Legally it operates as a supporting duty to the broader cyber security governance and risk framework — training is the human-control layer that makes technical controls enforceable.
Typically cascades from framework-level obligations down to periodic delivery, coverage and record-keeping expectations for the regulated entity.

data.theme: The end-to-end cyber security risk management lifecycle expected of supervised entities: identify, analyse, respond to, and continuously monitor cyber risk within the institution's overall risk governance.
how_members_connect: A parent obligation (risk management) explicitly references each lifecycle stage, creating a hierarchical obligation chain rather than four independent duties.
The stages are sequentially dependent: identification scopes the assets/threats, analysis assigns severity, response selects treatment, monitoring feeds results back into identification.
Shared defined terms (cyber risk, risk appetite, treatment/acceptance) run across all members, so a scope limit at the parent level constrains every downstream stage.
Interacts with enterprise risk governance and board/senior management accountability regimes — cyber risk is not carved out from general risk oversight duties.

data.theme: The general obligation to comply with applicable SAMA and other regulatory requirements, and to demonstrate that compliance on supervision or examination.
how_members_connect: Single-node cluster acting as a catch-all compliance duty that other regime-specific obligations ultimately roll up into.
Functions as a cross-reference anchor: breaches of specific rules (AML/CTF, payments, consumer protection) are also breaches of this general duty.
Sits at the top of the law → regulation → circular hierarchy, so it inherits scope from whichever instrument invokes it.

data.theme: Adherence to recognised industry and international standards where SAMA requirements incorporate or defer to them (e.g. security, operational or technical baselines).
how_members_connect: Single-node cluster operating by incorporation-by-reference: the regulatory obligation is to meet an externally defined standard.
Legally distinct from general regulatory compliance — the enforceable content is set outside SAMA instruments, which raises version/scope questions the entity must resolve.
Commonly paired with cyber security and operational resilience obligations, where standards supply the control baseline.

data.theme: Controlled change to information assets and IT environments as a supervised cyber security control domain under the SAMA Cyber Security Framework, where uncontrolled change is treated as a source of operational and cyber risk.
how_members_connect: Single-node cluster: the change management control stands alone in the graph but sits within the Framework's control-domain hierarchy (Framework -> domain -> subdomain control requirements).
Legally it is an obligation on the regulated member organisation's board/senior management to define, approve and periodically review a change process, not merely a technical practice.
Interacts with incident, vulnerability and infrastructure security domains, since remediation and patching are executed through the approved change path.

data.theme: Security of network, systems and hosting infrastructure as a defined control domain, addressing hardening, segregation and protection of the environments that support regulated financial services.
how_members_connect: Isolated node in the graph; its legal force derives from the parent cyber security framework's compliance and self-assessment obligations rather than from peer cross-references.
Supplies the technical control baseline that event/incident detection and vulnerability remediation domains presuppose.
Relevant to outsourcing and third-party arrangements where infrastructure is hosted or operated externally but accountability remains with the member organisation.

data.theme: Detection, triage, escalation and supervisory notification of cyber security events and incidents affecting SAMA-regulated entities, including the monitoring capability (SOC/SIEM) and threat intelligence that feed it.
how_members_connect: Definitional chain: an event is the raw observable, an incident is the qualified subset that triggers response and regulatory reporting duties; the two nodes are explicitly related.
Capability-to-obligation linkage: SOC and SIEM are the monitoring and correlation functions referenced by both event management and threat management requirements.
Supervisory hook: incident management connects to SAMA IT risk supervision, i.e. the reporting/escalation channel to the regulator and the basis for supervisory review of the entity's response.
Threat management is upstream input, informing detection use-cases and prioritisation rather than creating a separate reporting duty.

data.theme: Identification, assessment, prioritisation and timely remediation of technical vulnerabilities across the regulated entity's estate, as a standing control obligation rather than a one-off exercise.
how_members_connect: Standalone node whose obligation content derives from the cyber security framework's control-domain structure and periodic compliance reporting to SAMA.
Operationally chained to change management (remediation deployed via approved change) and to threat/incident domains (unremediated vulnerabilities as incident root cause).
Scope generally extends to systems operated by third parties where the member organisation retains regulatory accountability.

data.theme: Physical cash-in-transit and security services risk: who may be engaged to move and hold cash, and the controls applicable to secure-bag/cash transport arrangements between banks and licensed security companies.
how_members_connect: Both instruments are SAMA circulars constraining the same operational function — outsourcing of cash handling and transport to third-party security firms.

One sets an eligibility/counterparty restriction (prohibition on dealing with agents of non-Saudi security firms), the other sets operating conditions for cash transport and secure bags; together they form a permission-then-conduct chain.
Shared cross-regime relevance: third-party/outsourcing governance and operational risk, with implicit AML/cash-handling control consequences.
start_here: Cash Transport Companies and Secure Bags Circular

data.theme: Bank secrecy and the duty to protect customer banking information, including limits on disclosure and internal handling of client data by supervised institutions.
how_members_connect: Single-instrument cluster: a standalone SAMA circular stating the confidentiality obligation.

Interacts with other regimes rather than internal members — credit information sharing, AML information requests, and consumer protection disclosure rules — so read it as a constraint layered over those permissions.

data.theme: Sector participation in the national anti-narcotics awareness programme (Nebras) — a social/awareness obligation directed at financial institutions rather than a prudential or conduct rule.
how_members_connect: Single-member cluster with no internal legal cross-references.
Best read as an administrative/awareness directive; any enforceable consequence lies in the expectation of institutional participation, not in supervisory ratios or customer-facing duties.

data.theme: Prudential classification and treatment of non-performing exposures and forbearance — when an asset must be recognised as non-performing, how restructuring affects that status, and the resulting capital and provisioning consequences.
how_members_connect: Direct citation link: the SAMA prudential rules on non-performing assets draw on the Basel Committee's guidelines on prudential treatment of problem assets (definitions of non-performing exposure and forbearance).
Hierarchy is international standard → domestic supervisory rule, so the Basel text supplies the defined terms that the SAMA instrument makes binding in KSA.
Obligation chain runs from classification triggers to provisioning/capital treatment and supervisory reporting.

data.theme: Supervisory instruction to financial institutions on timely implementation of court and adjudicatory decisions, including execution orders affecting customer accounts and funds.
how_members_connect: Single-member cluster: a standalone SAMA circular imposing a compliance timeliness obligation rather than a substantive licensing regime.
Sits at the circular tier of the hierarchy, operating as an execution/enforcement overlay on customer account handling duties found in banking and consumer protection rules.
No internal cross-references captured; linkage to other regimes must be established externally (e.g. account freezing/seizure and customer notification duties).
start_here: Prompt Execution of Judicial Rulings Circular

data.theme: Statutory regime governing the licensed transport and physical protection of cash, precious metals and valuable documents, including who may carry out such activity and under what security conditions.
how_members_connect: Single-member cluster at the law tier; it is the primary instrument for the cash-in-transit activity and the source of any implementing rules.
Interacts with banking operational risk and physical security obligations, and indirectly with AML/CTF concerns over cash and precious metals movement.
No internal edges recorded; downstream regulations or licensing conditions would attach beneath this law.
start_here: Law on Transport of Money, Precious Metals and Valuable Documents

data.theme: Operational controls for banks' handling, retirement and disposal of old or damaged equipment, addressing residual risk in decommissioned assets.
how_members_connect: Single-member cluster: a SAMA controls instrument directed at local banks, sitting below general banking supervision requirements.
Relevant to information security, customer data confidentiality and physical asset control obligations, though no cross-references are captured here.
Treat as a specific operational duty rather than a definitional source for other regimes.
start_here: Controls for Dealing with Old or Damaged Devices in Local Banks

data.theme: The bancassurance regime: conditions under which banks may distribute insurance products of licensed insurance companies, and the allocation of duties between the two regulated parties.
how_members_connect: The Rules Governing Bancassurance Activities is the hub instrument, expressly referencing the required Bancassurance Agreement and the separate Bank Obligations and Company Obligations sets.
The Rules cite the Cooperative Insurance Companies Control Law, anchoring the insurance-side licensing and supervisory basis (law -> rules -> contractual agreement).

Bank Obligations and Company Obligations are the two mirrored duty sets that the Bancassurance Agreement must give contractual effect to, creating a cross-sector obligation chain over one customer relationship.

Cross-regime flag: the bank's consumer protection and disclosure duties run alongside the insurer's product and conduct duties, so responsibility for customer-facing conduct must be read from both duty sets together.

data.theme: Supervisory expectations for risk that a regulated entity transfers to external parties — outsourcing arrangements, cloud hosting, vendor contracting and third-party cyber exposure — where accountability remains with the licensed institution.
how_members_connect: Common control logic: materiality assessment, SAMA notification/no-objection where required, and non-delegable accountability for outsourced functions.
Contract and vendor management supplies the enforceable hooks (audit and access rights, data location, sub-contracting, exit) that the outsourcing and cloud requirements rely on.
Third-party cyber security cross-references both outsourcing and cloud computing, treating the vendor lifecycle as an extension of the institution's own control environment.
Hierarchy runs from framework-level governance requirements down to arrangement-specific rules for cloud and vendor onboarding.

data.theme: The SAMA repo framework: who may transact, in what collateral, under which master agreement, and how trades are confirmed, settled, held in custody and unwound on default.
how_members_connect: The Guidelines act as the parent instrument, defining eligible counterparties, eligible securities, risk management, custody and reporting/settlement duties.
Master agreement layer (conventional MRA and the Shariah-compliant master sale/purchase structure) carries the contractual obligation chain into events of default and early termination/settlement.
Annex confirmation and exercise-notice forms are the documentary evidence steps that operationalise the master agreements.
Settlement and reporting obligations tie into external infrastructure (SARIE, Saudi Exchange), fixing where legal transfer and finality occur.

data.theme: Consumer-facing real estate and vehicle finance/lease contracting: mandatory contract content, risk disclosure, insurance and loss allocation, early repayment/early ownership, and default and termination consequences.
how_members_connect: Finance Lease Law (M/48) sits at the top of the hierarchy; the individuals' lease contract, contract-registry powers decision and early-repayment guide all cite or implement it.
The early repayment calculation methodology is the shared computational rule linking real estate finance instructions, vehicle early-ownership provisions and BNPL treatment.
Mandatory instructions for real estate finance to individuals attach the variable-rate credit risk acknowledgment as a required consumer disclosure step.
Insurance, total/partial loss, default/termination and ownership transfer certificate operate as one allocation-of-risk chain within the individual lease contract.
Cross-regime note: BNPL sits in a separate licensing regime with its own 'Consumer' concept, so read the shared early-repayment logic without assuming identical scope.
start_here: Mandatory Instructions for Real Estate Finance for Individuals

data.theme: Mandatory adoption of the Legal Entity Identifier for entity identification in the Saudi financial sector, and the contractual route by which LEIs are issued, renewed and updated.
how_members_connect: The LEI circular is the obligating instrument; the SIMAH issuance agreements are the delivery mechanism giving effect to it.
SIMAH acts as local operating unit under GLEIF's global framework, so global LEI standards feed into the local issuance terms.
Issuance via a financial institution engages the Credit Information Law, raising consent, data-use and disclosure limits for entity data.
Cross-regime relevance: LEI supports customer/beneficiary identification used in AML/CTF KYB and payments-message obligations.

data.theme: SAMA's Regulatory Sandbox admission regime: how a firm applies to test an innovative financial product or service under a time-limited, supervised permission, and the criteria SAMA uses to decide readiness and progression.
how_members_connect: The Guidance Notes sit above and interpret the Application Form, telling applicants what disclosure SAMA expects at each field — a guide-to-form hierarchy rather than a standalone obligation set.
The Sandbox Stages document defines the lifecycle gates (application, evaluation, testing, exit), so obligations in the form and guidance attach to a specific stage.
The Operational Readiness Assessment Criteria supply the substantive admission test — governance, risk and consumer-protection safeguards a candidate must evidence before live testing begins.
Note scope limits: sandbox authorisation is a conditional, testing-only permission and does not displace licensing, AML/CTF or consumer-protection duties applicable to the eventual activity.
start_here: Guidance Notes on SAMA Regulatory Sandbox Application Form

data.theme: Prudential-accounting treatment of Zakat and income tax in supervised entities' financial statements — where these charges are recognised and how that recognition interacts with reported earnings and capital.
how_members_connect: A single SAMA circular carrying the operative instruction; it functions as a directive amending or clarifying accounting presentation for supervised institutions.

Cross-regime relevance: recognition of Zakat/tax feeds retained earnings and therefore regulatory capital and provisioning disclosures, linking it to prudential reporting obligations elsewhere in the corpus.
No internal cross-references in the graph — treat as a stand-alone instrument and read against the applicable accounting standards framework SAMA has adopted.
start_here: Accounting of Zakat and Income Tax Circular

data.theme: Credit risk recognition: how deposit-taking finance companies and other supervised lenders must classify assets by quality, review loan portfolios independently, and provision accordingly.
how_members_connect: Appendix C is the shared classification taxonomy (asset quality grades) that both the loan review and provisioning rules depend on — a common defined-terms anchor.
Loan Classification and Provisioning sets the substantive obligation chain: classify, then provision at the level the classification dictates.

The Loan Review Function rule imposes the governance layer — an independent internal function that tests whether classifications applied are accurate, making it a control over the provisioning obligation rather than a parallel duty.
Scope point: the loan review requirement is framed for DTFCs; confirm applicability before extending it to other licensee categories.

data.theme: Prudential capital adequacy reporting — the periodic return through which a supervised institution reports regulatory capital against risk-weighted exposures to SAMA.
how_members_connect: A single reporting instrument; the obligation is one of accurate, timely submission in SAMA's prescribed form, distinct from the underlying capital-adequacy calculation rules.
Depends downstream on asset classification and provisioning outcomes, since credit-risk weights and capital deductions reflect those determinations.
Isolated in the graph — read alongside the applicable capital framework and reporting circulars rather than as a self-contained standard.
start_here: Capital to Risk Weighted Assets Return

data.theme: Periodic liquidity reporting to SAMA — the prudential return through which a bank evidences its holding of liquid assets against deposit and other liabilities.
how_members_connect: Single-member cluster: the return is the reporting instrument, not a standalone regime, so its obligations derive from the banking control liquidity requirements it services.
Sits downstream of liquidity risk management expectations — the statement is the supervisory evidence of compliance with ratio and buffer obligations.
Cross-reads with the liquidity risk management principles cluster, which supplies the governance and measurement framework behind the reported figures.

data.theme: Opening, operating, restricting and closing bank accounts for customers — covering eligibility and documentation, term deposits, dormancy handling, and the circumstances in which balances may be frozen, blocked or account data disclosed.
how_members_connect: Hierarchical: the general account rules act as the parent framework, with each specialised rule set expressly referencing back to it for definitions, customer categories and documentation standards.
Shared defined terms (account holder, customer, operating/dormant status) mean any change in the general rules propagates into the term deposit, dormancy and freezing provisions.

Obligation chain into other regimes: freezing, blocking and data-disclosure duties are the account-level execution point for AML/CTF, sanctions/TFS and judicial or supervisory orders, while dormancy triggers customer-notification and consumer protection duties.
Disclosure of account data interacts with banking secrecy and data/credit information constraints, so permissive language must be read as an exception, not a general licence.

data.theme: Governance and measurement expectations for managing liquidity risk — risk appetite, funding strategy, stress testing, contingency funding planning and board/senior management accountability.
how_members_connect: Single-member cluster stating principles-level obligations that other liquidity instruments (ratios, returns) operationalise.
Functions as the qualitative counterpart to quantitative liquidity reporting: supervisory assessment weighs process adequacy alongside reported ratios.
Feeds the broader governance/risk regime, including ICAAP-style internal assessment and board oversight duties.
start_here: Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management

data.theme: Identification, measurement, governance and supervisory reporting of interest rate risk arising from banking book positions, and its treatment within internal capital adequacy assessment.
how_members_connect: The IRRBB framework is the operative Saudi requirement and references the Basel principles as the international standard it implements.
IRRBB feeds the ICAAP reporting chain: measured exposure and stress outcomes must be surfaced in internal capital assessment and risk reporting to SAMA.
Shared technical concepts (economic value and earnings perspectives, shock scenarios, banking book scope) are defined once and relied on across all three members.
Hierarchy runs from international principles to domestic framework to periodic reporting obligation.
start_here: Interest Rate Risk in the Banking Book (IRRBB)

data.theme: SAMA directives on the payment-acceptance technology layer — POS device standards and connectivity upgrades, use of locally sourced technology products, and extending electronic acceptance to charities and non-profit entities.
how_members_connect: Shared subject matter: the physical/technical POS estate that banks, payment service providers and merchant acquirers must deploy and maintain to SAMA specification.
Obligation chain runs from acquirer/PSP to the merchant or beneficiary entity — the 4G upgrade instruction sets the device baseline that the charities/NPO acceptance directive relies on.
The local technology products guidance sits alongside as a sourcing/procurement expectation applied to the same device and terminal population.
Cross-regime touchpoint: NPO acceptance sits close to AML/CTF concerns over cash collection by non-profits, so acceptance mandates carry indirect financial-crime rationale.
start_here: Electronic Payments for Charities and NPOs

data.theme: Pricing and fee treatment for e-wallet funding transactions within the national payment scheme, specifically amendments to top-up charges applied through mada.
how_members_connect: Single-instrument cluster: a scheme-level fee amendment binding on issuers, PSPs and e-money/wallet providers participating in mada.
Interacts with the consumer protection regime on fee transparency and disclosure of charges to wallet holders.
Sits under the payments/PSP regime, where SAMA sets or approves interchange and service pricing for scheme participants.

data.theme: Compliance expectations placed on, or in relation to, licensed real estate brokers as a regulated counterparty within the KSA financial and payments perimeter.
how_members_connect: Standalone item; its legal weight comes from the interface between real estate brokerage licensing and SAMA-supervised entities dealing with brokers.
Relevant to AML/CTF designated non-financial business and profession concerns, and to KYB/merchant onboarding where a broker is treated as a customer.
Also engages escrow/account-handling and payment acceptance duties for property transactions.

data.theme: Mandating or expanding acceptance of electronic payment at grocery and retail food outlets, addressing cash displacement in a high-volume consumer sector.
how_members_connect: Standalone directive addressed to acquirers, PSPs and, through them, merchants in the defined retail category.
Depends on the POS device and acceptance infrastructure standards handled elsewhere in the payments cluster.
Consumer protection angle: merchants may not refuse or surcharge electronic payment where acceptance is mandated.
start_here: Electronic Payment for Grocery Retail Sector

data.theme: Wage payment integrity for employers using the Wage Protection Program and the Mudad platform, sitting at the intersection of payroll disbursement obligations and the banks/PSPs that execute salary transfers.
how_members_connect: Single-member cluster: the obligation chain runs from labour-sector wage protection requirements to the financial institutions that must support compliant salary payment channels.
Links outward to payment account and transfer rules, since wage disbursement is effected through regulated payment/banking services.
Cross-regime interaction with CDD/customer identification where the employer is the institution's customer and employees are payees.
start_here: Wage Protection Program and Mudad Platform

data.theme: Customer identification and verification duties owed by payment service providers, i.e. how KYC obligations under the AML/CTF regime are applied within the licensed PSP perimeter.
how_members_connect: Single-member cluster anchored on the defined term 'Customer' and the verification steps required before or during establishment of a business relationship.
Sits in the hierarchy below the AML/CTF Law and Implementing Regulations, as applied to PSPs by payment-sector rules and circulars.
Interacts with merchant onboarding (KYB) and with reliance on third parties for CDD, which do not displace the PSP's own responsibility.
Feeds downstream controls such as monitoring, record-keeping and suspicious transaction reporting.
start_here: KYC Verification for Payment Service Providers

data.theme: How payment service providers must give effect to judicial orders and enforcement decisions affecting customer funds and accounts, including freezing, seizure or transfer directions.
how_members_connect: Single-member cluster where the obligation originates outside SAMA rules (courts/enforcement authority) but is executed by SAMA-supervised entities.
Cross-regime overlap with sanctions/TFS freezing duties and with consumer protection limits on account access and notification.
Constrains contractual terms with customers, since compliance with a lawful order overrides ordinary service obligations.
start_here: Execution of Judicial Orders by Payment Services

data.theme: Scope and treatment of payment services provided to entities established in the Integrated Logistics Zone, a special-status jurisdictional carve-out within KSA.
how_members_connect: Single-member cluster defined by a scope limitation: which SAMA payment and licensing requirements apply to zone entities and their service providers.
Raises defined-term questions on residency/establishment status of the customer, affecting onboarding and CDD risk classification.
Potential interaction with cross-border payment and FX treatment given the zone's distinct regulatory perimeter.
start_here: Payment Services for Integrated Logistics Zone Entities

data.theme: Cybersecurity and data-protection controls that SAMA-supervised entities must implement as part of operational risk and governance obligations, with data-specific controls layered on top of the general cybersecurity framework.
how_members_connect: Hierarchy: a SAMA circular issues/enforces the controls framework, while the dated data cybersecurity controls document sets the substantive control requirements.
Shared scope population — supervised financial institutions — and shared compliance/self-assessment and reporting duties toward SAMA.
Data-specific controls act as a specialisation of the broader cybersecurity control domains, so the two must be read cumulatively rather than as alternatives.
Cross-regime relevance: control obligations support confidentiality duties under consumer protection and credit/data information regimes.

data.theme: Governance of customer-facing SMS notifications by banks and payment participants, covering sender identity integrity and mandated notification content for card/mada transactions.
how_members_connect: Both impose conduct obligations on the same regulated population (banks/participants in the national payment scheme) regarding outbound customer messaging.
Sender tag governance protects the authenticity of the channel that the unified mada notification requirement mandates be used.
Consumer protection linkage: notification duties support customer transparency, disputes and fraud-detection rights.
Operationally sequential obligation chain: register/control sender identity, then send the standardised notification content.
start_here: Unified SMS Notifications for Mada Operations

data.theme: SAMA's prior-approval gate over establishment/incorporation documents of regulated entities, i.e. licensing and corporate-governance control at formation and at amendment of constitutive contracts.
how_members_connect: Single-member cluster: an approval requirement that conditions the legal effectiveness of corporate formation steps for supervised entities.
Connects upward to licensing regimes (banking, finance, payment services) where establishment documents form part of the licence application file.
Consequence for decisions: changes to the establishment contract cannot be treated as internal corporate matters — they trigger a separate supervisory consent obligation.

data.theme: Standardisation of merchant pricing/interchange arrangements across point-of-sale and e-commerce acceptance, addressing fee transparency and equal treatment of acceptance channels.
how_members_connect: Single-member cluster: a unified pricing model applying to acquirers/payment service providers in the domestic scheme.
Links to the payments/PSP regime (acquiring licence conditions) and to merchant-facing conduct duties on fee disclosure.
Decision consequence: channel-based fee differentiation between physical and online acceptance is constrained by the unified model rather than left to commercial negotiation.
start_here: Unified Pricing Model for POS and E-commerce

data.theme: Covers the arrangement by which judicial notifications are served electronically on financial institutions through a delegated channel, and the compliance duties that follow from receiving such notices (e.g. acting on court/enforcement instructions affecting customer accounts).
how_members_connect: Single-member cluster: the delegation instrument is the sole node, so linkage is external rather than internal.
Legally it sits at the intersection of judicial/enforcement authority and SAMA-supervised entities' duty to execute and acknowledge notified orders.
Interacts with account operation, freezing/attachment and customer-notification duties in the consumer protection and banking-operations regimes.

data.theme: Physical security and operational-risk requirements for the transport of cash and valuables, including licensing/authorisation of transport activity and the safety standards supervised entities and their contractors must meet.
how_members_connect: Isolated node: obligations are self-contained rather than cross-referenced within this cluster.
Sits in the operational-risk/outsourcing chain - the financial institution remains accountable for a third party performing cash transport.
Bridges to currency handling and branch/ATM operations rules in adjacent regimes.

data.theme: The statutory foundation for the Saudi riyal - issuance, legal tender status, and offences relating to currency - forming the primary-law layer above SAMA's operational currency rules.
how_members_connect: Single primary-law node that anchors, rather than depends on, lower-tier instruments.
Supplies defined terms (currency, legal tender, issuance authority) relied on by circulars on cash handling, damaged notes and counterfeit reporting.
Top of a law -> regulation -> circular hierarchy where implementing detail sits outside this cluster.

data.theme: Rules on how government subsidy/support is calculated and applied within responsible-finance products, affecting cost-of-borrowing disclosure and the amounts a consumer is actually charged.
how_members_connect: Single-member cluster; its legal weight comes from cross-regime effects rather than internal edges.
Feeds the finance-company and real estate finance regimes' pricing, APR/total-cost disclosure and early-settlement calculations.
Consumer protection consequence: support amounts must be reflected transparently in the contract and in consumer-facing statements.
start_here: Government Support Calculation for Responsible Finance

data.theme: Supervisory expectations for bank internal control and risk management in higher-risk exposures — dealings with highly leveraged institutions and derivatives activity. The problem-space is prudential risk governance rather than conduct or AML.
how_members_connect: All three are SAMA guidance-level instruments (guidelines/sound practices) that sit below the Banking Control Law rather than creating standalone licensing obligations.
The HLI sound practices document cross-refers to the derivatives risk management guidelines for counterparty exposure, collateral and valuation discipline.
Internal control guidelines supply the control-environment baseline (board oversight, segregation, independent risk and audit) that the two activity-specific documents presuppose.
Shared obligation chain: board/senior management accountability → risk limits and measurement → independent control and reporting.
start_here: Internal Control Guidelines for Commercial Banks

data.theme: Pre-launch regulatory clearance and governance for new banking products and services, including the specific regime for offering financial derivatives. Central question is when a product may be launched on notification versus requiring SAMA non-objection, and what internal governance must precede either.
how_members_connect: The New Banking Products and Services Regulation is the parent instrument; the governance, risk-assessment, compliance and notification/non-objection members are its constituent obligation sets.
Two-track procedural chain: product risk classification determines whether the bank notifies SAMA or must obtain prior non-objection before offering.

Board and senior management duties form an accountability hierarchy — approval of the product framework at board level, execution and risk assessment at management level, independent verification by compliance.

Cross-regime hooks: consumer protection requirements and the Counter-Fraud Framework must be addressed within the product risk assessment; derivatives offerings additionally trigger OTC trade repository reporting.
start_here: New Banking Products and Services Regulation

data.theme: Interaction between retail savings-product rules and the CTF statutory framework, notably identity-document validity as a precondition to operating accounts. Covers the legislative chain amending the terrorism-financing law.
how_members_connect: The Law on Combating the Financing of Terrorism is the apex statute; the Royal Decree and Council of Ministers Resolution are the enacting/amending instruments in the law-making hierarchy.
Savings product rules and the ID-expiry instruction are SAMA-level requirements that draw their identification and account-restriction rationale from the CTF law (and its CDD logic).
Shared defined-term dependency: customer identification and verification standards, applied to National ID / Iqama validity, link operational account handling to statutory CTF duties.
Practical consequence chain: expired identity document → identification no longer verified → restriction on account activity under the savings/AML-CTF regime.
start_here: Law on Combating the Financing of Terrorism
National and Resident ID Expiry Handling

data.theme: A single, isolated node on the development of QR code-based payment acceptance, sitting within the payments/PSP space. It is project- or initiative-level material rather than a standing obligation set.
how_members_connect: Singleton community with no internal legal cross-references in the graph.
Natural linkage points lie outside this cluster: payment service provider licensing, merchant acceptance and merchant-as-customer KYB duties.
Treat as context material; any enforceable requirement must be sourced from the payments regulations it would sit under.

data.theme: Periodic supervisory reporting: the prescribed return forms and the manual governing how supervised entities submit regulatory data to SAMA through the Returns Management System.
how_members_connect: The RMS guidance manual is the procedural hub; each form is a defined return whose content, frequency and submission channel it governs.
Members share a common data spine (entity identifiers, balance-sheet and customer/currency data), so definitions and reporting periods must be read consistently across forms.
Hierarchy runs from the supervisory reporting obligation down to the manual (process) and the individual forms (content), with annual, quarterly and comparative cadences distinguishing scope.
Accuracy and timeliness of these returns is an enforceable supervisory obligation, not a voluntary data exchange.
start_here: Guidance Manual for Returns Management System (RMS)

data.theme: Amendment to the Kingdom's general personal data protection regime, affecting how financial institutions lawfully collect, process, transfer and retain personal data.
how_members_connect: Standalone instrument at law level (Royal Decree), sitting above SAMA-issued data, credit information and consumer protection rules that presuppose lawful processing.
Interacts with AML/CTF record-keeping and CDD data retention duties, where the data protection regime must be read as constraining purpose and retention, not overriding statutory retention mandates.
Relevant to cross-border data transfer and outsourcing arrangements where customer data leaves the controller's direct control.
start_here: Personal Data Protection Law Amendment M/148

data.theme: Accessibility and safety obligations toward persons with disabilities in financial-sector premises, specifically emergency evacuation arrangements.
how_members_connect: Standalone guidance instrument; operates as a conduct/consumer-accessibility expectation rather than a prudential rule.
Connects conceptually to consumer protection principles on fair and equal access to financial services and premises.
Guide-level status means it sets expected practice; supervisory scrutiny attaches to whether the entity can demonstrate equivalent protection.
start_here: Emergency Evacuation Guide for Persons with Disabilities

data.theme: Labour-market localisation requirement applied to remote customer service functions, relevant where financial institutions outsource or offshore customer-facing contact activity.
how_members_connect: Standalone ministerial decision originating outside SAMA but binding on supervised entities as employers.
Cross-regime relevance: interacts with outsourcing governance and consumer protection expectations on service quality and customer contact channels.
Compliance consequence sits at workforce composition level, distinct from SAMA's own licensing or conduct conditions.
start_here: Ministerial Decision 112203 - Remote Customer Service Saudization

data.summary: A control domain within SAMA's Counter-Fraud Framework covering the detection pillar: identifying suspected fraud through monitoring, alerting, intelligence on emerging threats and analysis of internal and external data sources. It sits alongside prevention and response controls and relies on defined terms such as Fraud, Fraud case, External Fraud and Fraud Landscape. It binds Member Organizations supervised by SAMA, with Board and Counter-Fraud Governance Committee accountability for the wider programme.

The response pillar of SAMA's Counter-Fraud Framework, dealing with what a firm must do once fraud is suspected or confirmed — the Fraud Response Plan, reporting protocols, team responsibilities, information logging, investigation and corrective action. It interacts with cyber incident response and financial crime reporting obligations. Applies to Member Organizations under SAMA supervision, with oversight by the Counter-Fraud Governance Committee.

Addresses the technology component of the risk-based Counter-Fraud Programme — systems and tools used to prevent, detect and respond to fraud, supported by KPIs, Key Risk Indicators, enterprise-wide Fraud Risk Assessment and independent audit of control design. It also covers assessment of fraud vulnerabilities before launching new products, services or digital platforms, and vetting of third parties or managed services used for counter-fraud functions. Binds Member Organizations; proportionality to size and nature of business applies.

Covers enhanced counter-fraud solutions and controls applied where inherent or residual fraud risk is assessed as elevated — for example higher-risk products, channels, customers or newly identified threats. Control intensity is driven by the enterprise-wide Fraud Risk Assessment, the agreed Fraud Risk Appetite and monitored KRIs. Applies to Member Organizations supervised by SAMA.

The parent instrument: SAMA's Counter-Fraud Framework setting mandatory control requirements across governance, prevention, detection and response, plus a glossary of defined terms (Counter-Fraud Programme, Policy, Culture, Governance, CFGC, Fraud, Employee, Electronic Money, EMI). It assigns ultimate responsibility to the Board and requires a quarterly-meeting Counter-Fraud Governance Committee and coordination with cyber security and financial crime functions. Binds Member Organizations supervised by SAMA, proportionate to size and nature of business.

A referenced predecessor/related instrument: SAMA's anti-fraud rules issued to finance companies by circular, addressing fraud prevention, detection and reporting obligations for that sector. It is relevant for determining which fraud requirements apply to finance companies versus the broader Counter-Fraud Framework applying to Member Organizations generally. Check for supersession or continued application alongside the Framework.

A SAMA circular declaring the Founding Day (22 February) official holiday for 1447H and fixing the corresponding Sunday as a non-working day for supervised financial institutions. It also requires banks, currency exchange centers and payment service providers to keep designated branches at airports and border crossings operating during the holiday, notify SAMA of those branch names and hours, and publicise them. It binds all financial institutions under SAMA supervision.

A SAMA circular issuing the Regulation on Close-Out Netting and Related Collateral Arrangements, adopted by Governor decision and accompanied by an annexed list of Qualified Financial Contracts. It operates against the Bankruptcy Law and its Implementing Regulation, with the contract list determined by SAMA and the CMA in agreement with the Ministry of Commerce. It applies to financial institutions supervised by SAMA and takes effect from issuance.

A SAMA circular, issued under the money exchange business rules, directing currency exchange centers in Makkah, Madinah, King Abdulaziz International Airport and the Jeddah Hujjaj City to raise premises readiness and operate at full capacity for the 1447H Ramadan and Hajj seasons. An annex lists minimum operational and consumer-facing requirements (cash and denomination availability, suitable hours, crowd management, staff ID, displayed exchange-rate boards linked live to the system, receipts for all transactions, customer-rights signage, POS acceptance, CCTV, security staff, counterfeit-detection machines, mapping the location, and reporting unlicensed exchange activity to security authorities and SAMA). It binds the named currency exchange centers.

A SAMA circular setting Ramadan daily working hours and the Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha holiday dates for 1447H for supervised financial institutions. It fixes bank public-dealing hours, flexible six-hour hours for bank-affiliated money transfer centers and payment service providers, four working-day holidays for each Eid, continuous operation of branches serving pilgrims at Hajj entry points and the Holy Sites, and an obligation to open selected branches during Eid holidays and notify SAMA and the public of their names and hours.

A SAMA circular fixing the operating hours of the Saudi Arabian Riyal Interbank Express (SARIE) system during Ramadan 1447H and the Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha closure periods, noting that clearing houses will follow the system's hours and days. Issued under the SAMA Law and the Banking Control Law, it is addressed to banks operating in the Kingdom.

A SAMA circular setting the permitted hours for cash-in-transit and for ATM replenishment and maintenance during Ramadan 1447H, distinguishing 24-hour coverage in major cities, malls, airports and train stations from restricted hours elsewhere. It also reaffirms compliance with the security requirements of the Law on Transporting Money, Precious Metals and Valuable Documents, its Implementing Regulation and related SAMA circulars. It binds banks and currency exchange centers operating in the Kingdom, subject to any security-authority determinations.
lookup_terms: transport of money and precious metals law

data.summary: SAMA's Rules for Issuance and Operation of Credit Cards, issued under the SAMA Law and circulated to banks and finance companies operating in the Kingdom, replacing the earlier Credit and Charge Card controls. They cover the full product lifecycle — card issuance, the card agreement, repayment, statements, transactions, liability for unauthorised use, and fees and costs — and set defined terms such as Issuer, Customer, Credit Limit, Amount Due, Minimum Payment, Due Date, APR, Grace Period, Term Cost and Late Payment Fee. Binding on SAMA-supervised entities licensed to issue and finance credit cards, including charge (monthly settlement) cards, with a general compliance window from publication and a longer window for two specified provisions on repayment and on fees.

Duplicate instance of SAMA's Rules for Issuance and Operation of Credit Cards (same circular text and content as the primary node). Governs credit and charge card issuance, agreements, repayment, statements, transactions, unauthorised-use liability, and fees/costs disclosure, with annexes containing disclosure templates for fees, benefits and a term-cost worked example. Binds banks and finance companies licensed by SAMA to issue and finance credit cards.

SAMA circular adopting the Counter-Fraud Fundamental Requirements guide, issued under the SAMA Law and its supervisory powers to raise financial-sector maturity against evolving fraud typologies. It imposes procedural obligations on addressed institutions: a gap assessment against the guide, a board-approved remediation roadmap, submission of both to SAMA by a stated deadline, quarterly compliance reporting until full compliance, and full compliance by a fixed end date. Addressed to finance companies and payment service providers.

The Counter-Fraud Fundamental Requirements framework itself, structured as numbered control requirements addressed to Member Organizations, covering counter-fraud governance and risk management, fraud prevention, and related domains, together with a defined-terms section (e.g. Fraud, External Fraud, Fraud Risk Appetite, Fraud Risk Assessment, Electronic Money, EMI, Employee). It sets expectations for a proportionate, risk-based counter-fraud programme spanning people, process and technology, with board accountability and independent assurance. Applies to SAMA-supervised Member Organizations within its stated scope, including finance companies and payment service providers.

Section 3.1 of the Counter-Fraud Fundamental Requirements, setting the governance and risk-management controls: a risk-based Counter-Fraud Programme monitored via KPIs, ultimate Board responsibility for the governance structure and tone from the top, a Counter-Fraud Governance Committee meeting at least quarterly, an approved Counter-Fraud Policy, KRIs against fraud risk appetite, intelligence monitoring, and an enterprise-wide fraud risk assessment refreshed on change. It also requires counter-fraud input before launching new products or services, vetting and monitoring of third parties performing counter-fraud functions, and periodic independent audits, and encourages operational collaboration with cyber security and financial crime teams. Binds Member Organizations subject to the framework.

The Fraud Prevention part of the Counter-Fraud Fundamental Requirements, sitting after the governance controls and read against the framework's glossary (Fraud, Fraud case, External Fraud, Fraud Landscape, Fraud Response Plan, Fraud Risk Appetite, Fraud Risk Assessment, Electronic Money, EMI, Employee). It addresses preventive controls expected of Member Organizations to stop fraud before it occurs, complementing detection and response requirements elsewhere in the document. Applies to SAMA-supervised Member Organizations in scope of the framework.

SAMA circular transmitting the updated Debt Collection Regulations (controls and procedures) for individual customers, issued under the Central Bank Law and superseding the earlier collection circular. It defines key terms (Customer, Guarantor, Third Party, default, involuntary/voluntary change of circumstances, total disability, documented contact, telephone contact, complaint) and sets minimum conduct rules on contacting customers and guarantors, rescheduling for defaulting customers, death/total-disability waivers, telephone contact limits, and deduction of due instalments from customer accounts including joint/solidary borrowers per agreed liability shares. It binds banks and finance companies supervised by SAMA and, expressly, third parties carrying out collection on their behalf.

Duplicate publication of the SAMA circular issuing the updated Debt Collection Regulations for individual customers. Same content: definitions, objectives, scope, communication controls with customers and guarantors, collection procedures, collection-unit governance, and rules on rescheduling, death/total-disability relief and instalment deductions. Binds banks and finance companies under SAMA supervision and third parties performing collection for them.

SAMA circular permitting the Saudi Real Estate Refinance Company (SRC) to purchase residential real estate finance portfolios from real estate financiers after a shortened seasoning period of at least one month from the date the related financing was granted, or one month from receipt of the first instalment from the beneficiary, whichever is later, with recourse to the originator for six months from the financing date. It replaces the previous three-month seasoning requirement set in the earlier circular. Addressed to banks, finance companies operating in KSA and SRC.

SAMA circular, issued under the Finance Companies Control Law and its Implementing Regulation, requiring finance companies listed on the Saudi Exchange to notify SAMA before announcing periodic financial statements on Tadawul's website. They must provide SAMA with the draft financial-results announcement in Arabic and English at least five business days before publication, without prejudice to other applicable rules. Binds listed finance companies only.
lookup_terms: draft results announcement five business days

data.summary: SAMA circular directing supervised financial institutions to apply the new Commercial Register Law and Trade Names Law, including regularising their own commercial registers within the five-year grace period for branch registers and urging customers to do the same. It requires institutions to verify the continued validity of customers' commercial registration and to treat a suspended register (Article 15 of the Commercial Register Law) the same as an expired one, and addresses money-exchange licensees who must incorporate a company rather than a sole proprietorship if carrying on activities beyond exchange business. Binds all financial institutions under SAMA supervision.

SAMA instruction on the Countercyclical Capital Buffer (CCyB), issued under the Central Bank Law and the Banking Control Law, setting the CCyB rate applicable to banks' domestic private-sector credit exposures within the Basel range of 0% to 2.5% of risk-weighted assets. It is a macroprudential capital requirement binding banks licensed and supervised by SAMA.

Node from SAMA's counter-fraud control requirements covering counter-fraud governance and enterprise-wide fraud risk assessment. It requires Member Organizations to run a risk-based Counter-Fraud Programme with board-level accountability, a quarterly Counter-Fraud Governance Committee, KPIs/KRIs against an approved Fraud Risk Appetite, intelligence monitoring, pre-launch fraud assessment of new products/services, vetting of outsourced counter-fraud resources, and periodic independent audit. It binds all financial institutions and financial service providers regulated by SAMA (Member Organizations), with the fraud risk assessment refreshed periodically and on material internal/external changes.

Node covering the multi-factor authentication and remote-onboarding controls in SAMA's counter-fraud requirements for elevated-risk products and services. It prohibits reliance on SMS OTPs alone for identification and transaction verification, prescribes additional authentication factors, sets content and language expectations for SMS OTP notifications, and requires impersonation and mule-account risk controls where the customer relationship is initiated remotely (including one phone number/national ID per application, with extra due diligence for exceptions). It binds Member Organizations, mandatorily for EMIs, AISPs and providers of digital payment, credit card, microfinance, BNPL or safeguarding services, and on a risk-based basis for others.

Node covering fraud response, root cause analysis and counter-fraud technology requirements, together with the additional controls mandated for products and services of elevated risk. It requires a fraud case management repository, root cause and lessons-learnt processes, corrective and victim-remediation actions, and real-time 24/7 fraud detection able to freeze accounts, block transactions and screen high-risk accounts, IPs, devices and locations, including detection of mule accounts used to receive fraudulent funds and launder proceeds of crime. Mandatory for licensed EMIs, AISPs and Member Organizations offering digital payment, credit card, microfinance, BNPL or fund-safeguarding services; risk-based for other Member Organizations.

Short SAMA circular (Arabic) reminding finance companies to exercise due diligence before granting finance, proportionate to potential risk, and to verify the authenticity of income-evidence documents submitted by the customer, strengthening related procedures. Issued under the Finance Companies Control Law and its Implementing Regulation. Addressed to all finance companies operating in the Kingdom.

SAMA circular (Arabic) launching phase one of the supervisory Complaint Management System and mandating that supervised financial institutions handle complaints end-to-end through that system. It fixes handling deadlines (five business days at level one, three business days for customer-escalated level two, two business days to respond to SAMA queries on accepted escalations) and quarterly performance indicators on complaint handling quality, escalation rates, timeliness, response quality, repeat complainants and missing-document requests; it also requires resourcing of customer-care units and updating of internal policies, SLAs and escalation mechanisms. Binds all financial institutions supervised by SAMA, with enforcement action for non-compliance from Q4 of the stated year.

SAMA circular (Arabic) permitting electronic money institutions to contract with CMA-authorised capital market institutions to distribute units of publicly offered investment funds through their e-wallet applications. It sets conditions: prior notification to SAMA with confirmation that internal policies are updated, compliance with the Law on Payments and Payment Services and its Implementing Regulation (licence conditions and limits), due diligence on the products, contractual allocation of risk and liability to the CMA-supervised institution, a role limited to distribution and document handling (no investment account opening), no sale or redemption via the wallet, subscription completed only after the capital market institution confirms suitability to the customer, and clear disclosure that funds are not payment products. Addressed to payment service providers, principally EMIs.
lookup_terms: capital market institution / CMA authorised person
Law on Payments and Payment Services Implementing Regulation
separation of payment and investment activities

data.summary: A SAMA circular clarifying that technical connectivity and support services for e-commerce payment transactions are ancillary to payment services and therefore fall outside the current SAMA licensing perimeter, relying on the Implementing Regulation of the Payments and Payment Services Law provision excluding technical service providers from 'related payment services'. It fixes the boundary: such firms must obtain the necessary technical permits from Saudi Payments and must not contract with or onboard merchants, perform merchant KYC/verification, AML/CTF or anti-fraud checks, or complete settlement and deposit of funds into merchant accounts. It binds banks (which must deal only with licensed PSPs and report unlicensed activity to SAMA) and licensed PSPs (which may contract with technical support firms subject to outsourcing rules and mada operational, technical and fee requirements); it replaces an earlier circular on the same subject.

A SAMA circular activating the GCC-NET point-of-sale payment service with the Sultanate of Oman as of the stated go-live date, continuing earlier circulars on GCC-NET POS service and its tariff. It requires banks to make the technical and operational arrangements to accept and process cross-border POS transactions, apply approved pricing with GCC-NET cardholders and merchants, notify and educate cardholders that Omani purchases route through the GCC network, and accept GCC-NET branded cards on their POS terminals. It binds banks operating in the Kingdom.

A SAMA circular reinforcing compliance with the safeguarding-of-funds requirements in Article 93 of the Implementing Regulation of the Payments and Payment Services Law. It adds two obligations: a no-objection request for a safeguarding account must be accompanied by the policies and controls governing the account's management and operation (including named authorities, multi-level control based on risk assessment, involvement of control functions, and restriction of authority to leadership positions), and the PSP must perform and document reconciliation between total e-wallet balances or executed payment transaction values and the safeguarding account balance. It binds payment service providers operating in the Kingdom.

A SAMA circular introducing the eSAMA e-services portal (individuals, business and government tracks) for digital submission of requests such as no-objection for senior appointments and for product/service launches, with phased replacement of paper submissions and authentication via the National Single Sign-On (Nafath). It designates the financial institution's most senior executive (CEO or equivalent) as the mandatory main portal user, populated automatically via SAMA's link with the Ministry of Commerce, with authority to delegate submission rights. Responsibility for compliance with the circular and for requests filed through the portal rests with the board (or equivalent), while the CEO owns governance of user entitlements, including removal of departing users; it binds financial institutions supervised by SAMA.

SAMA's Internal Audit Principles setting out the definition, independence, mandate and organisation of the internal audit function, and the duties of the board, audit committee and executive management toward it, alongside expectations on internal audit directors and staff. Internal audit is framed as an independent assurance and objective consulting function over the adequacy and effectiveness of the internal control system, governance and risk management. The Principles bind finance companies and real estate refinance companies licensed by SAMA, and serve as guidance for finance support companies and finance lease contract registration companies, which SAMA may at any time require to apply them in whole or part.

SAMA's Compliance Principles establishing the compliance unit/function, the compliance officer's role and the unit's duties, including reporting lines to the audit committee, staff training and awareness, reporting irregularities to SAMA and the audit committee, quantitative and qualitative measurement of non-compliance risk, and maintaining a classified database of applicable instructions. They also require periodic review of the customer care department (semi-annual) and of collection activities or outsourced collection agents (annual), with real estate refinance companies excluded from those two reviews, and map the wider regulatory perimeter (AML/CTF, BNPL rules, consumer protection, anti-fraud, debt collection, governance and conduct instructions). They bind finance and real estate refinance companies, and guide finance support and finance lease contract registration companies, which SAMA may require to apply them.

Cross-reference node to SAMA's PSIAs Rules (September 2022) as invoked within the Risk Management Framework for Shari'ah Compliant Banking. It captures the obligations of banks offering profit sharing investment accounts to monitor that account holders' funds are used in line with agreed terms, to comply with the risk management requirements of the PSIAs Rules and later updates, and to adopt a formal policy managing the bank's potentially conflicting roles and fiduciary/agency duties toward current account holders and PSIA holders (including asset and profit allocation across investment periods). It binds domestic banks licensed under the Banking Control Law that conduct Shari'ah compliant banking, whether full-fledged Islamic banks or Islamic Windows.

Section of the Risk Management Framework for Shari'ah Compliant Banking setting Principle 2.0 on credit risk: banks must have methodologies, systems and resources to identify, measure, manage and report credit exposures arising from Shari'ah compliant financing. It requires defined criteria for approving, renewing and refinancing financing consistent with the approved risk appetite and SAMA's responsible lending requirements, plus processes for monitoring counterparty repayment ability, asset performance, exposure classification, documentation completeness, collateral and risk differentiation across contract stages. Binds banks conducting Shari'ah compliant banking in KSA.

Section of the Risk Management Framework for Shari'ah Compliant Banking setting Principle 3.0 on market risk for all assets held, including illiquid or highly volatile ones. It requires a market risk strategy and limits, an independent market risk function or middle office, pricing/valuation/income recognition policies, MIS and stress-condition reporting to senior management and board, and explicit treatment of product-specific exposures (Salam and Parallel Salam commodity price risk, Sukuk and Murabahah asset values) and FX risk. Binds banks conducting Shari'ah compliant banking in KSA.

Node on operational risk within SAMA's Shari'ah compliant banking risk framework, defined as losses from inadequate or failed internal processes, people and systems or from external events, and situated within the board/senior management oversight and risk management requirements of the framework. It sits alongside the requirement that the risk management function be independent of risk-taking functions and that policies establish clear roles, accountability and reporting lines for risks from Shari'ah compliant activities. Binds banks licensed under the Banking Control Law offering Shari'ah compliant products, including Islamic Windows.

Section of the Risk Management Framework for Shari'ah Compliant Banking setting Principle 6.0 on liquidity: banks must maintain liquidity management policies and a reporting framework addressing liquidity exposures for each category of current accounts and PSIAs, individually and in aggregate. It also requires periodic review of the liquidity risk profile and policies as market conditions change, with corrective measures. Binds banks conducting Shari'ah compliant banking in KSA.

Section of the Risk Management Framework for Shari'ah Compliant Banking setting Principle 7.0 on equity investment risk, covering profit sharing instruments such as Mudarabah and Musharakah. It requires banks to define investment objectives, risk tolerance, expected returns and holding periods; maintain policies, procedures and management structures for acquiring, holding and exiting profit sharing investments; monitor investee performance as partners; and track how risks transform across investment and contract stages. This node also carries the framework's definitions section (Bank, Full Fledged Islamic Bank, Islamic Window, credit/market/operational/SNCR/fiduciary/liquidity risk) and the 03 March 2024 effective date.
lookup_terms: Risk Management Framework for Shari'ah Compliant Banking

data.summary: Defines the trade identification convention for OTC derivative reporting to the SAMA-authorised Trade Repository: until a global Unique Transaction Identifier is available, the reporting counterparty (the "generating entity") must create an internal unique trade ID, unique to each contract and never reused, including in trades with foreign counterparties. It fixes the code's composition (an 'E02' prefix, the generating entity's 20-character LEI, and an entity-generated unique code) and its format limits, and states that the internal ID cannot itself be amended by a modification report. Binds all banks in KSA with reportable OTC derivative transactions.

Covers the manner of reporting to the SAMA authorised Trade Repository Operator: reporting banks must report directly, may not use agents or outsource to third-party service providers, and must sign a reporting service agreement containing counterparty consent for trade data reporting. It also requires electronic submission via system linkages and completed user testing, use of the TR's prescribed templates and fields, and reporting on execution plus subsequent life-cycle events (new trade, modification, novation/termination action types). Binds all banks in KSA entering reportable OTC derivative transactions.

Identifies the ISO 17442 Legal Entity Identifier as the required 20-character code for identifying parties in OTC derivative trade reports, including counterparties, the other counterparty's broker (as defined under the Capital Market Law), and clearing members of each counterparty. The LEI also forms the middle component of the internal unique trade ID generated by the reporting counterparty. Relevant to banks completing TR reporting templates.

Section A sets the trade reporting regime for OTC derivative contracts: which transactions are reportable, direct reporting to the SAMA authorised Trade Repository Operator, the required reporting service agreement and consent clause, electronic submission and template field completion, and reporting triggers at first execution and on subsequent life-cycle events such as modification, novation and termination. Applies to all banks in KSA with OTC derivative transactions.

Section B imposes risk mitigation requirements on banks that are contracting parties to non-centrally cleared OTC derivative transactions, applying regardless of outstanding notional amount or whether the trade is for hedging; centrally cleared trades (directly or through indirect client clearing) are outside its scope. Related reported data points include confirmation timestamps and master agreement details. Issued under SAMA's Law and the Banking Control Law, superseding the earlier circular, effective 1 February 2026.

The consolidated SAMA requirements for OTC derivative contracts, issued under SAMA's Law and the Banking Control Law, split into Section A (reporting to the SAMA authorised Trade Repository Operator) and Section B (risk mitigation for non-centrally cleared trades). It defines reportable transactions by product type (rates, FX, equity, credit, commodity), by the reporting counterparty's status as a KSA-licensed bank, subsidiary, SPV or SAMA-licensed foreign bank branch, and by the other counterparty's status, with examples resolving cross-border booking. Binds all banks in KSA with OTC derivative transactions; effective 1 February 2026, superseding the earlier circular.
lookup_terms: Trade Repository Reporting and Risk Mitigation Requirements
foreign bank branch licensed by SAMA

data.summary: Defines Shari'ah Non-Compliance Risk (SNCR) as the risk arising from failure of a bank's Shari'ah governance mechanism (systems and personnel) to ensure compliance with Shari'ah rules and principles as determined by its Shari'ah Committee, with potential financial and non-financial impact. Within SAMA's risk management principles for Shari'ah compliant banking, SNCR must be treated as part of operational risk and given higher priority than other identified risks, with policies to measure, mitigate and monitor it, Shari'ah-compliant contract documentation, and tracking of non-compliant income. It binds SAMA-licensed domestic banks conducting Shari'ah compliant banking, whether full-fledged Islamic banks or Islamic Windows.

Refers to the Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Plan as the vehicle through which banks conducting Shari'ah compliant banking must perform an annual assessment of Shari'ah Non-Compliance Risk, with the risk management function conducting the assessment, the Shari'ah compliance function reviewing compliance with laws and internal policies, and the Shari'ah audit function providing independent review. It sits alongside requirements on fiduciary duties toward current account and PSIA holders and liquidity risk policy. Binding on SAMA-licensed banks carrying out Shari'ah compliant banking activities.

A SAMA circular (Arabic) approving the official holiday schedule and working hours for financial institutions and for the Saudi RTGS system for the four coming years (1447–1450H), published on SAMA's website. It directs institutions to follow the published holiday dates and working-hours instructions, to notify SAMA in advance of branches operating during official holidays, and to announce them by suitable means. Addressed to all financial institutions supervised by SAMA.

SAMA requirements (version 4.0, September 2025) in two parts: Section A sets trade reporting obligations for OTC derivative transactions to the SAMA-authorised Trade Repository Operator, and Section B imposes risk mitigation requirements on banks entering non-centrally cleared OTC derivatives regardless of notional size or hedging purpose. It defines reportable transactions (interest rate, FX, equity, credit and commodity derivatives), counterparty scope including branches, subsidiaries and SPVs, and detailed reporting fields. Binds all banks in KSA, including locally incorporated banks and SAMA-licensed foreign bank branches; effective 1 February 2026, superseding the earlier circular.

Identifies the prior SAMA circular No. 42056371 dated 10-08-1442H on trade repository reporting and risk mitigation for OTC derivatives, which is expressly superseded by the version 4.0 requirements. Relevant mainly for determining which regime applies to a transaction before the 1 February 2026 effective date of the updated requirements. Applies to the same population of SAMA-supervised banks in KSA.

The Unique Product Identifier is the ISO 4914 twelve-character alphanumeric product identification code used in the trade repository reporting fields when no ISO 6166 ISIN is available, indicated by product identifier type 'U'. It sits within the contract information fields alongside the CFI code, internal unique trade ID and Unique Transaction Identifier (UTI) conventions for identifying reported OTC derivative contracts. Relevant to banks in KSA subject to the SAMA OTC derivatives reporting requirements.

Part of SAMA's trade repository reporting and risk mitigation framework for OTC derivative contracts, covering timely trade confirmation and the valuation of non-centrally cleared OTC derivatives. It requires banks to base valuations on economically similar transactions or other objective criteria, to be able to compute and corroborate valuations internally, to use mainstream (or justified novel) valuation methodologies, to review the agreed valuation process periodically, and to document fallback valuation approaches, change procedures and valuation dispute resolution with counterparties. It binds SAMA-supervised banks in their dealings with derivative counterparties, and interacts with the reporting fields and life-cycle event rules (new trade, modification, novation) in the appendices.
lookup_terms: valuation of non-centrally cleared OTC derivatives

data.summary: Sets the portfolio reconciliation obligation within SAMA's risk mitigation requirements for non-centrally cleared OTC derivatives. Banks must document the reconciliation process agreed with financial counterparties and their efforts with non-financial counterparties, and must set scope and frequency by reference to the counterparty's risk exposure profile, size, volatility and number of outstanding transactions, ensuring material terms and valuations (including variation margin) are exchanged and reconciled at regular intervals. It binds SAMA-supervised banks entering into bilateral OTC derivative transactions.

Covers the portfolio compression requirement for non-centrally cleared OTC derivative portfolios: banks must have policies and procedures to regularly assess and, where appropriate, engage in compression with one or more counterparties, proportionate to their exposure or activity level, considering risk exposure profile, size, volatility and number of outstanding transactions. The node also touches the collateral-related reporting fields (collateralisation status, portfolio collateral, portfolio code, initial margin posted and its currency) used in trade repository reports. It binds SAMA-supervised banks.

Addresses dispute resolution in SAMA's risk mitigation requirements for non-centrally cleared OTC derivatives. Banks must agree and document with counterparties the mechanism for determining when discrepancies in material terms or valuations amount to disputes and how they are resolved as soon as practicable, with material disputes escalated to senior management and the Board under clear criteria. It binds SAMA-supervised banks in their bilateral derivative relationships.

The governance section of SAMA's risk mitigation requirements for non-centrally cleared OTC derivative contracts, sitting alongside the reconciliation, compression and dispute provisions. It concerns board and senior management oversight of the bank's OTC derivative risk mitigation framework, including escalation of material disputes and ownership of the required policies and procedures. It binds SAMA-supervised banks.

Deals with counterparty identification and the allocation of the trade repository reporting obligation under SAMA's OTC derivatives reporting framework (Appendix A Table 1 counterparty data, read with the Appendix C allocation rules). It sets who reports in each pairing — financial versus non-financial counterparty, local versus international or qualified counterparty, transactions novated to a CCP, and two local financial counterparties each reporting with buyer/seller identification — and covers life-cycle reporting scenarios such as missing unique trade IDs, modifications and novations. It binds locally established reporting counterparties, principally SAMA-supervised banks.

Appendix A Table 2 of SAMA's Trade Repository Reporting and Risk Mitigation Requirements sets out the 'common data' reporting fields (economic terms and administrative details) that reporting banks must populate on the TR Operator's templates for each reportable OTC derivative transaction. Key referenced items include the Unique trade ID (item 15), Internal unique trade ID (item 14), Notional (item 19), Early termination date (item 27) and Action type (item 53). It binds SAMA-licensed reporting banks, which must report directly to the SAMA-authorised trade repository and may not outsource or use agents.

Defines the identification format for parties to a reported OTC derivative contract: the ISO 17442 Legal Entity Identifier, a 20-character alphanumeric code, used for the reporting counterparty, other counterparty, broker (as defined in the Capital Market Law), and clearing members. Where the other counterparty is a natural person or a KSA corporate without an LEI, a prescribed client code (CLC) convention based on National ID, ISO 3166 country code plus national ID, or commercial registration number applies. Binds reporting banks completing Appendix A counterparty data fields.
lookup_terms: broker ID Capital Market Law article 32

data.summary: Covers the trade identifier fields used in SAMA TR reporting: the 'Unique trade ID' (item 15), which may be provisionally left blank where a foreign generating entity has not supplied it by the T+1 deadline and must then be added by modification report, and the 'Internal unique trade ID' (item 14), which must match a previously reported code on all subsequent lifecycle reports and cannot itself be modified or corrected. It also underpins the 'Linked UTI' field used when a trade is novated for central clearing. Applies to reporting banks submitting lifecycle event reports.

Item 53 'Action type' is the field that classifies each submission to the SAMA-authorised trade repository — New (N), Modify (M), Error (E), Early Termination (C), Correction (R), Valuation update (V) and Compression (Z) — and drives which other fields are mandatory, conditionally mandatory, potential or not relevant. It governs how banks report lifecycle events such as modifications, novations (termination plus new report), notional increases/decreases, erroneous submissions and early terminations. Binds reporting banks under the OTC derivatives TR reporting requirements.
lookup_terms: action type codes N M E C R V Z

data.summary: Appendix B lists the reportable lifecycle events for OTC derivative transactions and the field-status conventions (mandatory, conditionally mandatory, potential, not relevant) that apply depending on the reported action type; it is also the source of guidance on reporting error amendments. It operates with the T+1 reporting timeline (before 23:59:59 of the next business day, excluding Fridays, Saturdays and KSA holidays) and the treatment of trades novated for central clearing via early termination plus a new report referencing the Linked UTI. Binds reporting banks, which must also keep records demonstrating compliance.
lookup_terms: field status mandatory conditionally mandatory potential
