Covers the mandatory liquidity stress testing programme for finance companies, requiring multiple scenarios of varying severity and time horizons, company-specific and market-wide, run individually and in combination, plus sensitivity analysis alongside scenario analysis. Includes the defined terms for stress test, HQLA, unencumbered assets, net cash outflows and contractual maturity mismatch, and notes SAMA may impose specific liquidity limits. Useful for confirming that stress testing is a requirement, not a recommendation.

Sets the requirement for finance companies to maintain a Contingency Funding Plan addressing strategy and procedures for handling liquidity crises and covering cash-flow shortfalls under stress. Prescribes minimum content: definition of a liquidity crisis event, quantitative and qualitative early warning indicators with monitoring ownership and frequency, response options by time horizon, roles and responsibilities, balance-sheet modification plans, prioritised alternative funding sources, activation authority, escalation, and periodic testing and updating. The Board must approve the CFP at least annually.

Concept node on internal controls and policy content for liquidity risk in finance companies. Senior management must implement adequate internal controls and audit mechanisms to safeguard the integrity of the liquidity risk management process, and liquidity risk policies must document sources of risk, appetite and tolerance, strategy, balance-sheet and off-balance-sheet composition, funding diversification, lines of authority and reporting, limits and ratios with exception escalation, cash-flow projections, stress testing parameters, liquid asset buffers, contingency funding and collateral management.

This node covers the IT Risk Management domain of SAMA's IT Governance Framework, setting out principles and control requirements for identifying, analysing, treating, reporting and monitoring IT risk across processes, technology and people. It requires a defined, approved and communicated IT risk management process aligned to enterprise risk management, a centralised risk register, treatment within board/senior-management-set risk appetite, KRIs, and reporting to senior management and the IT Steering Committee. It binds Member Organizations supervised by SAMA and allocates duties to risk owners, control owners, business owners and the risk committee.
data.label: IT Risk Management

data.summary: This node addresses the internal audit function's IT responsibilities under SAMA's IT Governance Framework, together with adjacent roles and the regulatory compliance and service level management requirements it interacts with. It requires internal audit to identify the auditable IT universe, perform IT risk assessment during audit planning and carry out IT audits, while the organisation maintains a process for compliance with IT-related regulatory requirements (including data privacy) and formal internal and third-party SLAs. It binds Member Organizations and, within them, internal audit, IT management and all staff.
data.label: Internal IT Audit

data.summary: This node sets out the System Change Management domain of SAMA's IT Governance Framework, covering governance of changes to information assets, change requirement definition and approval, system acquisition, testing, security requirements, release and configuration management, and patch management. Changes must be classified, risk-assessed, tested and approved (including Change Advisory Board endorsement and cyber security function review consistent with the SAMA Cyber Security Framework) before production deployment, with emergency changes documented and root-caused after the fact. It binds Member Organizations and their change requestors, asset owners, CAB and cyber security function.
data.label: System Change Management

data.summary: A concept node for the SAMA Cyber Security Framework as a companion instrument cross-referenced from the IT Governance Framework and related SAMA circulars. It is the source of cyber security control requirements (for example, cyber security review and approval of changes before CAB submission and definition of security requirements for system changes) that Member Organizations must satisfy alongside IT governance controls. It binds organisations regulated by SAMA and is used by SAMA to assess control maturity.
data.label: SAMA Cyber Security Framework

data.summary: A concept node for the SAMA Business Continuity Management Framework as an instrument referenced from the IT Governance Framework's risk, change and configuration control requirements. It is the SAMA-issued source of business continuity and resilience obligations that complement IT risk management, backup, configuration and change controls. It binds Member Organizations supervised by SAMA; the underlying BCM requirements sit in that separate framework rather than in the IT governance text.
data.label: SAMA Business Continuity Management Framework

data.summary: A concept node for SAMA's General Department of Cyber Risk Control, the supervisory unit associated with issuing and overseeing compliance with SAMA's IT governance, cyber security and related technology risk requirements. It is relevant as the supervisory counterparty for IT and cyber risk reporting, assessment and remediation expectations rather than as a substantive control set. It concerns Member Organizations in their dealings with SAMA supervision.
lookup_terms: General Department of Cyber Risk Control
data.label: General Department of Cyber Risk Control

data.summary: A concept node within SAMA's liquidity risk management guidance for finance companies, describing the requirement to hold a cushion of unencumbered high quality liquid assets — assets convertible to cash quickly at little or no loss of value even under market stress — as a readily available funding source for unexpected net cash outflows. It sits alongside expectations on funding diversification, liquidity risk tolerance and limits, cash-flow projections, stress testing and contingency funding plans. It binds SAMA-licensed finance companies and their boards/senior management, which set the liquidity risk appetite and review it at least annually.

SAMA's Rules Governing Credit Risk Exposure Classification and Provisioning, issued under the Finance Companies Control Law (Art. 13) and its Implementing Regulation (Art. 62), setting minimum requirements for classifying credit exposures and setting provisions on an IFRS 9 basis. It defines core terms (PD, EAD, LGD, financial asset, expected credit loss, 12-month and lifetime ECL, Stage 1/2/3, past due, problem loans) and requires an effective credit risk management framework proportionate to the company's risk profile. It binds SAMA-licensed finance companies, including their boards and regulatory reporting.

A concept node anchoring the IFRS 9 accounting framework as the reference standard used across SAMA's credit classification and provisioning rules for finance companies. It supplies the definitions relied on by the rules — probability of default, exposure at default, loss given default, financial asset, expected credit loss (12-month and lifetime), past due and the Stage 1/2/3 allocation, including SAMA's regulatory-only bifurcation into Stages 2A/2B and 3A/3B mapped to earlier regulatory categories. Relevant to finance companies applying the rules and to those reconciling accounting treatment with SAMA prudential reporting.

A concept node defining Expected Credit Loss as used in SAMA's credit classification and provisioning rules — the credit losses expected from default events, measured on a 12-month or lifetime basis per IFRS 9 — and the governance wrapped around it. The board of directors is responsible for maintaining adequate ECL provisions and overseeing credit risk practices, with documented definitions, roles, portfolio grouping, measurement methods (loss rate or PD/LGD), inputs, assumptions and qualitative adjustments, plus data integrity and model validation. Binds finance companies, their boards and those charged with governance.

A concept node covering how finance companies must allocate credit exposures across Stages 1, 2 and 3 and the conditions for moving between them, under SAMA's classification and provisioning rules issued pursuant to the Finance Companies Control Law. It sets documented re-staging criteria from Stage 2 to Stage 1 (no exposure over 30 days past due, a 90-day cure period for non-retail, improvement in the borrower's position and removal of the SICR indicators), with a shorter 60-day cure period for retail customers, and establishes a Stage 2A/2B bifurcation for quarterly prudential reporting only, not accounting. Binds SAMA-licensed finance companies and their regulatory reporting.

A concept node in SAMA's credit classification and provisioning rules distinguishing forbearance from renegotiation/refinancing/rescheduling. Forbearance arises where the borrower is in financial difficulty and the finance company grants a concession it would not otherwise consider; such exposures are identified at individual exposure level and may only be reported in Stage 2B, 3A or 3B, with defined situations (partial write-off, collateral repossession pending disposal, further forbearance) that do not permit re-categorisation as performing. Renegotiation applies only where there is no financial deterioration and no reduction in present value. Binds finance companies in their classification, ECL measurement and regulatory reporting.

A SAMA circular transmitting updated controls on the reproduction, photographing, printing or design of Saudi and foreign currency circulating in the Kingdom, issued under the penal law on counterfeiting and imitation of currency. It sets a general prohibition on unlicensed reproduction, a licensing route through SAMA, and specific conditions for print and electronic/digital reproductions (size limits relative to the original note, no distortion of the King's image, no risk of the public mistaking the image for genuine currency, 'specimen' marking, and destruction of plates, files and storage media after use). It binds any natural or legal person seeking to use currency images for commercial, media or other purposes, and supersedes earlier circulars on the topic.
lookup_terms: counterfeiting and imitation of currency law
use of Saudi riyal images in advertising

data.summary: A SAMA/Saudi Payments requirements document for the ATM Receipts initiative, aimed at reducing cardholder reliance on printed ATM receipts while keeping paper receipts available on request. It standardises ATM home-screen workflow across on-us and off-us ATMs for the four principal transactions (cash withdrawal, balance inquiry, mini statement, cash deposit) and splits requirements into cash and non-cash transaction streams. It binds mada Members (acquirers/ATM operators); it does not cover certification procedures or terms and conditions.

SAMA Rules standardising how the Annual Percentage Rate is calculated and disclosed for retail lending, including definitions (APR, amount of finance, total cost of finance, total amount payable by the borrower), a mandatory net-present-value calculation formula, and required use of SAMA's Excel-based APR Calculator. They bind finance providers — banks and finance companies licensed for retail lending — across advertising, offer stage, contracts, periodic statements and any other APR disclosure, including calculators published on their websites. They are read alongside the Finance Companies Control Law and its Implementing Regulation, consumer finance regulations and related disclosure rules.

Governor-approved controls, agreed with the Minister of Justice, on registration procedures in the finance lease Contracts Register — the data required for registration and the rules and procedures allowing third parties to view the register — issued under the Finance Lease Law and its Implementing Regulation. They cover definitions (registration, registered right, registrar, head and clerk of the register, executive deed extract), obligations of the licensed registration company to maintain and safeguard register data under SAMA supervision, and the lessor's duty to register contracts and amendments within a set number of business days via the register's electronic channel. They bind banks, finance companies and licensed finance lease contract registration companies operating in the Kingdom.

SAMA's 2020 regulatory framework for Deposit Taking Finance Companies, covering SAMA's supervisory approach, corporate governance, prudential requirements and operational rules for deposit accounts. It authorises DTFCs to mobilise savings and time deposits from non-individual customers only and to lend from those deposits, subject to liquidity and other prudential ratios, depositor record-keeping (retained five calendar years after the relevant financial year) and detailed conditions for opening and linking general and term deposit accounts. It binds all DTFCs in the Kingdom, in addition to the Finance Companies Control Law, its Implementing Regulation and general SAMA finance company rules.

A SAMA circular issuing a guide organising the operational procedures of money exchange businesses, grounded in the Rules Regulating Money Changing Business and the licensing requirement to conduct exchange activity. It distinguishes licence categories — Category A (permitted to carry out domestic and cross-border money transfer in addition to exchange) and Category B (buying and selling foreign currency, travellers' cheques and bank cheques) — and directs compliance with related instructions, ministerial decisions and AML/CTF rules. It binds all licensed exchange houses of Category A and B operating in the Kingdom.
lookup_terms: money changer Category A Category B

data.summary: Definitional node from SAMA's rules on credit risk exposure classification and provisioning for finance companies, setting out the IFRS 9-aligned vocabulary (probability of default, exposure at default, loss given default, financial asset, expected credit loss and 12-month/lifetime ECL, staging) and, separately, SAMA's regulatory definition of default. It binds licensed finance companies, which must adopt the regulatory default definition consistently for regulatory and financial reporting purposes or document justified reasons for departure. Default is triggered by either qualitative 'unlikeliness to pay' indicators (Stage 3B allocation, charge-off/specific provision, sale at material credit loss, concessionary restructuring, bankruptcy or enforcement action) or the quantitative 90-days-past-due criterion.

Governance provisions within SAMA's credit risk classification and provisioning rules for finance companies, covering board and senior management responsibility for approving and annually reviewing ECL methodologies, quarterly reporting on exposure and ECL adequacy, model validation and documentation, disclosure, and ECL-related KPIs. It requires the internal audit function, as third line of defence, to independently evaluate the credit risk assessment, measurement and rating systems annually, with an independent third party permitted where internal audit cannot perform the review. It also mandates a comprehensive policy for managing defaulted assets (recovery strategies, collateral revaluation, write-offs, board reporting) and states the rules take effect 1 July 2021, replacing the earlier Provisioning Guidelines.
lookup_terms: internal audit third line of defence

data.summary: Annexure and related provisions of the finance-company provisioning rules identifying eligible collateral for provision calculation (cash, gold, deposits and certificates of deposit, government securities and sukuk, listed shares, investment-grade corporate bonds/sukuk, receivables, financial and Kafalah guarantees, immovable and other physical collateral, leased assets) and setting collateral valuation and haircut expectations. It obliges finance companies to document valuation frequency, apply conservative haircuts feeding into LGD, stress-test collateral portfolios, and revalue immovable collateral securing Stage 3 or defaulted exposures at least annually by licensed appraisers, with the lower of two valuations used where judgement is involved.

SAMA instructions (Nov 2021) regulating the purchase/transfer of individual consumer finance debts between finance companies, issued under the Finance Companies Control Law. They bind finance companies licensed for consumer finance: no separate SAMA approval is needed per transaction, but the buying company must disclose new financing terms and costs and obtain documented customer consent, use a dedicated buyout request form, settle the outstanding debt through the SARIE system with prescribed payment details, and may not charge transfer costs other than early repayment or administrative fees. The selling company must issue liability statements and clearance letters, facilitate the transfer, and notify the customer of settlement, generally within one business day.

SAMA instructions fixing binding turnaround times for issuing clearance letters and for transferring customer accounts and debts, applying to banks and finance companies supervised by SAMA in respect of natural-person customers. They set one business day for a clearance letter where no outstanding obligations exist (seven business days where a credit or charge card is held), one business day for account transfer and for completing consumer finance debt transfer forms, and three/five business days for real estate finance transfer steps. They supersede the timeframes stated in several earlier SAMA circulars, do not otherwise derogate from related instructions, and exclude cases subject to judicial rulings or pending before competent authorities; compliance is required within thirty business days of issuance.

SAMA rules and procedures (Jan 2021) governing how lessors request, and licensed finance lease contract registration companies issue, executive bond extracts for registered finance lease contracts, issued under the Finance Lease Law and its Implementing Regulation, under which such an extract constitutes an executive deed for purposes of the Enforcement Law. They cover extracts for repossession of movable assets, for delivery of immovable leased assets, and for financial enforcement certificates, define the parties involved, and require all requests and issuance to be conducted electronically. Lessors are prohibited from repossessing movable assets except through companies specialised in repossession licensed by the Ministry of Justice; the rules supplement SAMA's earlier repossession controls and bind banks, finance companies and registration companies.

A KYC chapter within SAMA rules addressed to DTFCs, setting the minimum design of a Know Your Customer programme: customer acceptance policy, customer identification, ongoing monitoring of high-risk accounts and risk management. It prohibits anonymous, numbered-without-full-details, fictitious or inaccurate-name accounts, requires refusal of onboarding and reporting to SAMA's financial investigation unit where KYC doubts arise, and includes account-opening agreement acknowledgements (source of funds, real beneficiary, periodic data update at least every five years, freezing on non-update or suspected fraud) plus limits on remote opening of a General Account. It binds the licensed institutions themselves and, operationally, all their staff.

A SAMA circular (Arabic) instructing supervised financial institutions to use channels made available by the General Authority for Awqaf — technical integration, the data office email/data-sharing forms, the endowment deed verification service, and the public register of endowments — to verify beneficial owner data for awqaf (endowments) as part of customer due diligence. Institutions must also notify the Authority, via its designated form, of any discrepancies between CDD results and the Authority's beneficial owner data, without prejudice to STR obligations and personal data protection requirements. It binds all financial institutions under SAMA supervision from the date of publication.

Governor-issued controls (agreed with the Minister of Justice under the Finance Lease Law and Article 30 of its Implementing Regulation) covering registration procedures in the finance lease Contracts Register, the data registration requires, and the terms for third-party access to the register. Key duties include the lessor registering a contract and any amendment within ten business days via the register's electronic portal, and the licensed Contracts Registration Company maintaining, securing and — where SAMA licenses more than one company — unifying and exchanging register data under SAMA supervision. It binds banks, finance companies acting as lessors, and finance lease contract registration companies operating in the Kingdom.

Second edition of SAMA's General Rules on participation in events (conferences, forums, seminars and similar), updating the earlier rules on holding and sponsoring events and extending scope to presence via "temporary booths" for institutional promotion, which are exempted from the prior non-objection requirement. The rules set minimum requirements on board-approved internal policy, documentation and annual board reporting, selection and professional conduct of representatives (confidentiality, no politically sensitive or reputationally damaging statements, no unauthorised commitments), and event-related risk assessment. They bind all financial institutions licensed and supervised by SAMA.

The Law of Payments and Payment Services — the primary statute defining payment systems, payment services, payment orders, Members and Clients, and stating the Law's aims (integrity and efficiency of payment infrastructure, user protection, innovation and competition). It reserves to SAMA the powers to license, renew and revoke licences, set legal form, capital and solvency requirements, approve products and services, set outsourcing rules, and classify systems (including designation as a Systemically Important Payment System). It binds payment system operators and payment service providers, and prohibits operating a payment system or providing payment services in the Kingdom without a SAMA licence.
lookup_terms: Law of Payments and Payment Services

data.summary: The Implementing Regulation of the Finance Lease Law, setting definitions (Lessor as a licensed joint stock company including commercial banks, Lessee, Leased Asset, Contracts Register, Contracts Registration Company, Securitization) and the test for when finance leasing is a professional activity requiring licensing. It also covers securitization against lessor rights with continuing disclosure duties to SAMA, prior licensing before contracting, mandatory separation of lease value from ownership-right value in payment schedules with recovery on early termination, insurance indemnity, and SAMA's power to set contract standards. It binds lessors licensed to carry out finance lease and shapes lessee rights.

A SAMA circular (Ref. 482004268, 16/01/1448H) amending the Bank Account Rules to add account-opening requirements for a new customer category: non-resident non-Saudi natural persons and non-resident legal persons covered by the Non-Saudi Real Estate Ownership Law (Royal Decree M/186) and its Implementing Regulation. It sets the documentary requirements (Saudi-issued digital ID, passport, foreign bank statement, broker/developer agreement, commercial registration for legal persons) and general controls, including verification through a reliable independent Saudi source with biometric/attribute checks, a ban on joint accounts and non-resident authorised signatories, limits on remote accounts and no payment or credit card issuance, restriction of property-related transactions to approved Saudi electronic channels, and ongoing ID validity and data-update duties. It binds all banks operating in the Kingdom, effective from its date.

A SAMA circular (Ref. 482008.0.22, 29/01/1448H) directing supervised financial institutions to use the General Authority for Awqaf's channels — technical integration, the data office email/data-sharing forms, the endowment deed verification service, and the public register of endowments — when identifying and verifying beneficial owner data for waqf (endowment) entities. It is grounded in the Banking Control Law framework and the AML Law's Implementing Regulation CDD obligations, and requires institutions to notify the Authority, via its designated form, of any discrepancies found between Authority data and their own CDD results, without prejudice to STR reporting duties and consistent with the Personal Data Protection Law. It binds all financial institutions under SAMA supervision from the date of publication.

Concept node for the Finance Lease Law (Royal Decree M/48, 13/08/1433H) as the statutory basis for SAMA's Controls and Procedures for Requesting and Issuing Extracts of the Executive Deed for a Registered Finance Lease Contract (Jumada II 1442H / January 2021). Under Article 25(2) of the Law's Implementing Regulation, the extract of the executive deed for a registered lease constitutes an executive instrument under the Enforcement Law, and the controls define the extract types (recovery of movable assets, delivery of fixed assets, financial enforcement certificate), require exclusive use of Ministry of Justice-licensed specialised recovery companies, and mandate electronic processing by all parties. It binds lessors — banks and finance companies — and SAMA-licensed finance lease contract registration companies, alongside the separate SAMA controls on lessor recovery of movable assets.

Concept node for Consumer Financing Buyout — the purchase of an individual customer's outstanding financing debt by another financier — as referenced in SAMA's instructions on time limits for issuing clearance letters and transferring accounts and debts. The instructions define financiers (banks and finance companies under SAMA supervision), the Customer as a natural person, and account transfer as moving a balance to another bank with closure of the original account, with the stated aims of customer protection, fair dealing and enabling competition. They apply cumulatively with related SAMA instruments, including the Banking and Finance Company Consumer Protection Principles, the Consumer Finance Regulations, credit and charge card rules, and the circulars on inter-bank consumer debt buyout and real estate finance debt transfer.

Concept node for the Annual Percentage Rate (APR) as defined and governed by SAMA's Rules Governing the Calculation of the Annual Percentage Rate. APR is the discount rate equating the present value of all borrower payments (total amount payable, comprising principal plus total cost of finance) with the present value of finance amounts made available; the Rules prescribe the net present value formula, mandate use of SAMA's Excel-based APR Calculator, and require the APR to be disclosed consistently in advertising, offers, contracts, periodic statements and any other disclosure. They bind all finance providers engaged in retail lending — banks and licensed finance companies — including duties to update policies, apply internal controls and audit over automated calculators, and align customer-facing website calculators, and are read with the Finance Companies Control Law and its Implementing Regulation, consumer microfinance rules, interest-rate disclosure rules and the Consumer Finance Regulations.

Concept node for the Clearance Letter (khitab ikhlaa tarf) — the confirmation issued by a selling financier that a customer's debt has been settled — as it operates in SAMA's Instructions on the Purchase of Individual Consumer Finance Debts between Finance Companies (issued under the Finance Companies Control Law, RD M/51). The instructions require the purchasing company to hold a consumer finance licence, to disclose new financing terms and costs and obtain documented customer consent before buyout, to settle existing debt through the SARIE system with prescribed payment data, and to withhold release of surplus financing to the customer until the clearance letter is received from the selling company; the selling company must issue liability statements or debt-confirmation letters within one business day, facilitate transfer within one business day of complete requirements, justify any refusal in writing, and notify the customer of settlement. It binds finance companies operating in the Kingdom.

The Real Estate Finance Law is the primary statute governing residential real estate finance in the Kingdom: it defines core terms (Real Estate Finance Contract, Borrower, Consumer, Subsidy-Eligible Individual, primary and secondary markets) and assigns SAMA the mandate to regulate and license the sector, including banks conducting real estate finance and real estate finance companies. It also provides for licensing a real estate refinance joint stock company and cooperative insurers covering real estate finance risk, requires Sharia-compliant conduct via the Sharia committees referred to in the Finance Companies Control Law, and requires SAMA to set finance standards, review contract templates and set finance-cost disclosure principles. It binds real estate finance entities (banks and licensed finance companies) and allocates publication duties to the Ministry of Housing, Ministry of Commerce and Industry and Ministry of Justice.
lookup_terms: primary and secondary market real estate finance
Finance Companies Control Law Sharia committee

data.summary: The Saudi Central Bank Law (Royal Decree M/36, 2020) constitutes SAMA as an independent legal person reporting to the King and sets its objectives (monetary stability, financial sector stability and confidence, economic growth) and its full range of duties and powers. These include currency issuance, supervision and regulation of financial institutions, issuing regulations and directives, monetary and FX policy, operating and licensing payment/settlement/clearing systems and fintech platforms, consumer protection directives, prudential policy, and crime-prevention measures relating to financial institutions. It is the enabling instrument for essentially all SAMA rulemaking and binds any natural or legal person falling within the defined term "Financial Institution".

These Implementing Regulations give operative detail to the Law of Combating Terrorist Crimes and its Financing, notably by enumerating the financial activities and the commercial/professional (DNFBP) activities that bring a person within the Law's scope. They also set the mandatory content of AML/CTF policies, procedures and controls — risk management before customer verification, STR reporting procedures, a senior-level compliance officer, staff screening and training, independent audit — and extend group-wide compliance to foreign branches and majority-owned subsidiaries where local CTF requirements are weaker. They bind financial institutions, designated non-financial businesses and professions, and non-profit organizations.
lookup_terms: DNFBP designated non-financial businesses and professions
foreign branches and subsidiaries group compliance

data.summary: The Implementing Regulation to the Anti-Money Laundering Law (2017) elaborates the AML Law's definitions (Person, Transaction, Economic Resources, Correspondent Relationship) and the operative CDD regime. Key provisions address failure to complete due diligence (no account opening, termination of existing relationships, and consideration of an STR), the tipping-off exception permitting omission of CDD with a reasoned STR instead, and the conditions for relying on a third-party financial institution or DNFBP for customer/beneficial owner identification and verification. It binds financial institutions and designated non-financial businesses and professions, with ultimate CDD responsibility remaining with the relying entity.
lookup_terms: suspicious transaction report Directorate financial intelligence

data.summary: These Implementation Rules, issued by Ministerial Resolution under the Banking Control Law and circulated by SAMA, operationalise Articles 12, 16, 17, 18 and 22 of that Law. They cover fitness and prior SAMA approval for bank board members and senior managers (including multiple-board prohibition and disclosure of prior liquidation or removal), conduct of banking business consistent with monetary and credit policy, periodic supervisory and statistical reporting to SAMA, inspection and staff conduct requirements, and the procedures and penalties SAMA may apply. They bind all banks operating in Saudi Arabia and their employees.
lookup_terms: Implementation Rules for Banking Control Law
board member appointment prior SAMA approval
bank senior management fit and proper

data.summary: This is the Implementing Regulation of the Law of Payments and Payment Services (issued under Royal Decree M/26), which replaced SAMA's earlier Rules Regulating Payment Service Providers from its issuance date, with a corrective-action plan required within six months. It sets the framework for licensing payment service providers, agents and electronic money distributors, outsourcing/audit/risk management duties, customer protection and financial inclusion, contract and information disclosure requirements, e-money issuance and redemption, safeguarding of protected funds, account information and payment initiation services, and the designation, oversight and settlement finality regime for payment systems, plus supervision, enforcement and complaints handling. It binds licensed PSPs and payment system operators subject to the Law; note the source is largely in Arabic.
lookup_terms: Implementing Regulation Law of Payments and Payment Services
payment initiation and account information services

data.summary: The Saudi Central Bank (SAMA) is the independent legal person established under the Saudi Central Bank Law (Royal Decree M/36, 2020), reporting to the King, with objectives of monetary stability, financial-sector stability and confidence, and support for economic growth. The Law defines "Financial Institution" as any natural or legal person subject to SAMA's supervision, oversight and regulation, and vests SAMA with powers over currency issuance, licensing and supervision of financial institutions, monetary policy, payment/settlement/clearing systems, fintech platforms, consumer protection directives, prudential policy and crime-prevention measures. It is the constitutive authority underpinning essentially every SAMA rulebook cited by supervised entities.

SIPS is a classification category under the payment systems regime: SAMA may designate any payment system as a systemically important payment system and set tailored classifications and requirements for it. The surrounding provisions define the licensing, capital/solvency, product approval and outsourcing powers SAMA holds over payment system operators and payment service providers, and define core terms such as Payment Services, Payment Order, Member and Client. Relevant to operators and PSPs assessing whether heightened oversight applies to their system.

This node covers the Finance Lease Law and its Implementing Regulation, defining Lessor (a licensed joint stock company, including commercial banks), Lessee, Leased Asset, the Contracts Register and the Contracts Registration Company, and setting when finance leasing counts as a professional (licensable) activity. It imposes obligations on lessors regarding contract terms, ownership-right payment schedules, disclosure to SAMA of risks including those arising from securitisation, insurance indemnity and compliance with supervisory requirements. It binds licensed finance lessors and banks conducting finance lease activity in the Kingdom.

This node is the Capital Market Law as cross-referenced within SAMA's finance regime, chiefly the Real Estate Finance Law, where it governs public offering of shares in real estate refinance companies and refinancing through the issuance of securities. It marks the boundary between SAMA-supervised finance activity and CMA-regulated securities activity. Useful when a question involves securitisation, secondary-market refinancing or offerings by SAMA-licensed entities.

The Banking Control Law (Royal Decree M/5, 1386H) and its Implementation Rules (Ministerial Resolution 3/2149) form the core prudential and supervisory framework for banks operating in Saudi Arabia. Key provisions addressed include Article 12 (fit-and-proper approval for board members and senior managers, prior SAMA written approval, no dual bank directorships), Article 16 (conduct of banking business consistent with monetary and credit policy), Article 17 (periodic returns to SAMA), Article 18 (inspection, staff conduct, compliance with SAMA findings) and Article 22/25 (violations, procedures and penalties). It binds licensed banks, their boards and employees, including prohibitions on facilitating unlicensed banking or commercial activity.
lookup_terms: Implementation Rules for Banking Control Law

data.summary: The General Directorate of Financial Intelligence (formerly the Financial Investigation Unit) is the national FIU that receives and analyses suspicious transaction reports under the AML Law and its Implementing Regulation. The cited provisions govern STR filing where CDD cannot be completed or would tip off the customer, the FIU's operational and strategic analysis functions, its confidentiality and information-security duties, and its required operational independence and autonomy. It binds financial institutions and DNFBPs as reporting entities, and frames the FIU's own institutional obligations.
lookup_terms: customer due diligence failure terminate relationship

data.summary: Sets out the customer due diligence obligations owed by financial institutions and designated non-financial businesses and professions (DNFBPs), including the triggers for applying CDD (account opening or establishing a business relationship, occasional and linked transactions, wire transfers for non-relationship customers, suspicion of terrorism financing, and doubts about the adequacy of customer particulars). It covers risk-based calibration of measures, ongoing monitoring and record refresh for existing customers and beneficial owners, limited postponement of identity verification subject to risk controls, and the mandatory consequences where CDD cannot be completed (refuse the account/relationship/transaction, terminate existing relationships, and report to the General Directorate of Financial Intelligence). It binds all reporting entities supervised under the AML/CTF framework, including SAMA-supervised financial institutions.
lookup_terms: refusal to open account / termination of relationship

data.summary: A dedicated part of the Implementing Regulation of the Payments and Payment Services Law dealing with the protection and safekeeping of protected funds, i.e. customer/e-money holder funds received by licensees. It governs how such funds must be segregated, held and safeguarded against the licensee's own money and creditors, and is a core safeguarding obligation for licensed payment service providers and electronic money issuers operating in the Kingdom.

Concept node for the electronic money company / e-money issuer category under the Implementing Regulation of the Payments and Payment Services Law. It relates to the licensing category authorised to issue, distribute and redeem electronic money, and to the associated obligations on issuance and redemption, use of e-money distributors, safeguarding of protected funds and customer protection. It binds entities licensed by SAMA to issue electronic money in Saudi Arabia.

Concept node for the Payment Service Provider (licensee) under the Implementing Regulation of the Payments and Payment Services Law, which replaced SAMA's earlier Rules Regulating Payment Service Providers. It anchors the licensing requirements, scope of application, outsourcing, audit and risk management duties, customer protection and financial inclusion obligations, contract and disclosure requirements, and supervisory/enforcement powers applicable to PSPs. It binds all persons licensed by SAMA to provide payment services in the Kingdom, including banks where relevant.
lookup_terms: payment initiation and account information services

data.summary: Concept node for the Payment System Operator under the Implementing Regulation of the Payments and Payment Services Law. It relates to the parts of the Regulation on payment systems, including designation and classification of important payment systems, application of the CPMI-IOSCO Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures, system powers and rules, and settlement finality and insolvency protection. It binds operators of payment systems subject to SAMA oversight in the Kingdom.

Concept node for agents and electronic money distributors under the Implementing Regulation of the Payments and Payment Services Law, addressed in a dedicated part of the Regulation. It concerns the conditions for a licensee to appoint and use agents/distributors, the licensee's continuing responsibility for their conduct, and related oversight expectations. It binds licensed payment service providers and e-money issuers that operate through third parties, and is relevant to AML/CTF and outsourcing analysis of agent networks.

This node covers the Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures (CPMI-IOSCO, April 2012 and subsequent amendments) as incorporated by the Implementing Regulation of the Payments and Payment Services Law, including the defined term and the chapter imposing PFMI-based requirements on payment system operators. It addresses periodic self-assessment of PFMI compliance by operators of unclassified payment systems on terms agreed with SAMA under their licence, and related disclosure expectations drawn from the CPMI-IOSCO disclosure framework. It binds payment system operators (both systemically important/designated and unclassified) supervised by SAMA, and indirectly their participants through cooperation duties.

This node gathers the financial resources and capital adequacy obligations in the Implementing Regulation of the Payments and Payment Services Law (with a second SAMA source), covering the duty of payment system operators to maintain adequate financial resources and assess capital adequacy relative to the systems they operate. For unclassified payment systems it sets a floor expressed as at least six months of the highest operating cost of the system plus paid-up capital of ten million riyals. It binds payment system operators and, through the licensing chapter, payment service providers subject to SAMA licensing.

This node covers the complaints and disputes part of the Implementing Regulation of the Payments and Payment Services Law, together with the regulation's definition of a "complaint" as an expression of dissatisfaction or objection submitted by a customer or consumer to the licensee through available channels. It sits alongside the customer protection and financial inclusion part, and governs how licensees receive, handle and escalate complaints and disputes. It binds SAMA-licensed payment service providers and payment system operators dealing with customers and consumers.

This node covers payment initiation service as regulated under the Implementing Regulation of the Payments and Payment Services Law, in particular the part setting requirements for providing payment account information and payment initiation services. It is relevant to the open-banking style licensing category, contractual and information disclosure duties, and the scope-of-application provisions for licensees. It binds SAMA-licensed payment service providers offering initiation services and, indirectly, account-holding institutions.

This node covers the account information service (payment account information service) under the Implementing Regulation of the Payments and Payment Services Law, addressed in the part on requirements for providing payment account information and payment initiation services. It is relevant to licensing scope, customer consent and information/contract requirements for accessing payment account data. It binds SAMA-licensed providers of account information services and interacts with data protection and customer protection obligations.

SAMA Circular 1607 informs supervised finance providers of the phased rollout of real estate in-kind (title) registration under the Real Estate In-Kind Registration Law and its implementing regulation, following notification that Al Falah district in Riyadh is the first declared real estate area. It requires financing entities holding rights in a declared area to accept the ownership registration deed issued by the General Real Estate Authority as the recognised ownership document for that area, and places on them the ongoing duty to monitor subsequent GREA announcements. It is addressed to banks and finance companies operating in the Kingdom.
lookup_terms: General Real Estate Authority / الهيئة العامة للعقار

data.summary: Sub-rule 300.1.7 of SAMA's Rules Governing the Opening of Bank Accounts and General Operational Guidelines, sitting within the chapter on resident juristic persons. It sets the account-opening conditions and documentation for accounts used in liquidation and financial restructuring proceedings of entities, distinguishing them from ordinary operating accounts. It binds SAMA-licensed banks onboarding liquidators/restructuring trustees and the entities under those procedures.

Section 300.2 of SAMA's bank account rules, covering account opening for non-resident juristic persons, with sub-categories for GCC commercial non-banking companies, non-GCC companies with or without contracts/projects in Saudi Arabia, non-resident banks, international investment companies and funds, insurers, money changers and non-resident payment card companies. It sets the permitted account types, required documents and verification conditions for each category. It binds banks operating in Saudi Arabia when onboarding foreign legal entities.
lookup_terms: foreign company account with contract in Saudi Arabia
international investment companies and mutual funds accounts

data.summary: Chapter/section 400 of the SAMA bank account rules, addressing account opening for resident and non-resident foreign investors that fall outside the Foreign Investment Law, including investment-deposit linkage accounts and accounts for foreign financial institutions qualified by the CMA to invest in listed securities. It prescribes licensing/CR evidence, articles of association, identification and verification of beneficial owners holding ultimate control (25% threshold benchmark) and mapping of ownership and control structure. It binds banks onboarding such investors and interacts with CMA's QFI rules and FATF-based country risk screening.
lookup_terms: foreign investors not covered by Foreign Investment Law

data.summary: Section 500 of the SAMA bank account rules, governing accounts for Saudi ministries and government entities (including donation accounts, non-budget-funded activity accounts and Wilayah trust-fund investment accounts) as well as for foreign states and GCC/non-GCC government and quasi-government bodies; section 600 covers clearance accounts. It requires Ministry of Finance approval routed through SAMA, naming the account in the entity's name with a stated purpose, and specified authorized-signatory documentation. It binds banks and, procedurally, the government entities seeking accounts.

Chapter IV of the SAMA bank account rules, setting the ongoing operating regime for accounts after opening: deposit rules, account closure, and the dormancy lifecycle (dormant after 24 months without a customer-initiated debit or documented contact, then unclaimed and abandoned status). It imposes dual-control reactivation, restrictions on withdrawals/transfers from dormant accounts, customer notification duties, internal audit of unclaimed/abandoned accounts at least biennially with reports to the Audit Committee, and an annual statistical report to SAMA each March. It binds all banks operating in Saudi Arabia across all customer types, including embassies and government entities.
lookup_terms: Chapter IV operation of bank accounts

data.summary: The supervisory rules and controls in the SAMA bank account framework that anchor the Know Your Customer principle and require the Rules to be read together with the Anti-Money Laundering Law and its Implementing Regulations and the Law on Terrorism Crimes and Financing and related guidelines. It covers Compliance Department access rights to CDD and transaction data, verification of curators, legal agents, custodians and authorized persons, and ongoing risk-based monitoring of customers' transactions using automated systems integrated with core banking. It binds banks operating in Saudi Arabia at both onboarding and throughout the relationship.
lookup_terms: ongoing monitoring of accounts and transactions
Law on Terrorism Crimes and Financing
Compliance Department access to CDD data
legal agents curators custodians authorized persons

data.summary: Section 200.1 of SAMA's Rules Governing the Opening of Bank Accounts and General Operational Guidelines sets the account-opening and identification requirements for natural persons resident in Saudi Arabia, broken down by category (Saudi nationals, GCC nationals, expatriates, tribe members, Beluchis and Turkistanians, airline/ship crew, salary-payment prepaid records, credit cards for non-resident employees, and blood-money collection accounts). It prescribes acceptable identity documents, authorised signatories/delegation limits and risk classification at onboarding. It binds banks and other SAMA-supervised entities licensed to take deposits in the Kingdom.

Rule 200.1.3 governs bank accounts for expatriates residing in Saudi Arabia, including accounts for holders of temporary 90-day work visas opened on an employer's official request, employer notification duties on final exit, mandatory freezing and closure steps, and limits on delegation and joint accounts (permitted only for specified spouse/first-degree relative combinations with valid Iqama). It also caps standing orders for expatriates at one-year renewable, monthly domestic or cross-border transfers with verified customer data. Certain expatriate account types are expressly classified as high risk and subject to ongoing monitoring; the rules bind banks operating in the Kingdom.

Section 300 sets the documentary and authorisation requirements for opening accounts for juristic persons, split between resident entities (licensed businesses and shops, SPEs, foreign schools, e-commerce without premises, freelance permit holders, money changers, all company forms, foreign-investment entities, non-profit and public bodies, diplomatic missions and liquidation/restructuring accounts) and non-resident entities (GCC and non-GCC companies, banks, funds, insurers, money changers and payment card companies). It also covers specialised accounts such as real estate escrow, payment companies' client collection accounts and debt-based crowdfunding collection accounts. It binds banks onboarding corporate and institutional customers in the Kingdom.

Rule 300.1.5.1 governs bank accounts for Hajj, Umrah and Prophet's Mosque visit activity, including pilgrim affairs offices and tourism companies, agencies and associations organising pilgrim arrivals from abroad. It requires Ministry of Hajj and Umrah approval letters specifying the entity, its ministry-issued computer number and named authorised signatories, Saudi riyal denomination, attested lists of contracted counterparties, and a formal reactivation process for each Hajj season. It binds banks servicing pilgrimage-sector customers.
lookup_terms: Ministry of Hajj and Umrah approval letter

data.summary: Rule 300.1.5 sets account-opening conditions for the non-profit and public sectors, covering private associations and foundations, public welfare committees, charity change/halala donation collection accounts, cooperative associations and funds, homeowners' associations, endowments and bequests, clubs, public corporations, chambers of commerce, mosque construction accounts, national societies and committees, court-related and personal debt settlement accounts. It specifies supervising-authority approvals, authorised signatories and purpose limits for each category. It binds banks onboarding NPOs and public-sector bodies, a segment carrying elevated terrorist-financing sensitivity.

Rule 300.1.6.5 sits within the diplomatic and international-body part of Section 300 and sets the conditions for opening and operating accounts for multilateral international organizations resident in Saudi Arabia, alongside neighbouring rules on embassies, resident and visiting diplomats, foreign airlines, relief committees and campaigns, friendship committees and economic/technical liaison offices. It addresses required host-authority documentation, recognition of the organization's status and authorised signatory arrangements. It binds banks onboarding international organizations and diplomatic-sector customers.
lookup_terms: international organization bank account Saudi Arabia

data.summary: SAMA circular permitting credit information companies to conclude membership agreements with fintech firms that hold, or have applied for, a licence/permit from SAMA or the Capital Market Authority without first obtaining SAMA's written no-objection, relaxing the earlier general no-objection requirement. It sets conditions: verification of the licence/permit application before signing, that the fintech's intended activity involves entering a credit relationship with the consumer, suspension of membership rights (including access to consumer credit records) until a copy of the licence/permit is provided, and limiting ceased or expired-licence fintechs to updating records of their existing dealings rather than enquiring on new consumers. It binds credit information companies operating in the Kingdom, which retain full responsibility for compliance with the Credit Information Law, its Implementing Regulation and related SAMA instructions.

SAMA circular issuing the mandatory standard-form consumer finance contract for individuals, aimed at reducing divergence between financiers' contracts and limiting disputes. The template covers scope, definitions, formation and term, financed asset, financial obligations, instalments, payment methods, late payment/default, termination, early repayment, fees and administrative charges, guarantees, undertakings of financier and beneficiary, breach, death or incapacity, documentation, amendment, notices and governing law, plus a contract summary sheet and repayment schedule annex. It binds banks operating in the Kingdom (local banks, foreign bank branches, digital banks) and finance companies, which may not conclude contracts departing from or amending the template from the stated compliance date.

The early repayment provisions (Article 10) of SAMA's mandatory standard consumer finance contract for individuals, cross-referenced in the contract summary sheet that must be signed by the beneficiary. As part of the standard form, these terms cannot be varied by the financier and set the contractual basis on which a beneficiary may settle a consumer finance facility ahead of schedule. Binds banks and finance companies offering consumer finance to individuals in the Kingdom.

The late payment and default provisions (Article 8, with the related contract-termination procedure in Article 9) of SAMA's mandatory standard consumer finance contract for individuals; the consequences of late instalment payment must also be flagged in the signed contract summary sheet. As standard-form terms they are non-negotiable and govern the financier's remedies and the beneficiary's exposure on missed instalments. Binds banks and finance companies providing consumer finance to individuals.

SAMA circular reaffirming that lessors are responsible for the accuracy of the data they submit when applying to a finance lease contract registration company for issuance of executive-bond (writ of execution) extracts for a registered finance lease contract. Lessors must only apply where one of the cases set out in the existing controls and procedures for requesting and issuing such extracts is met, and bear liability for any prejudice to lessee rights arising from incorrect data; registration companies remain obliged to verify the lessor's entitlement and obtain the lessor's written undertakings before issuing extracts. Binds banks, finance companies and SAMA-licensed finance lease contract registration companies.

SAMA's Rules for Bank Accounts, in the part governing inactive account classifications: accounts become dormant 24 calendar months after the last customer-initiated debit or last reliable documented contact, with staged treatment thereafter as unclaimed and then abandoned. It sets operational controls including dual supervision for reactivation, restrictions on withdrawals and transfers, continued acceptance of incoming deposits and transfers without changing status, customer contact obligations before the five-year point, balance-return and account-closure conditions for small balances, separate secure file-keeping, and recognition of balances as liabilities on the bank's balance sheet. Binds banks operating in the Kingdom.

Node within SAMA's bank account opening and operation rules covering customer identification, due diligence and AML/CFT-linked controls that banks must apply when establishing and maintaining relationships, including correspondent banking. It requires senior management approval for new correspondent relationships, AML/CFT self-certification and control assessment of the correspondent (including no shell-bank access), adverse-information screening, restrictions on how correspondent accounts may be used, and prohibits accounts for certain non-resident financial institutions, funds and investment companies. Binds SAMA-licensed banks, and is expressly to be read together with the AML Law, its Implementing Regulation and the counter-terrorism financing law and guidelines.

Defines the lifecycle classification of inoperative bank accounts — dormant (24 calendar months from the last customer-initiated debit or documented contact), then unclaimed, then abandoned — and the operational controls attaching to each stage. Sets requirements for reactivation under dual control at a higher authority, permitted credits that do not restore active status, customer contact obligations, segregated and dual-controlled file custody, treatment of balances as bank liabilities, deduction of outstanding obligations before transfer to suspense, and a limited closure option for balances of SAR 1,000 or less with prior notice. Binds banks operating in Saudi Arabia and governs their handling of affected customer funds.

Node addressing restriction and suspension of activity on bank accounts, drawing on the inoperative-account rules that limit withdrawals and transfers once an account is classified dormant, unclaimed or abandoned, and on the constraints banks face regarding balances in those accounts. Sets who may transact on a restricted account (customer in person, legal agent, heirs' agent or authorised signatory for juristic persons, with defined exceptions for electronic channels), the dual-supervision requirement for reactivation, and the prohibition on banks disposing of balances. Binds banks; should be read alongside the disclosure and enforcement node for blocking imposed at SAMA's instruction.

Requires every bank to build and maintain an electronic registration system as a unified database underpinning the opening, operation and follow-up of bank accounts, with prescribed minimum data fields differentiated by customer category (Saudi natural persons, GCC nationals, non-Saudi natural persons and others per the annexed classification), sourced from approved identity documents and reliable independent sources. The node also carries related obligations: Compliance Department access rights to identification, due diligence and transaction data; verification of curators, legal agents, custodians and authorised persons; and ongoing risk-based monitoring of customers and transactions where manual monitoring is expressly insufficient. Binds banks and interacts directly with the AML Law and its Implementing Regulation.

Governs how banks respond to requests to disclose, and to enforce against, customer balances, accounts and banking relationships. Defines enforcement as blocking, compulsory deduction, cheque issuance and transfer from customer accounts; requires strict confidentiality; channels requests through SAMA except where SAMA's instructions provide otherwise; and mandates a full relationship search (active, closed, suspended and inoperative accounts, deposits, safe deposit boxes, credit cards, remittance memberships and other products), including sole proprietorships and company participations of the person searched, in the form and within the timeframe SAMA specifies. Binds banks; relevant also to court-related accounts and enforcement court arrangements described in the same instrument.

Concept node for credit information companies as they arise within SAMA's bank account rules; the surrounding material concerns documentation for opening accounts for legal persons (joint-stock companies including those under formation, LLCs, partnerships, GCC commercial entities) and the periodic updating of customer identification and information. It sets when identity documents must be refreshed (on expiry for documents valid under five years; every five years or on expiry for longer-dated ones; five years maximum for accounts opened under official letters or open-term licences), permits online identity updating with exclusions for incompetent persons, and lists triggers for updating customer information including behavioural change and ML/FT risk-driven due diligence. Binds banks; open it for entity KYC documentation and refresh cycles rather than for credit bureau licensing rules.

Concept node within SAMA's bank account opening rules covering the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Development as the licensing authority for private associations (and comparable Da'wah offices and branches) whose bank accounts banks may open in Saudi riyal only, subject to specified documentation and operating controls. The surrounding rules also address Hajj/Umrah organisers' account segregation and account opening for minors, persons with upper-limb disabilities and legally incompetent persons through legal representatives. It binds SAMA-supervised banks as part of customer identification and account-opening due diligence.
lookup_terms: Ministry of Human Resources and Social Development
Rules Governing the Opening of Bank Accounts

data.summary: Concept node identifying the Ministry of Finance's approval role in SAMA's bank account opening rules for government entities: foreign-currency government accounts, transfers of government accounts between banks, closure requests routed through SAMA, limits on credit/overdrafts to government bodies, Saudi-only signatories, and donation-receipt accounts; MoF approval is also required for sports club accounts. It binds banks opening or maintaining accounts for government entities and public-sector bodies.
lookup_terms: Deputyship for Financial and Accounts Affairs

data.summary: Concept node covering the General Authority for Awqaf's role in SAMA's account opening rules for endowment (waqf) and bequest accounts, including the endowment registration certificate, endowment deed, authorised signatories and administrator ID requirements. It sets restrictions on cross-border transfers and receipts, checkbook-only withdrawals, prohibition of ATM/credit cards, and notification of SAMA, distinguishing endowments administered by the Authority, those outside its administration, and foreign endowments. It binds banks opening such accounts.

Appendix C of SAMA's bank account opening rules explains the structure of the Ministry of Interior ten-digit computer number: the first digit denotes identity type (Saudi national, resident, entities such as government bodies, companies, charities, clubs and diplomatic missions), digits two to nine are serial, and the last digit is a check digit issued via the National Information Center. It supports the electronic record and identification requirements banks must maintain for natural and juristic persons, alongside Appendices A and B listing government entities and public-sector legal persons.

SAMA circular requiring licensed debt-based crowdfunding entities to prepare a quarterly risk report for discussion by the risk and credit committee (if any) and the board, covering the risks identified in the Rules for Engaging in Debt-Based Crowdfunding, mitigation measures, limit breaches, assumptions underlying risk assessment, and adequacy of disclosure standards. It sets submission deadlines to SAMA for the risk report, quarterly and audited annual financial statements with auditor and board reports, and annual/quarterly prudential returns (externally audited annually and certified by Chief Accountant, CFO and CEO/Managing Director), plus publication of specified reports and statements on the company's website.
lookup_terms: audited annual financial statements finance company

data.summary: SAMA circular establishing a statutory reserve for money exchange centers, requiring them to appropriate a minimum share of annual net profit (after covering accumulated losses) until the reserve reaches a set proportion of paid-up capital, with appropriation suspendable at that point. Use of the statutory reserve requires SAMA's prior written no-objection, and the requirement is stated to be without prejudice to the separate cash reserve obligation under the Rules Governing Money Exchange Business. It binds money exchange centers operating in the Kingdom with immediate effect.

A cluster of provisions in SAMA's bank account rules requiring the bank's head-office compliance department to obtain SAMA's prior approval (and, for certain categories, the approval of the sector supervisor such as the Ministry of Hajj and Umrah or MHRSD) before opening or transferring specified account types. It fixes escalation and turnaround timelines (same-day referral to compliance and SAMA, maximum two working days to open), documentation of refusals at branch level, dual control over the account, and restrictions such as holding all Hajj organizer accounts at a single bank and limiting sub-account use to defined purposes. It binds licensed banks operating in Saudi Arabia and their compliance functions.

Marks where the Bankruptcy Law interacts with the account rules: opening dedicated liquidation / financial restructuring accounts (court order, appointment of the bankruptcy officeholder or committee, prescribed account naming and operation), and the mandatory freezing of accounts on death, loss of legal competence, judicial or general-assembly liquidation, or the commencement of liquidation or administrative liquidation procedures. It also touches SAMA-directed compulsory deductions from salary accounts as priority claims. Binds banks holding the relevant customer accounts.

Marks the Companies Law as the reference framework for opening and operating accounts of Saudi juristic persons under the rules — joint-stock companies (including companies under formation and formation-expense accounts requiring Ministry of Commerce approval), limited liability companies, general and limited partnerships, and GCC companies holding a Saudi commercial register. It also underpins liquidation of a company under the Companies Law as a freezing/account-closure trigger, and drives the constitutive documents banks must collect. Binds banks opening corporate accounts.

A scope marker: Part 400 of the account rules covers resident and non-resident foreign investors that fall outside the Foreign Investment Law regime, including foreign financial institutions qualified under CMA's rules to invest in securities listed on the Saudi Exchange. It sets the documentary conditions (home-country licence or commercial register, activity licence from the CMA/SAMA counterpart, constitutive documents), beneficial-owner identification at the 25% threshold and mapping of the ownership and control structure, plus the bar on non-Saudi owners delegating account management. Binds banks opening accounts for foreign investors.

Marks the cross-reference obliging these account rules to be read together with the AML Law and its Implementing Regulations, the Law on Terrorism Crimes and Financing and the guidelines issued thereunder. It carries the associated ongoing due diligence duties: verifying the status of curators, legal agents, custodians and authorised persons; automated (not manual) transaction monitoring proportionate to the bank's risk profile and integrated with core systems; and the compliance department's right of timely access to CDD data, transaction records and identification information. Binds banks as AML/CTF-obliged financial institutions.
lookup_terms: Law of Terrorism Crimes and Financing
ongoing monitoring of accounts and transactions
compliance department access to CDD data

data.summary: Sets the Ministry of Hajj and Umrah as the gatekeeper authority for accounts of pilgrim affairs offices and of tourism companies, agencies and associations organising pilgrim arrivals: an approval letter naming the entity, its ministry computer number and the authorised signatories is required to open, and a fresh letter plus attested contracted-party list is required to reactivate the account each Hajj season. It confines such accounts to Saudi riyal, channels deposits and withdrawals to listed contracted service providers (with cash carried through ports evidenced by Zakat/Customs documentation), restricts petty-cash payments, requires compliance department sign-off to operate the account, and bars investing balances. Binds banks holding Hajj/Umrah organiser accounts.
lookup_terms: Ministry of Hajj and Umrah approval letter
cash disclosed at ports of entry

data.summary: A SAMA supervisory circular reminding financiers that, when outsourcing debt collection to external service providers, the financier remains responsible for verifying that those providers comply with SAMA's Collection Controls and Procedures for Individual Customers and have procedures in place to ensure compliance. It was issued in response to observed negative collection practices and warns that SAMA will take regulatory action against violators. It binds banks and finance companies operating in the Kingdom.

A SAMA circular directing finance companies to update their credit granting policies and procedures to keep pace with rapid changes in the finance sector and the activities being financed, adopt prudential measures to limit rising non-performing loans, and ensure provisions and collateral are proportionate to the risks of the activity. Issued under the Finance Companies Control Law and its Implementing Regulation. It binds licensed finance companies and SAMA-licensed crowdfunding entities.

A SAMA circular encouraging all financiers to develop periodic financial awareness programs tailored to small and medium enterprises, aligned with the Financial Sector Development Program under Vision 2030, and to use varied awareness channels. It asks institutions to submit a quarterly report on their contribution to a designated SAMA email address. Addressed to banks and finance companies; framed as encouragement rather than a hard prohibition, but with a reporting expectation.
lookup_terms: financial education small and medium enterprises

data.summary: A SAMA circular confirming that a real estate financier that transfers its contractual rights in the secondary market (including through licensed real estate refinancing companies) is not released from its obligations under the Real Estate Finance Law, its Implementing Regulation, related instructions and the contracts, and must continue performing them for the contract term. It cites examples such as prompt updating of customers' credit records within the period set in the Credit Information Law Implementing Regulation, and handling early repayment and debt rescheduling. It also addresses enabling a third party assigned collection duties while the financier retains responsibility; binds banks and finance companies.
lookup_terms: transfer of rights real estate financier

data.summary: SAMA's AML/CTF Guide setting out expectations for financial institutions under SAMA supervision, including board and senior management responsibilities, appointment of an independent senior-level AML/CTF compliance officer reporting to the board, establishment of a dedicated AML/CTF unit staffed by Saudi nationals with adequate human and technological resources, and the officer's timely access to customer due diligence data and transaction records. It also covers the AML/CTF program, risk identification for new products, services, channels and customers, at least annual policy review, training, and follow-up on audit and supervisory recommendations. It binds SAMA-supervised financial institutions.

The legal-basis and definitions component of SAMA's AML/CTF Guide, identifying the Law on Combating Terrorism Crimes and Financing (Royal Decree M/21, 12/02/1439H) alongside the Anti-Money Laundering Law (Royal Decree M/20, 05/02/1439H) and their Implementing Regulations, and confirming SAMA as a designated supervisory authority empowered to issue instructions, rules and guidance to financial institutions. It also references KSRelief as the sole authority for collecting donations destined outside the Kingdom and the Council of Ministers resolution making SAMA the competent authority for payment and financial settlement systems. Relevant to institutions determining the statutory source of their AML/CTF and TF obligations.
lookup_terms: Law on Combating Terrorism Crimes and Financing

data.summary: This node covers the risk-based approach (RBA) as set out in SAMA's AML/CTF guidance for financial institutions, describing the sequence of steps from identifying and assessing ML/TF risks through to implementing mitigating preventive measures and reviewing/updating the approach. It fixes an update cadence of at least once every two years or whenever risk factors change, and requires customer risk classification (e.g. high/medium/low) proportionate to the institution's size and business. It binds financial institutions supervised by SAMA, and drives the intensity of CDD, monitoring and senior management approval for high-risk customers.

This node is the institutional ML/TF risk assessment section of SAMA's AML/CTF guide: financial institutions must assess, understand and document their money laundering and terrorist financing risks across customers and beneficial owners, products/services/transactions, geographies, and delivery channels. It requires pre-launch risk assessment of new products, services, business practices and new or developing technologies, regular updating of customer risk profiles, and a mechanism to furnish the underlying information and reports to SAMA on request. It explicitly discourages wholesale de-risking, requiring mitigation rather than exclusion of high-risk customer classes.

This node covers customer due diligence obligations, with particular emphasis on reliance on third parties (another financial institution or a DNFBP, including group entities) to perform CDD under the AML Law Implementing Regulations. Reliance is conditional: the third party must be regulated and supervised and apply CDD and record-keeping, information must be obtainable immediately and without delay, high-risk country exposure must be considered, and the relying institution must assess and manage the associated ML/TF risk, verify the third party's capability at least annually, and monitor such relationships. Ultimate responsibility remains with the financial institution.

This node is the enhanced due diligence (EDD) section: where a customer or business relationship is classified as high risk under the institution's risk-based approach, additional information gathering, closer transaction monitoring and intensified controls are required. Financial institutions must define the risk factors used to place customers in the high-risk category, identify high-risk customers individually or by category, and apply EDD including to relationships onboarded through third-party reliance. It binds SAMA-supervised financial institutions and interacts with senior management approval requirements for high-risk relationships.

This node covers simplified due diligence (SDD), permitted where ML/TF risk is assessed as low and there is no suspicion of ML/TF, based on the AML Law and CTF Law Implementing Regulations. SDD is a streamlined, proportionate application of CDD rather than an exemption: identity of the customer (or person acting on their behalf) and the beneficial owner must still be verified from reliable independent sources, and the nature and purpose of the relationship and the ownership/control structure of legal persons must still be understood. The simplified measures applied must be set out in the institution's approved AML/CTF policies and procedures.

This node defines and operationalises the beneficial owner concept: the natural person who ultimately owns or controls the customer directly or indirectly, never a legal person. It sets the 25% ownership/control reference point for legal persons, with cascading fallback measures where no such person exists or where the controlling shareholder is suspected not to be the true beneficial owner (senior managing officials, sub-25% controllers, high-risk treatment and record-keeping of reasons). Financial institutions must verify beneficial ownership from authenticated independent sources and may not rely primarily on the customer's written statement.
lookup_terms: person acting on behalf of the customer

data.summary: This node covers the PEP element of customer due diligence within SAMA's AML/CTF risk-based approach guidance, requiring financial institutions to take reasonable measures to determine whether a customer or beneficial owner is a politically exposed person, whether foreign or domestic. Where the PEP relationship is high risk, enhanced due diligence must be applied and extended to family members and close associates. It binds financial institutions supervised by SAMA and links to Article 8 of the AML Law and its Implementing Regulations, which require internal procedures and tools for PEP identification.

This section sets the ongoing transaction and activity monitoring obligation under SAMA's AML/CTF risk-based approach guidance, grounded in Article 13 of the AML Law and Article 69 of the Law on Combating Terrorism Crimes and its Financing. Financial institutions must document and effectively implement risk-calibrated monitoring measures approved at senior management level, use adequate automated systems alongside manual review, test those tools at least annually, and keep customer information and risk classification current.
