It binds SAMA-supervised financial institutions and feeds directly into suspicious transaction reporting to the SAFIU.

This node covers the suspicious transaction reporting regime in SAMA's AML/CTF guidance: financial institutions must adopt board-approved STR procedures, resource internal investigation, and report immediately and directly to the SAFIU whenever there is suspicion or reasonable grounds to suspect ML/TF, including attempted transactions regardless of amount. It also requires confidentiality and no tipping-off, response to SAFIU information requests, and separate notification to SAMA of accounts or transactions linked to UN Security Council (1267/1989/2253 and 1988) and national 1373 designated names. Binds SAMA-supervised financial institutions and their designated reporting officer.

This node sets governance requirements for the AML/CTF compliance function: an independent, specialised AML/CTF unit with adequate human and technological resources, staffed by Saudi nationals, headed by a senior-management-level officer who reports administratively and technically to the board and has timely access to customer and transaction data. It lists the officer's mandated duties, including designing the AML/CTF programme, reviewing policies, monitoring transactions, handling internal suspicion reports and reporting to the SAFIU, and dealing with SAMA submissions. It binds SAMA-supervised financial institutions, their boards and senior management.

This section requires financial institutions to subject their AML/CTF controls, policies and procedures to independent testing of adequacy and effectiveness, referencing Article 14/1 of the AML Law Implementing Regulations and Article 18 of the Implementing Regulations of the Law on Combating Terrorism Crimes and its Financing. The auditor must be independent of the AML/CTF function and uninvolved in the areas audited, must apply a risk-based scope focused on higher-risk areas, and senior management must remediate identified weaknesses; extension of scope to the external auditor is to be considered where necessary. It binds SAMA-supervised financial institutions and their internal/external audit functions.

This node covers AML/CTF training obligations under SAMA's guidance: institutions must budget for and deliver ongoing training to senior management and staff, including annual specialised training for compliance function personnel, reflecting current ML/TF typologies and the institution's internal controls. The requirement derives from Article 14/1 of the AML Law Implementing Regulations and Article 18 of the Implementing Regulations of the Law on Combating Terrorism Crimes and its Financing, with the institution responsible for determining appropriate level and type of training. It binds SAMA-supervised financial institutions, their boards and senior management.

Section 13 of SAMA's AML/CTF guidance/rules for financial institutions, setting the due diligence expected before and during a correspondent banking relationship: gathering sufficient information on the respondent's business, reputation, supervision and AML/CTF standards, clarifying each party's AML/CTF responsibilities, applying ongoing transaction monitoring to correspondent accounts, and obtaining senior management approval (with input from the AML/CTF compliance officer) before onboarding. It anchors on Article 9 of the AML Law and Article 68 of the Law on Combating Terrorism Crimes and Financing, and imposes an absolute bar on relationships with shell banks or with foreign institutions that permit shell bank use of their accounts. Binds SAMA-supervised financial institutions.

Section 14 of SAMA's AML/CTF requirements governing cross-border and domestic wire transfers in any currency (including serial and cover payments) sent, received or processed in Saudi Arabia, including card- and mobile-initiated transfers. It sets the minimum originator and beneficiary data that must accompany and be verified with each transfer, a customer declaration on knowledge of the beneficiary and legitimate purpose, batch/combined transfer treatment, a domestic exemption with a three-working-day information response deadline, obligations of receiving and intermediary institutions to detect and act on missing information, confidentiality of exchanged data, and currency restrictions on inbound transfers routed to beneficiaries abroad. Binds financial institutions and intermediary institutions operating in Saudi Arabia.

Concept node for the Saudi Arabia Financial Intelligence Unit (SAFIU) as referenced in SAMA's AML/CTF rules — the national body to which financial institutions report suspicious transactions and activities identified through monitoring. Appears alongside the Kingdom's international AML/CTF commitments (UN conventions, FATF and MENAFATF membership) framing the domestic reporting architecture. Relevant to all SAMA-supervised financial institutions subject to STR obligations.

Concept node for the Financial Action Task Force as used in SAMA's AML/CTF rules, principally in the transaction and activity monitoring section (Section 7): institutions must develop and continually update ML/TF indicators and typologies proportionate to their business, observing instructions from SAMA, the PCCML, the PCCT and international bodies such as FATF. It signals that FATF standards and typologies are an expected input to a risk-based monitoring framework, not merely background. Binds SAMA-supervised financial institutions.

SAMA's Rules for Advertising Products and Services, issued under the Saudi Central Bank Law (Royal Decree M/36), governing the content, language and mandatory disclosures of any advertisement by a SAMA-supervised financial institution. Requires due diligence against misleading, tempting or exaggerated messaging and prescribes minimum advertisement content (institution identity, product name, key terms and conditions, target customer/consumer, all fees and commissions including VAT, and for finance products the APR and finance term, with fixed/variable term cost disclosure for real estate finance). Applies to all financial institutions supervised by SAMA when advertising any product or service to Customers and Consumers as defined.

The conduct and consent provisions of SAMA's Rules for Advertising Products and Services (Articles 8–14), covering fair competition and sector reputation, prohibition on using customer personal data in advertising without written consent, a ban on advertising insurance or credit products to individuals under 18 Hijri years or where unsuitable, opt-in consent and easy permanent opt-out for marketing channels, the binding effect of advertised offers and specifications on the institution and their inclusion in the contract, use of official channels or licensed third parties with the institution retaining responsibility for third-party non-compliance, and the requirement to adopt an internal advertising policy aligned with SAMA rules. Binds all SAMA-supervised financial institutions.
lookup_terms: use of customer personal data in marketing

data.summary: Article 15 of SAMA's Agent Banking Regulation requires each Bank engaging in Agent Banking to maintain a CDD programme tailored to its circumstances, agent types and risk level, covering KYC, information security and data privacy/confidentiality. Agents must identify customers by means the Bank deems appropriate and verify the purpose and nature of the banking relationship; where an Agent doubts the credibility of customer information it must cease dealing with the customer and report to the Bank's MLRO. The obligation binds the Bank, which remains responsible for its Agents' compliance — a delegated-performance, non-delegable-liability model relevant to AML reliance analysis.

This node covers the Bank board of directors' accountability under the Agent Banking Regulation (notably Articles 3 and 25): the board must ensure regulatory compliance, approve the policies and procedures governing agent selection and management, and ensure mechanisms exist for departments to implement SAMA instructions and to monitor agent activity proportionate to risk. It confirms the Bank is solely responsible for agent selection and fully liable for all acts and omissions of its Agents, including unauthorised acts connected to Agent Banking. Binds Banks contracting Agents; relevant where responsibility for outsourced customer-facing activity is contested.

Article 9 sets the minimum eligibility conditions an entity must meet to be contracted as a banking Agent, including satisfying the Article 13 fit and proper requirements, holding a commercial register permitting Agent Banking activity, obtaining any approval from its own supervisory/regulatory authority before the Bank seeks SAMA's non-objection, and adequate IT infrastructure. The Bank must submit a CEO (or designated senior officer) declaration confirming the fit and proper assessment and that eligibility minimums are met. Binds Banks proposing Agents and, indirectly, prospective Agents.

Article 13 establishes the fit and proper assessment the Bank must perform on a prospective Agent, its proprietors and persons managing the Agent Banking business, testing competence, integrity, adequacy of management structures and funding sources. It is a gating condition referenced by the eligibility and application provisions and underpins the Bank's declaration to SAMA. Binds Banks; sits within the Agent Banking Regulation's contracting section.

Article 14 requires Banks to run due diligence on prospective and existing Agents, covering moral/business/professional suitability, adverse credit bureau or other credible-source information, criminal records (particularly ML/TF, fraud and integrity), business experience, sources of funds, and verification of the Agent's legal status and address. It also requires defined internal roles for agent management, periodic reviews with early-warning indicators and corrective actions, and monitoring processes for AML/CFT, embezzlement and financial fraud, with requirements communicated to and monitored at Agents. Binds Banks; distinct from customer-level CDD under Article 15.

Article 29 concerns the registry of banking Agents maintained in connection with the Agent Banking Regulation, sitting in the section on Agent Registration alongside annual reporting obligations. It complements the transparency duties requiring Banks to publish and update Agent details (including terminated Agents, relocations and transfers) and the SAMA non-objection process for contracting Agents. Binds Banks operating Agent Banking arrangements.

Article 19 of SAMA's Rules for Agent Banking, which delimits the banking activities and services a contracted agent may carry out on behalf of the principal bank. It operates as the positive scope boundary of the agency arrangement, read together with the prohibited-activities article and the consumer protection and supervision sections of the same rules. It binds banks that outsource customer-facing activity to agents, and indirectly the agents themselves through the agent banking contract.

Article 20 of SAMA's Rules for Agent Banking, setting out activities a banking agent may not perform, forming the negative counterpart to the permissible activities article. It constrains what banks may lawfully delegate under an agent banking contract and is relevant to breach analysis, contract drafting and supervisory inspection of agents. It binds licensed banks as principals and, through contract, their appointed agents.

SAMA's Guide to Rules Governing Banks' Remittance Centers (Jumada Al-Akhir 1438H) consolidates operating, customer-acceptance, AML/CFT and service-quality rules for bank remittance centers and licensed remittance companies. It covers definitions, working hours, membership opening, KYC/CDD, domestic and international remittance execution, and contracting with money transfer service providers. It binds banks operating remittance centers and licensed remittance companies in the Kingdom.
lookup_terms: Guide to Rules Governing Banks' Remittance Centers

data.summary: The Know Your Customer provisions of the Remittance Centers Guide, requiring identity verification from official ID documents, prohibition of fictitious or anonymous names, assessment of source of funds and purpose of the relationship, identification of persons acting on behalf of the customer and of owners/controllers, and enhanced due diligence for high-risk customers, PEPs and high-risk jurisdictions. It also permits simplified measures for low-risk relationships but not where ML/TF is suspected, and discourages wholesale de-risking of customer categories. It binds remittance centers and licensed remittance companies alongside SAMA's AML/CFT rules and FATF standards.

Defined term in the Remittance Centers Guide: a register held with a bank's remittance center created under a signed Remittance Membership Opening Agreement between the center and the customer, containing the customer's information and creating mutual rights and obligations. Related provisions govern membership opening conditions, mandatory bilingual name and national/resident ID fields, linkage of membership numbers to identity, manager approval, approvals for high-risk customers, and termination where identification or source of transactions cannot be verified or the membership is misused. Relevant to defining the customer relationship for AML/CFT purposes in remittance services.

Reference in the Remittance Centers Guide to the Saudi Arabian Riyal Interbank Express (SARIE) system as an approved channel—alongside SWIFT—for executing outbound and inbound domestic and international remittances. It frames the expectation that remittance activity flows through recognised interbank transfer infrastructure, and sits next to requirements on contracting with and supervising money transfer service providers. Applies to bank remittance centers and licensed remittance companies.

A concept node sitting inside SAMA's Rules for Advertising Products and Services, covering the internal compliance ownership of advertising: the requirement to adopt an advertising policy aligned with these Rules and other SAMA/competent-authority instructions, and to monitor adherence including by licensed third-party advertisers. It also frames the substantive advertising duties the function must police — fair competition and sector reputation, no use of customer personal data without written consent, no unsuitable insurance/credit ads or ads to under-18s, opt-in/opt-out consent for marketing channels, and the binding nature of advertised terms. It binds all financial institutions supervised by SAMA, which remain liable for third-party non-compliance.

A concept node within SAMA's corporate governance principles for financial institutions dealing with board-formed committees, their composition, meeting quorum and voting, secretaryship, member duties and reporting lines to the Board. The surrounding text sets out committee frequency (at least six meetings a year for the committee in question), the chairman's reporting duty to the Board, and the Audit Committee's composition, appointment by the Ordinary General Assembly, term limits and required qualifications. It binds boards of SAMA-supervised financial institutions; forming committees does not relieve the Board of its responsibilities.

A concept node in SAMA's corporate governance principles addressing independent board membership: annual board assessment of independence, notification duties when independence may be impaired, and minimum numbers of independent members (not fewer than two or one third of the Board, whichever is greater). It also covers SAMA's prior written no-objection for board/committee nominations and leadership appointments, five-working-day notification of departures or loss of independence, multiple-directorship restrictions, tenure guidance and conflict-of-interest disclosure. It binds boards, nominees and members of SAMA-supervised financial institutions.

A version of SAMA's Rules for Advertising Products and Services, issued under the Saudi Central Bank Law, setting the regulatory framework and minimum content standards for advertising financial products and services. It defines Financial Institutions, Customer, Consumer, Products and Services and Advertising, and imposes due diligence on advertisement content, an Arabic-language requirement, and mandatory disclosures (institution identity, product name, key terms, target customer, all fees and VAT, APR and finance term, fixed vs variable term cost for real estate finance). It binds all financial institutions supervised by SAMA when advertising any product or service. Marked as a duplicate of the same instrument recorded elsewhere in the knowledge base.
lookup_terms: Rules for Advertising Products and Services

data.summary: SAMA's Regulation of Agent Banking in the Kingdom, setting minimum standards for banks that contract agents to deliver permissible banking products and services on their behalf, including agent eligibility, commercial register requirements, fit and proper assessment, prior SAMA non-objection, and the contract template and application package. It also requires descriptions of customer due diligence (KYC and AML/CFT compliance), information security and confidentiality, and risk management, and covers data and network security, consumer protection and conflict of interest. It binds all banks wishing to appoint agents; the board of directors is responsible for compliance and the bank remains fully liable for its agents' acts and omissions.

A concept node defining the banking Agent under the Agent Banking Regulation: an entity contracted by a bank to provide permissible banking services on its behalf, either as an Exclusive Agent (one bank) or Multiple Agent (non-exclusive or multiple banks). It sets agent-side conditions — a commercial register permitting agent banking, prior approval from its own supervisory authority, proper IT infrastructure, and satisfying the bank's fit and proper assessment before SAMA non-objection is sought. The bank selects the agent, contracts with it directly, and bears responsibility for all its actions and omissions, including CDD/KYC and AML/CFT compliance.

Defined term in SAMA's Guide to Rules Governing Banks' Remittance Centers identifying the Saudi Arabia Financial Investigation Unit as the national body receiving and analysing suspicious transaction reports relating to money laundering and terrorist financing from financial and non-financial institutions. Within this Guide it is the designated recipient of STRs from banks' remittance centres and licensed remittance companies, including where wire transfers lack complete originator information and the correspondent institution fails to respond. Binds remittance centres and their parent banks operating in the Kingdom.
lookup_terms: money laundering and terrorist financing reporting

data.summary: Defined term in the Guide to Rules Governing Banks' Remittance Centers describing the Financial Action Task Force as the inter-governmental standard-setter for AML, terrorist financing and proliferation financing measures. It serves as the reference framework underpinning the Guide's CDD, beneficial owner identification, risk-based approach and KYC obligations for remittance centres. Relevant to banks' remittance centres and licensed remittance companies applying SAMA's AML/CFT rules.

SAMA guidance document setting out the licensing process and minimum criteria for carrying on banking business in Saudi Arabia under the Banking Control Law, issued under SAMA's Charter and the BCL. It covers general licensing guidelines, restricted use of the word "bank", minimum criteria (capital, ownership, corporate governance, risk management, compliance/AML-CTF, IT and outsourcing, audit, home-supervisor oversight) and the application procedure. Binds all applicants for a banking licence, including foreign banks seeking to establish a branch, with the parent treated as the applicant.

The substantive criteria section of SAMA's Banking Licensing Guidelines, listing the minimum standards an applicant must satisfy: capital adequacy, bank ownership, corporate governance, risk management and controls, compliance and AML/CTF, IT and accounting systems and outsourcing, audit arrangements, and home-supervisor oversight for foreign branches. The criteria are expressly non-exhaustive and SAMA may impose additional prudential conditions case by case, including on newly licensed banks. Applies to all banking licence applicants, local and foreign.

Reference in SAMA's Banking Licensing Guidelines to the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision's Core Principles for Effective Banking Supervision, used as the benchmark for assessing whether a foreign bank branch applicant is subject to adequate prudential supervision at home. SAMA considers whether the home supervisor consolidates supervision in line with Basel principles and will co-operate with SAMA on the Saudi branch. Relevant to foreign bank branch applicants and their home regulators.

SAMA guidance issued under its Charter and the Banking Control Law setting additional licensing conditions for Digital-only Banks — banks conducting banking business mainly through digital channels — to be met alongside the general Banking Licensing Guidelines and Minimum Criteria. It addresses local joint-stock incorporation, promoter experience and financial capacity, business plan content, ICAAP/ILAAP submissions, physical head-office presence, corporate governance parity with conventional banks, risk management, and AML/CFT compliance in a fully digital environment. Binds applicants seeking a Digital-only Bank licence in Saudi Arabia.

Defines the Digital-Only Bank concept under SAMA's Additional Licensing Guidelines and Criteria — a bank conducting banking business mainly through digital channels such as web and mobile applications. It sets licensing conditions layered on top of the general Banking Licensing Guidelines and Minimum Criteria: local joint-stock incorporation, promoter experience and financial capacity, a detailed business plan, ICAAP/ILAAP submissions, a Saudi head office (branches not expected, though SAMA may exceptionally require customer service centres), and adherence to the same corporate governance, risk control and AML/CFT expectations as conventional banks in a fully digital environment. It binds applicants for a digital-only banking licence in Saudi Arabia and, once licensed, the resulting banks.
lookup_terms: Banking Licensing Guidelines and Minimum Criteria

data.summary: Concept node for the SAMA Cybersecurity Framework as invoked in the digital-only bank licensing context, alongside the SAMA BCM Framework and National Cybersecurity Authority requirements. It covers information system security, resilience and availability expectations proportionate to the proposed products and services, and the possibility that SAMA requires an applicant-funded independent third-party assessor to review technology/cybersecurity and AML/CFT arrangements at both design and implementation phases before operations commence. It binds licence applicants and licensed digital-only banks.

The Implementing Regulation of the Real Estate Finance Law, issued under SAMA's mandate to regulate the real estate finance sector. It sets definitions (Real Estate Finance, Borrower, Consumer, Originator, Secondary Market), licensing and activity limits for real estate finance entities, contract content requirements, insurance and disclosure duties, and the regime for real estate refinance companies including the Saudi Real Estate Refinance Company. It binds commercial banks and real estate finance companies licensed for real estate finance, plus licensed refinance companies.

Defined term and Chapter Two subject matter: a deferred payment contract extended to a borrower to own a dwelling. The regulation requires such contracts (written or electronic) to comply with the Law, SAMA rules and any SAMA standard contract form, requires a SAMA no-objection letter before products are offered, and prescribes minimum contract content including parties and ID details, term, total finance amount, term cost and its reference rate and change conditions, APR calculated per the Finance Companies Control Law regulation, and total amount payable. It binds real estate finance entities contracting with borrowers.

Covers Chapter Three of the Implementing Regulation: SAMA licenses real estate refinance companies restricted to refinance activity with minimum capital of SAR 5 billion, and PIF (or a wholly owned entity) incorporates the Saudi Real Estate Refinance Company with SAMA's initial approval. It governs share offerings (SAMA no-objection required), the conditions and 30% cap on aggregate shareholding by real estate finance entities after market stability and a five-year period, and the requirement that PIF or the founding entity retain at least 51%. It binds the refinance company, PIF as founder, and real estate finance entities seeking to invest.

Defined term: trading of the rights of real estate finance entities arising from primary market contracts. It frames the Real Estate Refinance Company's objectives — stability, growth and liquidity in the secondary market, intermediation between the sector and domestic/foreign funding sources — and the enabling powers to acquire and manage finance obligations, issue securities under the Capital Market Law with SAMA no-objection, and assign real estate assets and derived rights in refinancing transactions without borrower, debtor or guarantor consent. Relevant to real estate finance entities, refinance companies and SAMA pricing oversight.

SAMA's Responsible Lending Principles for Individual Customers, issued by circular in 1439H/2018 and amended shortly after, setting the framework for credit granted to individuals. It defines core terms (Creditor, Consumer, Finance Amount, Term Cost, Monthly Credit Obligations, Gross Salary) and imposes qualitative conduct duties plus quantitative deductible-ratio caps. It binds all creditors supervised and licensed by SAMA — banks and finance companies — across personal, vehicle, credit card and real estate finance directed at individual consumers, including where related work is assigned to third parties.
lookup_terms: total amount payable by the consumer

data.summary: The quantitative limb of the Responsible Lending Principles: caps on how much of a consumer's income may be absorbed by monthly credit obligations, tiered by total monthly income bands (e.g. up to SAR 15,000; above SAR 15,000 and below SAR 25,000). Separate sub-limits apply to salary-deduction-linked obligations (33.33% for employees, 25% for retirees), to obligations excluding real estate finance, and to total obligations, with a higher ceiling for consumers benefiting from Ministry of Housing or Real Estate Development Fund mortgage support. It binds creditors when assessing affordability before granting finance to individuals.

Chapter III of the Responsible Lending Principles, setting the conduct and process duties on creditors: a documented, board-approved and annually reviewed creditworthiness methodology; examination of the consumer's credit record with consent; written disclosure by the consumer of other credit obligations; registration and ongoing updating of credit information with licensed credit bureaus; and mandatory rejection of the application where consent is withheld. It binds banks and finance companies granting finance to individuals, and interacts with the credit information regime.

SAMA's Rules on Outsourcing for Finance Companies, setting regulatory requirements for companies licensed under the Finance Companies Control Law that have entered or intend to enter outsourcing contracts. They require a board-approved and annually updated outsourcing policy, risk review at inception and renewal, due diligence and licence verification on the External Service Provider, SAMA and auditor access rights, record retention, business continuity contingency planning, and transitional steps (policy filing within 180 days, review of legacy contracts within 365 days, notification of legal or regulatory breaches). Non-compliance is treated as a violation of the Finance Companies Control Law and its Implementing Regulations; responsibility for the provider's non-compliance remains with the finance company.

The defined term and classification test under the Outsourcing Rules: a function is material where its default or disruption could affect the finance company's activities, reputation or financial position, or where the outsourcing involves sharing, transferring, processing or storing consumer data and information. Finance companies must classify each proposed outsourcing case-by-case and obtain SAMA's written non-objection at least 30 working days before commencement, renewal or material change, submitting prescribed details. Appendices give non-exhaustive examples (e.g. external and internal audit, customer care and complaint handling, IT/cloud and security operations, brokerage and agency activity, HR provision, debt collection, archiving).

The required content and governance of the written outsourcing policy under the Rules on Outsourcing for Finance Companies: board and senior management responsibilities, which functions may be outsourced, eligibility and due diligence criteria for the External Service Provider (experience, financial and technical capability, effect on the firm's risk profile), and safeguards for confidentiality of consumer data including retrieval or destruction on contract expiry or termination. It also frames ongoing monitoring, reporting to senior management, business continuity and the deadline to file the board-approved policy with SAMA. It binds finance companies licensed under the Finance Companies Control Law.

A SAMA circular (Arabic, dated 1443/08/21) notifying the market of two regulatory amendments: the Minister of Finance's decision deleting Article 4 of the Implementing Regulation of the Real Estate Finance Law, and the Governor's decision amending Article 16 of the Implementing Regulation of the Finance Companies Control Law. The amended Article 16 confirms that SAMA specifies in the licence which financing activity or activities a finance company may conduct and may attach special conditions limiting geographic area, permitted beneficiaries or other matters. Addressed to banks and finance companies operating in the Kingdom.
lookup_terms: Real Estate Finance Law Implementing Regulation Article 4 deletion
Finance Companies Control Law Implementing Regulation Article 16

data.summary: SAMA's Financial Consumer Protection Principles and Rules, setting the overarching principles (fair treatment, disclosure and transparency, education, conduct, data privacy, complaints handling, competition, outsourcing) and detailed general conduct rules for dealings with consumers. Rules cover contract and initial disclosure form requirements, Arabic drafting, 30-day advance notice of changes to terms, fee and commission caps and publication, application acknowledgement and decision timelines, and complaint channels. Binds financial institutions supervised by SAMA in all consumer-facing activity, including through outsourced service providers.
lookup_terms: Financial Consumer Protection Principles and Rules

data.summary: The principles component of SAMA's Financial Consumer Protection framework: the general standards financial institutions must observe in every consumer dealing, including equitable and fair treatment (with special attention to vulnerable groups), disclosure and transparency of product information and pricing, and consumer education and awareness. Read together with the general conduct rules that operationalise them (documents provision, no post-contract fee increases, fee schedules, application notification timelines).
lookup_terms: no increase of fees after contract

data.summary: The complaints-handling and related privacy/competition/outsourcing elements of SAMA's consumer protection framework. It requires financial institutions to offer multiple accessible complaint channels (toll-free number, branches/website, apps, email), publish the complaint mechanism, issue reference numbers and handling periods by SMS, document communication channels and retain records for at least five years, and resolve complaints fairly and without delay. Principle 6 additionally ties consumer data privacy mechanisms to the Personal Data Protection Law.
lookup_terms: Personal Data Protection Law financial institution
consumer education on fraud and debt default

data.summary: SAMA's Rules Governing Real Estate Refinance Companies, defining the licensed real estate refinance activity and the permitted business of a Real Estate Refinance Company (a joint stock company licensed to refinance real estate financiers and trade real estate finance contractual rights in the secondary market). Sets objectives, permitted activities (acquiring finance rights, issuing securities under the Capital Market Law, providing finance solutions, investing surplus cash) and multiple SAMA no-objection requirements. Applies to companies licensed by SAMA for real estate refinance activity, alongside the Real Estate Finance Law and the Finance Companies Control Law and their implementing regulations.

Defines the Real Estate Refinance Company as a joint stock company licensed by SAMA to carry on real estate refinance activity, together with the related defined terms (Real Estate Financier, Real Estate Finance, Borrower, Primary/Secondary Market, Real Estate Finance Contractual Rights). Scope limit: the Company must direct its services and products to real estate financiers, and may only deal with non-real estate financiers after obtaining SAMA's no-objection. Subject to SAMA supervision under both the Real Estate Finance Law and the Finance Companies Control Law regimes.
lookup_terms: scope of dealings non-real estate financiers

data.summary: Node covering the governance body/committee layer of SAMA's Counter-Fraud Framework, sitting above the Counter-Fraud Department and responsible for oversight, approval and escalation of the Counter-Fraud Programme, Fraud Risk Appetite and periodic reporting to senior management and the Board. It operates alongside the maturity-model expectations that policies, standards and procedures be formally approved and monitored. It binds Member Organisations supervised by SAMA and, in practice, their boards and senior management.

Node identifying the senior individual accountable for the Counter-Fraud Programme and the day-to-day running of the Counter-Fraud Department, including reporting line considerations, independence and escalation to senior management. Relevant to allocating personal accountability for fraud risk assessment, detection systems, investigations and intelligence sharing with SAMA. Applies to Member Organisations under the SAMA Counter-Fraud Framework.

Sets the requirement for Member Organisations to establish and maintain a Counter-Fraud Department owning day-to-day operation of the Counter-Fraud Programme, with a minimum mandate covering policy compliance monitoring, enterprise fraud controls, Fraud Risk Assessment, intelligence analysis and sharing with SAMA and the sector, system tuning, investigations and root-cause analysis, Fraud Risk Appetite monitoring and crisis escalation, and periodic senior management reporting. It also requires alignment with Cyber Security and Financial Crime functions, which is the main cross-regime touchpoint with AML/CTF. Binds SAMA-supervised Member Organisations.
lookup_terms: alignment with financial crime and cyber security

data.summary: Describes the six-level Counter-Fraud Maturity Model (0 non-existent to 5 continuous improvement) used to measure a Member Organisation's counter-fraud maturity, with levels 3, 4 and 5 requiring cumulative satisfaction of all preceding criteria. Level 3 requires defined and embedded policies, standards, procedures and fraud detection capability monitored via KPIs; level 4 adds effectiveness measurement through KRIs; level 5 requires continuous improvement. Used as the assessment yardstick for SAMA supervision of Member Organisations.

Sets the principle and control requirements for a defined, approved and implemented fraud Intelligence Monitoring process drawing on internal and external sources to identify and monitor emerging fraud threats, including scanning, analysis, dissemination, action and sharing with internal and external stakeholders including SAMA. It requires alignment with SAMA's Cyber Threat Intelligence Principles, periodic effectiveness evaluation, sharing of confirmed-fraud log-in data through the Sectorial Anti-Fraud Committee and analysis of data shared by peers. Binds Member Organisations.

Requires Member Organisations to define a Fraud Risk Appetite stating tolerated fraud risk, derived from the Fraud Risk Assessment and aligned to overall risk appetite, with measures, thresholds and limits addressing impact on both the organisation and its customers. Breach of a customer-impacting limit triggers escalation to senior management and a CEO-level crisis management process with at least weekly meetings until resolution; the appetite must be reviewed annually, Board-endorsed and updated for material business model changes. Connects to the KRI requirements and the Fraud Risk Assessment methodology.

A SAMA circular (Arabic) addressed to debt-based crowdfunding institutions operating in the Kingdom, issued under the Central Bank Law and the Finance Companies Control Law, on pooled accounts used to manage financing value. It requires that such accounts be used solely to manage participants' financing amounts and be segregated from the institution's own funds, be named "Financing Value Management Account – [name of the debt-based crowdfunding institution]", and that SAMA be notified on opening or closing them at banks in the Kingdom. It also mandates a written policy and controls on account operation (authority matrix, multiple-control principle by risk, periodic reporting to senior management, no linkage to the institution's own financial obligations or rights), documented reconciliation of executed financing volumes against the pooled account balance, and that the bank account agreement reflect the regulatory requirements and allocate responsibilities between the bank and the institution.

SAMA's Counter-Fraud Framework, a principle-based instrument structured around four domains (Governance, Prevent, Detect, Respond) with Principles and mandated Control Requirements, plus a six-level Counter-Fraud Maturity Model (0–5) used to measure a Member Organisation's counter-fraud maturity. It obliges Member Organisations to establish a Counter-Fraud Programme and a dedicated Counter-Fraud Department responsible for day-to-day operation, including fraud risk assessment, control design, intelligence sharing with SAMA and the sector, systems tuning, investigations, root-cause analysis, monitoring of fraud risk appetite and periodic senior-management reporting. It binds SAMA-supervised Member Organisations and is the entry point for scope, applicability, responsibilities and maturity-level expectations.

The Governance domain of SAMA's Counter-Fraud Framework, placing ultimate responsibility for creating the Counter-Fraud Programme, providing direction and setting counter-fraud culture on the Board and Executive Leadership. It requires a Counter-Fraud Strategy, a Counter-Fraud Policy setting responsibilities and mandatory requirements, and a Governance Structure with internal and external reporting proportionate to the organisation's size and complexity, including a dedicated Counter-Fraud Governance Committee chaired by an Executive Committee member and with prescribed minimum membership (e.g. Head of Counter-Fraud, CRO, COO, Head of Digital). It binds Member Organisations' boards and senior management.

The Prevent domain of SAMA's Counter-Fraud Framework, covering proactive controls that stop fraud before harm occurs to the organisation or its customers. It requires a defined, approved and implemented Fraud Risk Management Framework aligned with enterprise risk management and addressing intelligence monitoring, fraud risk assessment, fraud risk appetite and KRIs, together with fraud prevention standards (internal and external fraud) that are periodically reviewed, monitored for compliance, measured for effectiveness, and risk-proportionate, including the approach to limits and thresholds for preventive controls. It binds Member Organisations and their business, risk and control owners.

The Detect domain of SAMA's Counter-Fraud Framework, addressing risk-based identification of actual or attempted fraud where preventive controls fail, using indicators in customer behaviour and transactional and non-transactional data. It requires defined, approved, implemented and maintained fraud detection standards covering internal and external fraud, periodically reviewed and effectiveness-tested, with prescribed minimum content on data sources, detection controls (including Wholesale Payment Endpoint Security monitoring), systems, roles and responsibilities and rationale, with enhanced measures where inherent fraud risk is higher. It binds Member Organisations.

The Respond domain of SAMA's Counter-Fraud Framework, governing the reaction to actual or suspected fraud incidents to limit losses and support recovery. It requires a defined, approved, implemented and maintained Fraud Response Plan, aligned where appropriate with enterprise incident management, monitored for compliance and effectiveness, and requiring prompt and competent assessment, investigation and resolution, with minimum content on alerting and reporting channels for customers, employees and third parties, roles and responsibilities, and decision-making authority and escalation/referral procedures inside and outside the organisation. It binds Member Organisations, including their investigation and customer-resolution functions.

A concept node within SAMA's Counter-Fraud Framework covering Key Risk Indicators used to measure a Member Organisation's position against its approved Fraud Risk Appetite. It requires KRIs built on a documented methodology, mapped to risks identified in the Fraud Risk Assessment, forward-looking rather than merely loss-counting, with defined thresholds showing whether results sit below, at, or above appetite, and complete, accurate, timely metrics. It binds Member Organisations subject to the Framework, with Board/Senior Management oversight of appetite breaches.

Concept node for the Case Management System required under the Respond domain of SAMA's Counter-Fraud Framework. It obliges Member Organisations to implement and maintain a system acting as the fraud case database — recording and monitoring suspected fraud alerts, internal and external reports, and investigations from initial assessment through to resolution — with access restriction, case ownership, workflow configurability, categorisation for trend analysis, audit of investigative steps, and retention of case evidence. It binds Member Organisations and supports the Fraud Response Plan and fraud reporting/trend analysis obligations.

Concept node for the Fraud Response Plan, the core requirement of the Respond domain of SAMA's Counter-Fraud Framework. It requires Member Organisations to define, approve, implement and maintain a plan — aligned where appropriate with enterprise incident management — covering alert and reporting channels for customers, employees and third parties, roles and responsibilities, escalation and decision-making authority, and prompt assessment, investigation and resolution of suspected or identified fraud, with compliance monitored and effectiveness periodically evaluated. It binds Member Organisations and is assessed against the Counter-Fraud Maturity Model.

Concept node for the authentication standard required under the Counter-Fraud Framework's prevention controls. Member Organisations must define, approve, implement and maintain a risk-based authentication standard — developed jointly by the Counter-Fraud Department and Cyber Security Team, informed by the Fraud Risk Assessment and Cyber Security Risk Assessment — covering customer, employee and third party credentials and instructions across digital and non-digital channels, with multi-factor authentication for higher-risk activity. It cross-refers to identity and access management and electronic banking provisions of SAMA's Cyber Security Framework.

Governance-domain node of SAMA's Counter-Fraud Framework, covering the Counter-Fraud Governance Structure and its interaction with SAMA's wider governance instruments. It places ultimate responsibility on the Board and Executive Leadership for the Counter-Fraud Programme (Strategy, Policy, governance structure and internal/external reporting) and requires a dedicated Counter-Fraud Governance Committee headed by an Executive Committee member, with mandated representation including the Head of Counter-Fraud, CRO, COO and Head of Digital. It binds Member Organisations proportionately to their size and complexity.

Concept node for whistle blowing obligations under the Counter-Fraud Framework's Detect/internal fraud controls. Member Organisations must define, approve, implement and maintain a multi-channel process allowing employees and third parties to report suspected fraud violations without fear of repercussion, must comply with SAMA's Whistle Blowing Policy for Financial Institutions, and must take no action against whistle blowers who report in good faith. It sits alongside internal-fraud monitoring controls such as employee activity logging and monitoring of anonymous reporting lines.
lookup_terms: Whistle Blowing Policy for Financial Institutions

data.summary: A control section (3.7) of SAMA's Counter-Fraud Framework requiring Member Organisations to notify SAMA immediately of newly observed fraud typologies and significant fraud incidents, whether or not a financial loss occurred. Notifications go to SAMA's General Department of Cyber Risk Control and cover external fraud attempts, significant internal employee fraud against customers, and serious integrity/honesty misconduct touching regulatory obligations. It binds all Member Organisations within the framework's scope and sits alongside fraud MI/reporting duties to senior management.
lookup_terms: General Department of Cyber Risk Control

data.summary: SAMA's Shariah Governance Framework setting minimum governance requirements for local banks conducting Shariah-compliant banking. It allocates roles across the board, executive management, the Shariah committee, compliance, risk management and internal audit, and covers committee formation, internal control, and Shariah-compliant product development. It complements rather than overrides other SAMA regulations and binds licensed local banks offering Islamic banking.

The provisions governing the bank's Shariah committee: meetings at least quarterly, majority quorum and majority voting with a casting vote for the chair, a 75% individual attendance requirement, and documented minutes and voting records. It also sets the committee's substantive mandate — supervising Shariah compliance of Islamic banking transactions, issuing binding Shariah decisions the board must rely on, and reviewing compliance and internal Shariah audit findings. Disclosure of member CVs and performance-assessment procedures, plus integrity screening of nominees, applies.

Chapter Seven (Article 16) establishes the three internal control pillars for Shariah governance: a Shariah compliance function performing regular assessment of Islamic activities and corrective actions; Shariah non-compliance risk management embedded in the bank's integrated risk framework and staffed by suitably qualified risk officers; and an independent internal Shariah audit providing objective assurance. It binds local banks conducting Shariah-compliant banking and links to the product development chapter.
lookup_terms: three lines of defence Islamic banking

data.summary: Chapter Nine (Article 18) governs how banks develop Shariah-compliant products, requiring all Shariah issues in product design and process to be referred to the Shariah committee with sufficient detail, and committee approval for every Islamic banking product and any subsequent amendment, including detailed review of contracts and documentation. It distinguishes pre-product approval (structuring, Shariah research, contract review before launch) from post-product approval review after the product is offered to customers.

SAMA guidelines on how to apply for a licence to engage in consumer microfinance activity under the Finance Companies Control Law and its Implementing Regulation. They set application submission rules, the definition of Applicant (founders/shareholders), the accuracy obligation with false or omitted material information treated as a violation of Article 7 and grounds for rejection or licence cancellation, and the checklist of required documents (articles of association, shareholder list, organizational structure, feasibility study and business plan, fit and proper forms for founders, 5%+ owners and board/committee candidates, and an irrevocable bank guarantee equal to 20% of minimum capital).

This is the corporate governance chapter (and related board/senior-management provisions) of SAMA's Rules Governing Real Estate Refinance Companies, issued under the Real Estate Finance Law and Finance Companies Control Law. It sets fit-and-proper and eligibility criteria for board and committee members, mandates board committees (audit, risk and credit, executive, nomination and remuneration) and a senior-management assets and liabilities committee, requires board-approved refinance policies that take effect only after a SAMA no-objection letter, and imposes personal liability on directors, the CEO/general manager, managing director and senior executives for breaches. It also requires adherence to SAMA's Principles of Corporate Governance for supervised financial institutions and the adoption of internal governance regulations submitted to SAMA. It binds licensed real estate refinance companies (joint stock companies) and their boards and senior management.

This is the risk management chapter of SAMA's Rules Governing Real Estate Refinance Companies, read alongside the adjacent internal-organization and outsourcing provisions. It requires a board-approved and annually updated business strategy and risk management policy covering all risk types (including outsourced processes), plus a comprehensive framework to identify, assess, manage, monitor and report risks with early identification, assessment of risk correlations and escalation to the board, audit committee, risk and credit committee and senior management. Related provisions require separation of executive and supervisory functions, adequate and tested IT systems safeguarding data availability, integrity and confidentiality, business continuity planning, and residual company liability for outsourcing providers' non-compliance. It binds licensed real estate refinance companies.

This node covers the definitions chapter and the secondary market chapter of SAMA's Rules Governing Real Estate Refinance Companies, including the concluding provisions. It defines key terms (real estate refinance company, real estate financier, real estate finance contractual rights, borrower, primary vs secondary market, refinance activity) and conditions trading of real estate finance contractual rights in the secondary market on a prior SAMA no-objection letter and a submitted comprehensive plan covering sukuk structuring, collection procedures, credit enhancement and a feasibility/impact study; SAMA may restrict or prohibit such trading. It binds licensed real estate refinance companies and is read together with the Real Estate Finance Law and Finance Companies Control Law and their implementing regulations.

SAMA instructions (Arabic original) regulating the purchase/transfer of individual consumer finance debts between finance companies, issued under the Finance Companies Control Law. The buying company must hold a consumer finance licence but needs no separate SAMA approval per transaction; it must disclose the new financing terms and costs, obtain documented customer consent, use a dedicated purchase request form with prescribed data, settle the existing debt via the SARIE system with specified payment details, give the customer the payment reference, charge no transfer fees beyond early settlement or administrative fees, and withhold release of surplus funds until a clearance letter is received. The selling company must issue outstanding-obligation statements or debt-confirmation letters and effect the transfer and settlement notification within one business day, refusing only with written justification. It binds finance companies operating in the Kingdom, with consumer protection obligations toward the individual customer.

A SAMA circular (Arabic original) making the "Compliance for the Finance Companies Sector" certificate mandatory for compliance managers at finance companies, relying on SAMA's mandate under the Implementing Regulations of the Finance Companies Control Law to develop the sector and raise staff competence. Incumbent compliance managers must obtain the certificate within one year of the circular, and it is required when a company seeks a no-objection letter to appoint someone to the role; the company must supply SAMA with the certificate once obtained. It binds finance companies operating in the Kingdom and their compliance function heads.

A SAMA circular (Arabic original) on pooled/collective accounts used to manage financing value at debt-crowdfunding entities, issued under the SAMA Law and the Finance Companies Control Law and reinforcing the Rules for Practising Debt-Based Crowdfunding. It requires that pooled accounts be used solely to manage financing value and be segregated from the entity's own funds, be named "Financing Value Management Account – [entity name]", that SAMA be notified on opening or closing such accounts at banks in the Kingdom, that written policies and authority matrices with multi-level control and periodic reporting govern operation, that the account carry no financial obligations or rights of the entity, that reconciliation between executed financings and account balances be performed and documented, and that the bank account agreement reflect the regulatory requirements and allocate responsibilities. It binds debt-based crowdfunding entities operating in the Kingdom.

This node covers SAMA's Fit and Proper Form as a mandatory attachment in the licensing pack for consumer microfinance activity, alongside the licence application letter, articles of association, shareholder list, organisational structure, feasibility study/business plan and a bank guarantee equal to 20% of minimum capital. A separate form must be completed and signed by each founding member, by each natural or legal person holding 5% or more where a founder is an entity, and by each board and sub-committee candidate, then endorsed by the person authorised to submit the application. It binds founders/shareholders (the "Applicant") and proposed directors of a finance company seeking a licence under the Finance Companies Control Law and its Implementing Regulation.

The Large Exposure (LEX) Rules for Banks are SAMA's prudential framework capping and monitoring concentration risk, setting definitions (exposure, large exposure, eligible capital base, control relationship), exposure measurement, eligible credit risk mitigation, exemptions, board-level governance duties and quarterly regulatory reporting. Limits are calculated on the Tier 1 eligible capital base per the latest published quarterly financial statements, with exposures reported gross and net of CRM. It binds all banks licensed in KSA, with the board ultimately responsible for oversight and policy approval.

This node sets the binding concentration caps under the LEX Rules: exposures to a single non-bank counterparty (excluding individuals, sole proprietorships and commercial undertakings majority owned by the Saudi Government) are capped at 15% of eligible capital, with a 25% limit applied to non-banking financial-sector subsidiaries, and it lists the exemptions. Exempted items include direct exposures to the Saudi Government, SAMA, Entities Connected with the Saudi Government, GCC central governments and central banks, government-guaranteed portions, intra-day interbank exposures, consolidated intra-group entities and central counterparties. All non-exempt exposures are fully subject to the limits; banks must still control and monitor exempted exposures.
lookup_terms: Entities Connected with the Saudi Government

data.summary: Defines when two or more natural or legal persons must be aggregated as a single risk for large exposure purposes, based on a control relationship, economic interdependence, or other connections identified in the bank's own assessment. It includes indicative interdependence criteria (contagion of financial difficulty, correlated default, common dominant funding source), a 5% of eligible capital investigation trigger, and a route for banks to rebut connectedness to SAMA's satisfaction. It also distinguishes Entities Connected with the Saudi Government from commercial undertakings 50%-or-more government owned, which remain subject to the limits.
lookup_terms: commercial undertakings majority owned by Saudi Government

data.summary: Sets which credit risk mitigation techniques may reduce exposure values under the LEX Rules: only unfunded credit protection and financial collateral eligible under the standardised approach for risk-based capital, expressly excluding equities, convertible bonds, UCITS and IRB-only collateral. Recognition is mandatory where the same technique was used for risk-based capital purposes, and it covers maturity-mismatch treatment and on-balance sheet netting of loans and deposits. Applies to banks measuring and reporting exposures net of eligible CRM, and interacts with the substitution rule that shifts exposure to the protection provider.

This node anchors the LEX Rules' key definitions to the Basel risk-based capital framework: exposure covers on- and off-balance sheet items in the banking and trading books plus counterparty credit risk instruments; a large exposure is 10% or more of eligible capital to one counterparty or connected group; and eligible capital base is effective Tier 1 capital under Basel III. It also defines SAMA, subsidiary (>50% shareholding) and control relationship, including voting agreements and influence over appointment or dismissal of governing bodies. These definitions bind banks when scoping, measuring and reporting exposures.

This node covers the regulatory reporting obligations under SAMA's Large Exposure (LEX) Rules for Banks (Section 7), including reporting of exposures to groups of connected counterparties and, for foreign bank branches otherwise outside the substantive limits, the requirement to report their 50 largest exposures and document large exposure/risk concentration policies. It sits alongside the scope provisions setting application to locally incorporated banks (including their foreign branches and subsidiaries) and foreign banks operating in the Kingdom, on both consolidated and standalone bases. It binds licensed banks supervised by SAMA; foreign branches under home-country consolidated supervision remain subject to the reporting element even where the limits do not apply.

A definitional node in the LEX Rules appendices explaining Systemically Important Financial Institutions per the FSB (institutions whose distress would materially disrupt the financial system) and the Basel Committee methodologies for identifying G-SIBs and D-SIBs, as adopted through named SAMA circulars. It also touches the definition of regulated and unregulated financial entities used when applying exposure treatments. It is relevant to banks determining whether tighter interbank exposure limits apply.

Defines Globally Systemically Important Banks under the Basel/FSB methodology (cross-jurisdictional activity, interconnectedness, size, substitutability, complexity), adopted by SAMA circular, with the G-SIB list reviewed annually by the FSB. Its operative consequence in the LEX Rules is that where the lending bank and/or counterparty bank is a G-SIB (or D-SIB), the bank-to-bank exposure limit tightens from 25% to 15% of the lending bank's eligible capital base. Binds banks licensed and operating in the Kingdom when calculating interbank large exposure limits.

Defines Domestic Systemically Important Banks — banks whose failure would seriously harm the domestic financial system or real economy — by reference to the BCBS D-SIB framework adopted through identified SAMA circulars. In the LEX Rules this status reduces the permissible interbank exposure limit to 15% of the lending bank's eligible capital where either the lending or counterparty bank is a D-SIB (or G-SIB). Applies to banks subject to SAMA's large exposure regime.

Sets out how exposure value is measured for large exposure purposes across instrument types: banking book on-balance sheet non-derivative assets at accounting value, OTC derivatives and other counterparty credit risk instruments via SA-CCR, securities financing transactions, trading book positions (including options and credit derivatives with sold protection), and exposures to central counterparties with a table of clearing-related exposure values (segregated initial margin at zero, non-segregated at nominal, default fund contributions, equity stakes). It notes that large exposure measurement can differ from risk-based capital measurement. Binds banks computing exposures against LEX limits.

Identifies the Standardised Approach for Counterparty Credit Risk (SA-CCR), adopted by SAMA circulars implementing the March 2014 Basel document, as the required method for determining exposure at default for derivatives and other counterparty-credit-risk instruments in the large exposure calculation. The surrounding text also sets eligible credit risk mitigation techniques for LEX purposes, expressly excluding equities, convertible bonds and UCITS, and limits recognition of IRB-only collateral. Binds banks measuring and mitigating exposures under the LEX Rules.
lookup_terms: Standardised Approach for Counterparty Credit Risk

data.summary: Appendix VII of SAMA's Large Exposure (LEX) Rules for Banks, setting out how banks must measure exposure values for trading book positions and aggregate them with banking book exposures to the same counterparty. It confirms that single-counterparty default risk in instruments such as bonds, equities, derivatives and options is captured by the large exposure limit, while commodity and currency concentrations are not, and specifies valuation conventions for swaps, futures, forwards, credit derivatives, credit-linked notes and options. It binds all banks licensed and supervised by SAMA.

Appendix VIII of SAMA's Large Exposure Rules defines covered bonds and sets the eligibility conditions for assigning a reduced exposure value (as low as 20% of nominal) rather than the default 100%, with the issuing bank treated as the counterparty. Conditions cover the composition of the cover pool, 10% over-collateralisation, LTV caps for residential and commercial real estate, and the operational requirements for eligible CRE/RRE collateral referenced to the Basel II standardised approach and SAMA's local guidance. It binds banks holding covered bonds when measuring large exposures.

Appendix IX of SAMA's Large Exposure Rules governs how banks assign exposures when investing through funds, securitisation vehicles and other structures with underlying assets. It sets the 0.25% of eligible capital base threshold that determines whether a bank may treat the structure itself as a distinct counterparty or must look through to underlying assets, addresses pari passu and tranched structures, and requires identification of third-party risk factors (manager, originator, liquidity provider, protection seller) that can create a group of connected counterparties. It binds banks measuring large exposures.

Appendix X of SAMA's Large Exposure Rules addresses bank exposures to central counterparties, exempting clearing-related exposures to qualifying CCPs (QCCPs) from the large exposure limits while retaining regulatory reporting, and requiring non-QCCP clearing and other exposures to be aggregated and held within the 25% eligible capital base limit. It adopts the risk-based capital definition of QCCP and disapplies the connected-counterparties concept to clearing-related CCP exposures. It binds banks that clear through CCPs.
lookup_terms: CPSS-IOSCO Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures

data.summary: The core body of SAMA's Large Exposure (LEX) Rules for Banks, localising the BCBS supervisory framework for measuring and controlling large exposures. It sets maximum exposure limits (including 15% of eligible capital to a single non-bank counterparty and 25% generally), exemptions and carve-outs for intra-day interbank and consolidated intra-group exposures, board-level governance, policy, stress-testing and monitoring duties, and quarterly regulatory reporting before and after credit risk mitigation. It binds all banks licensed by SAMA and their boards.

SAMA guidance explaining how founders apply for a licence to conduct debt-based crowdfunding activity under the Finance Companies Control Law and the Rules for Engaging in Debt-Based Crowdfunding. It specifies submission channels, the unmodifiable application form, the checklist of required documents (articles of association, organisational structure, fit and proper forms for founders and board/committee candidates, feasibility study and business plan, a bank guarantee for 20% of minimum capital, third-party and related-party contracts) and the consequences of false or omitted information under Article 7 of the Law. It binds applicants (founders/shareholders) seeking a DBC licence.
lookup_terms: Rules for Engaging in Debt-Based Crowdfunding

data.summary: A Governor-level SAMA circular announcing the launch of the SARIE instant payments system (effective 21 February 2021) and setting binding conditions on participating banks. It requires signing the system joining agreement, adherence to the latest technical/operational documents and SLAs, compliance with transaction caps (Single Transaction Limit and Quick Transfer Limit), a customer fee ceiling of SAR 0.50 for transfers up to SAR 500 and SAR 1 above that, adherence to the SARIE brand and customer journey guidelines, staff training, and rebranding of channels and public materials. It binds all banks operating in the Kingdom as system participants.

SAMA's Regulation on Branch Network sets the licensing and supervisory framework for opening, closing and relocating bank branches, service centers and remittance centers, including the use of inactive licenses, proposal content for new licenses, and prior-approval carve-outs by zone. It replaces the Annual Branch Expansion Plan requirement once a bank's Branch Network Policy is approved, and pursues financial inclusion, geographic diversification and consumer protection objectives. It binds all locally incorporated banks and licensed foreign bank branches (the latter only where expanding beyond three branches).

The Branch Network Policy is the mandatory bank-level document, required by SAMA's Regulation on Branch Network, governing criteria for opening, closing and relocating branches, service centers and remittance centers. It must address customer-service strategy (including elderly and disabled customers), target market, delivery channels, digital adoption, agent banking/bancassurance plans, and priority-area/CSR outreach; ATMs are excluded. It must be approved by the Board (or delegated committee), or by the Chief Executive/authorised senior executive for foreign bank branches, and submitted to SAMA within four months of the Regulation's issuance with specified historical data.

Financial inclusion appears here as a stated regulatory objective of SAMA's Regulation on Branch Network and as a mandatory content element of each bank's Branch Network Policy. Banks must set out their approach to promoting inclusion and extending outreach of financial services, including plans for priority areas as part of CSR and plans to promote digital delivery modes. It is an expectation on all in-scope banks rather than a standalone rulebook.

SAMA's Rules for Engaging in Debt-Based Crowdfunding sit under the Finance Companies Control Law and govern the licensing and conduct of debt-based crowdfunding activity — raising funds from Participants via a platform to lend to an Institutional Beneficiary under a loan contract. They define key terms (Participant, Eligible Participant thresholds, Institutional Beneficiary, Platform) and impose obligations on client-money segregation, electronic-only repayment, automatic participation consent, and platform disclosure and risk acknowledgment. They bind licensed Debt-Based Crowdfunding Companies operating in the Kingdom.

A Debt-Based Crowdfunding Company is a joint-stock company licensed by SAMA to operate a debt-based crowdfunding platform matching Participants' funds with financing for Institutional Beneficiaries. Its obligations include keeping Participants' funds in a segregated, dedicated Finance Amount Management Account used only for collecting and managing the Finance Amount, restricting repayment to electronic channels, obtaining prior consent for automatic participation with a right to cancel, and making platform disclosures including a pop-up risk acknowledgment from Participants.

This node covers SAMA's Fit and Proper Form as used within the licensing pack for debt-based crowdfunding activity under the Finance Companies Control Law and the Rules for Engaging in Debt-Based Crowdfunding. A completed and signed form is required for each founding member and each candidate board and sub-committee member, endorsed by the person authorised to submit the application, alongside the licence application letter, corporate documents, organisational structure, feasibility study/business plan, a bank guarantee equal to 20% of minimum capital, and draft third-party and related-party agreements. It binds Applicants (founders/shareholders) seeking SAMA approval to incorporate and license a debt-based crowdfunding company; false or omitted material information is treated as a breach of the Finance Companies Control Law and can lead to rejection or licence cancellation.

SAMA's Rules on Outsourcing (Version 2.0, December 2019) set the governance, policy, risk-assessment, contractual, monitoring, audit and documentation requirements for outsourcing arrangements. The Board retains ultimate responsibility for the outsourcing policy and all arrangements, must approve the policy covering Material business activities, and banks must notify SAMA of legal/regulatory breaches and file an annual outsourcing return within 30 business days of year-end. The rules bind banks licensed under the Banking Control Law, including local and foreign bank branches and banking subsidiaries in Saudi Arabia, and cover domestic, foreign and related-party service providers; insourcing under bank supervision and certain arrangements (market data vendors, clearing/settlement, correspondent banking, utilities) fall outside scope.

This node concerns the concept of Material outsourcing under SAMA's Rules on Outsourcing and the heightened obligations it triggers. Material arrangements require Board-approved policy coverage, a documented business case and risk-profile impact analysis, separate contingency planning, regular internal audit reporting to the Board or Board Audit Committee, immediate SAMA notification on termination with transition arrangements, and enhanced register entries (risk assessment date, approving body, commencement/expiry and notice periods, audit dates). SAMA may also require an external expert assessment of risk management around a Material outsourcing. It binds banks subject to the Rules.

Defines the Third-Party Service Provider as an entity undertaking an outsourced activity on behalf of a bank, expressly excluding head offices and related entities of foreign bank branches operating in KSA, and situates it against the definitions of Outsourcing and Overseas entities. It sets materiality factors (substitutability, ability to meet regulatory requirements, customer loss exposure, affiliation, sharing of personal/financial/credit or unpublished data, subcontracting complexity), SAMA and auditor access rights to records and data at provider premises, and register content on the provider. Outsourcing to a provider located overseas requires prior written SAMA no objection with specified information, given confidentiality and data-access risks under the Banking Control Law.

Sets the outsourcing regime specific to foreign bank branches in Saudi Arabia, covering both Material and non-Material arrangements. Branches must book KSA business locally unless SAMA agrees otherwise, maintain sufficient local staffing and control, and may not outsource key management responsibilities such as business decision-making, compliance and AML/CFT; other functions (e.g. internal audit, risk management) may be outsourced proportionately. Outsourcing to head office or a group member does not reduce the branch's or its management's legal obligations in KSA, must be audited annually by group internal audit or an independent third party with findings shared with SAMA, and any other regulator's report on the controls must be submitted to SAMA immediately.

Addresses business continuity expectations within SAMA's outsourcing framework: banks must ensure outsourcing does not compromise continuity and must hold a separate contingency plan for each Material outsourcing covering sudden termination or provider failure. Business continuity plans must document alternative third-party service providers or the process and timeline for selecting them, and set out procedures for bringing a Material outsourced function back in-house. It binds banks subject to the Rules on Outsourcing, and links to SAMA's and auditors' unrestricted access rights and to ongoing relationship monitoring proportionate to materiality.

Defines the Debt-Based Crowdfunding Platform as the web-based or other digital channel (websites, mobile apps) operated by a licensed Debt-Based Crowdfunding Company to conduct debt-based crowdfunding, sitting within the definitional chapter of SAMA's Rules for Engaging in Debt-Based Crowdfunding and linking to related terms (Debt-Based Crowdfunding Company, Institutional Beneficiary, Participant, Eligible Participant). The node also carries platform-level operating duties: segregation of Participant funds in a named Finance Amount Management Account, electronic-only repayment, opt-in and cancellable auto-participation, and disclosure of the business model, risks and party relationships including a pop-up risk acknowledgment. It binds joint-stock companies licensed by SAMA for debt-based crowdfunding.
lookup_terms: Rules for Engaging in Debt-Based Crowdfunding

data.summary: Covers the Institutional Beneficiary — a commercial enterprise registered in Saudi Arabia seeking or holding financing via a crowdfunding platform — and the diligence, disclosure and contractual obligations owed in respect of it. It requires documented CDD policies under the AML Law and the Law of Combating Terrorism Crimes and its Financing (legal status, identity, address, conflicts, solvency, credit history, business plan), publication of beneficiary-level project and financial information to Participants, and mandatory service-agreement terms including credit-record consent and material-change notification. Binds the licensed Debt-Based Crowdfunding Company; the Institutional Beneficiary bears the contractual undertakings.

Covers the Participant (natural or legal person funding an Institutional Beneficiary through the platform) and the protections attached to that status: a complaints-handling function with SAMA-specified response times, staff confidentiality of Participant data and transactions surviving termination of employment or licence, and exposure caps limiting a Participant to 25% of a requested Finance Amount and SAR 250,000 of aggregate outstanding financing (Eligible Participants excluded). Binds the licensed Debt-Based Crowdfunding Company and its employees.

Sets the risk governance requirement for Debt-Based Crowdfunding Companies: a board-approved, annually updated risk management policy covering an enumerated risk taxonomy (credit, market, operational, legal, reputational, technology, fraud, information security, cyber, ML/TF, outsourcing, platform cessation and Participant-protection/default risk) supported by an identification, assessment, monitoring and escalation framework. Adjacent provisions require an external auditor with SAMA non-objection, business continuity plans, ten-year record retention, staffing adequacy, wind-down planning, and compliance with SAMA information security and AML/CTF and financial-crime requirements proportionate to activity and risk. Binds the licensed company's board and senior management.
lookup_terms: money laundering and terrorist financing risk

data.summary: Covers the quantitative credit limits and the pre-financing credit checks in the debt-based crowdfunding rules: aggregate outstanding finance through the platform capped at 40 times the company's capital and reserves, financing restricted to Saudi-registered commercial enterprises with consumer-purpose financing prohibited, a SAR 7,500,000 cap per MSME Institutional Beneficiary (carve-outs for large enterprises and licensed real estate developers), and per-Participant concentration limits — each subject to SAMA written non-objection where relief is sought. It also ties in mandatory credit-record checking and credit bureau registration on beneficiary consent, with refusal of the finance request absent consent, plus KYC, information security and Electronic Transactions Law verification duties. Binds the licensed Debt-Based Crowdfunding Company.

SAMA's margin framework for non-centrally cleared derivatives, setting out instrument scope (all such derivatives except physically settled FX forwards and swaps, with a specific carve-out for the principal exchange leg of cross-currency swaps from initial margin) and entity scope. Covered entities are financial firms and systemically important non-financial entities — those whose group-wide month-end average notional of non-centrally cleared derivatives for March–May exceeds SAR 30 billion, excluding inter-affiliate trades — and they must bilaterally calculate and exchange initial and variation margin; central banks, sovereigns, MDBs, the BIS and non-systemic non-financial firms are outside scope. Only trades between two covered entities are captured.
lookup_terms: physically settled FX forwards and swaps
