data.summary: SAMA's general guidance package accompanying the amended Liquidity Coverage Ratio prudential return, explaining how Saudi banks are to complete and submit it and how SAMA has aligned its paragraph numbering with the BCBS January 2013 LCR standard. It sets reporting frequency and timing (monthly returns due 30 days after month end, with transitional relief for the first submission) and confirms continued parallel monitoring of NSFR under the earlier 2012 circular. It binds Saudi banks, with foreign bank branches carved out of the monthly return obligation.

The Liquidity Coverage Ratio as adopted by SAMA: the requirement that banks hold a stock of unencumbered high quality liquid assets sufficient to cover net cash outflows over a 30-calendar-day stress scenario, with a phase-in from 60% in 2015 to 100% in 2019. The node covers eligibility conditions for qualifying securities (ratings thresholds, issuer restrictions), caps and haircuts, and jurisdictional alternative liquidity approaches. It applies to Saudi banks subject to SAMA prudential supervision.

Defines High Quality Liquid Assets for LCR purposes through fundamental characteristics (low risk, ease of valuation, low correlation with risky assets, listing on a developed exchange) and market-related characteristics (active and sizeable market, low volatility, flight to quality). It sets the qualitative test that an asset's liquidity-generating capacity by sale or repo must survive severe idiosyncratic and market stress, and records SAMA's reading that qualifying instruments should at minimum be repo-able with central banks. Relevant to Saudi banks classifying assets in the LCR numerator.

Covers the Level 1 tier of the HQLA stock — assets includable without limit and generally without haircut, held as of the first day of the stress period regardless of residual maturity. It sits alongside the 40% cap on Level 2 and the 15% sub-cap on Level 2B, and connects to the alternative liquidity approach options available where a jurisdiction has insufficient Level 1 assets in domestic currency. Applies to Saudi banks computing the LCR numerator.

Covers the Level 2 tier of HQLA: Level 2A assets subject to a 15% haircut and capped, together with Level 1, at 40% of the stock, and the optional Level 2B category (including qualifying common equity shares at a 50% haircut) capped at 15% and counted within the 40% limit. It notes that caps apply after haircuts and after unwinding short-term securities financing and collateral swaps maturing within 30 days, and records that SAMA does not currently permit Level 2B assets in LCR computation. Binds Saudi banks calculating HQLA.

Reference node for the Basel Committee's January 2013 standard on the Liquidity Coverage Ratio and liquidity risk monitoring tools, endorsed by the GHOS, which SAMA adopts as the substantive basis for its amended LCR framework. SAMA's guidance and prudential return cross-reference the BCBS paragraph numbering, so the international text supplies the detailed rules where SAMA's circular does not restate them. It is not itself a SAMA instrument but is incorporated by reference for Saudi banks.

Concept node covering the initial margin obligation under SAMA's margin framework for non-centrally cleared derivatives: how the required amount is computed (approved quantitative portfolio margin model versus the standardised margin schedule, including the net standardised initial margin formula using NGR), when it must be collected (at trade outset and on an ongoing basis as potential future exposure changes), and the bar on switching between model and schedule bases to cherry-pick outcomes. It also carries the restriction that collected initial margin generally may not be re-hypothecated, re-pledged or re-used except on the narrow SAMA-approved basis. It binds covered entities — banks and other financial firms and systemically important non-financial entities — transacting with another covered entity.

Concept node for the margin calculation and model-governance side of SAMA's non-centrally cleared derivatives framework, sitting alongside the variation margin exchange obligation. The supplied material addresses calibration of initial margin models to a 99% confidence interval over a 10-day horizon using a stressed historical period not exceeding five years, the default expectation that banks use the standardised schedule, and the internal governance, validation, testing and SAMA approval required before any model may be used. It binds covered entities engaging in non-centrally cleared derivatives, and constrains their model risk governance.

Concept node on collateral eligibility, valuation and substitution for margin purposes under the SAMA non-centrally cleared derivatives margin rules, plus the treatment of provided initial margin. It covers dispute resolution over collateral value, the conditions for substituting alternative collateral (mutual agreement, continued eligibility, sufficiency after haircuts), and the requirement that initial margin be exchanged gross and held so it is immediately available on counterparty default while protecting the poster in the collecting party's insolvency. Binds covered entities exchanging margin bilaterally.

Concept node setting the prohibition on re-hypothecation, re-pledge or re-use of cash and non-cash collateral collected as initial margin, and the narrow exception permitting it. Re-use is allowed only to hedge the initial margin collector's derivatives position arising from customer transactions, only with SAMA's case-by-case approval, and only where the customer gives express written consent after disclosure of its right to refuse and of insolvency risks, is offered individual segregation, the collector is subject to liquidity risk regulation, and the collateral is treated and segregated as a customer asset by both collector and third party. Binds initial margin collectors (covered entities) vis-à-vis their customers.

Reference node for the BCBS-IOSCO margin requirements for non-centrally cleared derivatives, which SAMA's framework adopts and localises, including the phase-in timetable. It informs the instrument scope element: margin applies to all non-centrally cleared derivatives except physically settled FX forwards and swaps, with a carve-out for the fixed physically settled FX legs of cross-currency swap principal exchanges from initial margin (variation margin still applies to all components). Relevant to banks and other covered entities determining product scope and implementation dates.
lookup_terms: physically settled FX forwards and swaps exemption

data.summary: Concept node defining the entity scope of the SAMA margin framework: covered entities — all financial firms plus systemically important non-financial entities, the latter identified by group-wide aggregate month-end average notional of non-centrally cleared derivatives for March–May exceeding SAR 30 billion (inter-affiliate trades excluded). Central banks, sovereigns, multilateral development banks, the BIS and non-systemic non-financial firms are outside scope, and the requirements bite only where both counterparties are covered entities. It also sets the phased application from 1 September 2016 and the later thresholds (€50 billion, then €8 billion) for two-way initial margin subject to a €50 million threshold.

Node within SAMA's liquidity framework circular adopting the Basel III LCR text; despite the NSFR label, the captured material addresses unsecured wholesale funding run-off treatment, in particular funding from small business customers (treated like retail deposits where aggregated funding from one customer, on a consolidated/affiliated-group basis, is below the €1 million threshold) and the graduated run-off factors for non-financial corporates, sovereigns, central banks, MDBs, PSEs (20%/40%) and other legal entity customers (100%). It binds SAMA-licensed banks calculating liquidity ratios and defines counterparty categorisation for the outflow denominator.

Sets out the Basel III alternative liquidity approaches (ALA) available to jurisdictions with an insufficient domestic-currency supply of HQLA, including the qualifying criteria (structural insufficiency, mitigation capacity, commitment to supervisory monitoring, disclosure, self-assessment and peer review) and the supervisory obligations attaching to their use. Critically, SAMA records that it has not adopted any alternative treatment option, so the section is contextual rather than operative for KSA banks.

Explains the Basel discretion allowing national supervisors to recognise Shari'ah-compliant instruments (e.g. Sukuk) as alternative HQLA for Shari'ah-compliant banks, subject to conditions or haircuts, while preserving an equivalent minimum LCR standard. SAMA states it has not exercised any alternative treatment option, so no separate Shari'ah HQLA carve-out applies in KSA.

Defines the LCR denominator: total expected cash outflows less total expected cash inflows over the 30-calendar-day stress horizon (including expected interest), together with the no-double-counting rule and related outflow treatments such as secured funding roll-off by collateral quality and 100% treatment of net derivative cash outflows. Binds SAMA-supervised banks computing the LCR.

Covers the LCR treatment of retail deposits — deposits placed by natural persons, split into stable and less stable buckets with minimum floor run-off rates — including foreign-currency deposit treatment and exclusion of term deposits with over 30 days' residual maturity where the depositor has no legal withdrawal right. Two KSA-specific carve-outs are recorded: Saudi Arabia has no effective deposit insurance scheme (so deposit-insurance-based run-off rates do not apply), and run-off rates apply equally across currencies given the USD/SAR peg.

Defines unsecured wholesale funding for LCR purposes as uncollateralised liabilities raised from non-natural persons (including sole proprietorships and partnerships) callable or maturing within 30 days, excluding derivative obligations, and sets the counterparty-based run-off factors (small business, operational deposits, non-financial corporates/sovereigns/central banks/MDBs/PSEs at 20% or 40%, other legal entities at 100%). It also records SAMA's discretion to impose a higher-than-0% run-off on qualifying retail term deposits where withdrawal or reputational-repayment concerns arise.

A segment of SAMA's amended Liquidity Coverage Ratio guidance dealing with the classification of retail deposits as "stable" versus "less stable" and the resulting run-off assumptions for the 30-day LCR outflow calculation. It records Saudi-specific national discretion: KSA has no deposit insurance scheme (so the reduced stable-deposit treatment is unavailable), run-off rates follow BCBS for all currencies, and foreign-currency (mainly USD, pegged) deposits are not treated as inherently less stable. It binds banks licensed and supervised by SAMA when completing the LCR prudential return.

Part of SAMA's LCR guidance covering wholesale funding outflow assumptions, defining unsecured wholesale funding (obligations to non-natural persons not collateralised by designated assets, excluding derivatives) and the funding callable or maturing within the 30-day horizon. It sets the run-off factors by counterparty type — 20%/40% for non-financial corporates, sovereigns, central banks, MDBs and PSEs, and 100% for other legal entities including banks, securities firms, insurers and fiduciaries — plus SAMA's discretion to impose above-0% run-off on qualifying retail term deposits. Applies to SAMA-licensed banks calculating and reporting the LCR.
lookup_terms: operational deposits clearing custody cash management

data.summary: The framing and structure of SAMA's circular adopting the BCBS January 2013 Basel III LCR standard, including general and specific guidance notes, the prudential return, FAQs and national discretions, with paragraph numbering mapped to the BCBS text. It covers the objective of the LCR, the phase-in of the minimum ratio from 60% (2015) to 100% (2019), permitted use of the HQLA buffer under stress subject to SAMA assessment, and the Level 1 / Level 2 / Level 2B asset composition and caps (40% and 15%). Binds Saudi banks for LCR calculation and reporting; NSFR remains under the earlier 2012 circular.

SAMA's second-edition Controls for Establishing a Customer Care Department in Banks (issued 1444H/2023, replacing the earlier complaint-unit controls), setting the minimum requirements banks must meet for customer care, complaint handling and financial education. It requires the department to be created by board decision, report directly to the most senior executive, be independent of other departments, be adequately resourced, and comprise at least three units (complaint handling, quality and performance analysis, awareness and financial education); the department head's appointment needs SAMA's prior written no-objection. Binds all banks licensed by SAMA to operate in the Kingdom.

The Complaint Handling Unit is one of the three mandatory units of a bank's Customer Care Department under SAMA's 2023 controls, responsible for receiving and resolving customer complaints efficiently and within regulatory time limits. It must offer multiple accessible complaint channels — at minimum a toll-free number, website, mobile applications, email and branches — prominently published on the bank's homepage and platforms, and operate under service-level agreements and an escalation mechanism reaching the most senior executive. Binds SAMA-licensed banks; the department head (or delegate) holds decision authority for complaint settlements up to a defined riyal threshold.

The Quality and Performance Analysis Unit sits within the bank's Customer Care Department under SAMA's 2023 controls and supports the department's mandate to analyse complaint patterns and root causes, reduce recurrence and measure the effectiveness of remedial policies. The surrounding provisions require board-approved policies on root cause analysis, on protecting customer rights across the full customer journey (marketing and sales, after-sales quality, complaint handling, customer communication, credit advisor services) and on financial awareness, plus periodic capacity analysis and staff qualification requirements (retail banking and credit advisor professional certificates, annual training). Binds banks licensed by SAMA in the Kingdom.

This node sits within SAMA's customer care instructions for banks and concerns the bank-side financial awareness and education function. The instrument's introduction grounds SAMA's authority under the SAMA Law and the Banking Control Law to regulate customer rights and care, and adopts internationally recognised financial consumer protection principles on complaint handling, financial literacy and clear disclosure of customer rights, responsibilities and product risks. It sets a minimum standard binding on all banks licensed and operating in the Kingdom.

A SAMA circular (transmitted via the Finance Companies Supervision Department) reaffirming that supervised financial institutions must comply with circulars issued by SAMA. It announces the SAMA Circulars Portal as a transparency tool and expressly states that publication on the portal does not relieve any institution of its obligation to comply with instructions delivered through official written correspondence or official SAMA departmental email. Addressed to finance companies operating in the Kingdom, effective from the date of email transmission.

A SAMA circular reinforcing compliance with personal data protection requirements for customer data, referencing the Personal Data Protection Law and SAMA's data governance policies, rules and controls. It responds to observed practices where individual customers were required to disclose personal data not necessary for the product or service, directly or via a third party, and requires institutions to align with SDAIA and NDMO rules, review disclosure practices, secure data, use it only for the purpose collected, and report remedial actions to SAMA by a set deadline. Binds all financial institutions supervised by SAMA.

A SAMA circular notifying supervised entities of periodic improvements and amendments to IFRS and IAS endorsed by SOCPA, listing affected standards including IFRS 1, IFRS 9 (fees in derecognition/modification of debt), IFRS 3, IAS 41, IAS 37 (cost of fulfilling a contract in onerous contracts) and IAS 16 (proceeds before intended use). It directs readers to SOCPA's international standards page for the texts and requires compliance from the date of email transmission. Addressed to finance companies operating in the Kingdom.

A SAMA circular mandating biometric authentication when a customer relationship is established remotely, supplementing existing requirements to identify and verify an individual customer's identity using documents or data from a reliable and independent source. Institutions must adopt the biometric verification feature of the Nafath application at a high assurance level or above and complete integration with the approved service provider by the stated deadline, notifying SAMA of challenges beforehand. It binds banks (local, foreign branches, digital banks), finance companies and payment companies operating in the Kingdom.

A SAMA circular addressed to money exchange centers prohibiting employees from holding two jobs at the same time with more than one exchange center, and reaffirming job localization requirements. It relies on the SAMA Law and the Rules Governing Money Exchange Business, together with SAMA's requirements for appointment to leading positions and its professional conduct and work ethics principles. Exchange centers must verify and remediate dual employment within six months and notify SAMA, and must restrict all activity positions to Saudi nationals without seeking non-Saudi work permits elsewhere.
lookup_terms: professional conduct and work ethics principles

data.summary: A conceptual model within SAMA's Financial Sector red teaming framework describing an advanced cyber-attack as seven end-to-end stages (reconnaissance through actions on objective), used to structure attack scenarios and to position preventive, detective, responsive and corrective controls. It also frames the distinction between conventional penetration testing and red teaming (realistic access paths, TTPs, focus on detection and response). It binds Member Organizations and their Red Teaming Providers, who must explain the kill chains executed and depict them as attack vector diagrams in the evaluation report.

Covers the scenario phase of the SAMA red teaming framework, where the Green Team (sector-wide) and White Team (internal) independently supply threat intelligence, which the Red Teaming Provider combines with its own external and engagement-derived intelligence to build attack scenarios and TTPs. High-level scenarios, the test strategy and the detailed scenarios each require agreement with the Green Team before execution, and the phase is capped at about five weeks. It binds Member Organizations, their appointed teams and the Red Teaming Provider.

Defines the external party engaged to design and execute red teaming tests for a Member Organization, together with the selection, approval and procurement expectations set out in the framework and its Appendix A (experience, references, staff certification, defined methodology, governance, quality assurance and risk management). Procurement follows Green Team approval and covers NDA clauses, liability for test consequences and a Letter of Authorization. It binds the Member Organization as the procuring entity and shapes contractual duties on the provider.

The deliverable the Red Teaming Provider must produce at the end of the exercise, assessing the Member Organization's resilience against the executed attacks and covering scope, control framework references, execution methodology, kill chains and TTPs, timeline, tools, risk rating, recommendations and conclusions. It is issued to the White, Blue and Green Teams via secure channels under a need-to-know protocol and is classified Confidential. It feeds directly into the Blue Team Report discussion and the Remediation Plan.

The report prepared by the Blue Team during the lessons learned phase, setting out the exercise from the defender's perspective: alerts and events detected, actions initiated, their results, and recommendations for improvement. It is produced alongside the finalised Red Team report, supports the joint replay exercise and 360-degree feedback, and is a required input to the Remediation Plan. It binds the Member Organization's detection and response function.

The plan the White Team must draft after the exercise, built on the Red Team Evaluation Report and the Blue Team Report, identifying agreed areas of improvement, priorities and a roadmap for strengthening prevention, detection, response and recovery. Progress must be monitored and reported periodically to the Member Organization's Cyber Security Committee and to the Green Team. It binds the Member Organization as the remediating party.

SAMA circular (Arabic, dated 1444) reaffirming the standing obligation for staff of supervised institutions to hold prescribed professional certifications, supplementing earlier circulars on mandatory certification and on the updated target population for the credit advisor certificate. It identifies three certification tracks and the roles caught by each: retail banking fundamentals for customer-facing bank staff (customer care, call centre, branch staff and managers), the credit advisor certificate for staff directly involved in granting credit to individuals and branch managers, and the exchange/remittance certificate for front-line staff of bank-affiliated remittance centres and exchange houses; outsourced/third-party personnel are expressly included. It binds banks, their remittance centres, finance companies and exchange centres operating in the Kingdom, sets a one-year period from job commencement to obtain the certificate and a minimum compliance ratio, and carves out finance lease contract registration companies, the Saudi Real Estate Refinance Company and support-activity companies from the credit advisor requirement.

SAMA's Minimum Verification Controls (v1.0) sets a baseline set of cyber and customer-verification controls covering registration/onboarding, general operating controls and additional lending-specific controls. It applies to any member organization under SAMA supervision providing e-wallet services, lending products, crowdfunding or other fintech business models, subject to applicability against the stated objectives. Key themes include identity and phone-ownership verification through a licensed trusted party, OTP and multi-factor authentication, device binding, fraud handling, SMS notification, terms and conditions/data privacy consent, and board-approved internal policies reflecting these controls.

Section 3 of the Minimum Verification Controls governs registration and onboarding of users by member organizations offering e-wallet, lending, crowdfunding or other fintech services. It requires one-to-one linkage of a phone number or National ID/Iqama to a single application, a secure user validation process, strong authentication from an independent licensed trusted party (National Single Sign-On for e-wallets; an equivalent trusted-party authentication for lending platforms and analogous robustness for other models), verification that the mobile number is registered to the same user through a trusted party, OTP verification sent to that verified number, session timeout, SMS notification of registration and account status changes, single-device binding or per-login OTP with no concurrent sessions, and secure deactivation/reactivation and device re-registration processes. These are identity-verification and authentication duties that sit alongside, not in place of, AML/CTF customer identification and verification obligations.

This node covers the one-time-password requirements in the Minimum Verification Controls. OTP is required as a registration verification factor sent to a trusted-party-verified phone number, and for defined operational events including first-time wallet-to-wallet transfers below a defined value, marketplace transactions, first-time bill/utility/government payments, password resets, wallet reactivations and company-assessed risky transactions; out-of-band OTP delivery (a different channel) is required for higher-exposure transactions such as wallet transfers above the defined daily value, first-time IBAN transfers, international transfers and high-risk transactions. The defined value is set and periodically revised by separate SAMA memo, so the threshold is not fixed in the document itself. Binds member organizations providing e-wallet, lending, crowdfunding or other fintech services under SAMA supervision.

Refers to the general control in the Minimum Verification Controls requiring multi-factor authentication for each login to the member organization's application, complementing the OTP requirements and single-device/concurrent-login restrictions. It applies to member organizations under SAMA supervision offering e-wallet, lending, crowdfunding or other fintech business models. Relevant when assessing customer authentication adequacy and liability allocation in unauthorised-transaction and fraud disputes.

Section 5 of the Minimum Verification Controls imposes additional obligations on lending companies over and above the onboarding and general controls: assurance that the recipient IBAN belongs to the loan requester, use of a trusted and authorized digital signature provider, and secure creation, storage and management of promissory notes through a national trusted party such as Nafith. It binds SAMA-supervised member organizations providing lending products via digital applications, and interacts with finance/BNPL contracting and enforceability of security instruments.

A superseded SAMA control set specifying minimum cyber-security and customer-onboarding requirements for member organizations offering e-wallets, lending products, crowdfunding or other fintech business models under SAMA supervision. It covers registration/onboarding validation (one phone number or National ID/Iqama per application, strong authentication via an independent trusted party such as national single sign-on), terms and conditions and data-privacy consent, awareness programmes, inactive-account policy, contingency and back-up arrangements, and multi-factor/one-time-password requirements for wallet transfers, marketplace and bill payments, password resets, reactivations and high-risk or above-threshold transactions (thresholds circulated separately by memo). Because it is superseded, use it only for historical or transitional analysis; it binds SAMA-supervised fintech providers rather than customers.

SAMA's Financial Entities Ethical Red Teaming (F.E.E.R.) Framework sets out an intelligence-led, threat-based cyber-attack simulation regime for SAMA-supervised member organizations, structured in four phases (preparation, threat intelligence/scenario, execution, lessons learned) with defined Green, White, Blue and Red Team roles. It governs appointment of a Test Manager by SAMA, scoping of critical information assets, procurement and qualification of a Red Teaming Provider (contractual terms, NDA, Letter of Authorization, staff certification), execution controls, reporting and remediation tracking. It binds member organizations undertaking red teaming exercises and, indirectly, their external testing providers.

Defined role within the F.E.E.R. Framework: the Green Team is provided by SAMA's IT Risk of Financial Sector Supervision department and acts as regulator-side overseer of each red teaming exercise. It appoints the Test Manager (and backup), approves the member organization's selection of the Red Teaming Provider, supplies sector-specific threat intelligence where applicable, and participates in scoping, feedback and lessons-learned sessions. It guides and supports the White Team but is not accountable for the member organization's testing decisions.
lookup_terms: SAMA IT Risk Financial Sector Supervision

data.summary: Defined role within the F.E.E.R. Framework: the White Team is the small group inside the member organization (maximum five people, including a White Team Leader and SPOCs such as the CISO) that is aware of the red teaming test and controls its execution. It contracts and coordinates the Red Teaming Provider, defines scope with the Green and Red Teams, monitors the exercise, and decides whether to stop, postpone, adjust or continue when the Blue Team detects Red Team activity or where business disruption risk arises. It also organises debriefing, replay exercises and remediation follow-up.

Defined role within the F.E.E.R. Framework: the Blue Team is the member organization's cyber-security monitoring function (e.g. SOC) that analyses alerts and events and follows agreed incident response procedures, without prior knowledge of the simulated attack. Its detection and response performance is the object being evaluated; after the test it produces a blue team report covering detected alerts, actions taken, outcomes and improvement recommendations, and participates in the joint replay exercise and lessons-learned phase.

Defined role within the F.E.E.R. Framework: the Red Team comprises the external Red Teaming Provider's staff who execute the agreed attack scenarios against the member organization's defined critical information assets. It operates under contract with the member organization (NDA, liability terms, Letter of Authorization), is introduced to the White and Green Teams, must meet the framework's experience, methodology and staff-certification requirements, and adjusts or halts scenarios at the White Team Leader's direction. It reports observations and findings chronologically and joins the replay and feedback sessions.

A concept node within SAMA's Financial Entities Ethical Red Teaming (F.E.E.R.) Framework covering penetration testing as a component of adversarial security testing, and the team structure (Green Team from SAMA's IT Risk supervision function, the Member Organization's White Team and Blue Team) that governs controlled execution of red teaming exercises. Penetration testing is defined as evaluators mimicking real-world attacks to circumvent security features of applications, systems or networks, distinct from the broader threat-intelligence-led red teaming exercise. It binds Member Organizations affiliated with SAMA and the red teaming providers they engage.

The Banks Remuneration Rules (January 2023) set SAMA's minimum requirements and supervisory expectations for bank remuneration policies, governance, risk alignment, deferral, adjustment and reporting, superseding the 2010 Rules on Compensation Practices. They target risks arising from reward practices — particularly misconduct risk — rather than setting absolute pay levels, though regulatory caps still apply. They bind all locally incorporated banks licensed and operating in Saudi Arabia, extending on a group basis to majority-owned financial-sector subsidiaries inside and (subject to host-country law) outside the Kingdom.

Concept node on the mandatory written Remuneration Policy under the Banks Remuneration Rules: a policy for Senior Management approved by the General Assembly and a separate policy for all other employees approved by the Board. It prescribes minimum content, including objectives, scope covering all employee categories and outsourced third-party arrangements, pay structure and mix, perquisites, an approval authority matrix, and the roles of control functions and HR. It binds locally incorporated banks and their boards, with the Nomination and Remuneration Committee and Board holding oversight duties.
lookup_terms: Nomination and Remuneration Committee terms of reference

data.summary: Concept node covering ex post risk adjustment of variable pay: malus (reducing unvested deferred remuneration before vesting) and clawback (recovering paid or vested amounts), together with deferral thresholds — at least three years' deferral and above 60 percent deferred for the most senior and most highly paid employees. Adjustments must be documented in bank policies and applied for subsequent risk outcomes, misconduct, material error, performance downturn or risk-management failure, with justifications for reductions submitted to SAMA. Binds locally incorporated banks, their Boards and remuneration committees.

Concept node on misconduct risk as a driver of remuneration design under the Banks Remuneration Rules: ex ante non-financial performance criteria (risk management quality, legal and regulatory compliance, fair treatment of customers) must be embedded in individual performance and pay, and ex post adjustment must weigh proximity to the misconduct, rank, motivation, negligence, prior history and supervisory failures. It also requires severity to be assessed against fines, losses, reputational and customer impact, and permits freezing awards to individuals under investigation. Binds banks, their Boards, control functions and HR.

Concept node on the reporting and supervisory review obligations under the Banks Remuneration Rules: banks must file a semiannual Compliance Report to SAMA assessing alignment with the rules, disclosing gaps and action plans, with prescribed annexes on total fixed/variable remuneration, adjustments and the top 12 highest-paid employees, plus the Nomination and Remuneration Committee's terms of reference. Deadlines are before 31 March (second half-year) and 31 August (first half-year), with annual independent review results due before 31 March. Non-compliance may trigger SAMA-directed rectification, increased capital or liquidity requirements, penalties or limits on total remuneration; remuneration risk also feeds ICAAP and ILAAP.

This node marks the 2010 Rules on Compensation Practices (circular 26194/BCS/12580, 3 May 2010) as expressly superseded by SAMA's updated Banks Remuneration Rules, which set minimum requirements and supervisory guidance for bank remuneration policies to address misconduct risk and support sound risk management. The successor rules bind all locally incorporated banks licensed in Saudi Arabia and extend to majority-owned financial-sector subsidiaries at home and abroad (subject to host-country law). They impose semiannual compliance reporting to SAMA (due before 31 March and 31 August), disclosure of fixed/variable remuneration and the top 12 highest-paid employees, annual remuneration review results before 31 March, and expose banks to rectification directives, added capital/liquidity requirements or penalties for material deficiencies.

SAMA's Profit Sharing Investment Accounts Rules (Sep 2022), issued under the SAMA Charter and Banking Control Law, set minimum requirements for banks offering PSIA products, covering definitions, operation, board and senior management responsibilities, prudential treatment, disclosure and periodic statements, and separation of restricted from unrestricted PSIA accounts. They aim at consumer protection, transparency, financial stability and Shari'ah compliance, and bind all local Saudi banks licensed under the Banking Control Law that conduct Shari'ah compliant banking. The Rules took effect on 13 March 2023 and are to be read with the wider SAMA regulatory framework.

Defines the Profit Sharing Investment Account: an account managed by a bank on Shari'ah compliant terms under a management agreement in which the IAH and bank share profits in a specified ratio and the IAH bears losses not caused by the bank's negligence, misconduct, fraud or breach of contract. It distinguishes unrestricted PSIA (bank invests at its discretion and may commingle funds) from restricted PSIA (investment limited by IAH-specified conditions), which must be accounted for separately. The definition drives disclosure duties to IAHs and prudential treatment for banks offering these accounts.

Defines Mudarabah as a partnership contract where the capital provider (Rabb-ul-Mal / IAH) supplies capital managed by a partner (the bank as Mudarib), with profits shared per the contracted ratio and losses borne by the capital provider unless caused by misconduct, negligence or breach. It sits alongside Musharakah and Wakalah definitions and underpins how banks may raise PSIA funding and how loss-bearing and credit risk are allocated to IAHs. Relevant to banks structuring Shari'ah compliant deposit-like funding under the PSIA Rules.

Covers the Profit Equalization Reserve (appropriated from mudarabah profits to smooth returns) and the Investment Risk Reserve (appropriated from IAH profit after the mudarib share to cushion future investment losses), both maintained at the bank's discretion. The Board must oversee whether reserve levels are appropriate and fair between existing and new IAHs, and senior management must set guidelines on PER/IRR management and on who the reserves revert to on write-off or recovery. Prudentially, PSIA funds and PER/IRR are excluded from regulatory capital, must be reflected in LCR/NSFR and Large Exposure treatment, and outsourced IAH fund management must meet SAMA outsourcing rules; SAMA may direct whether an arrangement is treated as a PSIA.

Defines the Shari'ah Committee as the body responsible for supervising compliance with Shari'ah principles and rules and their application within the bank, with 'Shari'ah Compliant' meaning compliance with that committee's decisions. Related definitions include Islamic Window (the branch or dedicated unit of a conventional bank conducting Shari'ah compliant business) and Investment Account Holders. These terms scope the PSIA Rules, which apply to local Saudi banks licensed under the Banking Control Law that conduct Shari'ah compliant banking.

A prudential-requirements section of SAMA's Profit Sharing Investment Accounts (PSIA) Rules, addressing how banks must treat PSIA funds for regulatory capital risk-weighting and in liquidity ratio calculations (LCR and NSFR). It also bars PSIA funds and the associated Profit Equalisation Reserve and Investment Risk Reserve from counting toward regulatory capital, requires concentration risk from PSIAs to be managed under the Large Exposure Rules, and subjects outsourced management of investment account holder funds to SAMA outsourcing rules; SAMA retains discretion to classify an arrangement as a PSIA. It binds banks offering profit-sharing investment accounts.

SAMA's Related Parties Rules for Banks (2022 update), issued under the Central Bank Law and Banking Control Law, defining related parties and control relationships and setting governance, exposure limits, security, and quarterly reporting requirements for related-party exposures and transactions. It caps exposures to non-bank related parties (5% of eligible capital, 10% for listed Saudi companies, 25% for financial-sector non-bank subsidiaries, 50% cumulative), lists exemptions, and requires immediate notification of breaches with a remediation plan. It binds banks and local banks operating in KSA and supersedes the earlier related parties rules.

Reference node for the Central Bank Law (Royal Decree M/36, 11/04/1442AH), cited here as one of the statutory bases on which SAMA issued the Related Parties Rules for Banks alongside the Banking Control Law. It is the enabling authority establishing SAMA's supervisory and rule-making powers rather than a substantive conduct rule. Relevant to anyone tracing the legal basis and enforceability of SAMA banking instruments.

Cross-reference to SAMA's Rules on Large Exposures of Banks, which supply the measurement methodology for exposures and the group-of-connected-counterparties limits applied when calculating related-party exposures. Under the Related Parties Rules, related-party exposures are measured per the Large Exposures Rules, and where a related party sits within a connected group, both the related-party cap and the overall group exposure limit apply. Binds banks; open the Large Exposures Rules themselves for the measurement and aggregation detail.

Reference to the Islamic Financial Services Board (IFSB) standards, identified in the SAMA covering circular as the international benchmark with which the updated Related Parties Rules for Banks were aligned. It is a standard-setting reference, not directly binding of itself; its effect flows through the SAMA rules that adopt it. Useful for interpreting the treatment of Shari'ah-based and Shari'ah-compliant exposures and Shariah Committee members as related parties.

An Arabic-language SAMA circular confirming that real estate finance contracts concluded with individual (retail) customers are subject to the finance laws, their implementing regulations and SAMA instructions, whether the real estate financier contracts in its own name, as agent, or on behalf of another party. Financiers must not enter new contracts unless this is satisfied and must correct arrangements with third parties accordingly, including cases where the credit-granting decision does not rest with the real estate financier. It binds banks and real estate finance companies operating in the Kingdom.

This node covers the Core Cyber Threat Intelligence principles within SAMA's Financial Sector Cyber Threat Intelligence Principles, which set the baseline planning, production, processing and dissemination activities that underpin the strategic, operational and technical/tactical CTI domains. It includes expectations on classifying threat information under the Traffic Light Protocol, delivering actionable intelligence with defined actions, owners and response timeframes, sharing intelligence internally (e.g. with the SOC and IT), and continuously improving intelligence methods. It applies to all Member Organizations supervised by SAMA, including those that outsource their CTI capability, with phased implementation left to the entity's discretion.

This node concerns the MITRE ATT&CK framework as referenced and defined in SAMA's Cyber Threat Intelligence Principles: an open-source taxonomy of tactics, techniques and procedures used by threat actors. It is cited in the Operational CTI domain, where Member Organizations are expected to structure attack-phase analysis and adopt a TTP taxonomy for threat actors, tools and malware. Relevant to entities supervised by SAMA that must evidence a structured operational CTI practice.

This node covers the kill chain concept in SAMA's Cyber Threat Intelligence Principles — defined as the Lockheed Martin-derived model taxonomizing the phases of a cyber attack from reconnaissance through actions on objectives. Under the Operational CTI domain, Member Organizations are expected to define and taxonomize attack phases using recognised industry frameworks such as the kill chain or unified kill chain. It binds SAMA-supervised Member Organizations building an operational CTI capability.

This node addresses the Traffic Light Protocol classification scheme as applied in SAMA's Cyber Threat Intelligence Principles: all intelligence produced by Member Organizations must be classified under TLP in line with the SAMA Cybersecurity Communication Protocols, governing how threat information may be handled and distributed. It sits alongside the Core CTI expectations on collecting data from multiple intelligence sources, defining standard operating procedures, and securely processing and storing intelligence. Applies to all SAMA-supervised Member Organizations producing or sharing threat intelligence.

This node is a concept entry for the SAMA FEER framework as cross-referenced from the Financial Sector Cyber Threat Intelligence Principles. The supplied context does not set out FEER's own content; it only shows the CTI expectations on delivering actionable intelligence, internal sharing and continuous improvement of intelligence methods. Open the underlying CTI Principles document (and the separate FEER instrument) to confirm the actual scope and obligations before relying on this node.

SAMA's updated Guidelines on the Internal Liquidity Adequacy Assessment Plan (ILAAP), superseding the earlier guidelines issued under circular no. 381000120488 (3/12/1438AH) and effective from the 2021 ILAAP submission. They define the ILAAP as the bank's processes for identifying, measuring, managing and monitoring liquidity under SAMA liquidity risk management regulations, and set expectations on governance, board approval and challenge, risk appetite alignment, and strategic and liquidity planning. They bind banks supervised by SAMA, with ultimate responsibility resting on the Board of Directors and senior management; the guidelines are a starting point for supervisory dialogue, not an exhaustive standard.

An annexure-level component of SAMA's ILAAP guidelines setting out liquidity stress-testing expectations for banks, covering scenario and sensitivity testing, identification of liquidity strain sources (confidence loss, contagion, external and uncorrelated events), and institution-specific, market-wide and combined scenarios. It also frames how banks must document their liquidity-specific stress-testing framework, governance and challenge of assumptions, and feed results into risk appetite, strategic planning and the contingency funding plan. It binds banks supervised by SAMA and their governing bodies, which set liquidity risk tolerance.

Part of SAMA's ILAAP guidelines addressing how banks must express and disclose liquidity risk appetite and limits by reference to regulatory metrics — LCR, NSFR, Loan-to-Deposit Ratio and the SAMA Liquidity Ratio — under both normal and stressed conditions, and distinguish these from internally set treasury limits. It also covers the three-year funding strategy requiring Board (or delegated) approval and the quantification of liquidity risk, including comparison of internal assessments with LCR/NSFR outputs. Binds SAMA-supervised banks, their boards and treasury/risk functions.

A SAMA circular (Finance Companies Supervision) requiring lessors to use the standard/model form contract for vehicle finance lease agreements with individuals, prohibiting contracts that depart from or amend that form. It confirms the earlier compliance deadline was postponed during COVID-19 and then reinstated, with a revised final compliance date in July 2020. It binds finance companies (lessors) licensed and operating in the Kingdom.

A SAMA circular permitting finance companies to offer financing products and credit cards to individuals and SMEs through electronic channels using approved digital certification (e-signature) services, subject to the Electronic Transactions Law and its implementing regulations. It imposes minimum conditions including level-3 compliance with the Cyber Security Framework verified independently, prior SAMA no-objection for e-services, use of a provider accredited by the National Center for Digital Certification, preservation of KYC/identity and capacity verification, telephone confirmation of customer consent, cooling periods before approval (24 hours for individuals, three business days for entities), risk-based financing caps and record retention. It binds licensed finance companies and excludes products under SAMA's regulatory sandbox.

A SAMA circular clarifying the treatment of the VAT increase from 5% to 15% (effective 1 July 2020) for cooperative insurance contracts linked to finance lease contracts. It confirms the lessor must bear the increase and may not pass it on to the lessee, relying on the Finance Lease Law provision placing cooperative insurance of the leased asset on the lessor. It binds finance companies acting as lessors.

A SAMA circular directing finance companies to keep their websites continuously updated, to verify (or otherwise delete) their social media accounts, and to publish and maintain accurate branch locations and business hours on digital mapping platforms. It sets a one-month compliance window and requires reporting of steps taken to SAMA's liaison officer within two weeks. Issued under SAMA's supervisory mandate and framed as a customer-protection measure binding on finance companies.

A SAMA circular to all SAMA-supervised financial institutions transmitting the national guide on emergency evacuation of persons with disabilities, issued as a follow-on to SAMA's earlier instructions on services for persons with disabilities in financial institutions and to a letter from the Authority for the Care of Persons with Disabilities. The attached guide sets out definitions (emergency, evacuation routes, refuge/safe areas, emergency exits, first aider), disability types, building hazards, evacuation planning steps and self-preparedness, and safety/communication systems such as public address, assistive listening, visual alarms, tactile warning surfaces and access-card/security systems. It binds supervised financial institutions to strengthen premises security and safety arrangements so persons with disabilities can be evacuated safely.

Authority for the Care of Persons with Disabilities

data.summary: SAMA guidelines (version 3, September 2020) governing the quarterly regulatory return on weighted-average interest/commission rates and balances for assets and liabilities. They set the submission channel and deadline (30 calendar days after quarter end), CFO sign-off, domestic-only scope, three reporting templates (by product, by sector using ISIC4, and Sharia-compliant vs conventional), and definitions of rates, balances and maturity buckets, plus the asset/liability reporting categories. They bind all banks operating in Saudi Arabia, including branches of foreign banks, and supersede the earlier guidance note on quarterly prudential returns for loans and deposits commissions.
lookup_terms: Interest Rates on Assets and Liabilities report
loans and deposits commissions guidance note
banks operating in Saudi Arabia including foreign branches

data.summary: A defined classification basis used within SAMA's Interest Rates on Assets and Liabilities reporting guidelines: Template (2) requires banks to categorise reported assets and liabilities by economic sector using the International Standard Industrial Classification, revision 4 (ISIC4). It is a reporting taxonomy requirement, applying to all banks (including foreign bank branches) submitting the quarterly return, and works alongside the product-based and Sharia/conventional templates, with classifications required to be mutually exclusive.

A benchmark-rate element of SAMA's Interest Rates on Assets and Liabilities reporting guidelines: banks must include benchmark rates in the rate calculation based on booking value, illustrated by a SAIBOR rate at booking date plus a fixed spread. It clarifies how floating-rate exposures are reflected in the reported annual contractual weighted-average rates, and binds all banks submitting the quarterly return.

SAMA's Loans to Deposits Ratio Guidelines (version 2.0, March 2023), issued under the Central Bank Law and Banking Control Law and effective 1 June 2023, superseding the 1427H circular and the 1439H LDR calculation guidance. They define the ratio (net loans over weighted deposits), the numerator deductions, the deposit and long-term debt components of the denominator, exclusion of interbank and SAMA transactions, the maturity-based weighting table, and treatment of callable and perpetual sukuk/bonds. They bind banks, which must report LDR to SAMA monthly on a consolidated basis covering local and foreign currency, resident and non-resident transactions.

The defined regulatory metric within SAMA's 2023 guidelines: net loans (loans and advances less loan-loss provisions, unearned commission income and commission in suspense) divided by maturity-weighted deposits (deposits and repos plus long-term debt such as sukuk/bonds, syndicated and subordinated debt), with interbank and SAMA transactions excluded unless SAMA specifies otherwise. SAMA expects banks to keep total LDR below 90%, subject to the numerator not exceeding the unweighted denominator, with weights ranging from 100% for demand/overnight funding to 190% for over-five-year and perpetual instruments.
lookup_terms: subordinated and syndicated debt in denominator

data.summary: A SAMA circular activating the GCC-NET point-of-sale payment service for acceptance of transactions in Qatar as of a specified date, supplementing earlier circulars on the GCC-NET POS service and its tariff. It requires banks to make the technical and operational arrangements to accept and process GCC-NET POS transactions on their systems and terminals, to settle commercial terms with GCC-NET cardholders and acquiring merchants in line with approved pricing, to inform and educate cardholders that purchases in Qatar are routed through the Qatari national network linked to GCC-NET, and to accept and process all GCC-NET branded cards. It binds banks operating in the Kingdom.

Rules setting the minimum requirements exchange centres and bank-owned remittance centres must follow when receiving customer funds through electronic payment means for remittance or currency exchange purposes; they replace the earlier circular permitting such receipts. Requirements include a dedicated separate bank account, limiting inbound transfers to members with a unified reference number linked to the customer's ID and denominated in SAR, a prohibition on receiving customers' transfers from banks or exchange houses outside the Kingdom for currency exchange, verification and record-keeping on the transferring customer, restrictions on transfers back to customer accounts except for cancellations (refunded to the same payment instrument within three days), prior agreement and documentation of fees and exchange rates, customer awareness measures, and application of CDD under the AML and terrorism financing laws and their implementing regulations. It binds exchange centres and banks' remittance centres supervised by SAMA.

A circular confirming that finance companies must publish on their websites the reports and financial statements referred to in Articles 72 and 73 of the Implementing Regulation of the Finance Companies Control Law — audited annual and quarterly financial statements, the auditor's report and the board of directors' report — within ten business days of the end of the prescribed submission period. It supplements the earlier circular on providing SAMA with quarterly risk reports and financial statements. It binds finance companies operating in the Kingdom and the Saudi Real Estate Refinance Company.

A circular notifying a Governor's decision amending several articles of the Implementing Regulation of the Finance Lease Law issued under the Law's Article 27 rule-making power, agreed with the Minister of Justice. The amendments cover Article 10(5) (lessor must obtain a SAMA no-objection letter for finance lease products offered to individuals or microfinance beneficiaries before launch, to ensure fairness of terms), Article 17 (contract signing to take place at the lessor's premises with the lessor bearing the related costs), and Article 25(2) (aligned with Article 9(8) of the Enforcement Law). It binds banks, finance companies and finance lease contract registration companies in the Kingdom.

A circular extending SAMA's earlier acceptance of the Absher/Tawakkalna digital identity to the electronic Family Record document for citizens issued via Absher and displayed in Tawakkalna, readable by QR code. It obliges all financial institutions to accept this electronic Family Record in processes that do not require taking a copy of the document, with the same rules applicable to printed versions. It binds all financial institutions supervised by SAMA.

A circular reaffirming, by reference to earlier SAMA instructions on time limits for issuing clearance letters and transferring accounts and indebtedness, that real estate financiers must execute customer requests to transfer murabaha-based real estate finance indebtedness within the prescribed timeframes and comply with SAMA instructions on purchase and transfer of real estate finance debt between financiers. Business days linked to mortgage release procedures are excluded from those timeframes where the delay is caused by an external party, and financiers must update internal policies accordingly. It binds banks and real estate finance companies operating in the Kingdom.
lookup_terms: purchase of finance portfolios between financiers

data.summary: A SAMA circular (dated 02/02/1443H) instructing supervised financial institutions to accept the national Digital Identity issued through the Absher (Absher/Afrad) platform and the Tawakkalna application, including the QR-code-bearing digital ID, as valid proof of identity on the same footing as the physical civil-status identity document. Institutions must accept the electronic ID for existing customers in transactions that do not require retaining a copy, must continue assessing and reviewing risks arising from reliance on electronic identity, and must establish a suitable means of obtaining an electronic copy where a copy is required. It binds all financial institutions supervised by SAMA and is effective from its date.

The Banks Investment Rules (Version 1, April 2022) are SAMA's framework for how banks conduct and manage local and international investments across the trading and banking book. They set definitions, general prudential expectations on concentration and liquidity, documented investment rationale, governance, risk management and SAMA approval requirements. They bind banks licensed and supervised by SAMA, including foreign bank branches.

The governance section of the Banks Investment Rules allocates responsibility for investment oversight: the Board of Directors (or, for foreign bank branches, the head/regional office authority overseeing the branch) is ultimately accountable and approves the internal Investment Policy and Strategy, supported by a management-level investment committee. It prescribes minimum content of the Investment Policy, including controls and delegation of authority, eligibility criteria, prudential exposure limits and limits on local and international investments. It binds banks supervised by SAMA.

This part of the Banks Investment Rules covers the risk dimension of investment activity: the Investment Strategy must address credit, market (including IRRBB and FX), operational, liquidity and concentration risks, and its implementation must be overseen and supported by documented operational guidelines and monitoring mechanisms integrated into the bank's risk management framework. Banks must assess current and prospective investments, report identified risks to the responsible committee, and comply with SAMA's AML/CTF requirements before entering into any investment. It binds banks supervised by SAMA.

This section of the Banks Investment Rules covers portfolio monitoring, diversification, annual portfolio-level stress testing and resourcing, together with approval controls: banks must obtain SAMA's non-objection for investments requiring regulatory approval under the Banking Control Law and Ministerial Decree No. 3/2149, approved at portfolio level, with prior non-objection for changes to structure or limits. It also requires investment channels and product-level approval requirements to be set in bank policy, including that Money Market Fund investments be made through CMA-licensed entities and that Saudi riyal funds be invested onshore. It binds banks supervised by SAMA.

The Rules Regulating Money Changing Business set SAMA's licensing, regulatory and supervisory framework for money changers, defining Money Changing Business, Money Changer, Customer, Invested Capital and Third Party, and stating objectives including financial inclusion, innovation and customer protection. They prohibit unlicensed practice or use of money-changer style titles, with a narrow carve-out allowing licensed hotels, hotel apartments and travel agencies to exchange currency for their own customers subject to AML Law compliance and sale of currency to a licensed bank or money changer. Management of each licensed Money Changer is responsible for compliance and for approving the required policies and procedures.
lookup_terms: hotels travel agencies currency exchange exemption

data.summary: This node covers the licensing, ongoing licence-maintenance and supervisory-reporting obligations for Money Changers under SAMA's Rules for Money Changing Business, including the grounds on which SAMA may suspend or terminate a licence (failure to meet licence or business requirements, false information, obstruction of inspection, insolvency, accumulated losses of 50% or more of capital, dissolution or death of a sole proprietor). It also carries related supervisory duties: cooperation with SAMA inspectors, appointment of a licensed external auditor for a maximum of five continuous years (with SAMA able to appoint one at the Money Changer's expense), and periodic data returns on offices, senior position holders and staff. It binds licensed Money Changers, their owners and employees.

This node is the AML/CTF compliance article of SAMA's Money Changing Business rules, requiring Money Changers to observe the AML Law and its Implementing Regulations, the Law of Terrorism Crimes and Financing and its Implementing Regulations, related SAMA circulars and instructions, and the guideline implementing UN Security Council resolutions on proliferation financing of weapons of mass destruction. It sits alongside the enforcement provisions setting out SAMA's supervisory actions and penalties (warnings, corrective action, branch closure, service suspension, licence suspension or revocation, fines under SAMA's Charter, publication of decisions). It binds licensed Money Changers.
lookup_terms: Law of Terrorism Crimes and Financing

data.summary: This node sets the customer-protection floor for Money Changers: displaying customer rights and exchange-rate boards at head office, branches and electronic platforms; issuing transaction receipts (paper or electronic); providing complaint channels with resolution within seven days and escalation notice to SAMA; and safeguarding customer information against disclosure to unauthorised third parties without SAMA's prior non-objection. Adjacent provisions cover head office/branch and ownership changes requiring SAMA non-objection, and IT and operational requirements. It binds licensed Money Changers dealing with Customers.
lookup_terms: IT and operational requirements money changer

data.summary: This is SAMA's guidance document implementing the Basel III Net Stable Funding Ratio, covering scope of application, calculation and at-least-quarterly reporting frequency, minimum requirements, and detailed factor guidance for liabilities, capital and derivative positions (including replacement cost, eligible bilateral netting and cash variation margin treatment). It cross-references earlier SAMA Basel II and leverage-ratio circulars for scope and derivative measurement. It binds banks supervised by SAMA, primarily internationally active banks on a consolidated basis.
lookup_terms: Net Stable Funding Ratio Basel III
scope of application internationally active banks

data.summary: This node defines the Net Stable Funding Ratio itself — available stable funding over required stable funding, to be maintained at 100% or more on an ongoing basis — and explains its calibration by funding tenor, funding type and counterparty, and asset tenor, credit-creation and bank roll-over behaviour assumptions. It also records that SAMA may impose more stringent standards on an individual bank based on its funding risk profile and Sound Principles compliance. It applies to banks under SAMA supervision.

This node covers Available Stable Funding — the portion of capital and liabilities deemed reliable over the NSFR's one-year horizon — and the ASF factor schedule by liability category, from 100% for regulatory capital and long-dated liabilities, through 95%/90% for stable and less stable retail and small-business deposits, 50% for non-financial corporate, operational and certain six-to-twelve-month funding, down to 0% for residual liabilities, equity without stated maturity and net NSFR derivative liabilities. It supports NSFR computation and prudential return submission by banks.

Defines the Required Stable Funding (RSF) leg of the Net Stable Funding Ratio: the denominator measuring how much stable funding a bank's assets and off-balance-sheet exposures are presumed to need over a one-year horizon. RSF is computed by mapping carrying values of assets to prescribed categories, applying RSF factors calibrated to residual maturity, liquidity value, roll-over behaviour and credit-creation continuity, with LCR definitions applying unless stated otherwise. It binds banks subject to SAMA's NSFR scope, and SAMA may impose more stringent standards on an individual bank based on its funding risk profile.

Explains the Liquidity Coverage Ratio as SAMA's short-term liquidity standard requiring banks to hold sufficient high-quality liquid assets (HQLA) to survive a 30-day stress scenario, and positions it as complementary to the NSFR plus the associated liquidity monitoring tools. It cross-references earlier SAMA circulars implementing the amended LCR (2013) and the monitoring tools (2014). Applies to banks supervised by SAMA; LCR definitions are also used as the baseline for NSFR asset categorisation.

Node covering SAMA's adoption of the BCBS Basel III NSFR standard (October 2014): the definition of the ratio (available stable funding over required stable funding, minimum 100% on an ongoing basis), reporting frequency (at least quarterly), scope of application (consolidated basis for internationally active banks, extendable by SAMA), and specific treatment items such as derivative asset calculation, netting and margin. It also requires banks to monitor liquidity and funding risk at legal-entity, branch, subsidiary and group level. Binds banks subject to SAMA prudential supervision.

SAMA's August 2014 circular and enclosed framework establishing how domestic systemically important banks (D-SIBs) are identified and designated in Saudi Arabia, using an indicator-based measurement approach aligned with the BCBS D-SIB methodology. Designated banks must meet additional Higher Loss Absorbency capital requirements, effective 1 January 2016. Addressed to all banks operating in the Kingdom, at senior management level.

The assessment methodology component of the D-SIB framework: an indicator-based scoring approach reflecting size, interconnectedness, substitutability and complexity, calibrated to the operational dynamics of the Saudi banking system and the externalities a bank's failure would impose domestically and cross-border. It produces the scores used for D-SIB designation and bucket allocation. Applies to banks assessed by SAMA's Banking Supervision Department.

Sets out the scoring, bucketing and Higher Loss Absorbency (HLA) surcharge for designated D-SIBs: banks scoring above a 10% cut-off are automatically classified as D-SIBs (SAMA may add others by supervisory judgment), and are allocated to one of five buckets driving the HLA charge. HLA must be met entirely with Common Equity Tier 1 and sits on top of the bank-specific target capital adequacy ratio set by SAMA; SAMA may also impose recovery and resolution plans and other measures. Binds banks designated as D-SIBs.

This node covers SAMA's August 2014 circular and enclosed framework for identifying Domestic Systemically Important Banks (D-SIBs) in Saudi Arabia, developed by reference to the BCBS G-SIB assessment methodology and the G20/FSB mandate to extend it domestically. It sets an indicator-based measurement approach using size, interconnectedness, substitutability and complexity, and imposes additional Higher Loss Absorbency (HLA) capital requirements on designated banks. It binds all banks addressed by SAMA Banking Supervision, effective 1 January 2016.

A SAMA guidance note clarifying the scope of application of the Basel Framework in Saudi Arabia — risk-based capital and buffers, leverage, liquidity, large exposures, Pillar 2 supervisory review and Pillar 3 disclosure. It confirms that, since Basel II (Circular BCS290, June 2006), local banks apply SAMA's Basel requirements on both a standalone and consolidated basis, including at holding-company level and every tier of the banking group, with prudential returns aligned to that scope. It binds local banks and their banking groups.

This node concerns minimum Pillar 1 capital requirements for credit risk under SAMA's Basel framework (SCRE), together with the related Pillar 3 disclosure templates for RWA, capital requirements and capital distribution constraints. It delineates credit risk from counterparty credit risk, CVA, equity positions, settlement risk, securitisation exposures and threshold deductions, each reported and capitalised separately. It binds banks subject to SAMA's capital adequacy and disclosure rules.

This node addresses the standardised approach (SA) for credit risk as applied in SAMA's Basel framework, including use of the simple or comprehensive approach with standard supervisory haircuts for credit risk mitigation and treatment of failed trades and non-DvP transactions. It also covers the split between SA-computed RWA and modelled (IRB) RWA in disclosure, and the five-year linear phase-in of the prohibition on IRB for equity exposures. It binds banks calculating credit risk RWA under SAMA rules.
lookup_terms: credit risk mitigation simple comprehensive approach

data.summary: This node covers the Internal Ratings-Based approaches to credit risk — Foundation IRB, Advanced IRB and the supervisory slotting approach — which banks may use only with SAMA approval, and their interaction with the securitisation framework (SEC-IRBA, KIRB, attachment/detachment points) and equity investments in funds. It also reflects the phase-out of IRB for equity exposures. It binds banks seeking or holding SAMA approval to use internal models for credit risk RWA.

This node deals with eligibility conditions for External Credit Assessment Institutions whose ratings banks may use to determine risk-weighted exposures, with stricter conditions in the securitisation context: ratings and underlying methodologies must be publicly available on a non-selective, free basis, and the ECAI must show demonstrated expertise in securitisations. It also addresses multiple-ECAI conflicts, treatment of credit risk mitigation reflected in a rating, and when exposures must be treated as unrated. It binds banks relying on external ratings for capital purposes.

This node covers credit risk mitigation (CRM) as it appears in SAMA's Basel-aligned capital and Pillar 3 disclosure material: the qualitative and template disclosures on CRM techniques (Table CRC, Template CR3, and the CRM effects shown in CR4) and the rule that, under the standardised approach, mitigation is recognised via either the simple or the comprehensive approach with standard supervisory haircuts. It sits within the credit risk section that excludes securitisation exposures and counterparty credit risk, which are disclosed separately. It binds SAMA-supervised banks calculating risk-weighted assets and preparing Pillar 3 disclosures on a standalone and consolidated basis.

This node sets out SAMA's securitisation framework concepts and capital treatment: what counts as a securitisation exposure (including ABS, MBS, credit enhancements, liquidity facilities, swaps, tranched cover and originator-held reserve accounts), the definition of resecuritisation, and when a bank is treated as an originator. It also covers risk-weight mechanics under the standardised securitisation approach (SEC-SA), including the 15% risk-weight floor, inference of risk weights for market risk hedges, and the adjustments applied to resecuritisation exposures (supervisory parameter p of 1.5, delinquencies set to zero). It binds banks holding or originating securitisation positions for risk-based capital and related disclosure purposes.

This node is the Basel III anchor for SAMA's prudential rulebook, mapping the local glossary abbreviations (SACAP, SCRE, SCCR, SMAR, SOPE, SLEV, SLCR, SNSF) to the SAMA circulars adopting the post-crisis final reforms on capital, credit, counterparty credit and CVA, market, operational risk, leverage and liquidity. It also frames the Pillar 3 key metrics disclosure (Template KM1), a mandatory quarterly, fixed-format overview of capital, leverage and liquidity metrics with accompanying narrative. It binds all SAMA-licensed banks subject to the Basel framework.
lookup_terms: SACAP SCRE SCCR SMAR SOPE SLEV

data.summary: This node concerns SAMA's Guidance Note on the scope of application of the Basel Framework, tracing the position back to the Basel II Detailed Guidance Document Circular BCS290 (June 2006). It confirms that local banks must apply SAMA's Basel requirements on both a standalone and consolidated basis, including at holding-company level and every tier of a banking group, and that prudential return requirements follow the same scope. It binds local banks and their parent/holding entities within a banking group.

This node governs how banks may use external credit assessment institutions (ECAIs) recognised by SAMA when risk-weighting exposures under the standardised approach. It requires consistent use of chosen ECAIs across exposure types for both risk-weighting and risk management, prohibits cherry-picking between agencies, requires use of the global rating scale (national scales must be mapped), and sets the hierarchy for issue-specific versus issuer ratings; it also records the eligibility criteria expected of ECAIs (independence, transparency, disclosure). It binds banks applying the standardised approach for credit risk.

This node addresses the use of multiple external ratings in determining risk weights, including the rules for selecting between conflicting ECAI ratings, and the external-ratings-based approach for securitisation exposures (SEC-ERBA). It sets out the SEC-ERBA risk-weight tables for short-term and long-term ratings, the drivers of long-term risk weights (rating grade or inferred rating, seniority, tranche maturity and, for non-senior tranches, thickness) and the operational requirements for using external assessments and inferred ratings. It binds banks holding rated securitisation exposures and those relying on external ratings for standardised credit risk weighting.

A concept node covering the comprehensive approach to collateral within credit risk mitigation, as it surfaces in SAMA's Pillar 3 disclosure framework (including the CCR5 template on composition of collateral posted/received for derivatives and SFTs, cleared or bilateral). It explains that where banks use the standardised approach for credit risk, mitigation must be measured under either the simple approach or the comprehensive approach with standard supervisory haircuts, and how collateral is then reported. It binds SAMA-supervised banks for RWA calculation and semiannual disclosure purposes.

Concept node on supervisory haircuts used under the comprehensive approach: banks must volatility-adjust both exposure and collateral values to reflect possible future price movements before recognising collateral. Haircut size depends on the prescribed minimum holding period, instrument type, transaction type, residual maturity and the frequency of mark-to-market and remargining, with scaling rules for other holding periods. Applies to SAMA-supervised banks computing credit and counterparty credit risk exposure amounts; related supervisory parameters (supervisory factor, delta, maturity factor) appear in the SA-CCR context.

Concept node on the recognition of master netting agreements for securities financing transactions and margin agreements, covering how netted exposure (E*) is used as EAD, treatment where one margin agreement spans several netting sets, and collateral taken outside a netting set. It also notes the VaR models alternative to standard haircuts for SFT counterparty credit risk, subject to eligibility criteria and supervisory recognition of the internal model. Binds SAMA-supervised banks; use of the VaR approach requires SAMA approval.

Concept node distinguishing accounting balance sheet netting from regulatory (Basel) netting, as reflected in the LI1/LI2 reconciliation templates and in margin-agreement netting mechanics. It clarifies that regulatory netting rules may allow more or less offsetting than the accounting framework, producing incremental netting adjustments in the reconciliation between financial statements and regulatory exposure amounts. Relevant to SAMA-supervised banks preparing Pillar 3 disclosures and calculating counterparty exposure.

Concept node on guarantees and credit derivatives as credit risk mitigants and as exposures in their own right. It covers how exposures secured by financial guarantees versus credit derivatives are allocated and disclosed (Template CR3 illustrations), and the treatment of written credit derivatives where the bank sells credit protection, including when purchased protection may offset sold protection (identical reference names, equally or more conservative terms, strike price condition). Binds SAMA-supervised banks in exposure measurement and disclosure.

Concept node on the standardised approach for counterparty credit risk (SA-CCR) for derivatives and its place in SAMA's Pillar 3 counterparty credit risk disclosures. It covers the scope of CCR charges across banking and trading book (including exposures to CCPs), the CCRA/CCR1–CCR8 disclosure set, and the SA-CCR components reported in CCR1 (replacement cost, potential future exposure, alpha of 1.4, EAD post-CRM, RWA). Binds all SAMA-supervised banks; disclosure is mandatory and semiannual.

This node covers the rules on when a bank may map an external credit assessment to an exposure for standardised credit risk weighting, distinguishing issuer-level ratings (presumed to cover senior unsecured claims only) from issue-specific ratings, and how low-quality ratings contaminate unrated pari passu or subordinated claims. It also requires the relied-upon rating to reflect the full credit exposure (principal and profit/interest) and bars double-counting where credit enhancement is already embedded in an issue rating. It binds SAMA-supervised banks calculating minimum capital requirements for credit risk, with an adjacent passage on classifying instruments as equity exposures.

This node sets out how short-term external ratings may be used for risk weighting: they are treated as issue-specific, cannot be generalised to other short-term exposures or used for unrated long-term exposures, and apply only to bank and corporate exposures under a fixed risk-weight table. It also governs the interaction with the general preferential treatment for short-term interbank exposures, the ECAI eligibility criteria, the bar on using one group entity's rating for another entity, and the prohibition on unsolicited ratings. It binds banks applying the standardised approach to credit risk.
