This node describes the standardised approach to credit risk and its credit risk mitigation options for reporting and capital calculation purposes, requiring banks to use either the simple approach or the comprehensive approach with standard supervisory haircuts. It sits within the RWA/minimum capital reporting templates, delineating which exposures fall in the standardised bucket versus IRB, slotting, counterparty credit risk, CVA, equity and securitisation rows. It binds SAMA-supervised banks computing and disclosing Pillar 1 capital requirements.

This node governs recognition of credit protection where the hedge matures before the underlying exposure: maturity mismatches are not recognised under the simple approach for financial collateral, and elsewhere protection counts only if original maturity is at least one year and residual maturity at least three months, with a pro-rata adjustment formula. It also prescribes conservative measurement of both the exposure's effective maturity and the hedge's shortest possible maturity (including call options), alongside related maturity-scaling rules for default risk charge positions. It binds banks applying credit risk mitigation and market risk capital rules.

This node addresses capital treatment of collateralised and repo-style transactions, including exemptions from the one-year effective maturity floor for fully or nearly fully collateralised capital-market-driven and repo-style transactions with daily remargining, short-term self-liquidating trade finance, and other SAMA-defined short-term exposures. It also covers eligible collateral and haircuts for trading book repo-style transactions, counterparty credit risk on collateralised OTC derivatives, and minimum haircut floors for non-centrally cleared securities financing transactions. It binds banks calculating credit and counterparty credit risk capital.

This node sets out the simple approach to recognising financial collateral, under which the counterparty's risk weight is substituted by the risk weight of the collateral instrument for the collateralised portion, subject to the collateral being pledged for at least the life of the exposure and revalued at least every six months. Surrounding provisions address collateral segregation by custodians, capital charges on both legs of repo and securities lending transactions, agent-arranged repo-style transactions with a performance guarantee, and reuse of collateral. It binds banks using the standardised approach for credit risk mitigation.

SAMA's minimum capital framework for counterparty credit risk and credit valuation adjustment risk, setting out the definition of CCR (bilateral risk of loss before final settlement), the recognised CCR-related risks such as rollover risk and general/specific wrong-way risk, and the permitted CVA approaches (BA-CVA, SA-CVA and alternative treatment). It binds banks supervised by SAMA, effective 1 January 2023, and requires quarterly reporting of CCR and CVA risk-weighted assets and capital charges on SAMA's Q17 template within 30 days of quarter-end. Related disclosure guidance maps CCR and CVA amounts to specific rows of the Pillar 3 RWA overview template.

Provision within the standardised credit risk mitigation rules allowing the 0% risk weight for Saudi sovereign/SAMA exposures to be extended to the guaranteed portion of an exposure where the guarantee is denominated in and the exposure funded in Saudi Riyal. It also permits indirect sovereign counter-guarantees to be treated as sovereign guarantees where the counter-guarantee covers all credit risk elements, operational requirements for guarantees are met, and SAMA is satisfied the cover is robust. Binds banks applying the standardised approach to credit risk.

Overview provisions of the internal ratings-based approach to credit risk, covering how banks categorise banking-book exposures into asset classes and the conditions for adopting IRB. Notably it permits a phased rollout across asset classes, business units and from foundation to advanced approaches, but requires full application within an asset class in a given business unit, an implementation plan agreed with SAMA, and no capital relief for intra-group transactions designed to reduce group capital during rollout. Binds banks seeking or using SAMA approval for F-IRB, A-IRB or supervisory slotting.

The IRB definition of corporate exposures — broadly a debt obligation of a corporation, partnership or proprietorship — with an option for banks to separately identify micro, small and medium-sized entity (MSME) exposures, and five specialised lending sub-classes carved out within the corporate class. Sits within the credit risk framework's exposure categorisation rules and binds banks assigning banking-book exposures for capital purposes. Related disclosure guidance addresses how corporate versus retail loans are categorised for non-performing and forborne exposure reporting.

Rules identifying five specialised lending sub-classes within the IRB corporate asset class, defined by characteristics present in legal form or economic substance (typically exposure to an entity created to finance or operate physical assets). Part of the broader exposure categorisation requirement under which banks must demonstrate to SAMA that their asset-class assignment methodology is appropriate and consistent over time. Binds banks using the IRB approach; note the IRB approach is not permitted for equity exposures.

Standardised-approach criteria for the retail exposure class, including the low-value threshold (aggregate exposure to one counterparty not exceeding SAR 4.46 million), the granularity criterion (0.2% of the overall regulatory retail portfolio, excluding defaulted retail exposures), and the definitions of transactors and other retail. It sets the applicable risk weights: 75% for regulatory retail, 45% for transactor exposures and 100% for other retail. Binds banks classifying and risk-weighting retail credit exposures.

Defines the qualifying revolving retail exposure (QRRE) sub-class within the IRB retail asset class, alongside residential mortgages and other retail, and sets the cumulative criteria (revolving, unsecured, uncommitted, applied at sub-portfolio level) for that treatment. It also covers when small business exposures below the SAR 4 million threshold may be pooled and managed as retail. It binds SAMA-licensed banks using internal ratings-based approaches for credit risk capital, and interacts with Pillar 3 disclosure of problem assets and forbearance.

Sets out the eligibility and quantification treatment of purchased receivables under the IRB framework, splitting them into retail and corporate receivables and specifying when the top-down approach may replace obligor-by-obligor default risk assessment. It confirms that corporate purchased receivables may use A-IRB only where the individual obligors qualify, that retail receivables are A-IRB only, and that certain on-balance sheet uses require SAMA approval. Applies to banks adopting IRB, including the asset-class roll-out obligation.

Explains the structure of the IRB framework (risk components, risk-weight functions, minimum requirements) and distinguishes the foundation approach, where banks estimate PD only, from the advanced approach, where banks also estimate LGD, EAD and maturity. It records the exclusions from A-IRB (e.g. large corporate groups above the stated revenue threshold, bank and financial institution exposures, equities) and the phased roll-out and implementation plan that must be agreed with SAMA. Binds banks seeking or using IRB permission for credit risk capital.

Covers the IRB risk-weight functions that convert risk components into risk-weighted assets, including the chapter structure for default and dilution risk on purchased receivables and the recognition of credit risk mitigants such as guarantees and first-loss collateral. It sets substitution rules where a guarantee covers default risk, dilution risk, or both, and points to securitisation treatment (SEC-IRBA) where mitigants act as first-loss protection. Relevant to banks calculating IRB capital requirements.

Node for the IRB risk components (PD, LGD, EAD and effective maturity) as the bank-supplied or supervisory inputs to capital calculation; the surrounding context also carries definitional material on market risk concepts (risk factor, risk position, risk class, sensitivities) and internal risk transfers between banking and trading books. Useful as an entry point to definitions and to the boundary rules on regulatory capital recognition of internal hedges. Binds banks calculating credit and market risk capital under SAMA's framework.

Deals with probability of default as an IRB parameter and its supervisory validation, including the Pillar 3 backtesting template comparing modelled PD against realised default rates over at least a five-year average, and the related disclosure of movements in defaulted exposures. It also anchors the definition of a defaulted exposure (past due more than 90 days under the standardised approach, net of write-offs and gross of provisions). Mandatory for banks using F-IRB or A-IRB, with model-scope commentary obligations.

Concept node for Loss Given Default, the IRB risk component expressing the economic loss rate on a facility if the obligor defaults. The underlying material sets out the minimum requirements for banks permitted to use own-LGD estimates, including the downturn/long-run default-weighted average floor, treatment of dependence between borrower and collateral or guarantor risk, and currency mismatch; related context also covers loss data thresholds used in the operational risk capital calculation. It binds SAMA-licensed banks applying the advanced IRB approach and, for disclosure, banks completing Pillar 3 credit risk templates.

Concept node for Exposure at Default, the exposure measure that, with PD and LGD, drives IRB risk-weighted assets and expected loss, and that underpins several Pillar 3 credit risk templates. Related context covers carrying amounts of secured and unsecured exposures under credit risk mitigation reporting and the prudential treatment of non-performing and forborne exposures. Relevant to banks calculating credit risk capital and preparing mandatory disclosures.

Concept node for Effective Maturity (M), the maturity input to IRB corporate, sovereign and bank risk-weight functions. It fixes M at 2.5 years under the foundation approach (0.5 years for repo-style transactions), requires measurement of M per facility under advanced approaches subject to a one-year floor and five-year cap, and specifies treatment of cash-flow schedules, netted derivatives and revolving exposures; adjacent market risk material addresses maturity weighting and the three-month floor for default risk charge positions. Binds banks using IRB approaches and, for the DRC aspects, banks under the market risk framework.
lookup_terms: master netting agreement weighted average maturity

data.summary: Concept node for the supervisory slotting approach, the fallback IRB treatment for specialised lending (project, object, commodities finance, income-producing real estate and HVCRE) where a bank cannot meet PD/LGD estimation requirements. It requires mapping of internal grades to five supervisory categories with prescribed unexpected-loss risk weights, permits SAMA-approved preferential weights for strong and good exposures with short residual maturity, and sets the expected loss calculation for slotted exposures. Applies to banks using IRB approaches for specialised lending portfolios.
lookup_terms: project finance object finance commodities finance
strong good satisfactory weak default categories

data.summary: Concept node for the supervisory slotting criteria tables that define, for each sub-class of specialised lending, the assessment factors and characteristics corresponding to each of the five supervisory categories. Banks must assign exposures to internal grades using their own rating systems and then demonstrate that the mapping to the supervisory categories is consistent with the preponderance of the stated characteristics, guarding against overrides that undermine the mapping. Binds banks applying the slotting approach and their internal rating governance.
lookup_terms: mapping internal ratings to supervisory categories

data.summary: Concept node for the IRB treatment of purchased receivables, covering risk-weighted assets for default risk and for dilution risk, treatment of purchase price discounts and recognition of credit risk mitigants, together with eligibility conditions for the asset class. Purchased receivables also appear as a separate F-IRB/A-IRB line in Pillar 3 credit risk and credit derivative CRM templates. Relevant to banks with IRB approval that acquire receivables portfolios.

Part of SAMA's Basel-aligned capital framework dealing with the upkeep of rating systems: banks using internal ratings must document rating system design, criteria, review frequency, exception handling and the history of major changes to the risk rating process, and must periodically re-test criteria against the current portfolio and external conditions. The node also carries the eligibility expectations for external credit assessment institutions (ECAIs) regarding independence, timeliness of rating actions, transparency and disclosure of methodologies, default definitions and transition/default rates. It binds locally incorporated banks applying IRB approaches and, indirectly, conditions SAMA's recognition of ECAIs whose ratings banks may use.

Sets the rules for using external ratings in the standardised approach to credit risk: consistent use of SAMA-recognised ECAIs (no cherry-picking), use of global rating scales, and the multiple-ratings hierarchy (higher risk weight where two ratings differ; second-lowest logic where three or more). It also governs when an issue-specific or issuer rating may be extended to an unrated exposure, the requirement that the rating cover the full amount owed, and the bar on double-counting credit enhancement already reflected in an issue rating. Binds banks determining risk weights for rated and unrated exposures.

Covers data quality and retention obligations across two capital regimes: alignment, documentation and validation of risk-theoretical vs hypothetical P&L input data for market risk internal models (including notification to SAMA of changes to alignment processes), and the internal operational loss data standards under the standardised approach, including the ten-year observation period (five years exceptionally on transition) and linkage of loss data to current business activities. It also flags the consequence of failing loss data standards — capital at 100% of the business indicator component, a possible ILM above 1, and Pillar 3 disclosure. Binds banks using IMA for market risk and banks above the specified business indicator threshold for operational risk.

Relates to the capital adequacy disclosure and buffer machinery in SAMA's capital framework, notably the capital distribution constraints template — the CET1 ratio levels at which distributions become restricted once minimum ratios, the capital conservation buffer, G-SIB surcharge, countercyclical buffer, Pillar 2 and leverage buffer requirements are stacked. It also touches Tier 2 composition and the regulatory deductions for own instruments, reciprocal cross-holdings and holdings in financial sector entities/TLAC liabilities. Binds banks in respect of annual public disclosure and capital calculation.

Concerns the due diligence duty attaching to reliance on external ratings for risk weighting: banks must independently satisfy themselves that an external rating conservatively reflects the creditworthiness of the counterparty or covered bond, must notch up one bucket where their analysis shows higher risk, and may never notch down. It also sets the scope of the corporate exposure class (including securities firms and other financial institutions treated as corporates, exclusion of individuals, specialised lending) and the associated base risk weight table. Binds banks applying the standardised approach to credit risk.

Sets the organisational and control requirements for banks using internal models — an independent risk control unit separate from trading and model development, reporting to senior management, performing initial and ongoing validation (at least annually for IMA models), backtesting and P&L attribution at trading desk level. It requires active board and senior management involvement in risk control, use-test integration of model output into day-to-day risk management and trading/exposure limits, and documented policies and compliance routines. Binds banks approved to use IMM for counterparty credit risk and IMA for market risk.

Concept node covering how "default" is identified and reported for regulatory capital purposes, spanning the Pillar 3 disclosure templates on defaulted exposures (CR2 flows in/out of default, write-offs, returns to non-defaulted status) and the IRB backtesting of PD against realised default rates (CR9). It fixes the reference default definition used for both standardised (past due more than 90 days) and IRB exposures, including reporting net of write-offs and gross of provisions. It binds all SAMA-licensed banks for the mandatory templates, with the IRB backtesting elements binding only banks approved for F-IRB/A-IRB.

Concept node on the definition and measurement of operational risk loss: what counts as gross loss, net loss and recovery, the loss data set standards under the standardised approach, and the loss event thresholds (SAR 44,600 / SAR 446,000) used in the internal loss multiplier and related Pillar 3 disclosure rows. It specifies inclusions in gross loss (direct P&L charges, consequential external costs, provisions, pending losses) and that recoveries reduce losses only once payment is received. Binds banks calculating operational risk capital and disclosing operational loss data to SAMA.

Concept node on the required re-ageing policy governing the counting of days past due and the granting of extensions, deferrals, renewals and rewrites on existing facilities, including minimum policy content (approval authorities, minimum facility age, eligible delinquency levels, cap on re-ageings, reassessment of repayment capacity). It links re-ageing practice to the default trigger and the IRB 'use test', and sits alongside the treatment of authorised and unauthorised overdrafts. Binds banks using the IRB approach for credit risk.

Concept node on how the risk-mitigating effect of guarantees may be recognised in IRB parameters — through adjustment of either PD or LGD, with the LGD-adjustment option available only to banks approved for own LGD estimates — and the consistency, rating and documentation requirements that follow. It also covers related credit risk mitigation treatment for collateral, repo-style transactions and the foundation versus advanced recognition routes. Binds banks applying the IRB approach, including for retail pools where guarantees support individual obligations or pools.

Concept node on the treatment of credit derivatives, focused on written (sold) credit protection — the effective notional amount, reduction for negative fair value, and the conditions for offsetting against purchased protection on the same reference name. It sets the "same or more conservative material terms" test (subordination, optionality, credit events, reference obligation) and the rules for identical reference names and pool-versus-single-name offsets. Binds banks recognising credit derivatives for regulatory capital purposes.
lookup_terms: same or more conservative material terms

data.summary: Concept node on the risk quantification and validation standards for internal estimates of PD, LGD and EAD — the requirement that PD be a long-run average of one-year default rates, that estimates use all relevant material data (internal, external or pooled) and be demonstrably representative of long-run experience, grounded in historical and empirical evidence rather than judgement alone. Related material also covers internal risk transfer desks and their conditions for regulatory capital recognition. Binds banks approved to use IRB approaches and, for the internal risk transfer elements, banks with trading book activity.

Node covering the capital treatment of dilution risk on purchased receivables under SAMA's adopted Basel III credit risk rules, including how collateral and guarantees acting as first-loss protection are recognised when they cover default losses, dilution losses or both. It sets out the substitution and proportional/tranched treatments for guarantees and the interaction with the securitisation framework and SEC-IRBA exposure-weighted LGD. It binds SAMA-supervised banks calculating credit risk capital under IRB approaches; the extract also carries unrelated market risk internal risk transfer material.

Node on the recognition of expected losses and provisions in regulatory capital, sitting alongside the Pillar 3 historical loss disclosure (Template OR1) for operational risk. The extracted content specifies the ten-year aggregate loss data, loss event thresholds (SAR 44,600 and SAR 446,000), exclusions and their role in the internal loss multiplier and operational risk capital calculation. It binds banks in the relevant business indicator buckets and those with SAMA approval to use internal loss data.

Node covering the minimum requirements banks must meet to use the internal ratings-based approaches, together with the associated Pillar 3 templates (e.g. CR7 on the RWA effect of credit derivatives, CCR4 on IRB counterparty credit risk exposures by PD scale). It governs eligibility for F-IRB/A-IRB use, portfolio breakdowns and model-scope disclosure. It binds SAMA-supervised banks permitted to use IRB approaches for credit and counterparty credit risk.

Node setting out the design standards for internal rating systems under the IRB framework: the definition of a rating system, use of multiple rating methodologies, the two required rating dimensions (borrower default risk and transaction-specific factors), and documentation obligations for rating criteria, exceptions, default/loss definitions and statistical models. It prohibits cherry-picking borrowers across rating systems to lower capital. It binds banks seeking or maintaining IRB approval from SAMA.

Node covering SAMA's guidance on implementing the Basel III framework in Saudi Arabia, including the glossary of SAMA-issued components (capital reforms, credit risk, CCR/CVA, market risk, operational risk, leverage, LCR, NSFR) and the guidance note on scope of application. It confirms that the framework applies on a standalone and consolidated basis, including at holding company level and every tier of a banking group. It binds all local banks supervised by SAMA.

Node covering SAMA's minimum capital requirements for market risk, focusing on internal risk transfers between the banking book and trading book, the SAMA-approved internal risk transfer desk, GIRR hedge-matching conditions, CVA risk transfers, and the general provisions and structure of the standardised approach. It requires all banks, D-SIB and non-D-SIB alike, to compute the market risk capital charge under the standardised approach, with RWA derived by a 12.5 multiplier. It binds SAMA-supervised banks with trading book activity.

Node within SAMA's minimum capital requirements for credit risk covering the internal and external audit / independent review expectations attached to internal ratings systems and their governance. It bears on who must periodically review rating assignment, parameter estimation and compliance with the IRB minimum requirements, binding SAMA-licensed banks that use internal models for regulatory capital. Note that the extracted context attached to this node largely concerns internal risk transfers between the banking book and trading book and market risk capital recognition, so verify the underlying paragraphs before relying on the label.

Node addressing the "use test" — the requirement that internal ratings and default/loss estimates actually drive credit approval, risk management, internal capital allocation and governance, not merely regulatory capital calculation. It binds banks with SAMA approval to apply IRB (F-IRB/A-IRB) approaches. The extracted context here is drawn from Pillar 3 disclosure templates (qualitative disclosures for the internal models approach to market risk and RWA definitions by approach), so confirm the paragraph range before citing.

This node covers the IRB risk-quantification standards for loss given default (LGD) and exposure at default (EAD), including when banks must fall back on supervisory (foundation) parameter estimates instead of own estimates. It sets out that EAD must be no less than the current drawn amount for on-balance sheet items, must reflect additional drawings up to and after default for off-balance sheet items, and must be a long-run default-weighted average with a margin of conservatism. It binds SAMA-supervised banks using foundation or advanced IRB approaches for credit risk capital.

Overview node for the risk quantification section of the IRB framework: the general standards for banks' own estimates of PD, LGD and EAD, including the requirement to use all relevant material data (internal, external or pooled), to ground estimates in historical experience and empirical evidence rather than judgement alone, and to demonstrate representativeness of long-run experience. Binds SAMA-licensed banks using IRB approaches. The context also carries market risk definitional material (risk factor, risk class, sensitivity, delta risk), indicating mixed extraction.

This node covers the treatment of commercial and residential real estate as eligible collateral, including the regulatory definitions used for exposure classification (general vs income-producing RRE/CRE, land acquisition/development/construction) and the operational conditions for recognition under IRB. Eligibility requires legal enforceability and a perfected lien, valuation at or below current fair value, and revaluation at least annually. It binds banks calculating credit risk capital and related Pillar 3 disclosures.

Covers the probability of default estimation requirements under the IRB approach: PD must be estimated for each internal borrower grade (corporate, sovereign, bank) or each retail pool, and must be a long-run average of one-year default rates, subject to specific retail carve-outs. Also relevant to specialised lending and HVCRE sub-classes, where meeting PD estimation requirements determines eligibility for foundation versus advanced treatment. Binds SAMA-licensed banks applying IRB approaches for regulatory capital.

This node concerns receivables and financial collateral as credit risk mitigation, framed through the Pillar 3 disclosure templates (CR3 on CRM techniques and CCR5 on collateral composition for counterparty credit risk). It explains how secured, unsecured, over- and under-collateralised exposures are allocated across collateral, financial guarantees and credit derivatives, and how collateral posted/received in derivatives and SFTs is reported. It binds banks disclosing credit risk mitigation and counterparty credit risk exposures.

Sets out the requirements for banks' own estimates of loss given default under the advanced IRB approach: LGD must reflect economic downturn conditions where necessary and cannot fall below the long-run default-weighted average loss rate for that facility type, with explicit treatment of dependence between borrower and collateral/collateral provider risk and of currency mismatches. Also addresses partial recognition of collateral where the effect cannot be modelled, and LGD in repo-style transactions, guarantees and credit derivatives. Binds SAMA-licensed banks approved for A-IRB.
lookup_terms: credit risk mitigation guarantees and credit derivatives

data.summary: This node addresses other physical collateral and the residual collateral categories as they appear in the counterparty credit risk and CRM disclosure templates (CCR5 and CR3), covering cash, sovereign and government agency debt, corporate bonds, equities and "other collateral" posted or received in derivatives and securities financing transactions. It clarifies the reporting of both legs of a transaction and the allocation of multi-secured exposures. It binds all banks subject to the Pillar 3 templates and CRM recognition rules.

Sets out the requirements for banks' own estimates of exposure at default under the advanced IRB approach: EAD is the expected gross exposure at obligor default, floored at the current drawn amount for on-balance sheet items (subject to recognised netting), with the additional requirements focused on off-balance sheet facilities and conversion factors. Estimates must be long-run default-weighted averages with a margin of conservatism, must address instability in the undrawn limit factor approach, and reference data must not be capped to limits or outstanding principal. Binds SAMA-licensed banks approved for A-IRB.

This node relates to the recognition of leases and leasing activity within the credit risk framework, including how leasing performance is used in the supervisory slotting criteria for specialised lending (income-producing real estate in pre-stabilisation and construction phases), alongside adjacent netting and SFT collateral treatment. It informs how lease-backed and pre-leased/pre-sold projects are graded and how exposures are valued. It binds banks applying the credit risk capital rules, particularly slotting and specialised lending treatments.

This node covers Pillar 3 disclosure obligations for banks using IRB approaches, including template CR7 on the effect of credit derivatives on IRB risk-weighted assets, and the overarching disclosure principles (meaningful, consistent over time, comparable across banks, proportionate to complexity). It also requires a formal board-approved disclosure policy and assurance arrangements for Pillar 3 data. It binds SAMA-supervised banks, with CR7 mandatory for those on F-IRB or A-IRB.

A transitional provision within SAMA's Basel III-aligned capital and Pillar 3 disclosure framework addressing equity exposures. It records that the prohibition on using the IRB approach for equity exposures is phased in linearly over five years from 1 January 2022, with the applicable risk weight during that period being the higher of the IRB-calculated weight and the standardised phase-in weight, and permits SAMA to require immediate application of the fully phased-in standardised treatment; it also directs how phase-in equity exposures are reported (250% speculative unlisted equities, 400% other equities) in credit risk disclosure templates. Binds banks subject to SAMA's capital adequacy and Pillar 3 disclosure requirements.

Node covering the general provisions of the securitisation capital framework: what counts as a securitisation exposure (ABS, MBS, credit enhancements, liquidity facilities, rate/currency swaps, credit derivatives, tranched cover, originator-held reserve/cash collateral accounts), what constitutes a resecuritisation, what may sit in the underlying pool, and when a bank is treated as an originator. It also touches the SEC-SA risk weight mechanics, including the 15% risk-weight floor and the adjusted parameters for resecuritisations. Binds banks calculating regulatory capital on securitisation positions under SAMA rules.

Defines traditional securitisation for capital purposes: a structure where cash flows from an underlying pool service at least two stratified tranches of differing credit risk, with investor payments dependent on pool performance rather than on the originator's obligation, and where junior tranches absorb losses without interrupting payments to senior tranches (distinguishing it from ordinary senior/subordinated debt). Sits within the scope provision requiring banks to apply the securitisation framework based on economic substance rather than legal form, with SAMA consultation encouraged in doubtful cases. Binds banks determining regulatory capital on securitisation exposures.
lookup_terms: specialised lending real estate cash flows

data.summary: Defines synthetic securitisation for capital purposes as a structure with at least two stratified tranches of differing credit risk where credit risk of the underlying pool is transferred using credit derivatives or guarantees rather than by sale of the assets. Read together with the scope rule that banks must apply the securitisation framework to both traditional and synthetic structures (and hybrids) on an economic-substance basis. Binds banks calculating regulatory capital and assessing significant risk transfer.
lookup_terms: economic substance rather than legal form

data.summary: Concept node for resecuritisation exposure: a securitisation exposure where an underlying tranched pool includes at least one securitisation exposure, including exposures to other resecuritisation exposures, with a carve-out for retranching where the bank can demonstrate replication of cash flows by an exposure to a pool containing no securitisations. Carries the punitive SEC-SA adjustments (underlying capital requirement computed under the securitisation framework, delinquencies set to zero for securitisation tranches, supervisory parameter p of 1.5). Binds banks holding or originating such positions for capital calculation and related Pillar 3 disclosure.

Concept node for the special purpose entity used in securitisation structures — the vehicle (corporation, trust or other entity) organised for a specific purpose, whose activities are limited to those needed to effect the securitisation and which is structured to isolate the SPE from the credit risk of the originator. Relevant to originator status, consolidation scope and to capital-instrument disclosure where the issuer is an SPE rather than the bank itself. Binds banks applying the securitisation framework and completing regulatory capital instrument disclosures.

Node covering the simple, transparent and comparable (STC) criteria for traditional term (non-ABCP) securitizations under SAMA's minimum capital requirements for credit risk. It sets the scope of the STC framework, the disclosure duty on originators/sponsors, the investor's own obligation to assess STC compliance before applying alternative capital treatment, and the requirement that criteria be met on an ongoing basis. Binds locally incorporated banks acting as originator, sponsor or investor in securitization positions.

Node covering the short-term STC criteria applicable to ABCP conduits and transactions financed by them, together with related treatment of short-term external ratings in the credit risk framework. It determines when short-term securitization exposures qualify for the alternative (preferential) capital treatment and how issue-specific short-term ratings may and may not be generalised. Binds banks calculating credit risk-weighted assets, including sponsors and investors in ABCP programmes.

Node for KSA, the capital charge on the underlying pool used as an input to the standardized securitization approach (SEC-SA); the attached material also touches capital-composition and capital distribution constraint disclosure templates. Relevant to determining risk weights for securitization exposures where the standardized approach applies. Binds banks computing regulatory capital and the associated Pillar 3 disclosures.

Node on the operational requirements for using external credit assessments and inferred ratings under the external-ratings-based approach to securitization exposures (SEC-ERBA), including the risk weight tables for short-term and long-term rated positions and the drivers of the weight (rating grade, seniority, tranche maturity, tranche thickness). It conditions eligibility to apply SEC-ERBA on meeting the stated operational criteria. Binds banks risk-weighting rated or inferred-rated securitization positions.

Node for KIRB, the IRB capital requirement on the underlying securitized pool that serves as the key input to the internal ratings-based securitization approach (SEC-IRBA); linked material also covers capital composition and capital distribution constraint disclosures. It determines when and how a bank may use SEC-IRBA rather than fallback approaches. Binds IRB-approved banks holding securitization exposures and their Pillar 3 reporting.

Node on the supervisory parameter p used in the securitization internal ratings-based approach to set the capital surcharge above KIRB; the surrounding material also describes other supervisory-set parameters (supervisory delta, supervisory factor, maturity factor) and curvature risk weights used elsewhere in the capital framework. It fixes regulator-determined inputs that banks may not substitute with their own estimates. Binds banks calculating risk-weighted assets for securitization and counterparty/market risk exposures.

Defines the terminology used for asset-backed commercial paper structures within SAMA's credit risk capital rules — conduit (the special purpose vehicle issuing commercial paper), programme, asset pool, investor, obligor, seller, sponsor and transaction — and sets out how the simple, transparent and comparable (STC) criteria for short-term securitizations are applied. It distinguishes conduit-level exposures, where STC compliance must be met at both conduit and transaction level, from transaction-level exposures, where only the supported transactions' criteria matter, and imposes representation and warranty duties on the sponsor regarding asset nature and homogeneity. It binds SAMA-supervised banks holding or sponsoring exposures to ABCP conduits for regulatory capital purposes.

Covers the conditions under which internal risk transfers between the banking book and trading book, and between trading desks, receive regulatory capital recognition, including the requirement for a SAMA-approved dedicated internal risk transfer desk and exact matching of internal general interest rate risk hedges with external market hedges. It also links to the reporting of risk-weighted assets and Pillar 1 minimum capital requirements across credit, counterparty credit, equity, settlement and securitization exposures. It binds banks subject to SAMA's market risk and credit risk capital frameworks.
lookup_terms: banking book to trading book transfer

data.summary: Sets the conditions a clean-up call must satisfy in a securitization — it must not be structured to avoid loss allocation or to provide credit enhancement, and must only be exercisable when 10% or less of the original portfolio or reference portfolio remains. Where the criteria are not met, the originating bank must treat traditional securitization exposures as if unsecuritized and may not recognise gain on sale, while protection-buying banks in synthetic deals must hold capital as if unprotected; an exercised call functioning as credit enhancement counts as implicit support and is deducted from capital. It binds originating and protection-purchasing banks under SAMA's securitization capital framework.

Establishes the due diligence banks must perform to use the securitization framework's risk weight approaches, failing which a 1250% risk weight applies to the exposure, alongside the general credit risk due diligence duty to understand counterparty risk profiles at origination and at least annually. It defines securitization and resecuritization exposures and the range of underlying instruments, and requires due diligence proportionate to the bank's size and complexity, performed at solo entity level where possible and demonstrable to SAMA. It binds all SAMA-supervised banks holding securitization or credit exposures.

Sets out the ordered hierarchy of approaches banks must apply to calculate capital for securitization exposures, and how it interacts with credit risk mitigation — including full or pro rata credit protection, the decomposition of tranched protection into protected and unprotected sub-tranches, and the exclusion of SPEs as eligible guarantors. It also carries the core definitions of securitization exposure, resecuritization and originator status. It binds banks acting as originators, investors, protection buyers or protection providers under SAMA's credit risk capital rules.

Identifies the internal ratings-based approach for securitization exposures (SEC-IRBA), including the definition of KIRB, attachment and detachment points, the supervisory parameter p, risk weight calculation, and the alternative capital treatment available for term and short-term securitizations meeting the STC criteria. It sits alongside the external ratings-based (SEC-ERBA) and internal assessment (SEC-IAA) approaches and the treatment of non-performing loan securitizations, with dilution risk recognition illustrated separately. It binds banks with SAMA approval to use IRB modelled approaches for securitization positions, and feeds the RWA disclosure templates.

A concept node for the tranche-level parameters (attachment point A and detachment point D) used to locate a securitisation exposure in the loss waterfall and derive its risk weight under the securitisation capital approaches, principally SEC-IRBA. The source material sets out the definitions and illustrative worked examples, including how the parameters are adjusted where default and dilution losses do not share a single common waterfall. Relevant to SAMA-supervised banks calculating credit risk RWA for held securitisation positions, with supervisory consultation expected for non-standard structures.

Defines non-performing loan (NPL) securitisation for capital purposes by reference to a minimum threshold for the pool's W variable at origination and on subsequent pool changes, and limits the eligible underlying assets to loans and loan-equivalent or sub-participation instruments (no resecuritisation). It also records SAMA's discretion to apply a stricter definition, restricts use of SEC-IRBA where the foundation approach is used to compute KIRB, and applies a risk-weight floor across SEC-IRBA, SEC-SA and the look-through treatment. Binds banks holding or originating exposures to NPL securitisations.

Covers asset-backed commercial paper (ABCP) programmes and conduits: the roles of sponsor, seller and transaction, the credit and investment guidelines, seller credit analysis, minimum asset eligibility criteria and collection/servicing controls a programme must have, and how STC criteria are assessed at conduit versus transaction level. Relevant to banks sponsoring, administering or holding exposures to ABCP conduits, including liquidity facilities and credit enhancements, and to use of the internal assessment approach.

The look-through approach is the primary method for capitalising equity investments in funds, requiring the bank to treat the fund's underlying exposures as if held directly (adjusted for its equity share and fund leverage), and it also appears in the market risk sensitivities framework for indices and multi-underlying instruments. The source sets out eligibility conditions, consistency-of-application expectations and the interaction with the mandate-based and fall-back approaches, including for IRB banks and funds investing in other funds. Applies to SAMA-supervised banks calculating credit and market risk RWA and reporting them in Pillar 3 templates.

The mandate-based approach is the second-tier method for equity investments in funds, used where the bank cannot meet the conditions for look-through but can rely on the fund's mandate or applicable regulations to infer the underlying exposures. The source situates it within the hierarchy alongside the look-through and fall-back approaches, with rules on partial use, leverage adjustment, funds investing in other funds and application by IRB banks. Binds banks holding fund equity exposures and feeds the RWA figures disclosed in Pillar 3 overview templates.

The fall-back approach is the most conservative tier for equity investments in funds, applied where neither the look-through nor the mandate-based approach can be used, and it drives the capital outcome for opaque fund holdings. The source places it within the approach hierarchy for funds and links to how the resulting RWA and minimum capital requirements are presented in Pillar 3 overview disclosures. Applies to SAMA-supervised banks with fund equity exposures.

Node covering the external ratings-based approach for securitisation exposures (SEC-ERBA) within SAMA's Basel-aligned capital framework, together with the Pillar 3 securitisation disclosure section that reports such exposures (Table SECA and templates SEC1–SEC4). It sets out how risk weights are derived from external or inferred credit assessments, the operational requirements for using those assessments, and alternative treatment for term and short-term STC securitisations; the disclosure part distinguishes all securitisation exposures (SEC1/SEC2) from those actually treated under the securitisation framework with recognised risk transfer (SEC3/SEC4). Binds banks licensed and supervised by SAMA that hold, originate, sponsor or invest in securitisation exposures.

Node for the securitisation internal assessment approach (SEC-IAA), one of the approaches in SAMA's securitisation capital hierarchy, typically used for unrated exposures to ABCP conduits where the bank maps internal assessments to external rating equivalents. It sits alongside SEC-ERBA, SEC-IRBA and SEC-SA and feeds the risk-weighted asset figures reported in the Pillar 3 credit and securitisation templates. Applies to SAMA-supervised banks seeking to use internal assessments for securitisation capital purposes, subject to supervisory approval conditions.

Node for the securitisation standardised approach (SEC-SA), the formula-based fallback in SAMA's securitisation capital hierarchy used where SEC-IRBA and SEC-ERBA/SEC-IAA are unavailable or not permitted. It links the standardised credit risk treatment of underlying pools to securitisation risk weights and to how resulting RWA are reported in the Pillar 3 overview and securitisation templates. Binds SAMA-supervised banks calculating regulatory capital for banking book securitisation exposures.

Node on the caps that limit maximum capital requirements for securitisation exposures, applied on top of the SEC-IRBA/SEC-ERBA/SEC-IAA/SEC-SA calculations, including caps available to originators and sponsors and the maximum risk weight for senior positions. It operates within the definitional framework for securitisation, resecuritisation, originator and sponsor set out in the securitisation chapter. Binds SAMA-supervised banks holding securitisation exposures in the banking book.
lookup_terms: maximum risk weight senior securitisation exposure

data.summary: Node on credit risk mitigation as applied to securitisation exposures — recognition of collateral, guarantees, credit derivatives and tranched cover when determining risk weights for securitisation and resecuritisation positions. It interacts with the general CRM rules and with disclosure of secured versus unsecured exposures in the Pillar 3 credit risk templates. Binds SAMA-supervised banks recognising credit protection on securitisation exposures for capital purposes.

Node defining the simple, transparent and comparable (STC) securitisation framework and the conditions for alternative (preferential) capital treatment, limited to traditional securitisations including ABCP conduit exposures and transactions financed by such conduits. It allocates responsibility: the originator/sponsor must disclose sufficient transaction-level information, the investor must make its own STC compliance assessment before applying the alternative treatment, and STC criteria must be satisfied on an ongoing basis; retained positions with achieved significant risk transfer are assessed by the retaining originator. Binds SAMA-supervised banks acting as originator, sponsor or investor, and drives the STC columns in Pillar 3 template SEC1.

Concept node for Credit Valuation Adjustment (CVA) as used in SAMA's minimum capital requirements for counterparty credit risk, covering the CVA framework chapter and its treatment in Pillar 3 RWA disclosure rows. CVA is the counterparty-level adjustment to default-risk-free prices of derivatives and securities financing transactions for potential counterparty default; the framework distinguishes regulatory CVA from accounting CVA and converts CVA capital requirements into RWA via the 12.5 multiplier. Binds banks subject to SAMA's Basel-aligned capital and disclosure rules.

Concept node for the capital treatment of banks' equity exposures and equity investments in funds under SAMA's credit risk framework, including the look-through, mandate-based and fall-back approaches, funds investing in other funds, partial use, and the leverage adjustment. It also covers what counts as an equity holding (instruments conveying the economic substance of equity ownership) and the applicable risk weights, including the higher weight for speculative unlisted equity. Binds banks calculating credit RWA, with several determinations subject to SAMA's satisfaction or approval.

Concept node for the adjustments that reconcile published accounting total assets to the leverage ratio exposure measure, as set out in the LR1 disclosure template and its instructions. It covers adjustments for entities outside regulatory consolidation, securitised exposures meeting risk-transfer recognition, any temporary exclusion of central bank reserves enacted by SAMA, fiduciary assets, regular-way purchases and sales under trade date accounting, and eligible cash-pooling transactions, with sign conventions for increases and decreases. Mandatory for all banks reporting the leverage ratio, on a quarterly basis unless SAMA specifies or approves more frequent averaging.

Concept node for the capital treatment of unsettled securities, commodities and foreign exchange transactions and failed trades (settlement risk) under SAMA's credit risk framework, together with how such exposures are reflected in Pillar 3 capital and RWA disclosure templates. It sets out that unsettled transactions must be captured for regulatory capital from trade date regardless of booking or accounting treatment, and separates DvP from non-DvP (free delivery) treatment. Binds banks; the framework excludes instruments already subject to the counterparty credit risk and CVA requirements.

Concept node for delivery-versus-payment transactions within the capital treatment of unsettled transactions and failed trades. DvP systems provide simultaneous exchange of securities for cash, exposing the bank to loss on the difference between the agreed settlement price and current market price; a capital requirement arises where payment has not taken place five business days after the settlement date, while non-DvP legs trigger a requirement from the end of the business day. Banks must monitor failed trades from the first day of failure; SAMA may waive requirements in a system-wide settlement or clearing failure, and a counterparty's failure to settle is not itself a default for credit risk purposes.

Concept node for the standardised approach as used in SAMA's Pillar 3 RWA disclosure instructions (notably the overview of RWA template), which define standardised-approach RWA by contrast with modelled approaches the bank has SAMA approval to use. Despite the label, the supplied material concerns the standardised approach to credit risk (including simple and comprehensive credit risk mitigation with standard supervisory haircuts, failed trades and non-DvP transactions), the F-IRB, A-IRB and supervisory slotting rows, and the phase-in of the prohibition on the IRB approach for equity exposures. Binds banks completing SAMA's capital adequacy and disclosure returns.
lookup_terms: credit risk mitigation simple vs comprehensive

data.summary: Concept node for the Sensitivities-Based Method, one of the three components of SAMA's standardised approach to market risk capital (alongside the default risk charge and the residual risk add-on). It defines how banks compute delta, vega and curvature risk measures by applying prescribed risk weights to regulatory risk factor sensitivities and aggregating them with specified correlation parameters, including a requirement to run three correlation scenarios (medium, high, low) to reflect stressed conditions. It binds all SAMA-licensed banks, D-SIBs and non-D-SIBs alike, which are required to use the standardised approach for market risk capital.
lookup_terms: minimum capital requirements for market risk

data.summary: Concept node for Delta risk, the linear sensitivity component of the sensitivities-based method under SAMA's standardised approach to market risk. It covers sensitivities to regulatory delta risk factors across the risk classes (e.g. GIRR, credit spread, equity, FX, commodity), with prescribed risk weights and correlations feeding the aggregate market risk capital requirement; delta risk weights also anchor the curvature shocks. Applies to banks calculating market risk capital on trading book positions and in-scope banking book FX and commodity exposures.

Concept node for Vega risk, the optionality-volatility component of the sensitivities-based method in SAMA's standardised market risk framework. It applies to instruments whose cash flows cannot be expressed as a linear function of notional (i.e. instruments with optionality), which are subject to both vega and curvature capital requirements; non-optional instruments such as coupon bonds are outside vega and curvature scope, subject to a limited elective inclusion for curvature. Binds banks computing market risk capital under the mandated standardised approach.

Concept node for Curvature risk, the sensitivities-based method component capturing the incremental non-linear price risk of options not captured by delta, measured through upward and downward stress shocks to each regulatory risk factor. It specifies how curvature risk weights are derived (for GIRR, CSR and commodity, a parallel shift based on the most punitive delta risk weight) and how curvature correlations are obtained by squaring delta correlations, with special treatment for CSR non-securitisations and securitisations (CTP). Binds banks calculating market risk capital under SAMA's mandated standardised approach.

Concept node for the Default Risk Capital (DRC) requirement, the second pillar of SAMA's standardised approach to market risk, capturing jump-to-default risk on instruments subject to credit risk in the trading book. It is calibrated to the banking book credit risk treatment to limit capital discrepancies for similar exposures, with limited hedging offset permitted within comparable exposure types (corporates, sovereigns, local governments/municipalities). It binds banks computing market risk RWA and feeds Pillar 1 capital and related disclosure templates.

Concept node for the Residual Risk Add-On, the third component of SAMA's standardised approach to market risk, introduced because not all market risks can be captured by the sensitivities-based method and DRC without undue complexity. It applies a simple add-on to specified instruments carrying exotic or other residual risks (including certain instruments with embedded prepayment features and securitisation tranches), and interacts with the recognition rules for internal CVA risk transfers, which require an exactly matching external hedge with an eligible third-party protection provider. Binds all banks calculating market risk capital under the standardised approach.

Concept node covering the treatment of internal risk transfers — internal transactions moving risk between a bank's banking book and trading book, or between trading desks — for minimum capital purposes. It sets the conditions under which a banking book hedge executed internally is recognised for capital (documentation, a dedicated SAMA-approved internal risk transfer desk for general interest rate risk, and exact matching with an external market hedge), and specifies the consequences when those conditions fail, including exclusion of the trading book leg from market risk capital and capitalisation of short credit or equity positions under market risk rules. It binds SAMA-licensed banks calculating Pillar 1 market risk and banking book capital requirements.

Concept node for the correlation trading portfolio, one of the securitisation credit spread risk classes used in the market risk capital framework. It matters for bucketing, delta and curvature aggregation, and correlation parameters, where CSR securitisation (CTP) is treated differently from non-securitisation and non-CTP securitisation exposures. It binds banks computing market risk capital under the standardised sensitivities-based method and internal models, including backtesting expectations.

Concept node for general (generalised) interest rate risk, a defined risk class in the market risk capital framework alongside credit spread, FX, equity and commodity risk. It underpins delta, vega and curvature calculations (including parallel-shift curvature shocks on risk-free yield curves) and governs the dedicated internal risk transfer desk regime for hedging banking book interest rate risk into the trading book. It binds banks calculating market risk regulatory capital and managing banking book interest rate risk exposures.
lookup_terms: interest rate risk in the banking book hedge

data.summary: Concept node for credit spread risk as a market risk class, split into non-securitisation, securitisation non-CTP and securitisation CTP, and further split in the CVA framework into counterparty credit spread risk and reference credit spread risk. It drives bucketing, risk weights, correlation parameters and the assignment of eligible hedges, including the rule that a credit spread delta hedge must sit wholly in one risk class. It binds banks computing standardised market risk and SA-CVA capital requirements.

Concept node on the equity risk class within the standardised market risk capital framework: how equity exposures are grouped into buckets (by issuer characteristics) and the intra- and inter-bucket correlation parameters used to aggregate weighted sensitivities. It also connects to disclosure and RWA reporting lines that separate equity positions from general credit risk. It binds banks calculating Pillar 1 market risk capital and completing related regulatory reporting.

Concept node on the commodity risk class in the standardised market risk framework: the bucketing of commodity risk factors into defined groups and the correlation parameters applied when aggregating delta, vega and curvature sensitivities within and across buckets. It also intersects with the treatment of commodities risk in the banking book for internal risk transfer recognition. It binds banks calculating market risk regulatory capital requirements.
lookup_terms: commodities risk in the banking book

data.summary: Node covering the Internal Models Approach for market risk capital and, by contrast, the modelled versus standardised split used in Pillar 3 RWA reporting. It sets when a bank may compute market risk capital using SAMA-approved internal models (expected shortfall, default risk capital, stressed ES for non-modellable risk factors) at the trading desk level, and the qualitative disclosures (Table MRB) required of IMA users on model scope, trading desk structure and key modelling choices. Binds SAMA-licensed banks that have obtained supervisory approval to use internal models, at group-wide regulatory consolidation level.
lookup_terms: standardised approach vs modelled approach RWA

data.summary: Node on Expected Shortfall as the core risk measure in the internal models approach for market risk, including the distinction between unconstrained and constrained ES (sum of partial ES across regulatory risk factor classes), and its aggregation with the default risk capital requirement, the stressed ES capital add-on for non-modellable risk factors and any amber-zone surcharge. It also touches adjacent counterparty exposure measures (EE, EPE, Effective EPE, CVA) used elsewhere in the capital framework. Applies to banks calculating market risk capital under SAMA-approved internal models and reporting the associated disclosure templates.

Orientation node for the Internal Models Approach (IMA) to market risk capital under SAMA's Basel-aligned framework, covering the general architecture of IMA use (trading desk scope, SAMA approval, and the split between expected shortfall, default risk capital and stressed ES for non-modellable risk factors) and the related Pillar 3 qualitative disclosure expectations for IMA banks. It also situates IMA against standardised approaches in the RWA overview reporting. Binds SAMA-licensed banks that have SAMA approval to use internal models for market risk capital.

Node setting the backtesting regime for internal market risk models: daily comparison of a one-day 99th percentile VaR against actual and hypothetical P&L over the prior 12 months (250 trading days), at both bank-wide and trading desk level, with the green/amber/red zone framework driving supervisory consequences. Consequences escalate from no add-on, to a capital add-on scaled to the number of exceptions, to an automatic increase in the multiplication factor or withdrawal of model permission. Binds banks using internal models; SAMA holds the assessment, notification and disallowance powers, and banks must document and explain every exception.

Covers the qualitative and organisational conditions a bank must meet to use internal models for market risk: an independent risk control unit reporting to senior management, regular backtesting and P&L attribution at trading desk level, at least annual independent model validation by a unit separate from model development, and active board and senior management involvement in risk control. It also addresses alignment between regulatory capital models and day-to-day internal risk management models, and how risk factor data quality feeds model eligibility. Binds banks seeking or holding SAMA IMA approval.

Node on the profit and loss attribution test, the second gateway (alongside backtesting) determining whether a trading desk remains eligible for the internal models approach. It requires the PLA programme to start when the internal models capital requirement takes effect, a one-year backtesting and PLA report to support SAMA model approval, and quarterly reassessment of desk eligibility, with amber-zone desks attracting a capital surcharge and failing desks reverting to standardised treatment. Binds banks seeking or holding SAMA internal model approval for market risk.

Sets out the Risk Factor Eligibility Test used to decide whether a market risk factor is modellable (capitalised within the expected shortfall model) or non-modellable (capitalised as an NMRF via stressed ES). Addresses real price observation counting, maturity bucket allocation for credit spread risk factors, treatment of parametric curve/surface parameters, and systematic versus idiosyncratic credit and equity risk factors. Binds banks using the IMA; SAMA retains discretion over data suitability and exceptional relief in systemic stress.

Node defining the regulatory trading desk — the unit of observation for internal model approval, backtesting, PLA testing and market risk capital. It sets the mandatory attributes: an unambiguously defined group of traders or trading accounts, one (exceptionally two) head trader, one desk per trading account, a documented business strategy with annual budget and MI reporting, defined risk scope and permitted risk factors, and a clear risk management structure with reviewed trading limits. Binds banks proposing a desk structure for SAMA approval; internal operational sub-desks fall outside the approved structure and outside the capital framework.
lookup_terms: risk scope and permitted risk factors

data.summary: Node on the bucketing method for satisfying the Risk Factor Eligibility Test, i.e. how real price observations are allocated to standardised or own-defined buckets and counted for modellability purposes, with contextual material on RWA reporting rows distinguishing modelled from standardised approaches. Relevant to banks determining which risk factors qualify for the ES model versus NMRF treatment. Binds SAMA-licensed banks applying the IMA for market risk.

Node governing the boundary between the trading book and the banking book, focusing on internal risk transfers — internal written records of risk transfers within or between the books. It denies any regulatory capital recognition for transfers from the trading book to the banking book, and conditions recognition of banking-book credit, equity and general interest rate risk hedges on an exactly matching external hedge with an eligible third-party protection provider, with defined consequences when those conditions fail. Binds banks determining which positions attract market risk versus banking book capital treatment.
lookup_terms: external hedge eligible third-party protection provider
interest rate risk internal risk transfer

data.summary: States the principles a bank must apply, beyond the mechanical RFET count, to decide whether a risk factor that passed the RFET may actually be modelled in the expected shortfall model: data accuracy and source quality matter, and banks may not rely solely on the number of real price observations. Also records SAMA's power to deem data unsuitable and force NMRF treatment, and its narrow discretion during extraordinary systemic market stress. Binds banks using the IMA.
lookup_terms: risk factor excluded from ES model

data.summary: Node on the internally modelled capital charge for modellable risk factors (IMCC), the ES-based component of the IMA market risk capital requirement, alongside surrounding capital-adequacy reporting context such as RWA/minimum capital requirement templates and capital distribution constraint disclosures. Useful for understanding how modelled market risk capital aggregates into Pillar 1 requirements and disclosure. Binds banks with SAMA approval to use internal models.

A market risk node within SAMA's minimum capital requirements for market risk, covering how foreign exchange risk positions are grouped into buckets and correlated for capital purposes, alongside related material on internal risk transfers between the banking book and trading desks and on the simplified standardised approach (where FX risk is one of four recalibrated risk classes summed arithmetically). It binds banks calculating regulatory capital for market risk, including FX risk arising in the banking book. Relevant when determining FX capital charges, recognition of internal hedges, or use of the simplified standardised approach.

Defines gross jump-to-default (JTD) risk positions as the first step in the standardised default risk capital (DRC) calculation: each exposure's JTD is computed separately before offsetting against the same obligor, allocation to buckets and application of risk weights. It applies to banks computing DRC for non-securitisation portfolios, securitisations (non-CTP) and correlation trading portfolios, and interacts with look-through for credit and equity derivatives and LGD treatment. Binding on banks using the standardised approach for market risk.

Covers net jump-to-default positions: the offsetting of long and short JTD amounts to the same obligor (where permissible) to produce net long/short exposures, which are then allocated to buckets for the default risk capital requirement. Related material addresses net long and net short treatment for correlation trading portfolio positions and nth-to-default products. Binds banks applying the standardised approach to market risk default risk.

Sets out the default risk capital requirement for non-securitisation exposures under the standardised approach, including that no hedging is recognised across buckets (total DRC is the simple sum of bucket-level charges) and that no diversification benefit applies between non-securitisation, securitisation (non-CTP) and CTP DRC. Also covers zero risk weighting of certain sovereign, PSE and MDB claims and treatment of equity investments in funds. Binds banks calculating market risk capital under the standardised approach.

Addresses the default risk capital requirement for securitisation exposures in the correlation trading portfolio (CTP), computing gross JTD on the same basis as securitisations (non-CTP) — i.e. market value with no separate LGD ratio — with related rules on offsetting limits, tranche-based risk weights, the hedge benefit discount and simple summation across buckets. Binds banks holding CTP securitisation positions under the standardised market risk approach.

Concept node for the hedge benefit ratio (HBR), the partial-hedge discount applied to net short exposures within a bucket when aggregating weighted net JTD into the default risk capital requirement, reflecting that long and short positions in distinct obligors do not fully offset. Associated source material also includes SAMA Pillar 3 disclosure templates (e.g. capital distribution constraints, remuneration policy), so the node spans both the capital calculation and disclosure frameworks for banks.

Node covering the treatment of non-modellable risk factors (NMRF) under the internal models approach for market risk: where a risk factor fails the risk factor eligibility test (RFET) or the data quality/modellability principles are not met to SAMA's satisfaction, it must be excluded from the expected shortfall model and capitalised separately as an NMRF (stressed expected shortfall). It also records SAMA's narrow discretion, in extraordinary systemic stress, to continue treating widely non-modellable factors as modellable without reducing capital. Binds banks with IMA-approved trading desks, and frames SAMA's supervisory approval/rejection powers over model inputs.

Node on the default risk capital (DRC) requirement calculated under the internal models approach for trading book positions, sitting within the market risk capital framework and the wider RWA/minimum capital requirement disclosure architecture (Pillar 1 capital normally RWA x 8%). It relates DRC to other RWA components such as credit risk, counterparty credit risk, CVA and securitisation reported separately. Binds banks with SAMA approval to use internal models for market risk.

Node setting out liquidity horizons assigned to risk factors in the expected shortfall calculation under the internal models approach, including how to derive the horizon for multi-sector credit and equity indices by weighted average of underlying instruments mapped to the prescribed 10/20/40/60/120-day buckets, and how instrument maturity can cap the applicable horizon. It also frames the bank-wide ES calculation for modellable risk factors without supervisory constraints on cross-risk-class correlations. Binds banks with IMA-approved trading desks.

Node on aggregating components into the total regulatory capital requirement, covering how Tier 2 items are summed and how deductions (own instruments, reciprocal cross-holdings, investments in capital instruments and other TLAC liabilities of unconsolidated financial entities, 5%/10% thresholds) reduce the capital base. It links to the composition-of-capital disclosure rows and, for market risk, the aggregation of modelled and standardised charges into the total requirement. Binds banks calculating and disclosing regulatory capital.

Node describing the standardised (and simplified standardised) approaches used as the benchmark for comparing modelled RWA against fully standardised RWA across credit, counterparty credit, securitisation, market and operational risk, including definitions of each row/cell for the comparison disclosure. It also covers the phase-in for equity exposures out of the IRB approach and residual RWA not captured elsewhere. Binds banks, particularly those with SAMA approval to use internal models, which must also compute the standardised benchmark.

Node covering interest rate risk measurement under the simplified standardised approach for market risk, together with the framework's defined terms (risk factor, risk position, risk bucket, risk class, sensitivity/delta, look-through approach, embedded derivative) and how interest rate risk arises in commodities and funding positions (cost of carry, forward gap, basis risk). Binds banks applying the simplified standardised approach to trading book and FX/commodity positions.

A component of SAMA's simplified standardised approach for market risk capital, covering the equity risk class (capital requirement CR_EQ), including add-ons for non-delta option risks on equity instruments. Equity risk capital is summed arithmetically with interest rate, FX and commodity risk requirements, and the total is multiplied by 12.5 to derive market risk RWA. It binds banks licensed by SAMA that use the simplified standardised approach rather than the sensitivities-based standardised approach or an internal models approach.

The foreign exchange risk class within SAMA's simplified standardised approach to market risk capital (CR_FX), including additional charges for non-delta option risks arising from FX instruments. Its output is added to the interest rate, equity and commodity risk charges, with the aggregate scaled by 12.5 to produce market risk risk-weighted assets. Applies to banks under SAMA supervision that are eligible for and apply the simplified standardised approach.

The commodities risk class (CR_COMM) under SAMA's simplified standardised approach for market risk, capturing commodity price exposure plus non-delta option risks on commodity instruments. It is one of the four risk classes summed arithmetically before applying the 12.5 factor to obtain market risk RWA. Binds SAMA-licensed banks applying the simplified standardised approach, and is relevant to commodity positions held in the banking book that fall within the market risk capital scope.

Sets the specific risk capital treatment for basket credit derivatives: first-to-default protection is capped at the lower of the summed specific risk charges of the basket's reference credits or the maximum credit event payment, with limited offset where the derivative hedges an underlying position; for nth-to-default with n greater than one, the (n-1) lowest charges are disregarded and no offset is permitted. Externally rated first- or nth-to-default derivatives require the protection seller to use the rating-based treatment. Applies to banks holding or writing such positions in the trading book.

Concept node for SAMA's minimum capital requirements covering counterparty credit risk and credit valuation adjustment risk within the wider capital adequacy framework, alongside related capital composition, deduction and disclosure requirements (including capital distribution constraint disclosure). Useful as an entry point to where CCR and CVA charges sit relative to credit, market and securitisation RWA reporting. Binds banks subject to SAMA's capital adequacy and Pillar 3 disclosure rules.

Concept node for maturity-based treatment in market risk capital, covering the maturity ladder logic used for slotting positions by residual maturity and the related maturity-scaling and offsetting rules (for example, that derivative contract maturity, not underlying maturity, governs offsetting, and that maturities under three months are floored at three months for default risk charge purposes). Relevant to banks calculating standardised market risk capital, including the default risk charge and commodity/interest rate maturity bands.

Concept node for Operational Risk Capital under SAMA's adoption of the Basel standardised approach for operational risk, covering how the Business Indicator Component and Internal Loss Multiplier feed the capital charge and how the resulting RWA and minimum capital requirement are disclosed in Pillar 3 templates (including overview of RWA and capital distribution constraint disclosures). It binds banks licensed by SAMA that must compute and publicly disclose Pillar 1 operational risk capital.

Concept node on the minimum standards banks must meet to use internal operational loss data as a direct input to the operational risk capital calculation, including the 10-year (exceptionally five-year) observation period, documented identification and collection procedures, data quality and integrity expectations, and loss event thresholds. Non-compliance forces capital of at least 100% of the BIC, possible SAMA-imposed ILM above 1, and mandatory Pillar 3 disclosure of the exclusion. Binds banks, in practice those with a Business Indicator above SAR 4.46 billion.

Concept node covering the specific criteria for building the standardised approach loss data set: gross loss, net loss and recovery definitions, what must be included in gross loss (direct P&L charges, consequential costs, provisions, pending losses), reference date and grouped losses. It determines which operational loss events count and how they are measured for capital and Pillar 3 loss templates; binds banks using loss data in the operational risk capital calculation.

Concept node for Counterparty Credit Risk — the risk that a counterparty defaults before final settlement where there is bilateral risk of loss — under SAMA's minimum capital requirements framework for CCR and CVA, including related risks such as rollover risk and general/specific wrong-way risk. It also anchors the Pillar 3 rows where CCR RWA and capital charges are reported separately from general credit risk. Binds banks, with quarterly Q17 reporting to SAMA within 30 days of quarter-end and effect from 1 January 2023.

Concept node on the Internal Models Method for estimating exposure/EAD for counterparty credit risk, which requires prior SAMA approval, is available to both IRB and standardised credit risk banks, and must be applied to all in-scope CCR exposures (or to a full category such as OTC derivatives or SFTs) with a transition plan for remaining material exposures. Related model-governance expectations (independent risk control unit, backtesting, independent validation, board and senior management involvement) apply to internal models used for capital purposes. Binds banks seeking or using model-based capital treatment.

Concept node for Replacement Cost as a component of SA-CCR exposure at default, including the formula for margined trades using threshold, minimum transfer amount and net independent collateral amount, illustrated by worked margin-agreement examples. It also intersects with prudent valuation adjustment disclosure where fair-valued derivative positions are concerned. Relevant to banks calculating counterparty credit risk exposures under SA-CCR.

Node covering SAMA's Basel-aligned minimum regulatory capital requirement for operational risk, sitting within the wider Pillar 1 capital framework (alongside credit, market and counterparty risk RWA) and the related Pillar 3 disclosure templates, including capital distribution constraint disclosures. It sets out how operational risk RWA and capital charges are derived and reported. It binds banks licensed and supervised by SAMA on a consolidated and, where applicable, solo basis.
