lookup_terms: regulatory exposure amount vs carrying value

data.summary: Node covering the internal ratings-based (IRB) approach to credit risk under SAMA's risk-based capital rules, including the conditions for adoption: SAMA approval, phased rollout across asset classes and business units, movement from foundation to advanced approaches, and the requirement for an agreed, realistic implementation plan that is not driven by capital minimisation. Once IRB is adopted for an asset class in a business unit, it must be applied to all exposures in that asset class in that unit, and no capital relief is granted for intra-group transactions engineered to reduce the group charge during rollout. It binds banks seeking or holding SAMA permission to use F-IRB or A-IRB.
lookup_terms: own estimates of LGD and EAD

data.summary: Node within SAMA's Minimum Capital Requirements for Credit Risk covering the external ratings route for assigning risk weights — the External Credit Risk Assessment Approach used for rated bank exposures, and the parallel external-ratings-based treatment of securitization exposures (SEC-ERBA), including the 15% risk-weight floor, tranche maturity/thickness adjustments and the operational criteria for relying on external credit assessments. External assessments must come from an ECAI recognised by SAMA and must capture the full credit risk of all amounts owed. Binds SAMA-licensed banks calculating credit risk RWAs under the standardized approach.

Node in SAMA's Minimum Capital Requirements for Credit Risk setting out the Standardized Credit Risk Assessment Approach applied to unrated bank exposures, requiring classification into Grades A, B or C with base risk weights of 40%, 75% and 150% (20%/50%/150% for short-term exposures), and a 30% option where the counterparty bank meets CET1 and Tier 1 leverage thresholds and Grade A criteria. Related material addresses due diligence over external ratings and the allocation of provisions between standardized and IRB portfolios. Binds SAMA-licensed banks computing credit risk RWAs.
lookup_terms: Grade A Grade B Grade C

data.summary: Node covering the covered bond exposure class within SAMA's standardized approach to credit risk, sitting alongside the other individual exposure classes (sovereigns, PSEs, MDBs, banks, corporates, retail, real estate). It requires banks to perform due diligence so that external ratings conservatively reflect the creditworthiness of both the covered bond and the issuing bank, with an upward risk-weight adjustment where the analysis shows higher risk and no downward adjustment permitted. Binds SAMA-licensed banks.

Arabic SAMA circular clarifying that fees charged by the contract registration company fall within the fees, commissions and administrative service costs subject to the ceiling in Article 83 of the Implementing Regulation of the Finance Companies Control Law (the lower of 1% of the finance amount or SAR 5,000). It confirms such registration fees may not be passed on to the customer outside that cap, consistent with the earlier circular treating all unavoidable charges beyond the finance amount and term cost as within the ceiling. Addressed to banks, finance companies and the Saudi lease contract registration company.

Node setting SAMA's general due diligence obligation under the credit risk framework: banks must understand counterparty risk profiles at origination and at least annually, must not rely on external ratings alone, and must have policies, systems and controls demonstrable to SAMA showing that assigned risk weights are appropriate. It also links to the securitization external-ratings-based approach, where risk weights derive from external or inferred ratings subject to seniority, tranche maturity and thickness. Binds SAMA-licensed banks.

Node defining the corporate exposure class under SAMA's standardized approach to credit risk — loans, bonds and receivables to incorporated entities, associations, partnerships, proprietorships, trusts, funds and similar entities not falling in another class, including insurance companies and other financial corporates, and excluding individuals. It distinguishes general corporate from specialized lending exposures and confirms that securities firms and other financial institutions are treated as corporates. Binds SAMA-licensed banks calculating credit risk RWAs.
lookup_terms: securities firms and other financial institutions

data.summary: Definitional node within SAMA's standardised approach to credit risk setting out when a retail exposure qualifies as "regulatory retail" — product type, an absolute size cap per counterparty (SAR 4.46 million), and a granularity limit of 0.2% of the overall regulatory retail portfolio (excluding defaulted exposures). It also positions regulatory retail against "other retail" and drives the applicable risk weights (75% generally, 45% for transactor exposures, 100% for other retail). Binds banks calculating risk-weighted assets for credit risk under SAMA's minimum capital requirements.

Defines "transactors" for credit risk RWA purposes: obligors on credit card/charge card facilities whose balance was repaid in full at each scheduled repayment date over the previous 12 months, and overdraft obligors with no drawdown over the same period. The classification matters because regulatory retail exposures to transactors attract a 45% risk weight instead of 75%. Applies to banks applying the standardised approach for credit risk.
lookup_terms: credit card charge card repaid in full

data.summary: Sets the perimeter of the real estate exposure class under the standardised approach: immovable property (land and attached buildings), split into regulatory real estate, other real estate, and land acquisition, development and construction (ADC) exposures. It also gives the LTV-based risk weight table for regulatory commercial real estate materially dependent on property cash flows and the risk weights for "other real estate" (counterparty risk weight, or 150% where materially dependent). Binds banks classifying and risk-weighting property-secured lending.

Defines the "regulatory real estate" sub-class and its four buckets: residential and commercial exposures, each split by whether they are materially dependent on cash flows generated by the property. It also sets out the material-dependence test (loan servicing and recovery depending on rental, lease or sale proceeds rather than the borrower's other income), which typically but not exclusively applies to corporates, MSMEs and SPVs. Binds banks determining risk weights for property-secured exposures under the standardised approach.
lookup_terms: materially dependent on cash flows generated by the property
residential vs commercial real estate exposure

data.summary: Defines a "regulatory residential real estate" exposure as a regulatory real estate exposure secured by property having the nature of a dwelling and lawfully occupiable for housing purposes. The definition, read with the material-dependence test, determines which risk weight table applies to residential mortgage lending. Binds banks classifying property-secured credit exposures for capital purposes.

Defines "regulatory commercial real estate" residually as any regulatory real estate exposure that is not regulatory residential real estate, and locates it within the four-bucket regulatory real estate taxonomy split by material dependence on property cash flows. Determines which risk weight schedule applies to commercial property-secured lending. Binds banks applying the standardised approach for credit risk.

Part of SAMA's Minimum Capital Requirements for Credit Risk, this node sets the standardised-approach risk weights for specialised lending where no issue-specific external rating is used, and defines when a project finance exposure qualifies as "high quality" (80% instead of 100% operational-phase / 130% pre-operational). It also carries the IRB asset-class definitions of specialised lending and its sub-classes (project, object, commodities finance, IPRE, HVCRE). It binds SAMA-licensed banks calculating regulatory capital for credit risk.

This node covers the standardised-approach treatment of subordinated debt, equity and other regulatory capital instruments issued by corporates or banks, including the scope carve-outs for instruments deducted from capital, weighted at 250% under the Basel III capital framework, or at 1250%, and equity fund investments treated elsewhere. It also carries the substance-over-form test for identifying equity holdings and the remaining eligibility conditions for high-quality project finance. It binds banks computing credit RWAs.

Defines equity exposures for standardised credit-risk purposes on the basis of economic substance rather than legal form, covering direct and indirect, voting and non-voting ownership interests, instruments settleable in shares (subject to SAMA's satisfaction on debt-like treatment), and equity-linked liabilities, while excluding equity-structured debt or securitisation exposures. Sets the baseline 250% risk weight for equity holdings. Applies to banks subject to SAMA's minimum capital requirements for credit risk.

Identifies "speculative unlisted equity exposures" — investments in unlisted companies held for short-term resale, venture capital or similar price-volatile positions acquired for capital gain — and assigns them a 400% risk weight, against 250% for all other equity holdings. Relevant to banks classifying private-equity, VC and pre-IPO holdings in the banking book under the standardised approach.

Sets the two materiality thresholds for a bank's investments in significant minority- or majority-owned and controlled commercial entities — 15% of capital individually and 60% of capital in aggregate — with amounts below the thresholds risk-weighted under the normal equity/subordinated-debt rules and excess amounts at 1250%. Also carries the 150% weight for non-equity subordinated debt and capital instruments, plus related real-estate collateral definitions and operational requirements. Binds banks calculating credit RWAs.

Defines the standardised-approach retail exposure class (excluding real estate exposures), distinguishing "regulatory retail" (product, low-value SAR 4.46 million counterparty cap, and 0.2% granularity criteria), "transactors", and "other retail", and sets the corresponding risk weights of 75%, 45% and 100%. Covers exposures to individuals and to MSMEs that meet the regulatory retail criteria; non-qualifying MSMEs fall to the corporate treatment. Binds banks computing credit risk capital.

Defines when a regulatory real estate exposure (residential or commercial) is treated as "materially dependent on cash flows generated by the property" — i.e. where loan servicing and recovery on default depend on lease, rental or sale proceeds from the secured property rather than the borrower's other repayment capacity, with an indicative income threshold and expectation that it applies mainly to corporates, MSMEs and SPVs. The classification drives which risk-weight table applies under the standardised approach for credit risk, including the higher LTV-banded weights for commercial exposures and the 150% weight for cash-flow-dependent "other real estate". It binds SAMA-licensed banks calculating minimum capital requirements for credit risk.
lookup_terms: materially dependent on cash flows generated by the property
credit risk standardised approach real estate

data.summary: Sets out the definition and prudent calculation of the loan-to-value (LTV) ratio for real estate exposures — loan amount (including undrawn committed amounts, gross of provisions) divided by property value held at origination value, subject to downward revaluation on SAMA instruction or a permanent idiosyncratic value loss, and upward adjustment only for value-enhancing modifications. It also requires mortgage underwriting policies with defined repayment-ability metrics, including occupancy-type metrics where repayment depends on property cash flows. Binds banks applying the standardised approach to real estate exposures.

Refers to the "whole loan" method of risk weighting real estate exposures, under which a single risk weight determined by the exposure's LTV band is applied to the total exposure amount rather than splitting it into secured and unsecured portions. It is the treatment used for regulatory commercial real estate exposures that are materially dependent on property cash flows (and other specified real estate categories). Applies to banks computing standardised-approach credit RWAs.
lookup_terms: regulatory commercial real estate risk weights

data.summary: Refers to the alternative loan-splitting treatment for real estate exposures, whereby the exposure is divided into a portion covered by the property value (attracting a preferential risk weight) and a residual portion risk weighted as an exposure to the counterparty. It sits alongside the whole loan approach in the standardised approach to real estate and applies to banks calculating credit risk capital requirements.

Defines "other real estate" exposures as real estate asset class exposures that are neither regulatory real estate nor land ADC exposures, and sets their risk weights: the counterparty risk weight where not materially dependent on property cash flows (75% individuals, 85% SMEs, otherwise the unsecured counterparty weight), and 150% where materially dependent. Binds banks applying the standardised approach to credit risk.

Identifies "land acquisition, development and construction" (ADC) exposures as a distinct third category within the real estate asset class, separate from regulatory real estate and other real estate exposures, and carved out of those definitions. The full definition and applicable risk weights sit in the real estate section of the standardised approach; relevant to banks financing land purchase, development or construction.

A component of SAMA's Minimum Capital Requirements for Credit Risk (standardised approach) dealing with the risk weight multiplier applied to unhedged retail and residential real estate exposures where the borrower's income currency differs from the currency of the loan, alongside the related rule that domestic-currency ratings may only be used for domestic-currency exposures. It also touches on limited mitigation where a qualifying multilateral development bank guarantees convertibility and transfer risk. It binds SAMA-supervised banks calculating credit risk-weighted assets.

Bridging provisions in SAMA's credit risk capital rules that route exposures giving rise to counterparty credit risk — OTC and exchange-traded derivatives, long settlement transactions and securities financing transactions — to the exposure-amount calculation in SAMA's Counterparty Credit Risk (CCR) Framework for RWA purposes. Adjacent material covers credit conversion factors for off-balance sheet commitments, including unconditionally cancellable commitments and SAMA's discretion to require higher CCFs. Applies to banks licensed and supervised by SAMA.

Covers the capital treatment of credit derivatives under SAMA's credit risk framework from both sides: banks selling protection through first-, second- and nth-to-default baskets must aggregate underlying risk weights (capped at 1250%) against the notional protection, while as a mitigation technique only credit default swaps and total return swaps equivalent to guarantees are eligible and nth-to-default protection bought gives no capital relief. Also sets the protected/uncovered portion split and 1250% treatment of materiality thresholds. Binds SAMA-supervised banks.

The defaulted exposures section of SAMA's Minimum Capital Requirements for Credit Risk, which sits within the standardised approach chapter on individual exposures and determines risk weights for exposures that have defaulted; surrounding context includes the retail exposure class criteria (granularity, SAR 4.46 million counterparty threshold, transactor definition) from which defaulted retail exposures are excluded. It binds banks supervised by SAMA when computing credit RWAs.

Relates to residual risk weight treatments in SAMA's credit risk capital rules, including "other real estate" exposures (those outside the regulatory real estate and land ADC definitions) and commercial real estate materially dependent on property cash flows, plus recognition of credit risk mitigants and guarantees covering default and dilution risk on purchased receivables. It binds SAMA-supervised banks assigning risk weights to assets not captured by the main exposure classes.

Sets the rules for banks' use of external credit assessments under the standardised approach: SAMA recognition of eligible ECAIs, consistent and non-cherry-picked use of chosen ECAIs and the global rating scale, the multiple-ratings hierarchy (higher of two, second-lowest of three or more), issue-specific versus issuer ratings, short-term rating interactions with the interbank preferential treatment, no group-wide read-across of ratings, and a prohibition on unsolicited ratings. Binds SAMA-supervised banks determining risk weights from external ratings.

Sets out which external credit assessment institutions SAMA recognises for regulatory capital purposes (S&P, Moody's and Fitch) and the eight eligibility criteria an ECAI must satisfy on an ongoing basis, including objectivity, independence, international access/transparency, disclosure, resources, credibility and cooperation with SAMA. It also specifies the conflict-of-interest situations that must be disclosed, drawing on the IOSCO Code of Conduct Fundamentals for Credit Rating Agencies. It binds banks using the standardised approach to credit risk (which may only rely on recognised ECAI ratings) and conditions SAMA's own recognition decisions.
lookup_terms: conflict of interest disclosure rating agency

data.summary: Governs how banks apply recognised ECAI ratings to exposures: consistent use of chosen ECAIs across all exposure types (no cherry-picking), use of global rather than national rating scales unless mapped, and the hierarchy rules where one, two, or three or more ratings exist. It also introduces the issue-specific versus issuer rating principles for determining whether an exposure counts as rated. Binds banks calculating credit risk RWAs under the standardised approach.

Covers the securitisation external-ratings-based approach (SEC-ERBA), under which RWAs for externally rated or inferred-rated securitisation exposures are derived by applying prescribed risk weights to exposure amounts. Risk weights depend on short- or long-term rating grade, tranche seniority, tranche maturity and, for non-senior tranches, tranche thickness, subject to operational criteria for use of external assessments and inferred ratings. Binds banks holding securitisation exposures.

Addresses recognition of credit risk mitigants — collateral, guarantees and credit derivatives — including how mitigants on purchased receivables covering default and/or dilution risk are treated, substitution of the guarantor's risk weight, and proportional/tranched coverage of uncovered portions. It also touches credit conversion factors for commitments and capital treatment of nth-to-default credit derivatives. Binds banks applying IRB and standardised credit risk treatments, including where mitigants interact with the securitisation framework.

Specifies when credit protection with a maturity shorter than the underlying exposure may be recognised: not at all under the simple approach for financial collateral, and otherwise only where original maturity is at least one year and residual maturity at least three months, with a prescribed pro-rata adjustment to the protection value. It requires conservative measurement of both exposure and hedge maturities (including embedded call options) and extends the treatment to securitisation and synthetic securitisation exposures. Binds banks recognising credit risk mitigation for capital purposes.

A node grouping material on approach selection and use within the credit risk framework — the securitisation hierarchy (SEC-ERBA, SEC-IAA, SEC-IRBA), equity investments in funds (look-through, mandate-based and fall-back approaches), unsettled transactions, and the conditions for phased rollout and partial use of the IRB approach. It requires banks adopting IRB for an asset class in a business unit to apply it to all exposures in that class and to agree a realistic implementation plan with SAMA, with no capital relief for intra-group transactions during rollout. Binds banks moving between standardised and internal approaches.

Part of SAMA's Minimum Capital Requirements for Credit Risk dealing with currency mismatch between an exposure and its credit protection or collateral. It requires the protected amount to be reduced by an 8% foreign-exchange haircut (HFX) based on a 10-business-day holding period with daily marking to market, scaled up by the square-root-of-time rule where revaluation is less frequent; it also covers related collateral haircut rules (basket haircuts, non-eligible instruments in SFTs). Binds SAMA-supervised banks calculating credit risk-weighted assets under the standardized approach and applying credit risk mitigation.

Sets out how banks using the Internal Ratings-Based (IRB) approach must sort banking-book exposures into the asset classes of corporate, sovereign, bank, retail and equity, with five specialized lending sub-classes within corporate, three sub-classes within retail, and possible purchased receivables treatment; the IRB approach is not permitted for equity. Banks must apply the correct class-based treatment for minimum capital purposes and must demonstrate to SAMA that their assignment methodology is appropriate and consistently applied over time. Binds SAMA-supervised banks using IRB.
lookup_terms: corporate sovereign bank retail equity exposures

data.summary: Defines Income-Producing Real Estate (IPRE) lending as a specialized lending sub-class of corporate exposures where repayment and recovery depend primarily on cash flows generated by the property (lease/rental income or sale), distinguished from other real estate-collateralized corporate exposures by the strong correlation between repayment and recovery prospects. Related standardized-approach text defines the real estate exposure class, including exposures materially dependent on cash flows generated by the property and ADC exposures. Binds SAMA-supervised banks classifying and risk-weighting real estate lending.
lookup_terms: materially dependent on cash flows generated by the property

data.summary: Defines High-Volatility Commercial Real Estate (HVCRE) lending as financing of commercial real estate with higher loss-rate volatility than other specialized lending, covering property types SAMA categorizes as higher-volatility, loans funding their land acquisition, development and construction (ADC) phases, and other ADC loans repaid from an uncertain future sale or substantially uncertain cash flows. Sits alongside the IPRE definition and the standardized-approach real estate exposure class. Binds SAMA-supervised banks classifying real estate and ADC exposures for capital purposes.

Defines the sovereign asset class for IRB purposes as all counterparties treated as sovereigns under the standardized approach, including sovereigns and their central banks, PSEs identified as sovereigns, MDBs qualifying for a 0% risk weight, and certain other specified entities. Determines which exposures receive sovereign treatment rather than bank or corporate treatment in capital calculations. Binds SAMA-supervised banks classifying banking-book exposures.
lookup_terms: public sector entities PSEs treated as sovereigns

data.summary: Defines the bank asset class as exposures to banks, certain securities firms and other financial institutions treated as banks, covered bonds, domestic PSEs not treated as sovereigns, and MDBs not eligible for a 0% risk weight, plus subordinated debt and regulatory capital instruments of those entities subject to stated conditions (not equity exposures, not deducted from capital or risk-weighted at 250% under SAMA's Basel III guidance). The related standardized-approach text sets the regulatory retail criteria and risk weights, including transactor treatment. Binds SAMA-supervised banks classifying and risk-weighting counterparty exposures.
lookup_terms: securities firms and other financial institutions

data.summary: Defines the retail exposure class under the standardised approach to credit risk, splitting it into "regulatory retail" exposures (subject to product, low-value SAR 4.46 million and 0.2% granularity criteria), exposures to "transactors", and "other retail", and excluding real estate exposures. It sets the corresponding risk weights of 75%, 45% and 100%. Binds SAMA-supervised banks calculating regulatory capital for credit risk.

Sets out the IRB retail asset class sub-classes (residential mortgages, qualifying revolving retail exposures, other retail) and the cumulative criteria a sub-portfolio must meet to be treated as QRRE, including that exposures be revolving, unsecured and uncommitted, applied at sub-portfolio level. Also covers when small business exposures below SAR 4 million may be pooled and managed as retail. Binds banks using the internal ratings-based approach.

Defines eligible purchased receivables and divides them into retail and corporate receivables, setting when the top-down approach may be used instead of individual obligor default-risk assessment, and which IRB approaches (F-IRB or A-IRB) are available for each. Notes that use of the top-down treatment for on-balance sheet corporate exposures requires SAMA approval. Binds banks applying the IRB approach to purchased receivable portfolios.

Describes the supervisory slotting criteria approach for specialised lending, under which banks assign exposures to internal grades using their own criteria and then map those grades to the five supervisory rating categories set out in the slotting tables. It requires demonstrable, consistent mapping and controls over overrides. Applies to banks that cannot meet the IRB requirements for PD estimation on specialised lending exposures.

Governs adoption of the IRB approach across asset classes, permitting a phased rollout across business units, banking group entities and from foundation to advanced approaches, while requiring full application within any asset class in a unit once adopted. Banks must submit a realistic implementation plan agreed with SAMA, and no capital relief is allowed for intra-group transactions designed to reduce group capital during rollout. Binds banks seeking or holding IRB permission.

Provides the IRB corporate firm-size adjustment for MSME borrowers, defined by consolidated group revenues below SAR 223 million, with a revenue floor and a prescribed adjustment to the corporate risk-weight formula. Permits substitution of total assets for revenues, subject to SAMA allowance, where revenue is not a meaningful size indicator. Binds banks using the IRB approach for corporate exposures.

A concept node within SAMA's Minimum Capital Requirements for Credit Risk framework covering the adoption and phased rollout of the internal ratings-based (IRB) approach across asset classes and business units, alongside the structural map of the standard's securitization, fund-investment and unsettled-trade chapters. It sets expectations that a bank moving to IRB must apply it to all exposures in the relevant asset class within a business unit and must agree a realistic implementation plan with SAMA, with no capital relief for intra-group transactions designed to reduce group capital charges. It binds banks licensed and supervised by SAMA that calculate credit risk-weighted assets.

Defines which collateral qualifies for recognition in credit risk mitigation under SAMA's credit risk capital standard, distinguishing eligible financial collateral (as under the standardized approach) from additional eligible IRB collateral such as receivables, commercial and residential real estate and other physical collateral. It also sets the foundation IRB LGD floors for unsecured and subordinated claims and the legal-certainty, enforceability and documentation conditions for recognizing financial receivables. It binds SAMA-supervised banks calculating regulatory capital for credit risk.

Concept node on the standardized approach for counterparty credit risk (SA-CCR) as referenced in SAMA's credit risk capital standard, covering how exposures giving rise to counterparty credit risk (OTC and exchange-traded derivatives, long settlement transactions, securities financing transactions) are measured and fed into risk-weighted assets. It describes the netting-set calculation of replacement cost plus potential future exposure scaled by an alpha factor, including conservative proxies where inputs are unknown, notably when applying the mandate-based approach to equity investments in funds. It binds SAMA-supervised banks with derivative and SFT exposures.

Sets the operational conditions for recognizing credit derivatives as credit risk mitigation and the capital treatment where a bank instead sells protection. Only credit default swaps and total return swaps giving guarantee-equivalent protection are recognized (with a carve-out where total return swap income is booked without recognizing offsetting asset deterioration), while first-to-default and other nth-to-default derivatives give no capital relief and, when protection is sold, attract aggregated basket risk weights capped at 1250%. It binds SAMA-supervised banks using or writing credit protection.

Specifies which entities may be recognized as guarantors, counter-guarantors or credit protection providers for capital relief purposes, generally requiring a lower risk weight than the counterparty. Recognized providers include sovereigns and listed international bodies, PSEs, multilateral development banks, banks, securities firms and other prudentially regulated financial institutions, plus other externally rated entities, with a stricter rating condition where protection is given to a securitization exposure. It binds SAMA-supervised banks claiming credit risk mitigation from guarantees or credit derivatives.

Sets out how risk weights are applied where eligible credit protection is recognized: the protected portion takes the protection provider's risk weight while the uncovered portion retains the counterparty's, and amounts below a materiality threshold are treated as retained first loss and risk weighted at 1250%. It also covers substitution treatment for guarantees over purchased receivables covering default and/or dilution risk, including proportional and tranched coverage. It binds SAMA-supervised banks applying credit risk mitigation under the standardized and IRB approaches.

Sets out how loss given default is determined under the foundation IRB approach for corporate, sovereign and bank exposures, including the supervisory LGD values for unsecured senior and subordinated claims and the categories of collateral that may be recognised (eligible financial collateral plus eligible IRB collateral such as receivables, commercial/residential real estate and other physical collateral). It also prescribes the exposure-weighted LGD* calculation splitting an exposure into secured and unsecured parts, and bars the simple collateral approach for IRB banks. Binds SAMA-supervised banks using the IRB approach for credit risk capital.

Covers the capital treatment of guarantees and credit derivatives as credit risk mitigation, including which credit derivatives (credit default swaps and total return swaps equivalent to guarantees) are eligible, the exclusion of first-to-default and nth-to-default derivatives from CRM recognition, and the substitution of the protection provider's risk weight for the protected portion. It also addresses capital requirements for banks selling protection through basket credit derivatives and the 1250% treatment of materiality thresholds. Applies to banks calculating credit risk RWAs under SAMA's minimum capital requirements.

Addresses the interface between standardized and IRB treatments for provisions and the recognition of credit risk mitigants on purchased receivables, including attribution of general provisions on a pro rata or entity basis and SAMA discretion over internal allocation methods. It also explains how guarantees covering default risk, dilution risk or both are recognised, including proportional and tranched coverage. Binds banks operating partial-use or mixed standardized/IRB credit risk frameworks.

Explains how expected loss amounts are calculated under the IRB approach (PD x LGD x EAD, with best-estimate or supervisory LGD for defaulted exposures) and how the shortfall or excess against eligible provisions is deducted from or added to regulatory capital under the Basel III definition of capital rules. Securitization exposures are excluded from the EL amount and treated separately. Applies to IRB banks supervised by SAMA.

Part of the supervisory slotting approach for specialized lending: banks that cannot estimate PD must map internal grades of object finance exposures to five supervisory categories (strong to default) with prescribed unexpected loss risk weights, with slotting criteria set out separately. It also notes the standardized approach fallback risk weight for object finance where no issue-specific external rating exists. Binds banks holding specialized lending exposures under SAMA credit risk capital rules.
lookup_terms: supervisory categories strong good satisfactory weak

data.summary: Part of the supervisory slotting approach for specialized lending, covering commodities finance exposures where banks do not meet IRB PD estimation requirements and must slot internal grades into five supervisory categories with prescribed risk weights. It sits alongside the standardized approach fallback of a 100% risk weight for commodities finance without an issue-specific external rating. Binds SAMA-supervised banks with specialized lending portfolios.

Part of the IRB chapter on purchased receivables in SAMA's credit risk capital framework, addressing how collateral and guarantees are recognised against default risk and dilution risk. It sets out substitution of the guarantor's risk weight where a guarantee covers the pool's default and/or dilution risk, proportional or tranched treatment of partially covered exposures, and the interaction with securitisation first-loss treatment. It binds banks authorised by SAMA to use the internal ratings-based approach.

Chapter of the SAMA credit risk framework dealing with the IRB treatment of expected losses and eligible provisions, sitting alongside the unexpected-loss capital produced by the risk-weight functions. It covers calculation of expected loss amounts, calculation of provisions, and the comparison of EL against provisions for capital purposes. It applies to banks using the IRB approach under SAMA approval.

Defines total eligible provisions for IRB purposes as the aggregate of specific provisions, partial write-offs, portfolio-specific and general provisions attributed to IRB-treated exposures, plus discounts on defaulted assets, while excluding provisions against securitisation exposures. It also sets the attribution rules where a bank uses the standardised approach for part of its book, generally pro rata to credit RWAs, subject to SAMA discretion over internal allocation methods. Binds banks using IRB, including partial-use banks.

Node within the IRB minimum requirements on rating system design, concerning the dimensions a bank's internal rating system must capture (borrower risk versus facility/transaction characteristics, and the separate treatment required for retail-style pools). Related surrounding material governs use of external ratings, including consistent ECAI use, multiple ratings, issuer versus issue-specific ratings and short-term ratings. Applies to banks seeking or maintaining IRB approval from SAMA.

Node within the IRB minimum requirements addressing reliance on statistical models and other mechanical methods in assigning ratings or estimating risk components, including expectations on data quality, human oversight, model validation and documentation. It sits in the rating system design part of the IRB minimum requirements, adjacent to rules on external ratings and their mapping to risk weights. It binds banks using or applying for the IRB approach.

Section of the IRB minimum requirements governing quantification of risk components — PD, LGD, EAD and, where relevant, maturity — including estimation standards, data requirements, long-run and downturn considerations, and the treatment of defaulted exposures. It underpins the parameter inputs used in the IRB risk-weight functions and in purchased receivables and credit risk mitigation treatments. Applies to banks approved by SAMA to use foundation or advanced IRB.

A chapter-level node of SAMA's minimum capital requirements for credit risk dealing with how internal ratings-based (IRB) banks calculate risk-weighted assets for purchased receivables, which straddle the corporate and retail asset classes. It sets when foundation versus advanced IRB may be used (A-IRB only for corporate obligors themselves eligible for A-IRB; A-IRB only for eligible retail receivables) and lists purchased receivables as separate asset classes for the rule that IRB adoption must be extended across an entire asset class. Binds SAMA-licensed banks approved to use the IRB approach for credit risk.

Sub-section of the IRB purchased receivables chapter covering the calculation of risk-weighted assets for the default risk component of a receivables pool, including how credit risk mitigants such as seller or third-party guarantees and first-loss collateral are recognised and substituted into the pool risk weight. It interacts with the securitisation framework where the same mitigant covers both default and dilution risk. Applies to banks using IRB (and, where relevant, SEC-IRBA) for purchased receivable pools.

Sub-section of the IRB purchased receivables chapter addressing the separate capital treatment of dilution risk (the risk that receivable amounts are reduced by credits, offsets or disputes with the obligor) and how it is combined with or separated from default risk. It explains recognition of guarantees and collateral covering dilution risk alone, default risk alone, or both, including interaction with securitisation first-loss treatment. Binds IRB-approved banks holding purchased receivable pools.

Concept node for the foundation IRB (F-IRB) treatment, under which a bank supplies its own PD estimates while supervisory values are used for other risk components such as LGD and EAD. Relevant to the choice of approach by asset class, to purchased corporate receivables where obligors are not A-IRB eligible, and to the phased rollout from foundation to advanced approaches agreed with SAMA. Binds banks seeking or holding IRB approval.

Concept node for the advanced IRB (A-IRB) treatment, where the bank uses its own estimates of PD, LGD and EAD subject to minimum requirements and SAMA approval. It is the only approach available for retail exposures and eligible retail receivables, and is restricted for corporate purchased receivables to obligors eligible for A-IRB; movement from foundation to advanced forms part of the SAMA-agreed rollout plan. Binds IRB-approved banks and banking groups.

Concept node for KDilution, the capital requirement component attributable to dilution risk on a receivables pool, used alongside the default-risk capital charge in IRB purchased receivables and as an input where such pools sit within the securitisation framework (e.g. capital caps and KIRB-based calculations). It matters for determining aggregate capital requirements and maximum capital caps on securitisation exposures. Relevant to banks using IRB and SEC-IRBA.

Part of SAMA's Minimum Capital Requirements for Credit Risk framework, setting the eligibility, legal-certainty and risk-management conditions under which financial receivables may be recognised as credit risk mitigation. It defines eligible receivables (short-dated commercial/financial claims, excluding securitisation, sub-participation and credit derivative exposures) and requires perfected first-priority security, enforceable documentation, credit-risk assessment of the receivables pool, appropriate margining and ongoing monitoring. It binds banks in Saudi Arabia calculating regulatory capital for credit risk.

A section of SAMA's credit risk capital framework dealing with recognition criteria connected to leasing exposures, appearing alongside supervisory slotting criteria for income-producing real estate (pre-leasing, stabilisation and construction-phase indicators) and collateral/netting treatment for securities financing transactions. It informs how leasing and related property exposures are graded and how collateral value is recognised for capital purposes. Applies to banks calculating credit risk capital under SAMA rules.

A transitional-arrangements section within SAMA's credit risk capital framework, situated near the rules on off-balance sheet items and credit conversion factors and the eligibility criteria for external credit assessment institutions (ECAIs). It is relevant to timing of application of the credit risk standards and to how commitments and external ratings are treated during phase-in. Binds banks subject to SAMA's capital adequacy requirements.

General provisions of SAMA's securitisation capital framework: defines securitisation exposures (including ABS, MBS, credit enhancements, liquidity facilities, swaps, tranched cover and reserve accounts), resecuritisation, eligible underlying pools, and when a bank is treated as originator. It also covers risk-weight floors and adjustments for resecuritisation exposures under the standardised approach. Binds banks holding or originating securitisation positions for regulatory capital purposes.

Sets out the External Ratings-Based Approach for securitisation exposures, including the operational requirements for using external credit assessments and inferred ratings, and the alternative treatment for STC-compliant term and short-term securitisations. It sits within the hierarchy of approaches (SEC-IRBA, SEC-ERBA, SEC-IAA, SEC-SA) and the mixed-pool rules requiring SAMA approval in specified cases. Applies to banks in Saudi Arabia calculating capital for securitisation positions.

Governs the Internal Assessment Approach for unrated securitisation exposures to ABCP programmes (typically liquidity facilities and credit enhancements), requiring SAMA notification and approval, an existing approved IRB model, externally rated ABCP, and internal assessments mapped to ECAI criteria at investment-grade equivalent. Internal ratings must be embedded in the bank's risk management. Binds banks seeking to use internal assessments instead of external ratings for such exposures.

This node covers loss given default (LGD) determination under the IRB approach in SAMA's minimum capital requirements for credit risk, including how LGD for a collateralised transaction is split between the unsecured and collateralised portions after haircuts, and the supervisory LGD parameter floors for corporate exposures by collateral type (with sovereign exposures excluded). It also sets how the floor is pro-rated for partially secured exposures. It binds SAMA-supervised banks using foundation or advanced IRB models for regulatory capital.

This node sets the requirements for estimating exposure at default (EAD) under the IRB framework, covering the definition of EAD as expected gross exposure at obligor default, the floor at current drawn amount for on-balance sheet items, and the additional standards applying to own-EAD estimates for off-balance sheet items under the advanced approach. It requires long-run default-weighted average estimates with a margin of conservatism, conservatism where default frequency and EAD are positively correlated, and prohibits capping reference data at outstanding principal or facility limits. It binds banks approved by SAMA to use advanced IRB EAD estimates.

This node addresses the undrawn limit factor (ULF) method of estimating credit conversion factors and its known instability for facilities close to being fully drawn at the reference date. It requires banks to insulate EAD estimates from that instability, identifies acceptable alternatives (limit factor, balance factor, additional utilisation factor) and rejects capping/flooring or omitting affected observations as inadequate fixes. Applies to banks using advanced IRB EAD models under SAMA's credit risk capital rules.

This node governs how the risk-mitigating effect of guarantees may be reflected in IRB parameters — via adjustment to PD or LGD estimates, with the LGD route available only to banks approved for own LGD estimates, and consistency required across guarantee types and over time. It also requires borrower ratings for both obligor and each recognised guarantor at outset and on an ongoing basis, retention of information on the borrower absent the guarantee, and equivalent treatment for retail pool assignment. Adjacent context sets effective maturity (M) rules. Binds banks applying IRB to corporate, sovereign and retail exposures.

This node covers regulatory capital treatment of credit derivatives: eligibility of credit default swaps and total return swaps as guarantee-equivalent protection (with an exclusion where net swap income is booked without recognising deterioration of the protected asset), ineligibility of first-to-default and other nth-to-default derivatives as credit risk mitigants, and the capital treatment for banks selling such basket protection. It also sets the general substitution-based risk weighting of protected and uncovered portions and the 1250% treatment of amounts below materiality thresholds. Binds SAMA-supervised banks buying or selling credit protection.

This node sets when commercial and residential real estate may be recognised as eligible collateral for corporate claims under IRB — requiring legal enforceability and a perfected lien, objective fair-market valuation, and revaluation at least annually (more often in volatile markets) — and excludes income-producing real estate falling in the specialised lending asset class. It also carries the standardised approach definition of the real estate exposure class (regulatory residential/commercial real estate, other real estate, and ADC exposures). Binds banks calculating credit risk capital on real estate-secured exposures.

This node covers the operational conditions under which a bank may recognise credit risk transference and credit risk mitigants for purchased receivables and securitised pools under SAMA's minimum capital requirements for credit risk. It sets out how guarantees and collateral covering default risk, dilution risk or both are reflected (substitution of the guarantor's risk weight, tranched or proportional cover, first-loss treatment), and how master netting agreements and VaR-based approaches affect counterparty credit risk for SFTs. It binds SAMA-licensed banks calculating RWAs under the IRB and securitisation approaches.

This node describes the Simple, Transparent and Comparable (STC) framework as adopted in SAMA's credit risk capital rules, which limits alternative (preferential) securitisation capital treatment to traditional securitisations, ABCP conduits and conduit-financed transactions that meet defined criteria. It allocates disclosure duties to the originator/sponsor and an independent compliance assessment duty to the investor, with criteria required to be met on an ongoing basis. It binds banks holding or originating securitisation exposures that wish to apply the alternative capital treatment.

This node covers the general provisions of the securitisation framework, including scope, the definitions of traditional and synthetic securitisation, and the treatment of credit risk mitigation applied to securitisation exposures. It explains that capital treatment follows economic substance rather than legal form, how RWAs and exposure amounts are computed, and how provisions and purchase price discounts interact with 1250% risk-weighted positions. It binds banks with originated, retained, repurchased or invested securitisation exposures; SAMA consultation is expected where classification is uncertain.

This node identifies SAMA's issuance of the revised Basel III credit risk framework (Minimum Capital Requirements for Credit Risk), grounded in SAMA's Charter and the Banking Control Law, and its supersession of earlier circulars on ECAI rating mapping, IRB approaches, mortgage RWAs and MSME RWAs. It also anchors cross-references to the earlier Basel III guidance circular (No. 341000015689) for capital deduction and 250% risk-weight treatment. It binds SAMA-licensed banks calculating credit risk RWAs.
lookup_terms: minimum capital requirements for credit risk

data.summary: This node sets out the short-term STC capital criteria applicable to asset-backed commercial paper (ABCP) conduits and the transactions they finance, distinguishing criteria that must be met at conduit level from those tested at transaction level. Conduit-level exposures qualify only if criteria are satisfied at both levels, while transaction-level exposures qualify on transaction-level compliance alone. It binds sponsors and investing/supporting banks seeking alternative capital treatment for ABCP exposures.

This node defines the ABCP conduit and related terminology (sponsor, transaction, beneficial interest) used in the securitisation and short-term STC provisions of SAMA's credit risk capital framework. It clarifies that a conduit may finance transactions of different asset types provided each underlying transaction is homogeneous, and that programme-wide credit enhancement does not by itself defeat STC eligibility. It is relevant to banks acting as sponsor, liquidity provider or investor in ABCP programmes.

A concept node for the role of the "sponsor" as used in SAMA's Minimum Capital Requirements for Credit Risk. It covers two distinct uses: the sponsor/developer strength factor in the supervisory slotting criteria for specialised lending (project finance and income-producing real estate), where track record, financial standing and strategic commitment drive the slotting category; and the sponsor of an ABCP conduit under the STC criteria, where the sponsor must provide full liquidity and credit protection support and a single "main sponsor" must carry the majority of that support. It binds banks in Saudi Arabia calculating credit risk RWAs, particularly under the IRB/slotting and securitization frameworks.

Chapter 23 of SAMA's Minimum Capital Requirements for Credit Risk defines an NPL securitization by reference to the underlying pool's W variable being at or above 90% at the origination cut-off date and at any later replenishment or restructuring date, and limits eligible underlying exposures to loans and loan-equivalent or subparticipation instruments (re-securitizations excluded). It restricts use of SEC-IRBA where the foundation approach is used for KIRB and applies a risk-weight floor to exposures under SEC-IRBA, SEC-SA and the look-through approach. SAMA retains discretion to impose a stricter definition, including a higher W threshold or criteria for non-delinquent exposures; it binds banks holding or originating such exposures.

A concept node covering how dilution risk on purchased receivables is recognised in SAMA's Minimum Capital Requirements for Credit Risk. It addresses collateral or partial guarantees acting as first-loss protection (with a link to the securitization treatment), the exposure-weighted LGD calculation under SEC-IRBA where one mitigant covers both default and dilution risk, and the substitution/partial-coverage rules where a seller or third-party guarantee covers default risk, dilution risk or both. It binds banks applying the IRB and securitization frameworks to receivables pools.

This node covers the eligibility and use of External Credit Assessment Institutions under SAMA's Minimum Capital Requirements for Credit Risk. It sets recognition criteria (including resources, credibility, disclosure of conflicts of interest and cooperation with SAMA through notification of methodology changes and data access) and the stricter conditions for using ECAI ratings on securitization exposures, notably free, non-selective public availability of ratings and methodologies, demonstrated securitization expertise, treatment of multiple differing ratings, and no double-counting where credit risk mitigation is already reflected in the rating. It binds banks relying on external ratings for risk weighting and conditions ECAI recognition by SAMA.

A SAMA circular (Arabic) confirming earlier instructions that the ownership document issued by the Economic Cities Authority must be accepted as an official title document for any property or land owner inside the economic cities, standing in place of the title deed used outside those cities. It is a compliance/collateral-documentation instruction rather than a prudential rule. It binds banks operating in the Kingdom and real estate finance companies.

A SAMA circular (Arabic) requiring licensed banks and finance companies to begin registering finance lease contracts with the Saudi Company for Registration of Finance Lease Contracts (Sijil) from a specified commencement date. It relies on the Banking Control Law, the Finance Companies Control Law and the Finance Lease Law (including the registration company mandate) together with the Implementing Regulation obligation on the lessor to register the contract and its amendments within ten business days and to record dispositions affecting lessor and lessee contractual rights. It binds banks and finance companies operating in the Kingdom acting as lessors.
lookup_terms: lessor registration obligation ten business days
Implementing Regulation of the Finance Lease Law

data.summary: A component of SAMA's Rules on Management of Problem Loans setting the viability conditions a bank must satisfy before granting long-term or short-term restructuring measures to a borrower in difficulty. It requires documented evidence of borrower affordability, treatment of outstanding arrears, avoidance of serial or consecutive restructurings, and escalated internal controls (including designated Senior Management Committee approval) where a loan has been restructured before. It binds banks licensed under the Banking Control Law and interacts with the NPL strategy, workout unit independence and performance management requirements in the same instrument.

The collateral section of SAMA's Rules on Management of Problem Loans, setting governance, classification and general management requirements for collateral and guarantees taken by banks, applicable across the whole credit process regardless of loan performance. It requires Board-approved (or delegated) collateral policies reviewed at least every three years, valuer governance and quality assurance, internal audit review, documented collateral types (financial collateral, leased assets, other funded credit protection, guarantees) and legal enforceability review including for foreign branches and subsidiaries. It binds banks licensed under the Banking Control Law.

A cross-reference node linking SAMA's Rules on Management of Problem Loans to SAMA's Rules on Credit Risk Classification and Provisioning, which the problem-loans rules must be read alongside. The surrounding context sets eligibility conditions for credit risk mitigants — leased assets, third-party cash deposits/cash-assimilated instruments (pledge or assignment must be legally effective, unconditional, irrevocable and notified), and guarantees (direct, explicitly documented, clearly defined, no unilateral cancellation clauses). Relevant to banks determining classification, Loss Given Default inputs and provisioning treatment of secured exposures.

The definitional and scoping part of SAMA's Rules on Management of Problem Loans (issued under the SAMA charter and the Banking Control Law), which adopts the BCBS 403 definitions of non-performing exposures and forbearance as endorsed by SAMA circular no. 381000099757 dated 23/09/1438AH. It defines problem loans, non-performing loans, watch-list, early warning signals, cooperating and viable borrower, viability assessment, covenant and KPIs, and states the objectives (borrower rehabilitation, fair customer treatment especially for MSMEs, adequate controls). It applies to all banks licensed under the Banking Control Law.

The Executive Regulation of the Credit Information Law (issued under Royal Decree M/37 dated 5/7/1429H), the implementing framework administered by SAMA. It covers licensing of credit information (credit bureau) companies — including the joint-stock form, minimum paid-up capital of SAR 50 million, application contents, fees, five-year licence term and renewal, and prior written SAMA approval for branches, mergers and constitutional changes — plus scope of credit information services, governance, the credit record, supervisory requirements, confidentiality, member obligations, objections and complaints, and the committee for violations and credit information disputes. It binds licensed credit information companies and Members (government or private entities that exchange credit information with at least one bureau).

The Credit Record concept as defined in the Executive Regulation of the Credit Information Law: a report issued by a licensed credit information company containing credit information about a Consumer (natural or legal person having credit dealings). Related defined terms include credit information, public records (specialised funds, banks granting government loans, judicial bodies, government committees, bankruptcy and insolvency files), negative information and adverse decision — a decision by a Member against the consumer's interest based on the credit record. It is relevant to bureaus compiling records and to Members relying on them for credit decisions, consumer disclosure and dispute handling.

A defined risk class within SAMA's Minimum Capital Requirements for Market Risk framework, sitting alongside general interest rate risk, credit spread risk, FX risk and equity risk. It governs how banks identify commodity risk factors and compute capital requirements (including under the sensitivities-based and simplified standardised approaches), and it is one of the risks that may arise in the banking book and be moved via internal risk transfers with capital recognition. Binds SAMA-licensed banks calculating regulatory market risk capital.
lookup_terms: commodities risk in the banking book

data.summary: FX risk is one of the prescribed market risk classes in SAMA's market risk capital standard, capturing loss potential from exchange rate movements on positions whose currency differs from the bank's reporting currency. The node covers FX capital requirements under the simplified standardised approach and the treatment of FX positions in the banking book for internal risk transfer purposes. Applies to banks computing regulatory capital for market risk.

PV01 is the interest-rate delta sensitivity measure used in the sensitivities-based method: the change in an instrument's market value from a one basis point shift in the relevant rate risk factor. The standard requires sensitivities to be derived from the pricing models the bank's independent risk control unit uses for market risk or actual P&L reporting, with alternative formulations permitted only if demonstrated to SAMA as producing very close results. Binds banks using the standardised approach for market risk.

CS01 is the credit spread delta sensitivity used for credit spread risk classes (non-securitisation, securitisation non-CTP and CTP): the change in instrument value from a one basis point move in the credit spread at a given tenor. The standard permits proxying PV01 to CS01 where counterparty-specific money market curves are unavailable. Relevant to banks computing standardised market risk capital.

Jump-to-default risk is the exposure the default risk capital (DRC) requirement is designed to capture, i.e. sudden default losses not reflected in credit spread shocks under the sensitivities-based method. The node covers gross and net JTD computation, permitted offsetting against the same obligor, allocation to buckets, and partial hedge benefit across distinct obligors, for non-securitisation, securitisation non-CTP and CTP portfolios. Binds banks calculating standardised market risk capital.

The look-through approach requires a bank to treat the underlying constituents of index instruments, multi-underlying options and equity investments in funds as if held directly when calculating delta and curvature risk. It sets the narrow conditions for opting out (widely recognised listed indices meeting constituent-count, concentration and market-capitalisation tests), excludes index CTP instruments from decomposition, and demands consistent application over time and across identical instruments. Binds banks using the standardised approach for market risk.

A node within SAMA's Minimum Capital Requirements for Market Risk describing the simplified alternative to the standardised approach, one of the permitted methodologies for measuring market risk capital alongside the full standardised approach and the internal models approach (IMA). It sets indicative eligibility criteria (not a G-SIB or D-SIB, no IMA use on any trading desk, no correlation trading positions), makes use of the alternative conditional on SAMA approval and ongoing oversight, and preserves SAMA's power to require the full standardised approach where risks are complex or sizeable. It also covers the simplified treatment of commodity and options positions, binding SAMA-licensed banks with smaller or simpler trading books.
lookup_terms: simplified alternative to the standardised approach

data.summary: A concept node covering the trading book policy framework in SAMA's market risk capital rules, in particular the documentation and treatment of internal risk transfers within the banking book, between banking and trading books, and between trading desks. It sets the conditions under which a banking book credit, equity or general interest rate risk exposure is deemed hedged (exact matching external hedge with an eligible third-party protection provider, documentation, dedicated internal risk transfer desk) and the capital consequences where those conditions fail. It binds SAMA-licensed banks calculating regulatory capital for market risk.
lookup_terms: banking book to trading book hedge

data.summary: Defines the trading desk as the unit of observation for the market risk capital framework: an unambiguously defined group of traders or trading accounts with a head trader (or up to two with separated or hierarchical authority), a defined risk scope and permitted risk factors, a documented business strategy with annual budget and management information reporting, and a clear risk management structure with reviewed trading limits. Desk structures require SAMA approval, though banks may create operational subdesks internally without approval (which have no capital-framework effect). It binds SAMA-licensed banks organising trading activity for market risk capital purposes.
lookup_terms: desk risk scope permitted risk factors

data.summary: A defined-term node for the trading book under SAMA's market risk capital rules, drawn from the provisions on boundary treatment and internal risk transfers between the trading and banking books. It governs when a trading book leg of an internal risk transfer receives regulatory capital recognition, confirms that transfers from trading book to banking book get no capital recognition, and requires trading book legs to meet the same requirements as externally transacted trading book instruments. It binds SAMA-licensed banks determining market risk capital requirements.

A defined-term node for the banking book as used in SAMA's market risk capital framework, mainly through the internal risk transfer provisions. It sets when a banking book credit, equity or interest rate exposure is treated as hedged for banking book capital purposes, and requires banking book short credit or short equity positions created by internal risk transfers and not capitalised under banking book rules to be capitalised under the market risk rules. It binds SAMA-licensed banks allocating exposures across the banking/trading book boundary.
lookup_terms: interest rate risk in the banking book
FX and commodities risk in the banking book

data.summary: A concept node for equity risk as one of the defined risk classes in SAMA's market risk capital framework, alongside general interest rate risk, credit spread risk (non-securitisation and securitisation), FX risk and commodity risk. The surrounding material covers the treatment of internal risk transfers of equity and interest rate risk from banking book to trading book, and supporting definitions such as risk factor, risk position, risk bucket, sensitivity and delta risk. It binds SAMA-licensed banks calculating market risk capital requirements.

SAMA circular (Arabic) issued under the Finance Companies Control Law and its Implementing Regulation making use of the Ministry of Commerce/SOCPA "Qawaem" program mandatory as the source of financial statements for commercial entities that are required to file there, before any credit facility is extended. It binds all finance companies licensed in the Kingdom, with credit information companies also on the distribution list, effective from the date stated in the circular. Relevant to credit-underwriting evidence standards rather than prudential capital.

SAMA circular (Arabic) permitting the Saudi Real Estate Refinance Company (SRC) to purchase residential real estate finance portfolios from real estate financiers once at least three months have elapsed from grant of the underlying finance (or from receipt of the first instalment from the beneficiary, whichever applies). It is issued as an exercise of SAMA's power to exempt certain disposals of finance assets from the general Rules on Disposal of Finance Assets or Rights Arising Therefrom, and is addressed to banks and finance companies operating in the Kingdom.

The framework and definitional part of SAMA's Rules on Management of Problem Loans, issued under the SAMA Charter and Banking Control Law and applicable to all licensed banks. It sets the objectives (rehabilitating viable borrowers, fair customer treatment especially for MSMEs, and adequate controls over NPL and restructuring processes) and defines key terms such as problem loans, non-performing loans, watch-list, early warning signals, cooperating and viable borrower, viability assessment, covenant and failed restructuring. It must be read together with SAMA's Rules on Credit Risk Classification and Provisioning, with a separate SAMA guidance document offering good practice.

The early warning signals component of the Rules on Management of Problem Loans, requiring banks to build documented policies, tools and governance for EWS fully integrated into their risk management framework and calibrated to each lending portfolio. It sets out the categories of indicators banks must consider — economic environment, financial (including periodic interim financials or cash-flow/turnover data for MSMEs), behavioural, third-party and operational — so deterioration is detected and acted on before default. Applies to all banks licensed under the Banking Control Law.

Covers the NPL strategy and EWS-monitoring requirements under SAMA's problem loan framework: banks must adopt a Board-approved NPL strategy setting quantitative short, medium and long-term targets, resource allocation and controls, and must consider the full range of resolution options (hold/restructure, portfolio sales, write-offs, collateral repossession, legal and out-of-court routes) applying proportionality and materiality. It also requires monitoring of triggered EWS with corrective action plans, and periodic review of the strategy and its operational plan within the bank's risk management framework. Binds licensed banks.

Sets out the organisational and conduct requirements for problem loan workout: banks must establish a dedicated Workout Unit independent of business/loan-originating units, properly staffed, with performance appraisal and compensation matrices that are not based solely on NPL volume reduction. It also covers borrower-facing elements — standardised appeal forms with defined information and timelines, a documented workout fee policy assessed against borrower cash-flow impact and communicated transparently, and a code of conduct — plus workout plan requirements including Management Committee approval and time-bound criteria for mandatory transfer of loans to the Workout Unit.

Licensing chapter of the Implementing Regulation of the Credit Information Law (Royal Decree M/37), setting the prohibition on conducting credit information activity without a SAMA licence and the conditions for obtaining one. It binds founders and licensed credit information companies (bureaus): joint-stock form with head office in KSA, minimum paid-up capital of SAR 50 million, SAMA approval of constitutional documents and the credit information system, application contents and fees, five-year licence term with renewal fees and timing, grounds for licence expiry or cancellation, and prior written SAMA approval for branches, subsidiaries, mergers/acquisitions and amendments to constitutional documents. Relevant when assessing market entry, corporate change approvals, or the status of an entity handling consumer credit records.

SAMA's Minimum Capital Requirements for Market Risk framework (Basel FRTB as adopted in KSA), covering trading book/banking book boundary, internal risk transfers, the standardised approach, the internal models approach and related definitions. It obliges all banks — D-SIBs and non-D-SIBs — to compute market risk capital under the standardised approach, with RWAs derived by a 12.5 multiplier, and conditions recognition of internal risk transfers (including CVA-related transfers) on documentation and exact external hedging.

The standardised approach provisions of SAMA's market risk capital rules, mandating that all banks calculate the market risk capital charge under the standardised approach, with any alternative method requiring SAMA approval. It sets the RWA conversion (capital requirement × 12.5), SAMA's power to demand standardised-approach figures, and the conditions and indicative criteria under which a smaller bank may use the simplified alternative (non-G-SIB/D-SIB, no IMA desks, no correlation trading positions), subject to SAMA approval and oversight.

The internal models approach (IMA) provisions of SAMA's market risk framework, available only with prior SAMA approval and in parallel with standardised-approach calculation and reporting. It imposes governance and control obligations on banks: an independent risk control unit reporting to senior management, regular trading-desk-level backtesting and P&L attribution assessments, a separate model validation unit validating all IMA models at least annually, and active board and senior management involvement in risk control.

Concept node for the risk-theoretical P&L used in the P&L attribution (PLA) test under the internal models approach, produced by a trading desk's risk management model from the risk factors it captures. It underpins whether a desk remains IMA-eligible, and connects to the framework's defined terms (risk factor, risk position, risk bucket, risk class, sensitivities) and to rules on aligning and documenting RTPL input data with SAMA notification and justification.

Concept node for the hypothetical P&L used in backtesting and the PLA test, measuring the change in end-of-day portfolio value holding positions unchanged, excluding intraday trading and new or modified deals (unlike actual P&L). The rules bind banks on what must be excluded (fees and commissions, CVA and DVA-type adjustments capitalised elsewhere), which valuation adjustments must be included, the ban on smoothing non-daily adjustments, and the treatment of adjustments not computable at desk level, with SAMA agreement or support required in specified cases.

Concept node for the Expected Shortfall model used under the internal models approach (IMA) in SAMA's Minimum Capital Requirements for Market Risk. It covers which risk factors may be calibrated within the ES model (those passing the risk factor eligibility test and satisfying the modellability principles), SAMA's power to deem data unsuitable and force exclusion, and the backtesting/exception framework used to judge model accuracy. It binds banks in Saudi Arabia that use internal models for market risk capital, subject to SAMA supervisory approval.

Concept node for non-modellable risk factors: risk factors that fail the risk factor eligibility test (RFET) or whose data SAMA deems unsuitable must be excluded from the ES model and capitalised separately as NMRFs. It sets out the RFET observation thresholds (24 or 100 real price observations, with 90-day gap and monitoring conditions) and the criteria for what counts as a real price, including third-party vendor prices and committed quotes. Applies to banks using the internal models approach for market risk.

Concept node for the stress testing programme required of banks using the internal models approach for market risk capital. It requires rigorous, comprehensive stress testing at both trading desk and bank-wide level, covering low-probability market, credit and operational risk events, linear and non-linear positions, and both quantitative and qualitative elements, with results reported to senior management and periodically to the board. Banks must combine SAMA-specified scenarios with their own bank-specific scenarios.
lookup_terms: board reporting of stress test results

data.summary: Node for the Saudi Central Bank as the issuing and supervisory authority of the Minimum Capital Requirements for Market Risk (December 2022). SAMA sets scope of application, approves trading desks and internal models, imposes backtesting add-ons or multiplication factor increases, and may disallow model use or require standardised approach calculations. It is the counterparty of every supervisory obligation in the framework for banks operating in KSA.
lookup_terms: Minimum Capital Requirements for Market Risk

data.summary: Node marking the points where the market risk framework interfaces with credit risk capital treatment: specific risk capital for first-to-default and nth-to-default credit derivatives, internal CVA risk transfers between the CVA portfolio and the trading book, and the boundary between banking-book and trading-book credit exposures. It also records that all banks (D-SIBs and non-D-SIBs) must compute market risk capital under the standardised approach, with RWA derived by a 12.5 multiplier. Binds banks in KSA calculating credit-related market risk charges.

Concept node for risk buckets under the standardised approach sensitivities-based method: the prescribed groupings of risk factors by risk class to which risk weights and correlation parameters are assigned for delta, vega and curvature risk. It covers sector versus index bucket mapping for multi-underlying and index options (including the 75%-constituent test) and the liquidity-horizon calibration of weights and correlations. Applies to all banks computing market risk capital under the standardised approach.

A concept node within SAMA's Minimum Capital Requirements for Market Risk covering the default risk charge (DRC) treatment of securitisation exposures outside the correlation trading portfolio. It sets how gross and net jump-to-default positions are computed for tranches — market value rather than an LGD-adjusted exposure, since LGD is embedded in securitisation default risk weights — and restricts offsetting to tranches sharing the same underlying asset pool, with limited recognition of decomposition into replicating tranches or single-name equivalents. It binds banks calculating market risk capital under the standardised approach.

A defined-term node for Actual P&L (APL) in SAMA's market risk framework: the profit and loss produced by the bank's daily P&L process, including intraday trading, time effects and new or modified deals, but excluding fees, commissions and valuation adjustments capitalised elsewhere (e.g. CVA) or deducted from CET1. APL is compared against hypothetical P&L and model outputs in backtesting and profit-and-loss attribution, and governs which valuation adjustments enter the comparison and at what level (desk versus bank-wide). It binds banks seeking or maintaining internal models approach permission.

A concept node describing the Spearman rank correlation metric, one of the two profit-and-loss attribution test metrics used to assess how closely a trading desk's risk-theoretical P&L tracks its hypothetical P&L. It specifies ranking both 250-day time series by size and computing the rank correlation, and prohibits aligning HPL inputs to RTPL or adjusting either series for operational noise. It applies to banks running trading desks under the internal models approach.

A concept node covering the Kolmogorov-Smirnov distributional test metric — the largest absolute gap between the empirical cumulative distributions of risk-theoretical and hypothetical P&L — and its use, with the Spearman metric, to place a trading desk in the PLA green, amber or red zone. It carries the consequence that a red-zone desk loses internal models eligibility and must use the standardised approach until it returns to green and clears backtesting exception requirements. It binds banks with IMA-approved trading desks.
lookup_terms: PLA red zone amber zone green zone

data.summary: A defined-term node setting the regulatory liquidity horizons used to scale expected shortfall from a 10-day base horizon in the internal models approach. It prescribes the assignment of horizons (10 to 120 days) by risk factor category — interest rate, credit spread, equity, FX, commodity and their volatilities — including treatment of repo, dividend, inflation and basis risk factors. It binds banks computing daily ES for bank-wide and desk-level market risk capital.

A concept node relating to the aggregate internally modelled capital charge for modellable risk factors (IMCC) and the surrounding conditions for internal model use, including the risk factor eligibility test, the qualitative modellability principles, and SAMA's power to deem data unsuitable so that a factor is capitalised as a non-modellable risk factor. Context also covers the general standardised approach provisions, under which all banks — D-SIBs and non-D-SIBs — must calculate market risk capital, and internal CVA risk transfer recognition. It binds banks calculating market risk regulatory capital.
