Concept node covering the stress-scenario dimension of SAMA's market risk capital framework: the mandatory stress testing programme for banks using the internal models approach (desk-level and bank-wide), and the three prescribed correlation scenarios (medium, high, low) under which the sensitivities-based method capital requirement must be recalculated, with the highest result binding. It binds banks calculating market risk capital, with results to be escalated to senior management and periodically to the board. Relevant where a bank must combine SAMA-specified scenarios with its own bank-specific stress scenarios.

Concept node on stressed expected shortfall as the calibration basis for internal-model market risk capital, including the data-quality principle that inputs must reflect prices observed or quoted during the stress period and be sourced from the historical stress window where possible. It also touches adjacent IMA model-validation mechanics (front/back office versus risk price comparisons, data update frequency, P&L attribution zones and backtesting). Binds banks with IMA model approval for market risk.

Concept node defining the reduced set of risk factors used for the indirect calibration of the expected shortfall measure to a stress period, including the requirement for SAMA approval, compliance with modellable-risk-factor data quality standards, and the 75% explanatory-power threshold measured at group level across IMA-approved desks. It also frames identification of the stressed period by maximising the aggregate capital requirement for modellable risk factors. Binds banks using internal models for market risk capital.

Concept node on interest rate risk within the market risk capital framework, spanning the defined-terms layer (risk factor, risk position, risk bucket, risk class including general interest rate risk, sensitivity/delta) and the standardised and simplified standardised treatments of interest rate exposures, including interest rate risk embedded in commodity forward positions and funding of positions. Binds banks calculating market risk capital requirements for debt and rate-sensitive instruments.

Concept node on commodities risk as a market risk class, covering the risks captured (spot directional, basis, interest rate/cost of carry, forward gap) and the measurement options under the simplified standardised approach, alongside the general structure of the standardised approach and the RWA conversion using the 12.5 multiplier. Notes that all banks, D-SIB and non-D-SIB, must calculate market risk capital under the standardised approach. Binds banks holding commodity or commodity-derivative positions.

Concept node addressing issuer-specific market risk and the boundary/internal risk transfer rules that determine whether banking book credit, equity and interest rate exposures hedged internally receive capital recognition in the trading book. It sets conditions for exact matching with external third-party hedges, treatment of the internal risk transfer desk, and the consequence where conditions are not met (external hedge fully capitalised, trading book leg excluded). Binds banks operating trading desks and transferring risk between banking and trading books.

A concept node within SAMA's minimum capital requirements for market risk framework, covering general market risk as one of the risk components measured under the trading book regime, including the treatment of internal risk transfers between the banking book, trading desks and the internal risk transfer desk, and the mandatory use of the standardised approach. It sets when internal risk transfer legs receive regulatory capital recognition and how market risk RWA are derived (capital requirement multiplied by 12.5). It binds all SAMA-licensed banks, both D-SIBs and non-D-SIBs.

A concept node in SAMA's market risk capital rules dealing with when specific risk capital requirements on credit derivative positions may be offset against hedged cash or derivative positions. It sets full, partial or no allowance depending on matching of reference obligation, maturity, currency and contract features, and prescribes the treatment of first-to-default and nth-to-default basket credit derivatives for protection sellers. It applies to banks computing specific risk capital for trading book credit positions.

A concept node relating to the internal models approach under SAMA's market risk framework, where a multiplication factor is applied to modelled risk measures, alongside the rules on risk factor modellability, the risk factor eligibility test (RFET) and treatment of non-modellable risk factors (NMRF). It addresses data quality expectations, SAMA discretion to deem a risk factor non-modellable, and the evidence banks must produce on modellability. It binds banks seeking or maintaining model-based market risk capital treatment.

A concept node covering value-at-risk and the surrounding defined vocabulary of SAMA's market risk capital framework, including risk factor, risk position, risk bucket, risk class, sensitivity, delta risk, embedded derivative and the look-through approach. It functions mainly as a definitional anchor for how market risk measures and capital charges are constructed. It is relevant to all banks calculating market risk capital requirements under SAMA rules.

A concept node from SAMA's guidance on management of problem loans setting out early warning signals (EWS) as a mandatory framework element for identifying borrowers likely to face payment difficulties before default. It covers the three-stage EWS process (identification, action, monitoring), allocation of responsibility to an independent risk/middle or back office function, escalation to the Workout Unit, staff training, incentives and supporting data infrastructure. It binds SAMA-regulated banks in respect of corporate and MSME lending.

A concept node from SAMA's problem loan / NPL guidelines addressing the identification, monitoring and resolution of non-performing loans to large corporates and MSMEs, including restructuring, liquidation, foreclosed assets, provisioning and coverage levels. It sets expectations for granular NPL KPIs, portfolio monitoring, peer benchmarking and senior management reporting, and distinguishes borrower 'ability to pay' from 'willingness to pay'. It is directed at banks operating in the Kingdom and their workout and senior management functions.

A concept node within SAMA's Guidelines on Management of Problem Loans (2020) describing the watch list generated from the Early Warning Signals (EWS) process: how loans enter it, minimum data content (loan details, group/related-party status, materiality, inclusion date, review timestamps and outcomes, mitigation measures, reasons), and the governance around it. It sets expectations that risk management approves removal, that a loan may only stay listed for a bank-defined period before returning to the originating unit or moving to the Workout Unit, and that the list (or material exposures) is reported monthly to a designated management committee and, for major cases, the Board. Directed at banks' credit risk, relationship management and workout functions.

Concept node from SAMA's Guidelines on Management of Problem Loans covering segmentation of the non-performing loan portfolio into homogeneous groups as the first step of NPL resolution. It sets out the timing (immediately on transfer to the Workout Unit, before assignment to a workout officer), the principles of proportionality and materiality in resource allocation, and stage-one criteria such as nature of business (MSME vs corporate), legal status, arrears/days-past-due buckets and loan balance thresholds. Applies to banks managing NPL stock and designing workout strategies.

Concept node describing the stage-two initial viability assessment applied to non-performing loans not yet in legal proceedings, screening borrowers via financial ratios (or cash-flow ratios for MSMEs) and the loan-to-value ratio to classify them as viable, marginally viable or non-viable. It lists indicative, non-prescriptive benchmarks including Debt/EBITDA leverage, loan service coverage against sector averages, EBITDA trend comparison and an LLCR of 1.4 for project and multi-year finance, with thresholds to be set from general market indicators and adjusted for industry. Guidance for banks' Workout Units selecting resolution strategies.

Concept node on the loan-to-value ratio as used in SAMA's problem-loan guidelines: a readily available quantitative indicator of collateral coverage against the outstanding loan, applied alongside financial/cash-flow ratios in the stage-two screening of NPLs not in legal proceedings. Early LTV-based grouping informs the choice of workout strategy (hold/restructure, dispose, enforce) and related measures such as loan splitting or loan-to-asset swaps. Relevant to banks' Workout Units and credit risk functions.

Concept node covering the Loan Life Coverage Ratio as defined in Appendix 2 of SAMA's Guidelines on Management of Problem Loans: the present value of cash flows available for debt service over the loan life plus debt reserves, divided by the outstanding loan amount, discounted at the weighted average cost of capital. It is intended for project finance and other multi-year exposures where long-term viability must be assessed, contrasted with the point-in-time DSCR, with an indicative benchmark of 1.4. Used by banks' Workout teams in viability and risk-profile assessment.

Concept node on the Debt/EBITDA leverage measure used in SAMA's problem-loan guidelines as a proxy indicator in the initial viability assessment of a distressed borrower, signalling excessive leverage and repayment risk beyond a bank-set threshold. It sits within the broader illustrative (non-prescriptive) set of liquidity, solvency/leverage and profitability ratios that Workout Units — independent of the original loan approval — apply, with cash-flow analysis substituted where MSME financials are unreliable. Guidance for banks assessing borrower viability and restructuring options.

Concept node within SAMA's non-performing loan (NPL) management guidance covering the dedicated Workout Unit and the restructuring (workout) plan it produces. It sets expectations that the unit sits permanently in the organisational structure reporting to Risk Management rather than the originating business line, is staffed by qualified specialists, and tailors restructuring options to each borrower subject to two pre-conditions: sufficient projected cash flows and cooperative borrower behaviour. It also frames the preference for out-of-court settlement where documented recovery exceeds foreclosure, and points dissenting syndicate lenders to the Bankruptcy Law. Binds banks operating in KSA.
lookup_terms: segregation of duties from loan origination

data.summary: Concept node on the operational plan component of a bank's NPL strategy under SAMA's NPL guidance. It addresses how the approved strategy is designed, communicated, embedded across strategic, tactical and operational levels, monitored against targets with corrective action, and reviewed at least annually, including documented roles, reporting lines, staff incentives, and alignment with the business plan, budget, risk appetite framework and ICAAP. It also flags external drivers such as NPL investor demand, servicing capacity and capital implications. Binds banks.

Concept node describing the quantitative assessment a bank's Workout Unit performs to determine whether a defaulted borrower is viable, feeding the choice between restructuring, debt swaps or legal proceedings. It covers indicative liquidity, solvency/leverage and profitability ratios, balance sheet review of total debt burden and priority claims (wages, taxes), and cash flow as the ultimate determinant of repayment capacity; for MSMEs with weak audited data, cash-flow based analysis is expected. Independence is required: the analysis must be done by workout staff not involved in the original loan approval.

Concept node on the qualitative counterpart to financial analysis in NPL workouts: assessing the borrower's business model, medium- to long-term plan and projections, sustainable versus unsustainable debt, and alignment with existing credit terms. It also covers scenario and sensitivity testing of management assumptions, legal-documentation checks (cross-default clauses, notification obligations), collateral validity and enforceability, and the option to appoint a financial advisor for an independent business review. Binds banks resolving distressed exposures.

Concept node treating cash flow analysis as the core test of financial viability in an NPL workout, linking income statement and balance sheet to show forecast cash generation and repayment capacity, with weak cash generation signalling reliance on collateral, liquidation or bankruptcy. It also covers the forward-looking monthly cash budget, encouraged for all borrowers and particularly useful where micro and small enterprise financial statements are unreliable, with monthly monitoring and immediate corrective action.

Concept node explaining net present value analysis as the comparative tool for selecting the workout option that maximises recovery to the bank. It sets out discounting of net cash flows (principal, profit/interest and fees less out-of-pocket costs) at the bank's standard risk-adjusted discount rate or, alternatively, the original effective interest rate used for IFRS 9 provisioning, and lists the parameters to compare across restructuring, enforcement/legal action and insolvency scenarios.

Concept node covering restructuring/workout of distressed exposures under SAMA's problem-loan guidance, including the generic restructuring principles set out in the appendix (good faith, transparency, early engagement, sustainable rather than repeated short-term solutions) and the role of the restructuring agreement as the governing workout document. It addresses both the conduct expectations between bank and borrower and the documentation choice between a replacement agreement and an amendment to the original facility. Directed at banks dealing with borrowers, with simplified documentation contemplated for MSMEs; the principles are framed as encouraged practice rather than hard prohibitions, while surrounding supervisory expectations on problem-loan management remain binding.

Defines conditional loan forgiveness as a long-term restructuring option in which the bank waives part of the debt subject to conditions, typically to induce owners to inject additional funds and align their interests with the bank where the net present value of the company is below the total loan. It appears alongside other options (loan splitting, loan-to-asset swap, partial repayment, maturity extension) that banks may combine. Relevant to banks selecting and justifying restructuring measures for viable versus marginal borrowers.

Defines loan splitting as a restructuring technique addressing collateral and cash-flow shortfalls: the loan is divided into a serviceable portion repaid in equal principal-and-interest installments from sustainable cash flow, and an "excess loan" portion that may be subordinated, tranched, non-interest bearing, and repaid from asset sale proceeds or a bullet payment at maturity. It sits among the long-term restructuring options available to banks and is typically applied to marginal borrowers. Guidance addressed to banks structuring workouts.

Covers conversion of debt into equity (including conversion of owner loans into equity or another subordinated form) as a restructuring measure and as a supporting condition in workouts, alongside personal guarantees, capital increases, additional collateral and financial-indicator covenants. Debt-for-equity swaps are treated as measures requiring a supporting business plan, monitoring by asset/equity type, and compliance with applicable limits on such holdings. Applies to banks taking equity positions in restructured borrowers.

Defines the loan-to-asset (debt-for-asset) swap, under which a loan or part of it is transferred into "other assets owned" and ultimate recovery depends on selling the asset; it is normally combined with conditional loan forgiveness or partial repayment plus maturity extension. Banks are expected to support such swaps with a proper business plan, monitor volumes by asset type, respect regulatory limits on holdings, and weigh recovery outcomes against foreclosure and legal-route recovery rates. Addressed to banks managing repossessed assets and problem-loan recovery.

Explains short-term (temporary) restructuring measures — such as interest-only periods, moratoria, arrears/interest capitalisation and reduced payments — which do not themselves repay the obligation but give temporary relief for an identified short-term cash-flow disruption or time for the creditor to assess the case. Their use requires documented, non-speculative evidence that income will recover or that a long-term solution is not yet possible, and the guidance sets tenor caps (not exceeding 24 months, with a shorter limit indicated for certain cases). Binds banks choosing between short-term and long-term restructuring options.

A taxonomy node within SAMA's NPL/loan workout guidance distinguishing long-term (permanent) restructuring measures — such as debt-for-asset or debt-for-equity swaps, conditional debt forgiveness, profit/interest rate reduction, extension of maturity, debt consolidation, fresh money and additional security — from short-term/temporary relief measures, which are limited in tenor and used only where a documented, temporary cash-flow disruption exists. It informs how banks select and evidence a forbearance solution for distressed borrowers, including MSMEs, and how the chosen measure is then reflected in restructuring documentation. It binds banks conducting NPL workout and restructuring activity under SAMA supervision.

Guidance on how a bank should prepare and conduct negotiations with a distressed borrower over a rehabilitation/restructuring plan, including prior strategy formulation, SWOT-based assessment of the account, root-cause analysis, borrower education where the borrower lacks sophistication, and valuation issues in loan-to-equity conversions. It also situates negotiation within the wider NPL strategy implementation framework (monitoring of results, embedding roles, responsibilities and reporting lines). Applies to banks' workout units and management responsible for NPL resolution.

An analytical component of the workout process: the bank assesses account strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats alongside financial analysis (liquidity, solvency/leverage and profitability ratios, balance sheet composition, and cash-flow-based viability assessment) to determine borrower viability and shape the restructuring plan. For MSME borrowers lacking reliable audited financials, the emphasis shifts to cash-flow analysis and reasonableness testing. Directed at bank workout units, which must be independent of the original credit approval.

Sets out the coordinator role where a distressed borrower owes multiple banks: the bank with the largest exposure normally acts as coordinator, defining goals and deadlines, managing transparent communication and creditor meeting minutes, assessing the need for external financial or legal advisers, drafting the proposed restructuring solution, and potentially continuing as agent post-restructuring. It also covers use of advisers, guarantor involvement and re-confirmation of guarantees, and the preference for out-of-court workouts. Binds banks participating in multi-creditor NPL workouts.

Describes the standstill agreement as typically the first formal step in a multi-creditor workout: creditors agree not to enforce rights for defaults during a limited period, giving the borrower breathing space to prepare a survival strategy while creditors form a joint approach; it may also cover interim financing or deferral of principal/profit payments. For MSMEs a simplified template is contemplated, and in single-creditor relationships an informal understanding may suffice. Relevant to banks and their legal teams documenting NPL workouts.

Explains the restructuring agreement as the principal document governing a workout — setting out how the borrower will restructure debt and, where relevant, operations, and how and when creditors are repaid, including borrower conduct obligations during the agreement's life. There is no prescribed format; the bank's legal department should decide early whether the workout replaces the existing loan documentation or amends it by supplemental agreement, with simplified documentation contemplated for MSMEs. Addressed to banks structuring and documenting restructurings.
lookup_terms: amendment vs novation of loan agreement

data.summary: A cross-reference node pointing to the SAMA Cyber Security Framework as invoked within SAMA's Business Continuity Management (BCM) Framework, which sets resilience, recovery and continuity obligations for Member Organizations supervised by SAMA. The BCM context defines BCM, IT Disaster Recovery, Maximum Acceptable Outage and related recovery objectives, and requires an approved, maintained and tested Business Continuity Plan, incident response and escalation procedures, alternative workspace, and inclusion of cyber security requirements in continuity planning. It binds all SAMA Member Organizations, which must comply and embed the requirements in their BCM programme.

The Cyber Resilience Fundamental Requirements is a SAMA-issued, risk-based control set structured around Cyber Security Leadership and Governance, Cyber Security Operations and Technology, and Resilience domains, with uniquely numbered control requirements. It is aimed at newly established entities in early stages of operation, including firms testing solutions under SAMA's Regulatory Sandbox framework, rather than at mature Member Organizations subject to the full Cyber Security Framework. Useful for determining the baseline cyber and resilience expectations applicable to FinTech entrants supervised by SAMA.

The Cyber Security Leadership and Governance domain of the Cyber Resilience Fundamental Requirements, setting board- and management-level expectations: a resourced cyber security governance structure, approved and communicated policies, procedures and supporting security standards, periodic review against the evolving threat landscape, embedding cyber and fraud risk considerations in the business operating model, password controls, and documented, centrally registered IT/cyber risk assessments. It also carries the defined terms for cyber security governance, incident, incident management, policy and risk. Binds entities within scope of the Fundamental Requirements, with cross-references to other SAMA frameworks.
lookup_terms: IT and cyber risk assessment register

data.summary: The Cyber Security Operations and Technology domain of the Cyber Resilience Fundamental Requirements, one of the framework's core control areas covering day-to-day protective and detective security practices, supported by the framework's glossary definitions (cyber security incident, incident management, cyber security policy, cyber security risk). Applies to entities in scope of the Fundamental Requirements, principally newly established and sandbox-stage firms supervised by SAMA. Open this node for the operational control expectations rather than governance or continuity obligations.

The Resilience domain of the Cyber Resilience Fundamental Requirements, addressing continuity and availability of services and data for entities in scope, on a risk-based basis. It sits alongside the Leadership and Governance and Operations and Technology domains within the same numbered control structure. Relevant when assessing resilience expectations for early-stage or Regulatory Sandbox entities, as distinct from the fuller BCM Framework applicable to Member Organizations.

A concept node for the SAMA Cyber Security Framework as referenced within the Cyber Resilience Fundamental Requirements, where control requirements are cross-mapped to other SAMA frameworks. The surrounding material supplies the defining terms used across both instruments (cyber security governance, incident, incident management, policy, risk) and the baseline governance controls. Consult it to understand how the lighter Fundamental Requirements for new entrants relate to the fuller Cyber Security Framework applicable to Member Organizations.

A component of SAMA's credit workout/loan restructuring guidance describing the role and typical content of a term sheet in negotiating a restructuring with a distressed borrower. It sets out indicative headings (parties, closing date, representations and warranties, repayment and mandatory prepayment schedules, cash sweep, pricing and default interest, revised events of default, additional security, documentation, taxes, governing law) and a sequencing checklist from draft term sheet to signed workout documents. It is guidance addressed to banks' workout units and legal functions, not a binding documentary template.

Part of SAMA's NPL/workout guidance covering how banks should design, negotiate and follow through on a restructuring or rehabilitation plan, including SWOT-based strategy formulation, borrower education where the borrower cannot fully grasp the proposal, and the choice among workout options. It states the two pre-conditions for approving a restructuring (sufficient projected cash flows to repay past-due obligations within a reasonable timeframe, and cooperative borrower behaviour) and encourages out-of-court settlement where economic loss is lower than foreclosure. Binds banks' workout units; also touches syndicated/multi-bank cases where dissenting lenders may fall back on the Bankruptcy Law.

The performance-measurement strand of SAMA's restructuring guidance, listing metrics banks should use to assess the efficiency of workout activity (volume and value of evaluations, agreed modified solutions and resolved positions over a period; length of approval steps) and its effectiveness (success rate of each restructuring solution by portfolio segment). It links to the broader NPL strategy requirement for monitoring, annual review and defined roles and reporting lines. Directed at banks' management and workout functions.

Defines cure rate and re-default rate as the key measures of whether a forborne credit facility has genuinely returned to performing status, assessed by performance analysis after a designated cure period. Sets an expectation that the minimum cure period used for cure-rate measurement is 12 months, and points to vintage analysis of restructured exposures. Relevant to banks classifying and reporting restructured/forborne loans.

Appendix-level set of generic principles banks are encouraged to embed in their restructuring culture: treating restructuring as value-preserving rather than a cost centre, early identification of warning signs, good faith and seriousness by both sides, transparency and full disclosure between borrower and bank, prompt response to borrower proposals, adequate time for the borrower, sustainable rather than repeated short-term fixes, and confidentiality. It also explains restructuring agreement drafting choices (new agreement replacing prior documentation versus amendment of the original loan agreement), including simplified documentation for MSMEs. Expressed as encouraged good practice for banks dealing with borrowers.

SAMA Instructions (May 2023) issued under the Finance Companies Control Law setting minimum standards and procedures for entities licensed to practise aggregation activity — platforms that present finance offers from financiers to consumers. They define key terms (SAMA, Activity, Financier, Consumer, Entity, Platform, Documented Channels), require a licence before carrying on the activity, and impose obligations on technological capability, standard interfaces with financiers, verification of consumer identity and of information and documents from reliable and independent sources, accuracy of finance offers, and creation of an electronic record per consumer with phone-number authentication and up-to-date data such as the national address. They bind licensed aggregators and operate without prejudice to the Finance Companies Control Law and its Implementing Regulations, the Rules of Licensing Finance Support Activities, the Business Continuity Management Framework, the Financial Consumer Protection Principles and Rules, and the Electronic Transactions Law.
lookup_terms: Rules of Licensing Finance Support Activities

data.summary: Defines the "Entity" under SAMA's Instructions for Practicing Aggregation Activity — a firm licensed by SAMA (under the Rules of Licensing Finance Support Activities) that operates an electronic platform aggregating finance offers from Financiers for Consumers. It carries the operative duty set: platform cybersecurity and immediate breach notification to SAMA, restriction of the entity–financier electronic link to aggregation only, consumer complaint and disclosure channels, identity verification of the consumer against reliable and independent sources before passing data to the financier, electronic consumer records, and prohibitions on handling funds for financiers or joining financier marketing campaigns absent SAMA approval. Binds only SAMA-licensed aggregation entities; note the term is "Consumer", not the AML "Customer", so identity verification here is a conduct/accuracy duty distinct from full CDD.

A cross-reference node: the Aggregation Activity Instructions are expressly without prejudice to other SAMA and statutory instruments, including SAMA's cybersecurity/technology requirements, the Finance Companies Control Law and its Implementing Regulations, the Rules of Licensing Finance Support Activities, the BCM Framework and the Financial Consumer Protection Principles and Rules. Practically, it signals that aggregation entities must layer the Instructions' platform-security and breach-notification duties on top of the applicable SAMA framework obligations. Relevant to licensed aggregation entities and, more broadly, to member organisations subject to the referenced frameworks.
lookup_terms: Rules of Licensing Finance Support Activities
Financial Consumer Protection Principles and Rules

data.summary: A cross-reference to SAMA's Business Continuity Management Framework as one of the instruments preserved alongside the Aggregation Activity Instructions. It signals that an aggregation entity's technology, platform operation and interfaces with financiers must also satisfy SAMA's continuity and resilience requirements, in addition to accuracy-of-information and electronic record duties. Binds licensed aggregation entities and, in its own right, SAMA member organisations subject to the BCM Framework.

SAMA's Business Continuity Management Framework, setting principle/objective/control-consideration requirements for member organisations to build organisational resilience and ensure continuity and availability of operations and services. Covers BCM strategy, business continuity policy, BIA and risk assessment, resilient architecture and the crisis management plan (including crisis declaration criteria and command centre arrangements). Requirements are drawn from SAMA expectations and standards such as ISO 22301, and all member organisations must comply and integrate them into their BCM programme.

The governance layer of SAMA's BCM Framework: a defined, approved and maintained business continuity governance framework and structure, monitored by senior management and communicated to employees and third parties. Allocates ultimate responsibility for the BCM programme to the board or a delegated executive, requires board-mandated BCM committee with senior-management representation and a charter (including at least quarterly meetings), adequate budget, an established BCM function, and an appointed, suitably qualified BCM manager/head. Binds member organisations' boards and senior management.

The BCM Framework's requirements for Business Impact Analysis and Risk Assessment: member organisations must define and maintain a BIA/RA methodology and periodically identify, assess and treat threats (including single points of failure across people, process, technology and premises) that could disrupt critical activities. The BIA must prioritise products, services, functions and processes and determine financial, operational, customer, legal and regulatory impacts, RTOs, RPOs and MAO, interdependencies and recovery resources. Results and the prioritised list must be endorsed by the BCM committee and periodically updated.

This node covers the Business Continuity Plan and its surrounding governance layer in SAMA's BCM Framework: BCM governance (board/delegated executive ultimate responsibility, mandated BCM committee with a charter and at least quarterly meetings, a staffed BCM function and appointed BCM manager), BCM strategy, business continuity policy, and the BIA/risk assessment feeding recovery objectives. It also sets what a BCP must contain — key resources, roles and authorities, escalation, recovery within RTO/RPO/MAO, return to business-as-usual, communications and cyber security integration — plus alternative workspace and ongoing monitoring of effectiveness. It binds Member Organizations (SAMA-affiliated entities, banks in Saudi Arabia and their subsidiaries), with the board, senior management and BCM manager/coordinators as accountable roles.

This node addresses the IT Disaster Recovery Plan under the SAMA BCM Framework: a defined, approved and maintained IT DRP aligned to the BIA that restores data, systems, networks, services and applications after a disruptive incident. It requires an alternative data centre sited on a risk assessment showing it does not share the primary site's risks and subject to SAMA approval, capacity and configuration parity with the primary site, equivalent logical, physical, environmental and cyber security controls, backup/recovery processes with offsite storage, and formal third-party contracts aligned to BIA/RA outcomes. Accountability sits with the IT manager for keeping DR arrangements current, with the BCM manager accountable for integration into the BCM programme; it binds Member Organizations.

This node sets the crisis management requirement in the SAMA BCM Framework: a defined, approved and implemented crisis management plan enabling a managed response to major incidents, including rapid communication with internal and external stakeholders. Minimum content includes criteria for declaring a crisis and establishment of a command centre for centralised management and emergency command; compliance must be monitored and effectiveness periodically measured. It links to the testing requirements, since BCP and DR test scenarios must cover activation and involvement of the crisis management team, and it binds Member Organizations.

This node covers the testing obligations for business continuity and disaster recovery under the SAMA BCM Framework. Member Organizations must define, approve, execute and monitor BCP simulation exercises at least annually with well-planned scenarios (including cyber security scenarios) and consider an integrated BCM test across all critical services and functions, and must run a DR test combined with BCP at least annually, evaluating readiness of DR infrastructure supporting critical systems and producing improvement recommendations. Test scenarios must cover activation of the crisis management team, and testing serves both to validate the plans and to train employees and third parties.

This node draws together the cyber resilience dimension of the SAMA BCM Framework: BCM is framed as a holistic process for building organisational resilience, with IT Disaster Recovery defined as the part of BCM covering resilience, recovery and continuation of technology infrastructure supporting critical business processes. Practical cyber implications include applying the same logical, physical, environmental and cyber security controls at the alternative data centre as at the primary site, embedding cyber security requirements in continuity planning, and including cyber scenarios in testing. The framework cross-refers to the SAMA Cyber Security Framework for threat and vulnerability management controls; it binds Member Organizations.

This node covers the introductory and scope provisions of the SAMA BCM Framework, which states that its requirements are based on SAMA requirements, industry practice and international standards including ISO 22301 and ISO 27001, plus BCI and DRII guidance. It defines scope and applicability — all SAMA-affiliated Member Organizations, all banks operating in Saudi Arabia, banking subsidiaries of Saudi banks and subsidiaries of foreign banks in the Kingdom — and allocates responsibility: SAMA owns, interprets and periodically updates the document, while Member Organizations adopt and implement it. It identifies the target audience (board, CEO, CRO, CIO/CISO, BCM managers, internal audit) and the route for a Member Organization to request amendments through SAMA.

This node covers SAMA's Regulatory Sandbox arrangement as referenced in, and operationalised through, the Cyber Resilience Fundamental Requirements: a controlled 'live' testing environment (open to local and international firms) for new digital financial solutions in KSA, established in November 2019. The linked Fundamental Requirements set baseline cyber security and resilience controls for newly established entities in early operational stages, and SAMA may block a sandbox graduation or licence request where an entity cannot demonstrate compliance. SAMA owns and interprets the requirements; they are addressed to senior/executive management, information asset owners and heads of cyber security in participating entities.

A concept node for the glossary underpinning the Cyber Resilience Fundamental Requirements, where key terms (e.g. cyber security governance, cyber security incident, cyber security policy, availability, audit, business continuity) are defined by reference to NISTIR 7298r3 and ISO 22301. It supplies the defined-term layer used to interpret the control requirements rather than imposing obligations itself. Relevant to anyone construing scope of terms in SAMA cyber resilience instruments.

SAMA's Cyber Security Framework, the sector-wide instrument setting principles, objectives and control considerations for cyber security across domains (leadership and governance, risk management and compliance, operations, third parties), together with a maturity model used to measure compliance. Obligations attach to Member Organizations supervised by SAMA, with ultimate accountability placed on the Board of Directors, including approving policy and allocating budget. Central reference for any question on cyber security governance duties, policy content requirements and assessed maturity levels.

Concept node for the six-level cyber security maturity model (0 Non-existent through 5) used by SAMA to measure a Member Organization's compliance with the Cyber Security Framework. Levels are cumulative: a Member Organization must satisfy all criteria of lower levels before attaining level 3, 4 or 5, with level 3 requiring defined, approved, formally implemented and demonstrable controls. Determines the benchmark against which supervisory assessment and self-assessment outcomes are expressed.

Concept node for the Cyber Security Leadership and Governance domain of the SAMA Cyber Security Framework, covering the cyber security policy's mandatory content (definition, objectives and scope, board intent statement, allocation of responsibilities, links to standards and procedures) and the definition of cyber security roles and responsibilities. It places ultimate responsibility on the Board of Directors, including budget allocation and approvals, and requires that all stakeholders understand and discharge their roles. Binds Member Organizations subject to the Framework.

Concept node for the Cyber Security Risk Management and Compliance domain of the SAMA Cyber Security Framework, requiring a defined, approved and implemented cyber security risk management process covering identification, analysis, response and monitoring/review, aligned with the Member Organization's enterprise risk management process. The stated objective is protection of the confidentiality, integrity and availability of information assets, with compliance against cyber security controls subject to periodic review and audit. Applies to Member Organizations supervised by SAMA.
lookup_terms: cyber security compliance review and audit

data.summary: A domain node within SAMA's Cyber Security Framework covering the operational and technological control areas that Member Organizations must define, approve, implement and monitor — including asset and identity controls, secure disposal, payment systems and electronic banking services. It sits alongside the framework's maturity model, under which controls must be formally documented, approved and demonstrably implemented to reach the target maturity level. It binds Member Organizations supervised by SAMA (banks, insurers and financing companies), with ultimate accountability resting with the Board.

A domain node of SAMA's Cyber Security Framework addressing cyber security risk arising from outsourcing, cloud, vendors and other external service providers engaged by a Member Organization. It requires third-party arrangements to be governed by defined, approved cyber security requirements with contractual obligations and periodic measurement of effectiveness, consistent with the framework's maturity expectations. Responsibility remains with the Member Organization and its Board regardless of the outsourcing.

Defines the information security function headed by a Chief Information Security Officer, which must be independent of the IT function and report to the CEO/managing director or the general manager of a control function. The role covers security policy support, defining roles and goals, providing security and information risk management frameworks, identifying emerging issues and risk-appetite shifts, and assisting management with security processes and controls. It applies to Member Organizations under SAMA supervision.

The governance body within a Member Organization to which cyber security matters — including accepted risks within risk appetite — are reported and escalated, operating under the Board's ultimate responsibility for cyber security. It supports oversight of the cyber security policy, roles and responsibilities, budget allocation and approval of key framework documents. Relevant to Member Organizations assessing governance-layer maturity under the SAMA Cyber Security Framework.

Node covering the framework's mandatory compliance with international industry standards, under which Member Organizations must comply with PCI-DSS alongside the EMV technical standard and the SWIFT Customer Security Controls Framework. It connects to the framework's regulatory compliance process and to the payment systems control area referencing SARIE and mada rules and standards. It binds SAMA Member Organizations handling card and payment data.
lookup_terms: Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard

data.summary: Node covering the SWIFT Customer Security Controls Framework as one of the mandatory international industry standards a Member Organization must comply with under the SAMA Cyber Security Framework, together with PCI-DSS and EMV. It links to the framework's regulatory compliance and risk-response provisions, including the rule that accepted cyber risks must not conflict with SAMA regulations. Relevant to institutions operating SWIFT messaging and cross-border payment interfaces.

A cross-reference within SAMA's IT Governance Framework to SAMA's separate Business Continuity Management Framework, invoked where IT risk, availability and resilience obligations of Member Organizations connect to enterprise continuity requirements. It is a pointer node rather than a standalone rule set: the substantive continuity obligations sit in the referenced BCM Framework, while the surrounding IT governance provisions require IT risk management to be defined, approved, aligned to enterprise risk management and reported to senior management and the IT Steering Committee. Binds SAMA-supervised Member Organizations.

Provision of the SAMA IT Governance Framework requiring Member Organizations to document, approve and implement a system development methodology so that development of their systems is strictly controlled. It sets expectations on development approach, secure coding standards, testing types, version control, quality control, data migration, documentation and end-user training, plus an approved low-level system design document and secure code review (or an independent assurance statement where source code is unavailable). Binds Member Organizations supervised by SAMA, including where development is outsourced to vendors.

Sub-provision of the system change management chapter of the SAMA IT Governance Framework setting minimum testing expectations before changes enter production. It covers documented test cases and attributes, unit, system integration, stress, security and user acceptance testing, use of a separate test environment, formal business user acceptance, retention of UAT results, third-party certification where applicable, and a prohibition on using production data for testing (sanitized data only). Binds Member Organizations; the data-handling restriction has confidentiality/data-protection consequences.

Provision requiring cyber security requirements to be defined and fully tested in a test environment for all information system changes, so vulnerabilities are identified and mitigated before production deployment. It expressly links the change management process to the SAMA Cyber Security Framework for defining, testing and implementing those security requirements. Binds Member Organizations and creates a cross-reference between the IT governance and cyber security regimes.

Sub-provision of the SAMA IT Governance Framework governing how approved changes are released into production, including the requirement that changes be introduced within an agreed change window, with a separate approval process for exceptions which should rarely be permitted absent compelling reasons. It sits within the wider change management chapter requiring changes to be classified, tested and approved before deployment. Binds Member Organizations.

Provision requiring Member Organizations to define, approve, communicate, implement and periodically evaluate a system configuration management process that maintains reliable and accurate information about configuration items for their information assets. It addresses roles and responsibilities, identification and criticality of configuration items relative to supporting business processes, interrelationships between items, periodic verification, and implementation of a configuration management database. Binds Member Organizations supervised by SAMA.

SAMA's Information Technology Governance Framework (v1.0) sets principles and mandated control requirements for how SAMA-regulated entities (Member Organizations) govern and manage IT. It is structured into four domains (IT governance and leadership, IT risk management, IT operations management, system change management), each broken into subdomains with a stated principle plus numbered control requirements, and compliance is assessed through periodic self-assessment against a six-level maturity model, reviewed and audited by SAMA. Departures require compensating controls, internal risk acceptance and a formal waiver request to SAMA.

The first domain of the SAMA IT Governance Framework, covering board- and senior-management-level accountability for IT: governance structures, IT strategy, enterprise architecture, IT policies and procedures, and defined roles and responsibilities. It binds Member Organizations and typically routes oversight through an IT Steering Committee (ITSC), with performance and compliance trends reported to senior management. Useful when the question is who owns IT decisions and how IT direction must be approved and monitored.

Domain 3.2 of the Framework requires Member Organizations to define, approve, implement and communicate an IT risk management process aligned with enterprise risk management, covering risk identification and analysis, treatment, reporting, and monitoring/profiling. It extends to information assets (business processes and data, applications, infrastructure) and to third-party relationships and people aspects, and requires a centralized risk register, defined risk appetite, IT key risk indicators, and treatment plans approved consistent with governance arrangements. Relevant to outsourcing/third-party risk questions and to how IT risk acceptance is evidenced.

Domain of the Framework addressing day-to-day running of IT at Member Organizations, including managing assets and interdependencies, service level agreements, availability and capacity, data centre management, and system configuration and monitoring. It sets principles and control requirements for operational continuity and performance of information assets. Open this node for questions about IT service delivery, SLA governance with providers, and operational monitoring expectations.

Domain 3.4 requires a governed change management process so that changes to information assets (applications, software, devices, data) are classified, risk-assessed, tested and approved before deployment to production. Control requirements cover change governance policy, requirement definition and asset-owner approval, Change Advisory Board endorsement, system acquisition and development, testing (including UAT and prohibition on using production data in test), security requirements, release management, and emergency-change handling with post-implementation review and root cause analysis. Explicitly cross-references the SAMA Cyber Security Framework for security sign-off on changes.

A cross-reference node: the IT Governance Framework repeatedly defers to the separate SAMA Cyber Security Framework for security-related controls, notably requiring the cyber security function to review and approve changes to information assets before Change Advisory Board submission and requiring change security requirements to be defined and tested per that framework. It signals that IT governance obligations sit alongside, and do not displace, cyber security obligations on the same Member Organizations. Use it to trace which requirement set governs a security control question.

Subdomain 3.4.9 of SAMA's IT Governance Framework setting the principle and control requirements for a defined, approved, implemented and communicated patch management process so that functional and non-functional patches are applied in a timely way to close vulnerabilities. It sits within the System Change Management domain alongside system configuration management (CMDB, configuration items) and change windows. It binds Member Organizations supervised by SAMA and is assessed through the framework's self-assessment and maturity model.

Subdomain 3.4.10 of SAMA's IT Governance Framework requiring a formally defined and approved IT project management framework, policy and procedure covering the project lifecycle from initiation to closure. It prescribes minimum project documentation (project charter, requirements and information flow analysis, feasibility/cost-benefit, detailed plan), an IT project steering committee with business and technical representation, and risk assessment, mitigation and monitoring across the lifecycle. It binds Member Organizations subject to the Framework.

Subdomain 3.4.11 of SAMA's IT Governance Framework requiring a defined, approved and communicated quality assurance process that independently verifies changes and developments to information assets against business, user and regulatory requirements before release to production. Key points are an independent QA function with its own reporting line and authority for objective evaluation, mandatory pre-production QA assessment of all changes, minimum quality requirements, QA record management and reporting of results to stakeholders. It binds Member Organizations.

Appendices A and B of the IT Governance Framework describing the procedure and form for a Member Organization to request an amendment to the Framework. The request must be justified with pros and cons, approved by the CIO and then the IT steering committee, and submitted formally in writing by the CEO or managing director to the manager of SAMA's General Department of Cyber Risk Control, which evaluates and responds. The existing Framework continues to apply while the request is pending.
lookup_terms: General Department of Cyber Risk Control

data.summary: Appendices C and D of the IT Governance Framework setting out how a Member Organization requests a waiver from a specific control it cannot implement. The request must explain why the control cannot be met and describe available or suggested compensating controls, be approved by the CIO and IT steering committee, be signed by the CIO and business owner, and be issued formally by the CEO or managing director to SAMA's General Department of Cyber Risk Control. The control remains binding until the waiver is granted, and any waiver is valid for one year with renewal the Member Organization's responsibility.
lookup_terms: General Department of Cyber Risk Control

data.summary: Structural and interpretive material for SAMA's IT Governance Framework: how the Framework is organised into domains and subdomains, each with a Principle and mandated Control Requirements, the control numbering convention, and the compliance mechanics. It covers the periodic self-assessment questionnaire reviewed and audited by SAMA, the six-level IT governance maturity model (levels 0-5, with lower levels to be met before achieving 3-5), and the option of compensating controls plus a formal SAMA waiver. It applies to Member Organizations supervised by SAMA.

A definitional/reference node within SAMA's cyber security framework document, pointing to the US NIST body of information-security standards and its glossary (NISTIR 7298r2), from which many of the framework's defined terms are drawn (e.g. malware, mobile device, multi-factor authentication, confidentiality, compensating control, cryptography). It is interpretive rather than obligation-creating: it fixes the meaning of technical terms used in requirements addressed to Member Organizations affiliated with SAMA. Open it to confirm how a cyber-security term is defined, not to find a standalone duty.
lookup_terms: glossary of key information security terms

data.summary: A node covering business continuity concepts and related minimum expectations in SAMA's cyber security framework, including the ISO 22301-based definition of business continuity and the requirement that continuity arrangements be preserved when services are outsourced to cloud providers (alongside SAMA prior approval, data location in the Kingdom, data segregation, use limitation, audit/review rights and exit provisions). Binds Member Organizations affiliated with SAMA. Useful when assessing continuity obligations in a cloud or third-party context.

SAMA's framework setting minimum regulatory capital requirements for operational risk, issued under the Central Bank Law and Banking Control Law and superseding conflicting prior Basel II guidance. It fixes the calculation methodology (Business Indicator Component multiplied by the Internal Loss Multiplier), loss data collection standards, quarterly Q17 reporting and Pillar 3-plus disclosure. It applies to domestic banks on a consolidated and standalone basis; foreign bank branches in the Kingdom follow their home regulator's capital rules.

The single permitted methodology under the SAMA operational risk framework: operational risk capital equals the Business Indicator Component times the Internal Loss Multiplier, with marginal coefficients applied at defined BI thresholds and internal loss data feeding the ILM. It also governs which losses enter the data set, including the SAR 44,600 collection threshold (which SAMA may raise to SAR 446,000 for banks with a BI above SAR 4.46 billion) and the treatment of credit- and market-risk-related losses. Binds domestic banks calculating minimum regulatory capital.

Context node identifying the Basel Committee's December 2017 Basel III post-crisis reforms as the source of SAMA's revised operational risk regime, which adopts the revised standardized approach as the sole method and aims to reduce RWA variability. It also carries the legal basis (Central Bank Law, Banking Control Law), the supersession of prior Basel II detailed guidance, and the scope, reporting and disclosure provisions. Relevant when tracing why a national requirement departs from or mirrors the Basel text.

Detailed rules on identifying, collecting and treating operational loss data: defining gross loss, net loss and recoveries; listing what must be included (direct P&L charges, consequential costs, provisions, material pending losses, material timing losses giving rise to legal risk) and what must be excluded (general maintenance contracts, post-loss business enhancements, insurance premiums); and fixing the date of accounting as the reference date, including for legal loss events. It also requires SAMA approval for excluding losses from the Loss Component, which should be rare and strongly justified. Binds banks building the standardized approach loss data set.
lookup_terms: exclusion of losses from loss component

data.summary: The SAMA Rules on Stress Testing (issued November 2011 to all banks under SAMA's charter powers) set minimum regulatory requirements for bank stress testing as a risk management tool, covering framework design, methodologies, scenario selection, board and senior management responsibility, and half-yearly reporting to SAMA. Section 12 makes stress testing programs subject to supervisory review, ICAAP bilateral meetings and on-site examinations, assessing framework adequacy, assumptions, frequency, governance involvement and degree of compliance. It binds locally incorporated banks and branches of foreign banks above the specified asset threshold; banks may adopt more sophisticated techniques than the stated minimums.

This node covers the interaction between the SAMA Rules on Stress Testing and the BCBS "Principles for Sound Stress Testing Practices and Supervision" (May 2009), circulated to banks by SAMA circular of 2 August 2009. Banks must apply the BCBS guidance in addition to the Rules when designing and implementing stress testing programs, and must approach SAMA where the two are inconsistent. It also records the effective date provisions: immediate force, full framework compliance by 30 June 2012, and reporting from the half-year ending 30 June 2012 within three months of each half-year end.
lookup_terms: BCBS Principles for Sound Stress Testing Practices and Supervision

data.summary: Defines the categories of stress tests under the Rules — Regular (bottom-up, bank-conducted), Ad-hoc (irregular, bank- or SAMA-initiated), Reverse (viability-threatening scenarios, elaborated in Section 5.4), and Macro (top-down, conducted by SAMA on the Saudi banking system) — and establishes stress testing as a mandatory requirement. The mandate applies to all locally incorporated banks and to branches of foreign banks whose total assets exceed 0.5% of total Saudi banking system assets, each of which must build a program proportionate to its nature, size, complexity and risk profile.

Section 4 sets the minimum content of a bank's stress testing framework: a holistic approach covering all material internal and external risks, shocks of sufficient magnitude, capture of exceptional but plausible events, account of domestic, regional and global market developments, and an adequate historical time horizon. It also requires the stress testing process to be documented in policy or standard operating procedures, including allocation of responsibility (which may sit with the Chief Risk Officer). Compliance with the framework is assessed by SAMA through supervisory review and on-site examination.

Sensitivity Analysis is one of the methodologies described in Section 5 of the Rules: it measures the change in portfolio value from shocks of varying degrees to a single risk factor or a small set of closely related factors, without evaluating the relationships between factors, with impact typically estimated on capital. The Rules leave methodology choice to each bank based on business nature, size, complexity and risk profile; SAMA does not prescribe risk factors or a common covariance matrix.

Scenario Analysis measures portfolio value change from simultaneous moves in multiple risk factors, including changes in correlations and volatilities, using either historical (backward-looking) or hypothetical (forward-looking) scenarios, each with acknowledged limitations. Related scenario-selection requirements oblige banks to reflect their own business environment and risk profile, cover all material risk factors and both on- and off-balance sheet exposures, and include at least one viability-threatening (reverse) scenario. Risk coverage must span credit, market, operational, liquidity, reputational and off-balance-sheet vehicle risks.

Provision within SAMA's Rules on Stress Testing for banks that defines reverse stress testing as starting from a business-failure outcome and working backwards to identify the scenarios that would produce it. It makes reverse stress testing of the business plan to the point of non-viability a requirement for banks, including assessing the likelihood of such adverse circumstances and taking remedial measures where the resulting failure risk is inconsistent with risk appetite or tolerance. Related material covers SAMA's supervisory review of stress testing programs, including via ICAAP discussions and on-site examinations.

Section of SAMA's stress testing rules setting out the board of directors' duties: overall responsibility and oversight of the stress testing framework, approval of the stress testing policy and its revisions, ensuring adequate resources and infrastructure, reviewing major stress test findings and remedial actions, and requiring periodic management reporting on framework effectiveness. It binds boards of banks subject to the Rules and permits the board to require independent evaluation by internal audit or an external consultant.

Companion provision to the board section, allocating to senior management responsibility for designing, developing and implementing the stress testing framework, including organizational structure, qualified staff, supporting infrastructure and data processes. Senior management must oversee scenario definition and methodology, ensure results are clearly compiled and communicated to the board, committees, business areas and SAMA, prepare action plans, and periodically reassess and update the framework subject to board approval where needed.
lookup_terms: stress test results reporting to SAMA

data.summary: Part of the stress testing rules describing SAMA's supervisory top-down (macro) stress testing alongside banks' bottom-up tests, comprising use of banks' submitted bottom-up results, requiring banks to run SAMA-specified sensitivity or scenario tests and report results, and SAMA's own system-wide tests using macroeconomic and bank data. It obliges banks to submit data and results in prescribed formats and clarifies that SAMA will not formally share its own test results, and that stress testing reporting is separate from ICAAP reporting.
lookup_terms: ICAAP reporting vs stress testing reporting

data.summary: SAMA circular (Arabic) issued to credit information companies under the Credit Information Law and its Implementing Regulations, addressing the sensitivity of data held by those companies. It requires credit information companies to obtain SAMA's no-objection before providing any data or statistics to governmental or non-governmental entities, except as covered by member agreements concluded under the Law and Regulations.

Component of SAMA's Pillar 3 disclosure requirements covering the overview of risk management and key prudential metrics: Template KM1 (key metrics on capital, buffers, RWA, leverage ratio, LCR and NSFR), Template KM2 (TLAC, G-SIBs only), Table OVA (risk management approach) and Template OV1 (RWA overview). It sets out completion instructions, treatment of ECL transitional arrangements and pre-floor RWA/ratios, and cross-template linkages, binding banks subject to SAMA's Pillar 3 regime; TLAC disclosures are not required unless SAMA specifies otherwise.

Pillar 3 disclosure template TLAC2, requiring a material subgroup entity that has issued internal TLAC to a G-SIB resolution entity to disclose its creditor hierarchy at legal entity level, showing nominal capital and liabilities, excluded liabilities, TLAC-eligible amounts and residual maturity buckets. It binds only banks designated as G-SIBs, completed per material subgroup entity within each resolution group and grouped by resolution group, semiannually, in fixed format with narrative on jurisdiction-specific credit hierarchies. Relevant only from the TLAC conformance date; not applicable to foreign bank branches in KSA.

Cross-references to SAMA's SACAP capital rules used as the definitional backbone for the Pillar 3 capital composition disclosures (Template CC1 line items), covering regulatory adjustments and deductions such as goodwill and intangibles, DTAs, cash flow hedge reserve, provision shortfall, own-credit-risk gains, pension fund assets, own shares, reciprocal cross-holdings and the 10%/5% threshold deductions for investments in capital instruments and other TLAC liabilities. It binds banks in computing CET1, AT1 and Tier 2, with certain threshold conditions applying only to G-SIBs.

Sets the scope, effective date and five guiding principles for banks' Pillar 3 disclosures — clarity, comprehensiveness, meaningfulness, consistency over time and comparability across banks — plus the requirement for a formal board-approved disclosure policy and assurance over Pillar 3 data. It applies to all domestic banks on both consolidated and standalone bases and expressly excludes foreign bank branches operating in Saudi Arabia; requirements took effect 1 January 2023 with first reporting as at 31 March 2023.

Pillar 3 disclosure template TLAC3, the resolution-entity counterpart to TLAC2, showing the creditor hierarchy of each G-SIB resolution entity at legal entity level with nominal capital and liabilities, excluded liabilities, potentially TLAC-eligible amounts and residual maturity/perpetual breakdowns. Identical in structure to TLAC2 except that no exposure-to-resolution-entity information is collected, so only one column per hierarchy layer. Mandatory for G-SIBs, semiannual, fixed format, effective from the TLAC conformance date.

Table LIA is the mandatory narrative accompanying Templates LI1 and LI2, explaining the main drivers of differences between financial statement carrying values and regulatory exposure amounts, including valuation differences, netting rules, provisions and prudential filters. Accompanying Q&A clarifies treatment of 1,250% risk-weighted exposures, which liabilities go in the unallocated column of LI1, and the distinction between balance-sheet netting and incremental Basel netting. Binds all banks within the Pillar 3 scope.

Template LI1 reconciles the balance sheet under the accounting scope of consolidation with the regulatory scope of consolidation and maps carrying values to the credit risk, counterparty credit risk, securitisation and market risk frameworks (or to a not-subject-to-capital-requirements column). It feeds Template LI2 and the three-step link between published financial statements and Template CC1 capital composition. Mandatory for all banks in scope, annual frequency, with narrative in Table LIA.

Pillar 3 disclosure template LI2 within SAMA's Pillar 3 Disclosure Requirements Framework, requiring banks to explain the main drivers of difference between accounting carrying values (under the regulatory scope of consolidation) and the exposure amounts used for regulatory capital purposes, broken down by credit risk, counterparty credit risk, securitisation and market risk frameworks. Differences arising purely from scope of consolidation belong in LI1; LI2 covers off-balance sheet amounts, valuation and netting differences, provisions and prudential filters. Mandatory for all banks, annual frequency, flexible format, with narrative support via Table LIA.
lookup_terms: regulatory exposure amounts vs carrying values

data.summary: Table CRA is the general qualitative credit risk disclosure in SAMA's Pillar 3 framework, requiring banks to describe their credit risk management objectives and policies — how the business model shapes the credit risk profile, criteria for credit risk policy and limits, the structure of the credit risk management and control function, its interaction with risk control, compliance and internal audit, and credit risk reporting to executive management and the board. It sits at the head of the section 19 credit risk disclosure suite (CR1, CR2, CRB, CRB-A, CRC, CR3, CRD, CR4, CR5). Mandatory for all banks, annual, flexible format.

Table CRB is the additional qualitative and quantitative disclosure on the credit quality of assets under section 19 of SAMA's Pillar 3 framework, supplementing the quantitative CR1 and CR2 templates. It sits alongside Table CRB-A (prudential treatment of problem assets) in the general credit risk information block and is addressed to banks subject to the credit risk RWA disclosure regime.

Table CRB-A requires banks to disclose additional qualitative and quantitative information on non-performing and forborne exposures, including the bank's own definitions of non-performing and forborne exposure, whether it applies SAMA's Rules on Management of Problem Loans (No. 41033343, January 2020), materiality thresholds for past due, exit criteria and probation periods, and differences in treatment between corporate and retail lending. Values are accounting carrying amounts stated on the regulatory scope of consolidation. Mandatory for banks, annual, flexible format.
lookup_terms: Rules on Management of Problem Loans 41033343

data.summary: Table CRC is the qualitative disclosure on credit risk mitigation techniques in section 19.2.2 of SAMA's Pillar 3 framework, paired with the quantitative Template CR3. It supports understanding of how banks recognise CRM (including the simple versus comprehensive approach with supervisory haircuts under the standardised approach) when computing credit risk RWA, excluding securitisation and counterparty credit risk positions covered elsewhere.

Template CR3 is the quantitative overview of credit risk mitigation techniques in SAMA's Pillar 3 framework, showing exposures secured by collateral, financial guarantees and credit derivatives against unsecured exposures, and complementing the qualitative Table CRC. It forms part of the section 19 credit risk disclosure set, which reports carrying values on the regulatory scope of consolidation and excludes securitisation and counterparty credit risk positions disclosed in other sections. Binding on banks subject to the Pillar 3 disclosure framework.

Template KM2 is a fixed-format Pillar 3 disclosure template setting out key metrics on total loss-absorbing capacity (TLAC) available and TLAC requirements measured at resolution group level, under both single point of entry and multiple point of entry resolution approaches. It prescribes the reported items (TLAC available, RWA, leverage exposure measure, TLAC ratios, subordination exemption indicators), the quarterly frequency, the five-period reporting series (T to T-4), and the requirement for narrative explanation of material changes. It is mandatory only for resolution groups of G-SIBs, with the template reproduced per resolution group under MPE.
lookup_terms: single point of entry / multiple point of entry

data.summary: Template OV1 is the Pillar 3 overview of risk-weighted assets, mapping RWA and minimum capital requirements across credit risk, counterparty credit risk, CVA, securitisation, market risk, operational risk, equity investments in funds, settlement risk and amounts below deduction thresholds. It fixes the row-by-row definitions and cross-references to the SAMA-adopted Basel standards (SCRE, SCCR) for each approach, including which lines capture standardised versus internal-model approaches used with SAMA approval. It binds banks subject to SAMA's disclosure framework.

Template CMS1 is the Pillar 3 comparison template requiring banks that use internal models to disclose actual RWA alongside RWA as they would be if the full standardised approach were applied, broken down by risk type (credit, counterparty credit, CVA, securitisation, market, operational and residual RWA). Its instructions define, per row, what counts as the standardised approach and which exposures fall into modelled versus standardised cells. It applies to banks with SAMA approval to use modelled approaches under the disclosure framework.
lookup_terms: comparison of modelled and standardised RWA

data.summary: Template CMS2 breaks the modelled-versus-standardised RWA comparison down by credit risk asset class, disclosing actual RWA and the RWA that would result from applying the standardised approach to the same exposures. The accompanying instructions define the scope of each credit risk row, its exclusions (counterparty credit risk, equity positions, settlement risk, securitisation, below-threshold amounts) and the relevant Basel/SAMA standard references, together with the derivation of minimum capital requirements. It binds banks using IRB or supervisory slotting approaches for credit risk.

Template CC1 is the fixed-format Pillar 3 disclosure of the composition of regulatory capital, itemising CET1, Additional Tier 1 and Tier 2 components and each regulatory adjustment and deduction, with row-level cross-references to the SAMA capital standard (SACAP), including treatment of investments in the capital instruments and other TLAC liabilities of financial entities and the 5%/10% thresholds. The surrounding material also covers capital distribution constraint disclosure (buffers, Pillar 2, leverage). It binds banks subject to SAMA's regulatory capital and disclosure framework, with certain rows applicable only to G-SIBs.

Table CCA is the Pillar 3 disclosure of the main features of regulatory capital instruments (and, where relevant, other TLAC-eligible instruments), covering issuer, governing law, regulatory treatment, tier eligibility, amount recognised, maturity, call, coupon, conversion and write-down terms and subordination ranking. It is read together with the capital composition and regulatory adjustment rules cross-referenced to the SAMA capital standard. It binds banks issuing regulatory capital instruments under SAMA's disclosure framework.
lookup_terms: main features of regulatory capital instruments

data.summary: Table CRD is a Pillar 3 qualitative disclosure item within SAMA's Pillar 3 Disclosure Requirements Framework, requiring banks to explain how they use external credit ratings when risk-weighting exposures under the standardised approach for credit risk. Disclosure covers the ECAIs used, the asset classes each is applied to, the issuer-to-issue rating transfer process, and the mapping of each agency's rating scale to SAMA risk buckets. It binds all SAMA-supervised banks that use the standardised (or simplified standardised) approach and rely on external ratings; annual frequency, flexible format, with a reasoned explanation permitted where amounts are negligible.

Template CR4 is a Pillar 3 quantitative disclosure showing, for portfolios under the standardised approach for credit risk, exposures before and after credit conversion factors and credit risk mitigation, together with resulting RWA and RWA density. It sits alongside definitions of the standardised approach (including simple vs comprehensive CRM treatment with supervisory haircuts) used across the disclosure framework. It binds SAMA-supervised banks using the credit risk standardised approach.

Template CR5 is a Pillar 3 quantitative disclosure breaking down standardised-approach credit exposures post-CCF and post-CRM by regulatory asset class and applied risk weight band. It is part of the same SAMA Pillar 3 framework document that also sets out related disclosures on reconciliation of accounting and regulatory exposure amounts and asset encumbrance. It binds SAMA-supervised banks applying the standardised approach for credit risk.
lookup_terms: exposures by asset class and risk weight

data.summary: Table CRE is a Pillar 3 qualitative disclosure on internal ratings-based (IRB) models used to compute credit RWA, covering model development, approval and change governance, independence between model development, risk management and internal audit, model reporting, the scope of SAMA's approval by entity/portfolio/exposure class, and EAD coverage split between standardised, F-IRB and A-IRB. It is mandatory for banks using F-IRB or A-IRB for any exposures; annual, flexible format.

Template CR6 is a Pillar 3 quantitative disclosure presenting IRB credit risk exposures by regulatory portfolio and PD range, with associated parameters (PD, LGD, EAD, maturity), RWA, RWA density, expected loss and provisions. It supports comparison of model outputs against actual outcomes for banks with SAMA approval to use F-IRB or A-IRB approaches. It binds SAMA-supervised banks using IRB approaches for credit risk.

Template CR7 is a Pillar 3 quantitative disclosure showing, by IRB portfolio (sovereign, banks, corporate, specialised lending, retail sub-classes, equity, purchased receivables, split F-IRB/A-IRB), hypothetical pre-credit derivatives RWA against actual RWA, to isolate the mitigating effect of credit derivatives used as a CRM technique. It is mandatory semiannually, fixed format, for SAMA-supervised banks using F-IRB and/or A-IRB, with narrative commentary explaining the RWA impact.

A Pillar 3 credit-risk disclosure template (CR8) within SAMA's Pillar 3 Disclosure Requirements Framework, covering movements in credit risk risk-weighted assets for exposures treated under the internal ratings-based approach. Surrounding material sets out how standardised versus modelled (F-IRB, A-IRB, supervisory slotting) RWA are delineated, including exclusions for counterparty credit risk, CVA and banking-book securitisation, and the phase-in for equity exposures. It binds banks subject to SAMA's Pillar 3 regime that use IRB approaches; open it to confirm row/column definitions and reporting frequency.

Pillar 3 template CR9 requires banks to disclose backtesting of probability of default per portfolio, comparing PD used in IRB capital calculations against observed obligor default rates over at least a five-year average annual default rate.
