It concerns damage short of total destruction of the leased vehicle and the treatment of the parties' rights and rental obligations in that event, disclosed to the lessee in the contract summary. It binds lessors (banks and finance companies) that must contract on the approved form.

Node for the insurance provisions of the standard-form individual vehicle finance lease (Ijarah) contract mandated by SAMA, covering cover on the leased vehicle and the disclosure of insurance in the contract's financial summary. It sits alongside the loss, maintenance and inspection clauses and determines how insurance costs and duties are allocated between lessor and lessee. It binds banks and finance companies as lessors, which may not conclude non-conforming or amended contracts.

Section of SAMA's mandatory model vehicle finance lease (Ijarah) contract for individuals, issued by circular to banks and finance companies under the Banking Control Law, the Finance Companies Control Law and the Finance Lease Law and its implementing regulation. This node covers the breach, default and contract-rescission provisions, alongside related consequences of late payment, lessee withdrawal, expiry without ownership transfer, and death or incapacity of the lessee. It binds lessors, who must use the approved form without amendment and may not conclude contracts conflicting with it.

Annex/clause of SAMA's mandatory model vehicle finance lease (Ijarah) contract for individuals dealing with transfer of ownership of the leased asset, including the ownership transfer certificate and the related procedures (including early ownership acquisition and delays in completing transfer formalities). It sits within the standard form that lessors must apply unchanged. Binds banks and finance companies acting as lessors to individual lessees.

Royal Decree-approved Law on the Practice of Transporting Money, Precious Metals and Valuable Documents, defining those terms and setting a licensing regime administered by the Ministry of Interior / Public Security, with three-year renewable licences, fees, geographic scope, mandatory insurance cover, and advance notification of high-value transports. It applies to financial institutions whose business requires such transport (banks, exchange houses, investment and insurance firms), precious metal factories, showrooms and outlets, and licensed private security companies. Relevant to SAMA-supervised entities as an external statutory obligation layered on their cash operations.
lookup_terms: transport of money and precious metals law
نظام مزاولة نقل النقود والمعادن الثمينة

data.summary: SAMA circular on controls for handling old or damaged bank equipment and assets being disposed of, such as ATMs, POS terminals, computers, imaging devices and associated documents, tapes and discs. It requires banks to adopt policies and procedures for disposal that preserve the confidentiality of information held on such items and prohibits ordinary discarding that could allow misuse. Addressed to local banks and licensed exchange houses, which retain regulatory responsibility for the information contained in the equipment.

SAMA's Rules Governing Bancassurance Activities, defining key terms (Company, Bank, Bancassurance Activities, Agreement, Authorised Employee, Client) and setting the scope, objective and core requirements for marketing and distributing insurance products through banks. The rules regulate the bank–insurer relationship, requiring the activity to be conducted directly through the bank as a distribution channel rather than as an insurance agency relationship. They bind licensed banks and licensed cooperative insurance companies, with the Cooperative Insurance Companies Control Law, the Banking Control Law and other SAMA instructions applying residually.

Part of the Bancassurance Rules setting out the mandatory minimum content of the bank–insurer Agreement (term, termination, distribution channels, training, KYC, compliance, covered insurance products, marketing, premium collection, commission and its calculation, client care and complaints, claims handling) together with the bank's obligations and professional conduct duties. It makes the bank fully responsible for Authorised Employees' conduct of bancassurance activities and imposes honesty, competence, disclosure, accuracy and confidentiality standards toward Clients and the insurer. Binds banks conducting bancassurance in the Kingdom.

An obligations article within SAMA's draft Rules Governing Bancassurance Activities, setting out what the licensed insurance Company must do when a Bank markets and distributes its insurance products. Duties include obtaining SAMA's prior approval for material amendments to the Agreement, submitting an annual training plan for Authorised Employees (covering marketing/distribution techniques, product workshops and AML/CTF training), preserving confidentiality of Bank and Client data, periodically reviewing the Bank's conduct of Bancassurance Activities across electronic and non-electronic channels, and paying commission within SAMA-set limits. It also carries a tying prohibition barring the Bank from conditioning banking products on insurance purchase or vice versa, unless coverage is required by a competent authority.
lookup_terms: tying / bundling prohibition insurance banking products

data.summary: The defined term "Agreement" in SAMA's draft Rules Governing Bancassurance Activities: the contract under which an insurance Company and a licensed Bank agree that the Bank will carry out Bancassurance Activities. The node also carries the surrounding definitions, scope, objective and practice requirements, including that Bancassurance Activities must be conducted directly through the Bank as one of the Company's marketing and distribution channels and that the contractual relationship must not amount to an insurance agency relationship. It binds both the insurance Company and the Bank.

A cross-reference node for the Cooperative Insurance Companies Control Law as used in SAMA's draft Bancassurance Rules: it is the licensing basis for the "Company" (an insurer authorised to conduct insurance business in KSA), alongside the Banking Control Law for the "Bank". The Rules' scope article makes that Law, its Implementing Regulation, the Banking Control Law and other SAMA and competent-authority instruments residually applicable to anything not specifically addressed in the Rules. Relevant to determining which regime governs a given bancassurance question.

The preventive-measures provisions of the KSA Anti-Money Laundering Law binding financial institutions and DNFBPs: risk-based customer due diligence, PEP identification and additional measures, cross-border correspondent banking safeguards and the shell-bank prohibition, and originator/beneficiary information requirements for wire transfers (with a bar on executing transfers where required information cannot be obtained). The excerpt also includes the supervisory authorities' powers and duties, including information collection, on-site and offsite supervision, sectoral risk assessment, issuing binding guidance, international cooperation and fit-and-proper screening.

The confiscation and international-cooperation provisions of the KSA Anti-Money Laundering Law: on conviction for money laundering or a predicate offence the competent court must confiscate laundered funds, proceeds (including intermingled funds up to the intermingled value) and instrumentalities, subject to good-faith third-party rights. It also covers non-conviction-based confiscation (death, flight, absence), value-based confiscation of substitute assets, and mutual legal assistance, information exchange, recognition of foreign confiscation judgments and extradition. These provisions bind courts and competent authorities rather than supervised entities directly, but are relevant to asset-freezing and cooperation requests.

SAMA guidance notes accompanying the Regulatory Sandbox application form, explaining the four-stage operating model: application submission and eligibility assessment (60 business days), operational readiness against the Assessment Criteria (120 days) leading to a temporary permission (Letter of Authorisation), live testing for six to twelve months, and exit/graduation toward a full regulatory licence. It clarifies that the initial approval letter permits company formation as a FinTech but does not authorise commencing operations or onboarding customers. Addressed to innovators/FinTech applicants seeking to test in the Sandbox under SAMA supervision.
lookup_terms: Letter of Authorisation LoA temporary permission

data.summary: Describes SAMA's Regulatory Sandbox operating model as four sequential stages: application assessment (decision within 60 business days), operational readiness against the Assessment Criteria (120 days, ending in a temporary permission/Letter of Authorisation), live testing of six to twelve months, and graduation/exit. It also sets out the two possible outcomes of initial screening, including grounds for rejection where regulations already exist, the concept falls outside SAMA's regulatory perimeter, or no regulatory oversight is needed. Binds FinTech innovators seeking temporary permission to test in the KSA market; it is process guidance rather than a licensing regime.

Guidance notes for completing the SAMA Regulatory Sandbox Stage 1 application form, setting out its four sections: about your business, about your innovation, minimum viable product and technological readiness, and team background. It explains the information SAMA expects (contact details, business name, country of incorporation, registered address) and confirms a 60-business-day response window, with further information requested at Stage 2. Relevant to applicants preparing a sandbox submission; it does not confer permission to operate.

Covers Stage 2 of the Regulatory Sandbox: after a favourable initial screening the applicant receives an initial approval letter allowing company formation/update at the Ministry of Commerce as a FinTech, but expressly not permitting operations. Compliance with the Operational Readiness Assessment Criteria (AC) — covering fit and proper approvals for management, shareholder approval, a three-year financial model, performance metrics, IT/helpdesk support and other minimum compliance items — is assessed and monitored by the sandbox Risk Management Unit, culminating in a No Objection Letter to go live at Stage 3. Binds sandbox applicants before customer onboarding.

April 2017 SAMA circular addressed to all banks, insurance companies and finance companies clarifying the accounting treatment and financial statement presentation of Zakat and income tax. It withdraws the SAMA Accounting Standards for Commercial Banks with effect from 1 January 2017 and requires financial statements under IFRS as adopted by SAMA (IFRS except IAS 12 and IFRIC 21 insofar as they relate to Zakat), with a standalone guidance annexure applied consistently across the banking, insurance and finance sectors.
lookup_terms: SAMA Accounting Standards for Commercial Banks

data.summary: Part of SAMA's Rules Governing Credit Risk Exposure Classification and Provisioning, issued under the Finance Companies Control Law and its Implementing Regulation (notably the provisioning duties in Article 13 and Article 62). It requires finance companies to classify exposures, individually or collectively, into three stages mapped to regulatory categories (Regular, Special Monitoring/Substandard, Doubtful, Loss), with Stage 1 covering exposures showing no significant increase in credit risk since origination and Stage 2 those with SICR. It supersedes the category definitions in the earlier Provisions Guidelines circular and binds licensed finance companies.

The expected credit loss elements of SAMA's Rules Governing Credit Risk Exposure Classification and Provisioning for finance companies: definitions aligned to IFRS 9 (probability of default, exposure at default, loss given default, financial asset, 12-month and lifetime ECL, Stage 1/Stage 2 exposures) and governance duties such as documented and board-approved ECL methodologies reviewed at least annually, quarterly board reporting on provision adequacy, annual independent internal audit review, and a default-asset management policy covering recovery strategies, collateral revaluation and timely write-offs. Effective 1 July 2021, replacing the earlier Provisioning Guidelines circular.

A section of SAMA's credit risk classification and provisioning rules for finance companies dealing with restructuring of exposures, distinguishing forbearance (concession granted because of the borrower's financial difficulty) from renegotiation, refinancing and rescheduling. It sets identification criteria for forbearance and financial difficulty, mandates stage allocation of forborne exposures (Stage 2B, 3A or 3B), and prescribes cure/probation periods and repayment conditions for re-staging out of Stage 3, with shorter cure periods for retail customers. It binds finance companies licensed under the Finance Companies Control Law.

The governance section of SAMA's liquidity risk management rules for finance companies, allocating ultimate responsibility for liquidity risk to the Board and setting out its duties: setting liquidity risk tolerance, approving strategy, policies, the contingency funding plan and stress testing framework at least annually, and monitoring the liquidity profile. It also defines senior management responsibilities and recommends an ALCO, plus reporting of cash flow mismatches, funding concentration and early warning signals to management, the Board and SAMA. It binds finance companies and their boards and senior management.

Sets the requirement for finance companies to maintain a Contingency Funding Plan addressing liquidity crisis strategy and cash flow shortfalls under stress, including definition of a liquidity crisis event, early warning indicators, activation authority, roles and escalation, and periodic testing and updating. Adjacent text covers funding diversification, funding concentration limits and the cushion of unencumbered high quality liquid assets. It binds finance companies subject to SAMA's liquidity risk management rules.

SAMA's 2020 Regulations for Deposit Taking Finance Companies, applicable to all DTFCs in KSA and issued under the Finance Companies Control Law and its Implementing Regulation. It sets the conditions for exercising deposit-taking activity — mobilising savings and time deposits from non-individual customers and lending out of those deposits — together with corporate governance, prudential, liquidity and depositor record-keeping requirements (records preserved five calendar years), and applies in addition to the general finance company regime.

Chapter 5 of the DTFC Regulations, requiring every DTFC to have a Board-approved liquidity risk management plan covering management structures, net funding requirements, contingency funding planning and internal controls. It imposes hard statutory limits: a minimum 20% liquid asset holding against deposit and short-term liabilities, statutory deposits with SAMA of at least 4% of deposit liabilities, and a cap on deposit liabilities of 15 times total capital, with a one-month remediation route. It also sets monthly liquidity reporting to SAMA by the 15th business day and completion instructions for the liquidity return.

Chapter 3 of the DTFC Regulations setting SAMA's internal governance and risk management requirements for deposit taking finance companies, proportionate to the nature, scale and complexity of their business. It requires a clear organisational structure, job descriptions for each senior manager tied to SAMA fit and proper pre-approval, a Management Responsibilities Description Document, and segregation of functions. Associated material addresses the compliance officer's role, KYC account acceptance standards, ongoing monitoring of accounts and transactions, suspicious transaction reporting to the FIU with notification to SAMA, and risk-based classification of accounts.

Chapter 6 (Asset Quality) provisions of the Deposit Taking Finance Companies Regulations 2020 establishing the mandatory loan review function in every DTFC. It requires the loan portfolio and lending activity to follow a board-approved written lending policy, timely identification and internal classification of problem accounts, board/management reporting on credit risk and control effectiveness, and continuous maintenance of adequate loss provisions. It binds deposit-taking finance companies licensed by SAMA, with duties allocated to the board or its delegated authority and senior management.

Sets the classification and provisioning rules for DTFC loan portfolios: quarterly review and classification per Appendix C, contagion of non-performing status across all loans of a single borrower, and specific treatment of renegotiated/restructured and twice-restructured facilities (Substandard, Doubtful or Loss depending on repayment of past-due principal and profit). It also mandates profit suspension on non-performing exposures, reversal of accrued but uncollected profit, conditions for return to accrual, and minimum provisioning percentages (Normal 1%, Watch 5%, Substandard 25%, Doubtful 75%, Loss 100%), with a floor where IFRS impairment is lower. Binds every deposit-taking finance company supervised by SAMA.

Covers the capital adequacy regime for DTFCs (Chapter 4) together with the completion instructions for the Capital to Risk Weighted Assets return. It sets the 20% capital adequacy requirement and record-keeping to compute it, SAMA's power to impose higher individual minimum ratios (e.g. for capital deficiency, high risk exposure, poor asset quality, rapid growth, or holding-company contagion), definitions of core and supplementary capital (including term subordinated debt and statutory loan loss reserve capped at 1.25% of RWA, supplementary capped at core), and the risk-weighting of on- and off-balance sheet exposures. Binds every DTFC; SAMA determines compliance.
lookup_terms: capital to risk weighted assets return

data.summary: Chapter 5 liquidity requirements for DTFCs plus completion instructions for the Appendix B liquidity statement. It mandates a board-approved liquidity risk management plan (management structures and MIS, net funding measurement, contingency funding, internal controls), a 20% minimum holding of liquid assets against deposit and short-term liabilities, statutory deposits with SAMA of at least 4% of deposit liabilities, a cap of 15 times total capital on deposit liabilities with a one-month remedy, and monthly reporting by the 15th business day. Binds every deposit-taking finance company; SAMA may vary the statutory deposit percentage.

Appendix C asset quality return and its completion instructions, read with Chapter 6, prescribing how DTFCs report loans by classification category (Normal, Watch, Substandard, Doubtful, Loss) with number of accounts, outstanding amounts, minimum provisioning percentages, provisions required, and security held. It also carries return definitions for on- and off-balance sheet items (loans reported net of provisions, treatment of reserves appropriated from retained earnings, credit risk equivalents at 100% weight). Binds every DTFC reporting to SAMA.

Operational rules for the DTFC General Account and linked Term Deposit Accounts. Credits are restricted to funds from the accountholder's own bank account(s) or their Term Deposit Account, with name-matching against the remitter (funds returned if mismatched) and recording of remitter name, IBAN and value date; withdrawals must go back to a source account of the accountholder, and transfers are permitted only between General Accounts in the same name. Term Deposit Accounts have a six-month minimum tenor and prescribed deal data, including Sharia-compliant commodity details. Binds deposit-taking finance companies; relevant to source-of-funds and account-integrity controls.

A SAMA circular to payment service providers reinforcing that KYC/customer verification procedures must be applied and tested for effectiveness before selling or activating POS terminals, including where marketing and promotion of terminals is outsourced to a party that must itself be SAMA-licensed. It also requires internal policies covering all customer segments, risk identification, monitoring and reporting, and confirmation that a POS device is linked only to the merchant's own bank account with no transfer to another account. It binds licensed payment service providers, with grounding in the Banking Control Law and the Payment Service Provider Regulations (licensing scope and fraud-detection obligations).
lookup_terms: marketing and promotion of payment services

data.summary: A SAMA circular amending the pricing applied to e-wallet top-up transactions funded by mada cards through the e-commerce path, replacing percentage-based pricing with capped/fixed amounts for the Merchant Service Charge and the Interchange Fee. Use of these amended fees is restricted to that specific transaction type, and all fees must be disclosed in new and updated Merchant Service Agreements with documented merchant acceptance before signing. It binds banks, payment service providers and Saudi Payments from the stated effective date.

A SAMA circular requiring supervised financial institutions to deal and contract only with real estate brokers licensed by the Real Estate General Authority, relying on the Real Estate Brokerage Law's prohibition on unlicensed brokerage or real estate services. It directs firms to verify broker licensing status through the Authority's public register. It binds all institutions under SAMA supervision and licensing.

A SAMA circular implementing the mandatory provision of electronic payment acceptance by all groceries and food supply stores in the Kingdom from the stated date, as part of the anti-commercial-concealment programme and cash-reduction strategy. It obliges banks and payment service providers to be ready to open merchant bank accounts and e-wallets, to receive and process requests for SAMA-authorised acceptance channels (POS terminals and QR) across all service channels in line with the applicable regulatory and operational rules, to apply Merchant Category Code 5411 for this activity, and to brief staff internally.

A SAMA circular relaxing an earlier restriction that barred charitable associations and non-profit foundations from GPRS (mobile) POS terminals, now permitting all SAMA-authorised electronic payment solutions including GPRS POS for these entities. The permission is conditional on the association or foundation obtaining approval from the National Center for Non-Profit Sector Development. It binds banks and payment service providers operating in the Kingdom, effective from issuance, and should be read with the earlier circulars on charity POS restrictions and 4G POS upgrades.
lookup_terms: National Center for Non-Profit Sector Development

data.summary: A SAMA circular issuing the revised Basel framework for Interest Rate Risk in the Banking Book, updating the 2004 principles on identification, measurement, monitoring, control and supervision of IRRBB. Key changes include guidance on interest rate shock scenarios and behavioural/modelling assumptions, enhanced quantitative disclosure requirements, an updated standardised framework, and a tighter outlier threshold of 15% of Tier 1 capital (previously 20% of total capital); it is accompanied by regulatory returns and FAQs with national discretions. It applies to domestic banks only and not to foreign bank branches.
lookup_terms: interest rate risk in the banking book

data.summary: Operational rules within the Deposit Taking Finance Companies Regulations governing how a DTFC opens and maintains Term Deposit Accounts and their mandatory linkage to a General Account, whose sole purpose is to service Term Deposit operations. It sets preconditions for opening (an active General Account plus a signed/accepted Term Deposit Deal), naming and one-to-one linkage rules, the prohibition on de-linking or recycling an account for another deal, and the permitted credit entries to the General Account (funds from the accountholder's own bank accounts with remitter name matching, or maturity proceeds with principal and profit credited separately, including Islamic commodity deal details). It binds licensed deposit-taking finance companies dealing with their depositors.

Chapter 11 of the Deposit Taking Finance Companies Regulations sets when a DTFC must freeze a General Account, principally on expiry of the customer's or juristic entity's identification/authorisation documents (e.g. 90 days after expiry of a licence or commercial registration) or where opening documents carry no validity date, and requires monitoring of directors' and authorised signatories' IDs with suspension of their operating powers. It also requires the freezing right and customer notification to be documented in account opening forms and contracts, and interacts with SAMA-directed disclosure and blocking of balances. It binds deposit-taking finance companies in respect of all customer accounts.

Chapter 12 of the Deposit Taking Finance Companies Regulations defines when a General Account becomes Inactive (one year without customer movement) and Dormant (a further year), imposes dual control and higher-authority approval for reactivation, restricts withdrawals from dormant accounts to duly authorised persons, and requires board-approved policies for customer contact, file isolation, supervision and annual internal audit. It clarifies that a General Account linked to a live Term Deposit Account does not accrue inactivity, and that the rules apply to all customers including those with other active accounts. It binds deposit-taking finance companies.

Chapter 14 of the Deposit Taking Finance Companies Regulations governs disclosure of customer account data and balances and the blocking of funds at the request of official authorities, requiring that such communications pass through SAMA only. It requires searches to cover all relationship types (active, closed, suspense, inactive, dormant General Accounts and Term Deposit Accounts) and sets the scope and duration of blocking, including the carve-out for accounts of companies in which the customer is merely a shareholder and the requirement to maintain a block until SAMA notifies otherwise. It binds deposit-taking finance companies responding to authority or SAMA requests.

The Law on Combating Terrorism Crimes and their Financing, setting the statutory definitions (terrorist crime, terrorism financing crime, terrorist, terrorist entity), offences, and the institutional architecture for CTF in the Kingdom. It establishes the Permanent Committee for Combating Terrorism and its Financing (implementation of UN Security Council resolutions), the Committee for Mutual Legal Assistance, and the General Directorate of Financial Intelligence as the national FIU receiving, analysing and disseminating suspicious transaction reports and empowered to obtain further information from financial institutions via the supervisory authority. It binds state authorities, financial institutions, DNFBPs and any person within its criminal scope.
lookup_terms: Combating Terrorism Crimes and their Financing Law

data.summary: Chapter Six of the CTF Law imposes the core preventive obligations on financial institutions, DNFBPs and non-profit organisations: documented TF risk assessment (including customers, geographies, products, channels and new products/technologies before use) available to supervisors, risk-based customer due diligence with enhanced measures where TF risk is high, and record keeping of transactions and documents for at least ten years (extendable by the Public Prosecution) in a form allowing reconstruction of transactions. Related chapters cover reporting to the Financial Intelligence Directorate, information sharing with domestic and foreign counterparts, and supervisory authority powers including inspection, sectoral risk assessment, guidance-issuing and cooperation.

A concept node covering the Basel Committee's 2004 Principles for the management and supervision of interest rate risk, as referenced in SAMA's circular adopting the revised IRRBB standards. It frames the baseline supervisory expectations for identifying, measuring, monitoring and controlling interest rate risk in the banking book, and records the key revisions (shock-scenario and behavioural/modelling assumption guidance, expanded Pillar 3-style disclosure, an updated standardised framework, and a tighter outlier test moved from 20% of total capital to 15% of Tier 1 capital). It binds domestic banks in KSA; foreign bank branches are outside scope.
lookup_terms: interest rate risk in the banking book
IRRBB disclosure Table A Table B

data.summary: The Basel Committee sound practices paper, circulated by SAMA, on banks' credit relationships with highly leveraged institutions (HLIs), including hedge funds. It sets expectations on board-approved credit risk strategy and risk appetite, HLI-specific policies and procedures, due diligence and financial information, exposure measurement, limit setting, collateral and covenants, and ongoing counterparty monitoring. It applies to Saudi banks that deal with counterparties meeting the HLI/hedge fund definition, alongside SAMA's internal control guidelines and each bank's own credit policies.

A cross-reference node to SAMA's Internal Control Guidelines for Commercial Banks, invoked in the 1999 HLI circular as the existing framework under which exposures to highly leveraged institutions and hedge funds must be managed. It functions here as the domestic regulatory anchor that, together with a bank's internal credit policies and procedures, gives effect to the Basel HLI sound practices. It binds all banks addressed by the circular.
lookup_terms: Internal Control Guidelines for Commercial Banks

data.summary: A cross-reference node to the Basel Committee's earlier risk management guidelines for derivatives (and the related 1998 CPSS/Euro-currency Standing Committee report on OTC settlement and counterparty risk), which identify types and sources of counterparty risk in OTC transactions and sound practices for each risk type. Within the HLI paper these guidelines are the antecedent material drawn on and applied to the specific risks posed by highly leveraged counterparties. Relevant to banks running OTC derivatives books.

The SAMA circular transmitting the Basel Committee paper on sound practices for banks' interactions with highly leveraged institutions, issued after the near-collapse of LTCM. It requires banks to ensure credit, risk management and related function heads are conversant with the practices described, and to manage any HLI or hedge fund exposures in line with SAMA's internal control guidelines and prudent internal credit policies. Addressed to all banks, at general manager and managing director level.

The section of the HLI sound practices dealing with measuring and limiting counterparty exposure: banks taking OTC derivatives positions against HLIs should build meaningful measures of potential future exposure (PFE), apply timely and plausible stress tests reflecting market, credit and liquidity risk interaction and collateral value effects, and feed these into decision-making. It also covers limit setting, requiring aggregate counterparty-level limits across on- and off-balance-sheet exposures, monitoring of mark-to-market exposure against PFE limits, and procedures to reduce exposure as limits are reached. Limits should be binding and not driven by customer demand.

Extract from the counter-terrorism financing law covering Chapter 9 (Supervision) and related information-exchange provisions, setting out the mandate of supervisory authorities over financial institutions, DNFBPs and non-profit organisations. It grants inspection, information-demand, sectoral risk-assessment, rule-making and international cooperation powers, and lists the graduated enforcement measures available for breaches — from written warnings and compliance orders through fines up to SAR 5 million per violation, employment bans, restriction or removal of directors and senior management, suspension of activities, and licence withdrawal. It binds supervised entities and their directors, board and executive/supervisory management personally, and also frames the Financial Intelligence Directorate's information sharing and the Permanent Committee's national CTF policy role.
lookup_terms: Permanent Committee for Counter-Terrorism and its Financing

data.summary: SAMA circular to all banks (attention CFOs and CROs) revisiting the earlier BCS circular on Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management and Supervision, which transposed the 2008 Basel Committee principles into banks' internal systems and processes. It requires banks to commission an internal audit assessing their implementation of those principles and to report the findings to the Director of Banking Supervision by the stated deadline. Binds all SAMA-licensed banks.
lookup_terms: Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management and Supervision
internal audit report to Banking Supervision

data.summary: SAMA banking supervision communication specifying additional risk information banks must include in their ICAAP submissions, covering connected-party lending concentration, liquidity metrics (LCR, NSFR, top-ten depositor and wholesale funding concentration), off-balance-sheet derivatives activity by currency, and capital leverage ratios including the statutory ratio under the Banking Control Law. It sets reporting content and multi-year historical coverage rather than capital thresholds. Binds all banks preparing ICAAP documents for SAMA.
lookup_terms: Liquidity Coverage Ratio Net Stable Funding Ratio reporting

data.summary: SAMA circular to all banks on applying the Basel III countercyclical capital buffer (CCyB) in Saudi Arabia, explaining its macroprudential purpose and the 0%–2.5% range of risk-weighted assets. It sets out the calculation methodology — reciprocity with buffer rates published by the Basel Committee, a default maximum rate where no rate is published, inclusion of private-sector and non-bank financial exposures (excluding interbank and public sector), ultimate-risk geographic allocation, and weighted averaging across jurisdictions — together with the effective date and SAMA's pre-announcement mechanics for increases and decreases. Binds all banks operating in the Kingdom.

Short SAMA circular (Payment Systems and Companies Control Department) forwarding a communication from the Communications, Space and Technology Commission about its published guide to locally developed technology products, presented as an indicative, non-binding list serving sectors including banking, insurance and finance. The circular is for awareness only, but reiterates that supervised entities must continue to comply with SAMA's existing instructions, particularly those governing outsourcing to third parties. Addressed to SAMA-supervised financial and payment entities.
lookup_terms: CST / Communications Space and Technology Commission circular
Payment Systems and Companies Control Department circular

data.summary: SAMA circular mandating the migration of point-of-sale terminals in the Kingdom to at least 4G connectivity, prompted by the telecoms regulator's decision to update terminal specifications and the phased shutdown of 2G and 3G networks. It requires POS suppliers to provide 4G-capable devices and obtain technical certification from Saudi Payments (mada network compatibility), makes 4G support the minimum for new and replacement installations from the stated date, and obliges banks and payment service providers hosting electronic payment services to execute a replacement plan for their existing POS fleet with minimum annual completion percentages and periodic progress reporting to SAMA and Saudi Payments. Binds banks, PSPs operating in the Kingdom, POS suppliers and Saudi Payments.

A sound-practice section of the SAMA-circulated Basel Committee paper on counterparty credit risk with highly leveraged institutions (HLIs), requiring banks to run timely, plausible stress tests of counterparty credit exposures under volatile markets. It expects stress scenarios to capture large market moves, liquidation effects, liquidity impacts on underlying markets and positions, and impairment of pledged collateral, and warns that merely widening confidence intervals or horizons for potential future exposure (PFE) is insufficient. Binds banks with trading and derivatives exposures to HLI counterparties; results must feed into limit setting and monitoring.

Section of the counterparty credit risk sound practices addressing credit limit setting for HLI and other counterparties, requiring overall credit limits at individual counterparty level that aggregate different exposure types on a comparable basis. Limits should be anchored on meaningful PFE measures covering on- and off-balance-sheet activity, with mark-to-market exposures monitored against initial PFE limits and clear procedures to reduce exposure when limits are approached. Limits are expected to be binding on banks and not driven by customer demand or competitive pressure.

Section covering collateral, early termination and other contractual provisions in dealings with HLIs, requiring these terms to be aligned with counterparty credit quality rather than driven solely by net asset value. It addresses initial margin where financial information is insufficient, internal guidelines for minimum transfer amounts and loss thresholds, two-way margining and rehypothecation rights, and haircut policies reflecting price volatility and wrong-way risk between counterparty default and collateral impairment. Applies to banks using secured loans, repos and OTC derivatives with HLI counterparties.

Section requiring banks to monitor HLI creditworthiness and exposure development on an ongoing basis, with counterparty credit quality reviews of material HLI exposures at least quarterly and additional reviews triggered by exposure increases or market volatility. Monitoring must go beyond net asset value and balance-sheet measures, using quantitative risk data such as VaR supplemented by stress testing, reviews of the counterparty's risk management capability, and understanding of risk concentrations. Also requires collateral management practices capturing all positions with at least daily marking to market and timely collateral transfers.
lookup_terms: collateral management daily mark to market

data.summary: Defined term underpinning the whole instrument: highly leveraged institutions are large financial institutions subject to very little or no direct regulatory oversight and very limited public disclosure, that take on significant leverage (broadly, the ratio of risk to capital). Hedge funds are the primary example, though not all hedge funds qualify and other institutions may share some HLI attributes. The definition scopes which counterparty relationships attract the paper's enhanced due diligence, exposure measurement, limit, collateral and monitoring expectations for banks.

SAMA guidance setting out how founders apply for a licence to conduct Buy Now Pay Later activity under the Finance Companies Control Law and the Rules Regulating BNPL Companies. It specifies submission channel and format, the unmodifiable application form, the checklist of required documents (draft articles of association, organisational structure, fit and proper forms for founders and board/committee candidates, feasibility study and business plan, and an irrevocable bank guarantee equal to 20% of minimum capital), and the licensing procedure. Binds applicants (founders/shareholders) seeking BNPL authorisation; false or omitted material information is treated as a violation of the Finance Companies Control Law and may cause rejection or cancellation of the licence.

SAMA guidance setting out how founders/shareholders (the "Applicant") apply for a licence to conduct Buy Now Pay Later activity, including the mandatory application form, checklist of attachments (articles of association, organisational structure, fit and proper forms for founders and board/committee candidates, feasibility study and business plan) and an irrevocable bank guarantee equal to 20% of the minimum required capital. It binds prospective BNPL companies seeking authorisation; false or omitted material information is treated as a breach of the Finance Companies Control Law and can lead to refusal or cancellation of the licence. Useful for pre-licensing readiness, not for ongoing BNPL conduct obligations.

Node identifying the Rules Regulating Buy Now Pay Later (BNPL) Companies as the instrument that, together with the Finance Companies Control Law, provides the licensing provisions and defined terms for BNPL activity. Here it appears only as the interpretive source for terms used in SAMA's licence application guidance, which binds applicants for a BNPL licence. Open the Rules themselves for substantive BNPL definitions, scope and conduct obligations; this node gives the licensing cross-reference.

SAMA's New Banking Products and Services Regulation (November 2023, v2.0), replacing the 2017 guidelines, setting minimum requirements for how banks identify, assess, monitor and manage risks arising from new or materially modified products and services, and when they must notify SAMA or obtain non-objection before launch. It applies to all banks licensed under the Banking Control Law and defines "product or service", "new product or service" and "existing product or service". Consult it for pre-launch regulatory clearance, governance and post-launch monitoring/audit duties.

Provisions placing oversight duties on a bank's Board for the offering of new products and services: ensuring senior management develops and implements internal policies and procedures, ensuring product risks are managed and consumer needs and rights addressed, and testing whether product offerings remain within the Board-approved risk appetite. Where offerings fall outside appetite, the Board must review and revise the appetite with documented justification and risk assessment and ensure policies are updated. Binds boards of banks licensed under the Banking Control Law.

Provisions making senior management accountable for the design, implementation and compliance of new products and services with Board-approved policies, for keeping offerings within approved scope, and for periodically reviewing policy adequacy and proposing amendments to the Board. Senior management must also identify and mitigate actual or perceived reputational effects and confirm full operational readiness (processes, controls, systems) and any other authorities' approvals before launch. Binds senior management of SAMA-licensed banks.

Requirements for banks to assign responsibility for and conduct full risk assessments of new products and services across their life cycle, to maintain risk management standards (due diligence, approvals, identification/measurement/monitoring/reporting, change management), and to apply a risk classification process producing an overall rating such as high/medium/low. It also requires third-party risk management where products are offered with fintechs, agents or similar partners, and gives the risk management function documentation, review and approval duties over product risk profiles, alongside internal audit, product development and ongoing monitoring obligations. Binds banks licensed under the Banking Control Law.
lookup_terms: internal audit within one year of launch

data.summary: Node covering the compliance function's duties under SAMA's New Banking Products and Services Regulation, alongside the adjacent risk management, internal audit and product development (business unit) roles. It requires pre-launch review of every new product or service from a compliance, regulatory and financial-crime angle, ongoing conformity with SAMA and other regulators' rules, at least annual assessment of non-compliance risk, and annual reporting of that risk and its mitigation to the Board. It binds licensed banks and, internally, their control functions and product owners.
lookup_terms: financial crime review of new products
internal audit new products and services
New Banking Products and Services Regulation

data.summary: Node covering the documentation/reporting duties and the notification pathway in SAMA's New Banking Products and Services Regulation. It requires banks meeting the stated maturity levels in SAMA's Cyber Security, Counter-Fraud, Business Continuity and IT Governance frameworks (independently validated annually) to notify SAMA of new products and services, launch within 12 months of the acknowledgment receipt, and re-notify before reintroducing anything discontinued for over 12 months; SAMA may request further information or prohibit a product on safety-and-soundness grounds. It also mandates an annual CEO-signed products and services report filed by the compliance function to the Banking Licensing Division by 1 March, plus record retention and a product inventory.
lookup_terms: annual product report 1 March CEO signed

data.summary: Node covering when a bank must obtain SAMA's prior non-objection rather than merely notify before launching a product or service. Non-objection is required for home loan products, financial lease products, financial derivatives, and anything not covered by existing SAMA rules; banks failing the required framework maturity level must seek non-objection for all products. Launch must occur within 12 months of the non-objection, and re-offering a product discontinued for more than 12 months requires a fresh non-objection.
lookup_terms: products not covered by existing regulations

data.summary: Node on the additional conditions for offering financial derivatives and structured products under the New Banking Products and Services Regulation. Banks must disclose profit/loss scenarios over the product horizon, satisfy themselves of customer awareness, prior investment experience, suitability against the customer's objectives and risk appetite, and obtain signed terms; they must not recommend a derivative unless satisfied it suits that customer. New derivative products must also be shown to have a bona fide economic purpose (not mere speculation, leverage or regulatory arbitrage) with identified intended users, and the bank must demonstrate organizational capacity to manage the resulting risks.

Node capturing the consumer-facing design considerations banks must build into their internal products and services policies and procedures. It requires target-market-appropriate design, formal customer appropriateness and fairness assessments before approval, fairness and suitability of offerings, avoidance of conflicts of interest, mis-selling and unfair terms, proportionate product-risk control across the value chain (development, governance, pricing, marketing, sale, distribution), phased commercial launch, and compliance with related SAMA instruments including the Responsible Lending Principles, Financial Consumer Protection Principles and Rules, and the advertising rules. It binds banks, with duties allocated to the Board, senior management and control functions.
lookup_terms: Financial Consumer Protection Principles and Rules

data.summary: Node covering product and service risk assessment duties, which connect the regulation to SAMA's Counter-Fraud Framework and companion frameworks used as the maturity gate for the notification route. Banks must assign responsibility for new-product risk, conduct full life-cycle risk assessments as the basis for launch decisions, apply risk management standards and a risk classification (e.g. high/medium/low), and manage third-party risk where products are offered with fintechs, agents or similar partners; the risk management function must document, review and approve each product's risk profile and have the capacity to monitor risks to the bank, customers and market stability.
lookup_terms: cyber security business continuity IT governance frameworks

data.summary: A glossary-level concept within SAMA's operational risk management guidance for banks, describing finite risk insurance as an external risk financing option that blends conventional risk transfer with self-insurance and carries an upper limit on the insurer's exposure. It sits alongside captives, risk retention groups, rent-a-captives and risk sharing pools as alternatives to conventional insurance. Relevant to Saudi banks designing the risk financing policy element of their Operational Risk Management Plan.

Refers to the Bankers Blanket Bond / Financial Institution Bond, the principal crime and fidelity insurance cover identified in SAMA's operational risk guidance as a risk-transfer tool against employee dishonesty, loss of property on premises and in transit, forgery and related exposures. It is presented as one of a small set of coverages of primary concern to banks, used in combination with internal controls, fraud programmes and internal audit. Guidance-level material for bank directors and senior management, not a standalone binding rule.

Defines the Operational Risk Manager as the senior bank officer responsible for developing the Operational Risk Management Plan and for implementing and running the Operational Risk Management Programme, reporting directly to the Managing Director/General Manager. The role interacts with the Operational Risk Management Committee (which reports to it), the Board (which approves the Plan annually) and Internal Audit in reviewing risk assessment and control matrices. Applies to banks operating in the Kingdom under SAMA's operational risk guidance.

A cross-reference to SAMA's Internal Control Guidelines for Commercial Banks Operating in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia (1989), identified as a companion instrument to the operational risk guidance. It underpins the internal-controls leg of operational risk mitigation, to be read together with the disaster recovery planning and physical security guidelines to form an integrated operational risk control programme for banks.
lookup_terms: Internal Control Guidelines for Commercial Banks
commercial banks Kingdom of Saudi Arabia

data.summary: A cross-reference to SAMA's Guidelines on Physical Security for Saudi Banks (1995), including the Minimum Physical Security Standards issued that year, cited as a companion instrument to the operational risk guidance. It addresses the physical-security controls that mitigate robbery, burglary and related crime exposures at branches and ATMs, and is intended to be applied together with the internal control and disaster recovery guidelines by banks in the Kingdom.
lookup_terms: Guidelines on Physical Security for Saudi Banks

data.summary: A cross-reference to the Saudi Company Law issued by Royal Decree M/6 of 1985, specifically Articles 66–82, cited in SAMA's operational risk guidance as the domestic source of joint liability of board members towards the company, shareholders and third parties for damages. It is used to frame directors' and officers' liability exposure inside the Kingdom, alongside lender liability exposures arising from lending and workout conduct.

A concept node within SAMA's operational risk guidance for banks, defining professional risk as the exposure arising directly from providing financial products and services, and treating it as a leading and fast-growing component of operational (pure) risk. It covers professional errors and omissions by staff (mis-transfers, unauthorised trading, booking errors) and the resulting liability toward customers and third parties, noting that losses on the bank's own account are uninsurable and must be controlled internally. It is addressed to directors and senior management of banks operating in the Kingdom, as guidance rather than a prescriptive rule set.

Concept node explaining Directors and Officers (D&O) liability as a category of professional liability distinct from the bank's own liability, covering personal exposure of executive and non-executive directors and senior officers for alleged negligent or imprudent acts or omissions. It identifies the main sources of exposure (shareholder actions, client service relationships, employment practices, environmental claims) and explains that the bank purchases the policy to indemnify its directors and officers, including where the bank cannot legally or financially indemnify them. Relevant to boards and senior management of banks in the Kingdom considering risk transfer for governance-level liability.

Concept node describing Professional Indemnity (PI) cover, which indemnifies the bank itself against claims by customers and third parties alleging errors, omissions, misstatement or imprudence by its directors, officers and employees in performing services. It contrasts PI with D&O: PI is limited to specified professional services (trust, brokerage, investment advisory) but protects the institution, whereas D&O is broader in wrongful acts but narrower in insureds. Guidance for bank management structuring operational risk financing for service-related liability.

Concept node treating political and regulatory instability as a source of operational risk for banks with cross-border operations or significant involvement in international trade. It expects Saudi banks operating outside the Kingdom to maintain management systems and procedures for monitoring the political and regulatory environments, including red-flag/warning indicators and alternative action plans to prevent or mitigate losses. Sits within SAMA's broader operational risk guidance directed at directors and senior management.

Concept node covering self insurance as an internal risk financing option for operational risk, including unfunded and funded retention, single parent captives and contractual transfer of risk, governed by formal loss retention guidelines set in the bank's Operational Risk Management Plan. It also explains that risk retention groups, group captives and risk sharing pools, though formed as insurance companies, are in substance self-insurance vehicles whose participants bear virtually all their own losses. Guidance for bank boards and senior management deciding how much operational risk to retain versus transfer.

Concept node on conventional (regular) insurance as an external risk financing option for operational risk, alongside self insurance and alternatives such as risk retention groups, agency captives, pools and finite risk insurance. It frames insurance as a means of funding loss exposure rather than controlling risk, to be combined with internal controls, segregation of duties, audit and physical security in an integrated operational risk programme. Addressed to directors and senior management of banks operating in the Kingdom.

This node sits within SAMA's New Banking Products and Services Regulation (effective 1 March 2024, superseding the 2017 guidelines) and covers the derivatives-specific conditions banks must satisfy before launching new products, including suitability, disclosure of profit/loss scenarios for structured products, bona fide economic purpose, internal capacity to manage the risks, and no adverse impact on SAIBOR/SAR. It cross-refers to SAMA's 2019 Rules on Trade Repository Reporting and Risk Mitigation Requirements for OTC Derivatives Contracts (as updated) and to a separate circular on SAR-versus-foreign-currency derivatives, and sets the documentation/checklist required for notification or non-objection. It binds banks licensed in KSA introducing new derivative or structured products.
lookup_terms: new banking products and services regulation

data.summary: A SAMA guide for bank directors and senior management explaining the nature of operational risk (treated as pure risk: loss or no loss) and the techniques for identifying, controlling and financing it, including internal controls, retention and insurance transfer. It contains a defined-terms glossary (Operational Risk Manager, Operational Risk Management Committee and Plan, risk financing policy, retention guidelines, risk assessment and control matrices) and requires a board-approved plan reviewed at least annually, plus periodic independent review of the risk management function. Addressed to banks operating in the Kingdom and intended to be read with SAMA's internal control, disaster recovery and physical security guidelines.

A category within SAMA's Operational Risk Management Guide identifying criminal activity by employees or third parties as historically the largest source of operational loss in Saudi banks, based on insurance claims data. It groups fraud, forgery, counterfeit currency, robbery/burglary, electronic crime and retail electronic crime as distinct sub-elements to be addressed in a bank's operational risk plan and control framework. Relevant to banks' internal control, insurance and board-level risk oversight rather than to AML reporting duties as such.

A sub-element of criminal risk in SAMA's Operational Risk Management Guide, identifying fraud as the single largest source of operational loss in the Saudi banking system, with the majority perpetrated by employees (notably cash and travellers cheque theft from branches and ATMs). It also flags customer and third-party fraud exposures arising from high ATM cash limits and network interoperability, credit card internal fraud across application, account setup, embossing and statement processes, external card fraud, and merchant fraud at point of sale. Guidance for banks' boards and operational risk functions on where fraud loss concentrates.

A sub-element of criminal risk in SAMA's Operational Risk Management Guide covering forgery and cheque fraud, historically the second largest operational loss category for Saudi banks, typically involving failure of staff to verify authenticity of cheques or negotiable instruments such as letters of credit before negotiation. It anticipates fewer but more technically sophisticated and higher-value forgeries as document reproduction technology advances, and expects banks' risk policies to address forgery committed by electronic means, including in signature verification and payment card/payment systems contexts.

A sub-element of criminal risk in SAMA's Operational Risk Management Guide dealing with computer and telecommunications-related crime against banks, spanning ATM, credit card, POS, corporate/cash management, EDI and retail electronic channels. The accompanying insurance discussion explains Electronic and Computer Crime (ECC) cover as a companion to the Bankers Blanket Bond / Financial Institution Bond, responding to third-party fraud and unexplained loss involving computer systems, electronic data, communications, transmissions, forged fax and voice-initiated transfers. Directed at banks assessing how to control versus transfer electronic crime exposure.
lookup_terms: Electronic and Computer Crime coverage ECC

data.summary: A SAMA rulebook setting general requirements for savings products offered by banks operating in the Kingdom, issued in both Arabic and English. It binds SAMA-licensed banks in the design, disclosure and administration of savings/deposit products offered to customers. The available extract is limited to the title/issuance page, so the substantive obligations must be read in the full document.
lookup_terms: General Rules for Savings Products in Banks

data.summary: SAMA prudential instructions adding Shari'ah-specific capital adequacy requirements for credit and market risk, issued under the SAMA Charter and the Banking Control Law and effective 1 January 2024. It maps Islamic contract structures (Murabahah with binding/non-binding purchase order, Ijarah Muntahia Bi Al Tamlik, Qard Hassan, and equity-type Musharakah/Mudarabah/Wakalah) to risk-weight treatment at each stage of the contract. It binds all SAMA-licensed domestic banks conducting Shari'ah compliant banking, including their majority-owned foreign subsidiaries and foreign branches, and is read alongside the SAMA Basel framework.

Concept node for the SAMA Basel framework (issued by circular in December 2022 and subsequent updates), the baseline prudential regime setting minimum capital requirements for credit risk, market risk and equity exposures. It is the reference standard against which Shari'ah-compliant contract stages are risk-weighted, and it continues to govern areas carved out of the Islamic add-on (e.g. ijarah-structured real estate finance exposures). Relevant to any question about which capital rulebook applies to a given exposure.
lookup_terms: minimum capital requirements for credit risk
minimum capital requirements for market risk

data.summary: The Credit Information Law establishes the principles and controls for collecting, exchanging, protecting and correcting consumer credit information, and defines key terms including Credit Information, Consumer, Member, Companies, Credit Record and Public Records. It applies to licensed credit information companies, members, and government and private entities that maintain credit information, imposing licensing, accuracy, updating, confidentiality and consumer-consent duties, and listing the acts treated as violations. Note the broad definition of Consumer (natural or corporate person engaging in credit transactions), which differs from consumer definitions in other SAMA regimes.
lookup_terms: member consent to obtain credit record

data.summary: A SAMA circular on the QR Code payments development project run with Saudi Payments, issued under SAMA's authority over payment and settlement systems (confirmed by Council of Ministers Resolution No. 226). It directs entities that had already launched QR-based payment services to comply with the project's technical and commercial standards for the payment environment and to complete required testing and certification with Saudi Payments before end-2021. It binds banks and SAMA-licensed fintech/payment companies offering QR code payment acceptance.

A short SAMA circular, issued through the Payment Systems and Companies Control Department, reaffirming mandatory compliance with SAMA's cybersecurity policies, frameworks and controls as well as national cybersecurity authority requirements amid rising cyber threats to the financial sector. It directs supervised entities to implement the Essential Cybersecurity Controls and the Critical Systems Cybersecurity Controls and to prioritise cybersecurity in their approved budgets. Primarily addressed to payment systems operators and payment service providers under SAMA supervision.

A SAMA circular from the Payment Systems and Companies Control Department relaying a request from the communications and IT regulator to establish governance over the registration of bulk SMS sender tag names through a unified portal for SMS service providers, aimed at preventing misuse of text messaging. It directs supervised entities to cooperate promptly with their contracted SMS providers and complete registration within the transitional period set by the regulator. It binds payment institutions and other SAMA-supervised entities that send bulk SMS to customers.

A SAMA circular supplementing an earlier instruction on standardising the content elements of SMS notifications sent to customers of financial institutions, extending the unified elements to newly introduced mada transaction types. Financial institutions must send notifications for those operations in line with the attached standard elements, with full application before the end of Q1 2022 and an implementation plan submitted to SAMA by 4 November 2021. It binds banks and payment institutions servicing accounts, memberships and e-wallets.

An informational SAMA circular conveying the Ministry of Commerce's approach to approving company incorporation contracts and their amendments, under which partners and the submitting party bear responsibility for the content in accordance with the Companies Law. SAMA stresses that this streamlined ministry process does not diminish financial institutions' own obligations under SAMA-issued regulations. Addressed to payment systems and companies supervised by SAMA; issued for information rather than as a new obligation.

A SAMA follow-up circular on the unified pricing model for POS and e-commerce services for mada card transactions carried out at money exchange and remittance centres, and for transfers made through e-wallets. It requires banks and payment service providers to report the extent of their compliance with and application of that pricing model to SAMA by 15 June 2022. It binds banks and licensed payment service providers acting as acquirers or wallet operators.

A SAMA circular responding to the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Development's concerns about integration failures between the Mudad platform's payroll management system and partner financial institutions, which delay employers' compliance with the Wage Protection Program and workers' receipt of wages. SAMA stresses adherence to the service level agreement with Mudad and the exercise of due care in resolving technical issues. It binds financial institutions and payment companies connected to the Mudad payroll ecosystem.

A SAMA circular requiring supervised financial institutions to adopt the National Cybersecurity Authority's Data Cybersecurity Controls (DCC-1:2022), invoking the SAMA Cyber Security Framework provisions on regulatory compliance and compliance with national/international industry standards. Institutions must ensure continuous compliance, complete a self-assessment using the attached assessment tool, and achieve full implementation no later than end of September 2023, alongside urgent cyber risk assessment and management. It binds SAMA-supervised financial institutions, including payment systems and companies.

A Ministry of Human Resources and Social Development ministerial decision (No. 112203, dated 18/06/1442H) issued under the Labour Law that restricts remote customer-service roles to Saudi nationals. It covers all occupations and jobs in establishments that serve customers remotely — by telephone, email, chat/electronic channels, social media or direct interaction — and applies whether staff are engaged through direct employment or indirectly via outsourcing contracts covering work forming the entity's main activity. It binds establishments operating in KSA (including financial institutions and their service providers) and exposes non-compliant establishments to the penalties in the violations and penalties schedule.

A SAMA circular from the Payment Systems and Companies Control Department reminding payment service providers to verify the legal/regulatory status of the customers they serve, including checking the validity of official identification documents and reflecting this in service policies and agreements (e.g. obliging counterparties to notify changes in their legal status). It ties this to the PSP Regulations provision allowing a PSP to refuse payment orders where execution would breach its legal obligations, and transmits lists of entities with cancelled commercial registrations for re-assessment. Binds all licensed payment service providers in KSA.

A short SAMA circular issued by the Payment Systems and Companies Control Department directing addressees to act on its content with immediate effect; the extracted context contains only the closing/signature block, and the substantive instruction on handling judicial orders is not reproduced here. Nominally addressed to payment service providers and payment companies supervised by SAMA. Open the source document to obtain the operative requirements.
lookup_terms: Payment Systems and Companies Control Department

data.summary: A SAMA circular instructing payment sector companies to take account of the special nature of entities licensed under the Integrated Logistics Special Zone regime (Royal Order 17/1 dated 01/02/1440H) when providing payment services, and to update their policies and service agreements accordingly. It sets identity verification requirements for such entities: a copy of the commercial registration issued by the General Authority of Civil Aviation, the articles of association and annexes, and identification of persons authorised to open and manage accounts. Binds all licensed payment service providers dealing with ILSZ-licensed entities.

A SAMA circular urging financial institutions to use the Ministry of Commerce "Electronic Delegation" service to appoint a representative to receive judicial notifications served against them and to monitor judicial orders via the Najiz portal. It relies on the Royal Order approving electronic means of judicial service and on the Enforcement Law and its Implementing Regulations (notification timing rules under Article 34), with the aim of allowing institutions to settle claims within the notification period and avoid coercive court measures. Addressed to SAMA-supervised financial institutions, issued through the payments supervision department.

A SAMA (then SAMA agency) circular from the Exchange Centres Supervision Division reaffirming mandatory compliance with the rules and instructions governing the movement of cash and with the Security Safety Guide, following earlier circulars on contracting with cash transport companies, use of high-specification security bags, and organisation of cash movement for local banks and exchange houses. It highlights vehicle requirements for transporting cash and valuables above the stated threshold and refers to the Law on Trading in Money and Precious Metals. Binds all exchange centres (money changers) operating in the Kingdom.
lookup_terms: دليل السلامة الأمنية Security Safety Guide

data.summary: The Currency Law, issued by Royal Decree No. 6 dated 1/7/1379H, establishing the Saudi Riyal as the monetary unit, its subdivisions and par value in gold, and vesting the exclusive privilege of minting, printing and issuing Saudi currency in SAMA. It allocates decision-making between the Council of Ministers, the Minister of Finance and SAMA over denominations, design, withdrawal and replacement of worn notes and coins, seizure of counterfeit currency, full gold and foreign-currency backing of issued currency, legal tender status and limits on compulsory acceptance of subsidiary coin, signature of banknotes, withdrawal of the gold sovereign, and SAMA's record-keeping and periodic publication duties. It binds SAMA, government bodies and, as to legal tender and counterfeiting, all persons in the Kingdom.

SAMA circular to finance companies (transmitting earlier April 2020 email instructions) on how to treat expired National IDs and Iqamas (resident IDs) for customer due diligence purposes. It relies on the Ministry of Interior's two-month automatic extension of expired National IDs and the Passports Directorate's three-month extension of Iqamas for private-sector expatriates, and permits such IDs to be treated as valid when applying CDD requirements under the AML Law and its Implementing Regulations, Article 17 of the CTF Implementing Regulations and SAMA's AML/CTF Guide. It binds finance companies operating in the Kingdom, effective from the date of the email transmission.

SAMA circular confirming how government housing support from the Ministry of Municipality, Rural Affairs and Housing or the Real Estate Development Fund is treated when assessing an individual customer's income under the Responsible Lending Principles for Individuals. It restates that government subsidies may not be counted in monthly income except housing support paid periodically (non-periodic or one-off support is excluded), and that the debt burden ratio for such beneficiaries is computed on total monthly income where support is paid monthly. It binds banks, finance companies and credit information companies operating in the Kingdom.
lookup_terms: Ministry of Municipal Rural Affairs and Housing support

data.summary: Council of Ministers Resolution No. 637 dated 17/10/1441 AH approving an amendment to Article 12 of the Law on Combating the Financing of Terrorism (issued by Royal Decree M/21 dated 12/02/1439 AH), restricting provisional release of the accused to temporary release ordered by the Public Prosecution where investigations are not harmed and there is no flight or disappearance risk. It also approves repealing Article 9 of the CTF Implementing Regulations and annexes a draft Royal Decree giving effect to the amendment. It is a legislative instrument addressed to state authorities rather than a supervisory obligation on financial institutions.
lookup_terms: Law on Combating the Financing of Terrorism

data.summary: Royal Decree No. M/142 dated 19/10/1441 AH enacting the amendment to Article 12 of the Law on Combating the Financing of Terrorism, limiting provisional release of persons accused under that Law to temporary release ordered by the Public Prosecution subject to investigation and flight-risk conditions. It is the enacting instrument for Council of Ministers Resolution 637 and directs ministers and heads of independent entities to implement it within their competences.

Node for the Law on Combating the Financing of Terrorism, issued by Royal Decree M/21 dated 12/02/1439 AH, with its Implementing Regulations issued by Council of Ministers Resolution 228 dated 02/05/1440 AH. It is the primary KSA statute criminalising terrorist financing and underpinning CTF obligations that SAMA-supervised entities apply through CDD, reporting and targeted financial sanctions requirements. In the supplied context it appears as the instrument amended by Resolution 637 and Royal Decree M/142 (Article 12; repeal of Article 9 of the Implementing Regulations).
lookup_terms: Law on Combating the Financing of Terrorism

data.summary: Template bilateral agreement between the Saudi Credit Bureau (SIMAH), acting as the GLEIF-accredited Local Operating Unit for Legal Entity Identifiers, and a SAMA-supervised financial institution that grants credit to legal entities, enabling the institution to arrange LEI issuance, updating and renewal for its corporate clients. It sets fees per issuance/renewal request (VAT excluded), monthly invoice settlement terms, confidentiality and data-protection duties under the Credit Information Law, its Implementing Regulations, SAMA instructions and national cyber security requirements, plus amendment, severability, notice, governing law and dispute provisions. It is entered into pursuant to a SAMA circular permitting banks to sign the agreement with SIMAH.

A SAMA user/guidance manual explaining how supervised entities access the Returns Management System (RMS) portal and submit, validate and resubmit supervisory and prudential returns for each reporting period. It is procedural rather than substantive: it covers account creation by SAMA, period-opening notifications, template-based file upload, validation, submission and the resubmission request route where the supervisor raises observations. It binds/serves entities under SAMA supervision that are required to file periodic returns, and the SAMA supervisory staff who review, accept or return them.

A SAMA reporting template (Version 2.0) issued by the Exchange Centres Supervision Division requiring quarterly submission of foreign-currency sales and purchases (by counterparty type: local banks, other exchange houses, individuals, and cross-border), inward/outward remittance volumes, largest-customer data, counterfeit currency detected, and staff data. It is a supervisory data-collection instrument rather than a rule-making text, but the underlying filing duty is enforceable against licensed exchange centres. Relevant where customer-concentration and counterfeit-note reporting intersect with AML/CTF supervision of money changers.

An annual regulatory data return used by SAMA's Exchange Centres Supervision Division to collect licensing and corporate information from licensed exchange centres: licence issue/renewal/expiry dates, branch list and addresses, ownership and partner shareholdings, executive/non-executive designations, key control-function holders (CEO/manager, internal audit) and appointment dates, cash insurance policy expiry, and contracted external third parties. It supports fit-and-proper, licensing and outsourcing oversight rather than financial reporting.

A SAMA template (Version 2.0) from the Exchange Centres Supervision Division for comparative quarterly and annual financial statements of exchange centres, covering balance-sheet lines (foreign currency inventory, amounts due from/to related parties for cash drawings, credit sales and cash support, fixed assets, zakat provision, end-of-service benefits, equity and retained earnings) and income-statement lines. Income-statement data is reported for the three-month period in quarterly filings and for the full year in annual filings.

Royal Decree M/148 approving amendments to the Personal Data Protection Law (originally issued by Royal Decree M/19), together with the enabling Council of Ministers resolution. It revises core defined terms (destruction, disclosure, sensitive data, data subject), restates the data subject rights article, and touches the cross-border transfer adequacy assessment and the fees provision, with SDAIA as the competent authority. It binds all controllers and processors of personal data in KSA, including SAMA-supervised financial institutions, and applies from the effective date of the amendments.

A guidance publication of the Authority of Persons with Disabilities (APD) on emergency evacuation planning for persons with disabilities, setting out definitions (evacuation, emergency, first responder, safe assembly areas, escape routes), disability categories, building hazards, self-preparedness, evacuation plan steps, and accessibility features such as public address and assistive listening systems, visual alarms, refuge areas and tactile warning surfaces. It is advisory in nature and directed at facility operators and entities serving the public rather than a SAMA prudential or conduct rule, but is relevant to branch and premises accessibility obligations.

data.why: If you are computing capital for an object finance exposure under supervisory slotting, you cannot stop at the slotting risk weight — you must also determine the expected loss amount and compare it against eligible provisions. Both sections sit within the same IRB chapter of SAMA's capital framework, and the specialised lending slotting rules generate EL figures that feed the general IRB EL-versus-provisions treatment (shortfall deducted from capital, excess added back within limits). The practical consequence is that slotting decisions on object finance drive not only RWA but also a separate provisioning comparison that must be performed consistently. This link is inferred from the structure of the framework, so confirm the specific EL percentages and provision-offset rules in the primary text.

When assessing internal audit obligations of a finance or real estate refinance company, treat the Principles as an exercise of SAMA's supervisory powers under the Finance Companies Control Law rather than as free-standing good practice.
