The cross-reference is explicit: floors and equivalent constraints are set in parallel provisions of SA-CCR, the comprehensive approach under standardised credit risk, and IMM, so the same economic exposure must not be double-counted or measured on an inconsistent basis. The consequence is that any EAD reported for counterparty exposures should be traced back to the SA-CCR provisions and their floor, not to the general EAD text alone.

Where a bank holds an equity investment in a fund and looks through to the fund's underlying holdings, the capital treatment of any securitisation exposures inside that fund is determined by the securitisation hierarchy, of which SEC-IRBA is the top tier. The look-through approach therefore only delivers a lower capital outcome if the bank can meet the SEC-IRBA conditions for the underlying pool, including the ability to compute KIRB and the relevant attachment/detachment and supervisory parameters; otherwise the fall-back tiers or a punitive treatment apply. For a decision, the availability of underlying data and IRB approval for the pool type determines whether look-through is genuinely usable, so both provisions must be read together.

Delta risk cannot be assessed or capitalised as a standalone charge: it is one of the risk components of the sensitivities-based method under the standardised approach to market risk, alongside vega and curvature, and its output only becomes a capital requirement after bucketing and aggregation across the prescribed risk classes. The list of risk classes referenced in the delta provisions is the same list that drives the sensitivities-based method's scope and correlation structure. The consequence is that a delta-sensitivity calculation must be validated against the sensitivities-based method's instrument scope and aggregation rules before any capital figure is relied on.

The default risk capital requirement exists precisely because jump-to-default risk is not captured by the credit spread shocks in the sensitivities-based method, so a compliance review must confirm that both charges are computed and that the same risk is neither omitted nor double-counted. Liquidity horizons are the calibration concept underpinning the market risk shocks, which is why the DRC provisions are read against them when demonstrating that the split of coverage is complete. Note that the two extracted excerpts overlap in the same section of the standardised market risk rules, so the precise nature of the cross-reference should be verified against the primary text before it is relied on in an assessment.

Before a bank can compute any IRB capital number it must first decide which asset class an exposure falls into, and this categorization provision is the entry gate to the IRB approach rather than a standalone rule. Both sit within the same minimum capital requirements framework, so the asset-class definitions (corporate, sovereign, bank, retail and their sub-classes) determine which IRB risk-weight function, parameter estimation duties and minimum requirements attach. In practice, a misclassification at this step propagates into the wrong RWA treatment, so classification evidence should be documented before the modelling approach is defended.

When assessing a corporate facility, the reader must check whether it is in fact specialized lending, because SL is a defined sub-category carved out of the corporate asset class rather than a separate regime. The corporate exposure definition feeds directly into the SL sub-classes (project, object, commodities finance, income-producing real estate and high-volatility commercial real estate), each of which has its own risk-weight and expected-loss treatment, including the supervisory slotting approach where the bank cannot meet the estimation requirements. Consequently the general corporate IRB treatment cannot be applied to an SL exposure without first ruling out the sub-class criteria and the slotting fallback.

A cyber governance control cannot be assessed against one document alone: the governance and leadership requirements are expressly mapped back to the Cyber Security Framework's governance, policy and risk-management domains. The Framework supplies the overarching structure (policies, standards, procedures and the governance layer above them), while the linked control set articulates the specific control requirements that evidence compliance with it. For a compliance decision this means gap assessments and audit evidence should be traced to both instruments, since satisfying the detailed control does not displace the Framework-level obligation.

These are two Pillar 3 disclosure templates in the same disclosure regime, and the key metrics template reports summary figures that are derived from the fuller RWA breakdown template. The decision consequence is consistency: the aggregate risk-weighted asset and capital ratio figures published in the key metrics template must reconcile to the detailed RWA overview for the same reporting date. Any divergence between the two is a disclosure-accuracy issue in its own right, independent of whether the underlying RWA calculation is correct.

This appears to be a parent-law relationship: the Finance Companies Control Law and its Implementing Regulation are the statutory basis under which SAMA regulates finance companies, including provisioning duties, so rules addressing the purchase of residential real estate finance portfolios would operate as subordinate instruments within that authority. If so, the portfolio-purchase requirements must be read consistently with the Law's licensing, provisioning and prudential obligations, and cannot be treated as displacing them. Because this link is inferred rather than an express citation, the reader should verify the primary text of the purchase rules for an explicit authorising reference before relying on the hierarchy in an opinion.

When assessing whether an advertising control is binding on a supervised institution, treat the advertising rules as an exercise of SAMA's statutory supervisory powers rather than guidance. The advertising controls reference the Saudi Central Bank Law (M/36), which is the parent enabling statute conferring SAMA's authority to regulate and supervise financial institutions and to issue and enforce such instruments. Practically, non-compliance with the advertising controls engages SAMA's supervisory and enforcement powers under the Law, so the reader should not treat marketing rules as a soft conduct expectation.

If the decision is whether a financial institution needs a documented conflict-of-interest policy, the answer is set by the conflict of interest principle sitting inside the Code of Conduct and Work Ethics instrument, not by a separate rulebook. The principle is a component of that Code, so its defined scope, addressees and governance expectations inherit from the parent Code applicable to financial institutions. Consequently, the written policy requirement is an enforceable element of the Code's overall conduct framework and should be assessed alongside the Code's other principles and board/senior management accountability provisions.

When scoping internal audit coverage for a finance company, liquidity risk controls should be treated as within the control environment that audit must independently test, not as a treasury-only matter. Both provisions rest on the same governance logic: internal audit exists to identify control weaknesses and verify adherence to regulatory requirements, while the liquidity rules require an effective internal control system over liquidity identification, measurement, monitoring and reporting. This link is inferred rather than an express cross-reference, so the reader should verify the primary text of each instrument before relying on it to define audit scope or assurance obligations.

An institution cannot demonstrate IT governance compliance by reading the IT Governance Framework alone; cyber security and business continuity controls must be sourced from the dedicated frameworks. The IT Governance Framework expressly defers to SAMA's Cyber Security Framework (and the Business Continuity Management Framework) for those specific requirements, creating a signposted obligation chain rather than a duplicate standard. The consequence is that gap assessments, maturity ratings and remediation plans must be run against the cyber framework's requirements where the subject matter is cyber, with IT governance supplying the surrounding accountability structure.

For a finance company deciding where liquidity stress test results must land, the ALCO provisions and the stress testing provisions operate together within the same liquidity risk instrument. ALCO is the senior management forum drawing in risk, treasury and financial control, while the stress testing requirements (including sensitivity alongside scenario analysis) generate the outputs that inform asset and liability decisions and contingency funding. Practically, stress and sensitivity results should be escalated into the ALCO governance loop, and a company that runs the analysis without embedding it in that decision forum has a governance gap even if the modelling itself is adequate.

If you are a SAMA-licensed finance company, treat the Counter-Fraud Fundamental Requirements as an operational-conduct layer sitting on top of, not inside, the prudential obligations of the Finance Companies Control Law and its Implementing Regulation (e.g. provisioning for contingent operational losses). The link here is inferred from shared SAMA supervisory authority over the same licensed population rather than an express cross-reference in the excerpts, so the fraud guide should be read as a separately issued circular with its own scope and effective date. Practically, compliance with the fraud controls does not discharge the Law's provisioning or governance duties, and vice versa; the reader should verify the primary text of both instruments before relying on this connection in a decision.

Use this pairing to route a licence application to the correct regime: finance and refinance activities are licensed under the Finance Companies Control Law and its Implementing Regulations, whereas finance support activities are licensed under the separate Rules of Licensing Finance Support Activities, with SAMA issuing parallel application guidelines for each. The connection is inferred from the shared licensing architecture and common issuing authority rather than an explicit citation in the excerpts. The consequence is that an applicant cannot assume the FCCL licensing conditions, capital thresholds or defined terms carry across to support activities; confirm which instrument governs the specific activity in the primary text.

When interpreting the SAMA framework, read it as the domestic transposition of the December 2017 BCBS document on finalising post-crisis reforms, which both instruments expressly identify as their source. That means the Basel text is persuasive for interpreting intent, definitions and calibration, but only the SAMA-issued version is enforceable on Saudi-licensed banks. Where the two diverge, or where SAMA has applied national discretion, the SAMA instrument governs the compliance decision.

These two records appear to be the same Targeted Financial Sanctions Rules held twice in the knowledge base, so the decision point is version control rather than substantive difference. Because TFS obligations (asset freezing, no-delay implementation, reporting to the competent authority) are time-critical and strictly liable in character, citing a superseded or duplicate copy creates real advice risk. Confirm which record carries the current issue date and circular reference, and cite only that one; the similarity here is inferred from titles, so verify against the primary text.

Treat the Supervisory Framework for Payment Systems and Operators as an exercise of statutory power rather than guidance: it draws its authority from the Saudi Central Bank Law (M/36), which confers SAMA's oversight mandate over payment and settlement systems. That parentage means the framework's designation criteria, oversight expectations and information demands are enforceable supervisory obligations, and its scope is bounded by the statutory definitions in the Law. The supporting excerpt is a garbled footnote, so confirm the specific enabling article in the primary text before relying on it in a formal position.

When deciding where a suspicious transaction report or AML-related disclosure must be routed and who may lawfully receive or act on it, the Implementing Regulation's reporting duties resolve to the statutory financial intelligence unit rather than to the supervisor. The Regulation operates under the AML Law and adopts its defined terms, and the Law establishes the General Directorate of Financial Intelligence with its own oversight line and operational independence. Practically, reporting entities should treat FIU submission as the discharge point for the reporting obligation, and should not substitute notification to SAMA or another authority unless a separate rule requires it.

For a decision on whether a proposed senior appointment can proceed, the circular's requirements should be read as an exercise of SAMA's statutory power over bank management appointments rather than as free-standing guidance. The Banking Control Law reserves to SAMA the ability to object to or bar appointments, including where a candidate was removed from or associated with a failed banking concern, so the circular's criteria sit inside that consent framework. This link is inferred, so the reader should verify the circular's stated legal basis and its precise scope of covered positions against the primary text before relying on it.

In deciding whether a business model falls inside the debt-based crowdfunding licensing perimeter, the entity definition cannot be applied independently of the Rules that contain it. The definition of the company is tied to operating a debt-based crowdfunding platform and carrying out the defined activity, so the defined terms and the substantive Rules form one instrument. The consequence is that meeting the definition triggers the full set of licensing, conduct and prudential obligations in the Rules, not merely the definitional label.

When computing minimum capital, the operational risk requirement must be read against the framework-level glossary and the Basel III implementation guidance rather than in isolation. Both sit within SAMA's consolidated capital framework, so terms and cross-referenced components used in the operational risk calculation carry the meanings fixed at framework level. For a compliance decision this means any interpretation of operational risk inputs must be consistent with the framework's defined terms and with the capital reform guidance SAMA has adopted.

To decide how a purchased receivables exposure is capitalised, the IRB overview's asset-class definitions and adoption rules govern before the receivables-specific quantification provisions apply. The overview establishes the asset-class taxonomy, which separately identifies corporate purchased receivables, and requires that once IRB is adopted for part of an asset class it is extended across that class. The practical consequence is that classification and roll-out obligations are decided at the overview level, and a bank cannot selectively apply the purchased receivables treatment to only part of a qualifying asset class.

Treat these as one liquidity-risk obligation chain rather than two separate deliverables: the contingency funding plan cannot be assessed as adequate unless the stress and scenario work that defines the range of stresses it must survive has actually been performed. Both requirements sit in the same instrument and share the same supervisory purpose, so the scenario and sensitivity outputs are the evidential input that sets the plan's triggers, severity assumptions and escalation paths. For a compliance decision, review or sign-off on the plan should be conditioned on current, documented stress and sensitivity analysis; a plan calibrated to stale or narrower scenarios is exposed on both counts.

When applying the updated account rules for non-resident property owners, the relaxation concerns eligibility to hold an account, not the identification and verification duties that attach to any customer relationship. The link is inferred: the KYC definition here is drawn from an agent/payments context, while the account rules address a different customer category, so the shared element is the underlying obligation to identify the customer and any beneficiary before and during the relationship. Practically, do not read the update as a KYC concession, and verify the primary text of the circular and the applicable AML/CTF rules for the exact identification requirements for non-resident applicants.

If you intend to rely on the authority's data service to confirm beneficial ownership, treat it as a verification source feeding your KYC/CDD obligation rather than as a substitute for it. The connection is inferred from the shared subject matter — identifying customers and the beneficiaries behind them — and the KYC definition cited comes from a different instrument's scope, so the mapping is by concept, not by cross-reference. The consequence is that accountability for accurate beneficial owner identification remains with the institution even where an external source is used; confirm in the primary circular whether the service is permitted, mandated, or merely enabled, and for which customer types.

Read know-your-customer as the identification and verification component sitting inside the wider customer due diligence obligation, not as an alternative to it: completing identity checks does not discharge the further CDD duties of understanding purpose, ongoing monitoring and data refresh. The link is inferred because the KYC definition quoted is framed for an agent relationship while the CDD provisions here govern member and occasional customer acceptance, so the defined terms for who counts as a customer may not align exactly. For a decision, map your acceptance procedures to both layers and verify the primary Arabic text for the precise customer categories and update triggers.

Before a point-of-sale device is sold or activated, the merchant must be treated as a customer in its own right, so identification and verification has to be completed at onboarding rather than after deployment. The connection is inferred from the common identification duty, but note the scope shift: the definition cited addresses an agent identifying its customers, whereas the POS requirement operates as merchant-side due diligence within the payments regime. The consequence is that acquiring and terminal-distribution activity should be gated on completed merchant verification, including the parties behind the merchant; confirm the exact pre-sale conditions in the primary POS instrument.

If you are deciding how much capital a purchased receivables portfolio attracts under the IRB approach, you cannot read the RWA calculation in isolation from the parameter-quantification rules for that same exposure class. Both sit in the same SAMA capital framework and use the same asset-class taxonomy, in which corporate purchased receivables are carved out of the general corporate class, so the quantification requirements define the PD/LGD/EAD inputs the RWA provisions then consume. Practically, an internal model that satisfies the RWA formula but not the quantification conditions for the receivables class is not compliant, and the exposure would need to fall back to the treatment SAMA prescribes.

When determining which loss-given-default figures a bank may use, the choice between the foundation and advanced IRB approaches is the controlling gate. The LGD provisions set out how a long-run default-weighted average loss rate is derived and how it interacts with the PD estimate, but the F-IRB/A-IRB scope provisions decide whether the bank supplies its own LGD or applies supervisory values. For a compliance decision, confirm the bank's approved approach first; that permission fixes the extent to which internal LGD estimation and its evidentiary requirements apply, including for counterparty credit risk exposures within the template's scope.

The same approach-scope logic applies to probability of default: whether a bank uses its own PD estimates, and under what estimation and disclosure conditions, follows from its F-IRB or A-IRB permission for the relevant exposures. The linkage is at the level of the parameter chain (PD feeding RWA for counterparty credit risk exposures) rather than a specific numbered cross-reference, and the excerpt captured for the PD node concerns an unrelated basket default swap illustration. Treat this connection as directional guidance only and verify the primary PD provisions in the instrument before relying on it for a capital or disclosure decision.

For purchased receivables, dilution risk is a distinct capital charge that sits alongside default risk within the same IRB RWA computation, not an alternative to it. The framework's structure for purchased receivables expressly separates risk-weighted assets for default risk from risk-weighted assets for dilution risk, with further provisions on purchase price discounts and credit risk mitigants. The consequence is that a bank cannot treat dilution as immaterial by default; it must either quantify and capitalise it under the dilution provisions or demonstrate the conditions on which the framework permits it to be disregarded.

The treatment of expected losses and provisions is not a free-standing accounting question; it is a component of the Basel-based capital framework SAMA has made binding on banks in the Kingdom on both a standalone and consolidated basis. The guidance document is the parent instrument that gives the EL calculation, the provision calculation and their comparison their enforceable force and their scope of application. So when assessing a bank's regulatory capital position, apply the EL-versus-provisions rules as SAMA-mandated capital requirements rather than as optional Basel commentary, and check the applicable version and any SAMA-specific adjustments in the guidance document.

When deciding whether a bank may compute market risk capital under the internal models approach, the ES measure is not an optional add-on but the risk metric the approach is built on. The internal models rules define the capital requirement by reference to expected shortfall, so the two instruments form a single obligation chain: model approval conditions and the calibration/measurement requirements for ES must be read together. Practically, a model that does not meet the ES specification cannot be treated as compliant with the internal models approach, and the reader should assess both texts before signing off on IMA use.

For a decision on whether a bank's internal model remains fit for regulatory capital purposes, validation requirements and backtesting outcomes are best assessed as complementary evidence rather than separate exercises. Validation covers the approaches, assumptions and benchmarks used to test a model, while bank-wide backtesting supplies the quantitative exception counts and zone classification that can trigger supervisory consequences such as multiplier increases or model restrictions. This linkage is inferred from subject matter rather than an express cross-reference, so the reader should verify in the primary texts whether backtesting is formally incorporated into the validation obligation or stands as a distinct requirement.

When computing total RWA and capital ratios, market risk RWA and the CCR/CVA capital requirements are separate components of the same denominator and must be assembled consistently. The market risk framework defines the risk classes and RWA output, while the CCR and CVA framework sets the counterparty-side requirements that feed the same minimum ratios, buffers and Pillar 2 add-ons. The consequence is that scoping decisions (for example whether an exposure sits in the trading book market risk charge or attracts a CVA charge) affect where capital is held, not whether it is held, so both instruments should be checked before concluding on a capital treatment.

Any determination of counterparty credit risk exposure depends first on how transactions are grouped into netting sets, since the CCR calculation is performed at netting-set level. The netting set definition also governs how collateral is recognised, including collateral held outside a set but available against defaults on that set only, which is treated as independent collateral in the replacement cost step. In practice the reader must confirm netting set boundaries and legal enforceability of netting before relying on any reduced CCR exposure figure.

Whether a trade is cleared through a central counterparty changes the counterparty credit risk analysis, because the CCP becomes the relevant counterparty and a distinct treatment applies to cleared exposures and default fund contributions. The CCR rules and the CCP provisions therefore operate on the same exposure but assign different capital consequences depending on clearing status and CCP qualification. The reader should establish the clearing arrangement and the CCP's status first, since that classification drives which capital treatment, and which CVA consequences, apply.

When a bank is settling which capital approach applies to a given exposure, this link is a reminder that the CVA risk provisions and the look-through approach for fund exposures sit inside the same consolidated SAMA capital framework and use a common vocabulary of 'standardised' versus alternative approaches, but they govern different risk types. Selecting the standardised or basic approach for CVA risk carries no implication for whether look-through is available for equity investments in funds; each approach-choice condition must be met on its own terms. For an approach-selection or disclosure decision, treat this as a same-rulebook linkage rather than a substantive dependency: the mandate-based approach is the fallback tier for fund exposures where full look-through is unavailable, while the CVA provisions govern counterparty credit spread risk capital. The shared framework means consistent definitions and consistent Pillar 3 presentation, not interchangeable eligibility. Because the fund-side excerpt appears to be a contents listing, confirm in the primary text whether an operative cross-reference exists before treating one approach determination as informing the other.

If the bank hedges CVA risk through an internal desk rather than directly in the market, this link determines whether that hedge is recognised for capital purposes: recognition in the CVA capital calculation depends on satisfying the internal risk transfer conditions set out in the market risk framework, including how the internal transfer is externalised. The two instruments form an obligation chain — the CVA rules define the hedging benefit, the internal risk transfer rules define when an intra-bank transaction can carry that benefit. Practically, a CVA desk relying on internal hedges must evidence compliance with the internal risk transfer requirements or forgo the capital relief and accept the resulting SA-CVA or BA-CVA outcome.

Where a fund in which the bank invests holds securitisation positions, this link tells you the risk weight is not determined by the equity-funds provisions alone: under look-through, the underlying exposures are weighted as if held directly, which pulls in the securitisation hierarchy and, where the operational conditions for using external credit assessments are met, the external-ratings-based approach. The equity-funds rules therefore act as a routing provision into the securitisation framework rather than a self-contained treatment. For the decision at hand, the bank must confirm the SEC-ERBA operational requirements (including those on inferred ratings) are satisfied at the underlying-exposure level, or fall back to the next approach in the securitisation hierarchy.

These two provisions appear to interact at the point of deciding whether a trading desk may keep using the internal models approach: expected shortfall is the measure that produces the model-based capital number, while the P&L attribution test, alongside backtesting, is the gateway that determines desk eligibility and zone status. On that reading, a desk in the amber zone attracts a capital add-on and cannot return to green until it produces green-zone outcomes and clears its backtesting exceptions over the prior twelve months; failure ultimately pushes the desk to the standardised approach. This relationship is inferred rather than stated as an express cross-reference, so the reader should verify the primary text of the market risk chapters before relying on the sequencing for a capital decision.

Before computing replacement cost for a derivative netting set, the bank must first decide whether that netting set is margined or unmargined, and that classification is governed by the margin-agreement provisions in the counterparty credit risk rules rather than by the replacement cost text alone. The two instruments sit in the same Basel-aligned SAMA capital framework and share the defined terms 'margined netting set' and 'variation margin', so the RC formula is only correctly applied once the counterparty's obligation to post variation margin is confirmed. The practical consequence is that a one-way arrangement in which only the bank posts margin cannot be treated as margined, which changes the RC formula used and therefore the reported exposure and capital outcome.

The PFE add-on cannot be calculated without first constructing hedging sets, so a decision on add-on treatment depends on the hedging-set definitions and supervisory factors in the counterparty credit risk instrument. The relationship is an obligation chain within the same capital framework: effective notionals are determined at hedging-set level and then scaled by the prescribed supervisory factor to produce the add-on that feeds the exposure calculation. Note that the excerpt captured for the add-on node does not obviously address hedging sets, so the reader should verify the exact provisions in the primary text before relying on the specific paragraph mapping.

When a clearing member bank sizes capital for its default fund contribution to a CCP, the underlying trade exposures must be measured using the standardized approach for counterparty credit risk, so the two instruments must be read together rather than in isolation. The default fund methodology is a downstream calculation that takes SA-CCR exposure inputs (including applicable floors) as given, which makes SA-CCR the controlling measurement basis. Practically, any change in SA-CCR classification or parameters flows through to the default fund capital charge, and a compliance review of one should trigger review of the other.

Deciding the leverage ratio treatment of a derivative position requires both components: the current exposure measure and the potential future exposure add-on, which are specified in the same instrument. The derivative exposures provision is the operative rule and PFE is the defined input it depends on, so the two form a single obligation chain rather than alternatives. The consequence is that omitting or mis-scoping PFE understates the derivative component of the exposure measure and therefore overstates the leverage ratio.

Derivative exposures are one of the enumerated categories that must be captured in the leverage ratio exposure measure, so any question about whether a derivative position is in scope is answered by reading the derivative-specific rule as a component of the broader exposure measure provision. The relationship is hierarchical within one instrument: the exposure measure sets the perimeter (on-balance sheet, derivatives, SFTs, off-balance sheet items) and the derivative provision specifies how that category is quantified. For a compliance decision this means exclusions or netting claimed at the derivative level must still be reconciled against the exposure measure's overall scoping rules.

When a bank determines the denominator of its leverage ratio, it cannot stop at balance-sheet, derivative and SFT positions: the exposure measure provision expressly enumerates off-balance sheet exposures as a fourth component and therefore pulls in the off-balance sheet items section as the operative treatment. The link is a direct internal cross-reference within the same SAMA capital framework instrument, so the two provisions form a single obligation chain rather than parallel rules. Practically, any assessment of leverage ratio compliance must apply the off-balance sheet measurement rules; omitting commitments, guarantees or similar items understates the exposure measure and overstates the ratio.

The same leverage ratio exposure measure requirement reaches across to a separate SAMA instrument's off-balance sheet items provision, which supplies the credit conversion factor treatment used to bring those items into the measure. This is a cross-document reference within the risk-based capital hierarchy, so the CCF rules are incorporated by reference rather than duplicated. For a decision, confirm which document and version is in force for the reporting date before fixing the conversion factors applied, since the two off-balance sheet sections must be read as one consistent basis for the leverage denominator.

Off-balance sheet items are not risk-weighted directly; the provision requires them first to be converted into credit exposure equivalents using credit conversion factors, so the two sections operate as a mandatory two-step calculation. The link is an express internal cross-reference in the same instrument, with the CCF rule defining the mechanism and the off-balance sheet section defining the population. In practice, a review of credit RWA must test both the completeness of the off-balance sheet inventory and the correctness of the CCF assigned to each item type; an error in either step propagates to the capital ratio.

The output floor is calculated on total standardised risk-weighted assets, and the framework identifies market risk RWA as one of the components that must be included alongside credit and operational risk. The reference means the market risk RWA rules are incorporated into the floor calculation, so a bank using internal models for market risk must still produce the standardised equivalent. For a compliance decision, verify that the standardised market risk figure is computed and fed into the floor comparison; excluding it would understate the floor and could mask a binding capital constraint.

The output floor provision does not only set a calculation rule; it attaches a disclosure obligation discharged through the specified comparison templates, of which CMS1 covers modelled versus standardised RWA at risk-category level. The link is an explicit enumeration of required templates within the same disclosure section, so the template is the prescribed form of the obligation rather than optional guidance. Consequently, a bank subject to the output floor must publish CMS1 (and its companion asset-class template) in the mandated format; using an alternative presentation does not satisfy the requirement.

When computing credit risk RWA for derivative and other counterparty exposures, you cannot treat the credit risk rules as self-contained: the exposure amount input is determined under the standardized approach for counterparty credit risk, which the credit risk framework cross-references directly (including the floor applied consistently across SA-CCR, the comprehensive approach to collateral within standardized credit risk, and the internal models method). Both sit in the same SAMA Basel-aligned capital hierarchy, so the defined terms and calibration in SA-CCR govern the counterparty exposure measure that the credit risk chapter then risk-weights. Practically, a capital calculation or validation decision must reconcile both instruments; applying credit risk weights to an exposure measured outside SA-CCR would understate or misstate the requirement.

Deciding the capital treatment of counterparty credit risk and CVA requires reading the market risk framework alongside it, because CVA risk is measured using market risk concepts — notably the defined risk classes such as credit spread risk — that the market risk instrument establishes. The cross-reference means the definitions and risk-class taxonomy are sourced from the market risk rules rather than restated in the CCR/CVA rules, and both feed the same total RWA and capital ratio calculation. For the reader, a CVA capital determination should be evidenced against the market risk definitions to avoid inconsistent classification or double-counting across the two RWA components.

If you are preparing the main-features disclosure for capital and TLAC-eligible instruments, eligibility of the non-capital TLAC items is not decided in the disclosure table itself but by reference to the FSB TLAC term sheet criteria that the table imports. The disclosure obligation is therefore derivative: the table sets what must be published, the term sheet sets which instruments qualify to be listed as TLAC-eligible. In practice, an instrument's inclusion or exclusion from the disclosure must be justified against the term sheet criteria, and this only bites for banks within the TLAC scope.

When completing the composition-of-capital disclosure, the figures reported are not free-standing: they must be traceable to the published balance sheet through the reconciliation template, which exists to evidence how accounting amounts map to regulatory capital components and deductions. Both templates sit in the same SAMA disclosure framework and use the same defined capital tiers, so the reconciliation is the audit trail for the composition figures. For the reader, a disclosure sign-off is incomplete if the capital components cannot be reconciled line-by-line to the balance sheet items identified in the reconciliation template.

For a bank in scope, the TLAC composition disclosure builds on the regulatory capital composition disclosure: the CET1, Additional Tier 1 and Tier 2 amounts determined for capital purposes are the starting point, with TLAC-eligible non-capital instruments added and buffer-related capital excluded from TLAC. The cross-reference reflects a hierarchy — capital definitions govern, TLAC reporting applies them at resolution group level. The consequence is that the two disclosures must be internally consistent; scope also differs, since TLAC1 applies only to G-SIB resolution groups while the capital composition disclosure applies more broadly.

When preparing or reviewing Pillar 3 disclosures, the capital distribution constraints template cannot be signed off in isolation from the key metrics template: the framework prescribes explicit cross-template linkages so that the CET1 ratio and buffer-related figures reported in CDC must agree with the corresponding key metrics lines. Both templates sit under the same SAMA-adopted Basel disclosure regime, so the linkage is a reconciliation obligation, not a presentational convention. Practically, an inconsistency between the two is a disclosure defect in its own right, and the trigger ratios for distribution restrictions must be derived from the same capital figures disclosed in KM1.

Treat the prudent valuation adjustments disclosed in PV1 as an input to the regulatory capital composition shown in CC1, not as a standalone valuation note. Prudent valuation under the Basel prudent valuation guidance (as applied through the relevant SAMA circular) feeds the adjustments and deductions that determine CET1, which CC1 discloses line by line. The consequence is that any change in PVA methodology or amount has a direct capital-ratio effect, and the two disclosures must be internally consistent when assessing CET1 adequacy and buffer headroom.

This link appears inferred rather than expressly cross-referenced, so read it as interpretive: PD backtesting disclosure under CR9 is only meaningful for portfolios and exposure classes covered by SAMA's model approval, and the substantive parameter, estimation and F-IRB/A-IRB distinctions come from the minimum capital requirements rules on the IRB approach. The counterparty credit risk IRB template is a disclosure vehicle for parameters whose definition and permitted use sit in the IRB rules within the minimum capital requirements framework, so the two should be read together when assessing whether reported PD, LGD and exposure figures are properly derived. The connection is inferred rather than an explicit citation, so treat it as an interpretive aid. The practical consequence is that a bank may only populate this template for CCR exposures within its approved IRB permission; the reader should confirm the scope of approval and the governing IRB provisions in the primary text.

When classifying an exposure, start from the general definition of corporate exposures and then determine whether it falls into the general corporate sub-category or one of the specialised corporate sub-classes, because the second provision operates as a subset of the first within the same IRB asset-class taxonomy. This is a hierarchy relationship inside a single instrument, so the parent definition sets the outer boundary and the sub-category drives the applicable risk-weight function and parameter treatment. Misclassifying at either level changes the capital calculation, so both provisions must be applied in sequence rather than alternatively.

Treat these as the same BCM obligation set rather than two independent requirements: one item states the framework and its addressees (board, CEO, CRO, senior management, information asset owners, BCM managers, internal audit), while the other supplies the definitional and standards layer aligned to the ISO 22301 concepts the framework builds on. For a compliance decision, read the operative expectations together with the definitions so terms such as business continuity management and change management carry their framework meaning rather than an in-house one. This link is inferred from overlapping subject matter, so confirm in the primary text which document is the controlling issuance and which is supporting reference material before relying on either for a gap assessment.

When a supervised entity's obligations touch cyber security or continuity, the referring instrument does not itself set the detailed controls but points outward to SAMA's Cyber Security Framework and BCM Framework, so compliance cannot be demonstrated from the referring text alone. The referenced framework supplies the documentation hierarchy — policies, standards and procedures — that the entity must actually maintain and evidence. Practically, scope your control mapping to the cyber framework's requirements and treat the referring document as incorporating them by cross-reference; verify the exact wording of the cross-reference, as this link is inferred.

These are Pillar 3 disclosure templates within the same disclosure regime, so figures reported in the market-risk internal-models template must reconcile with the aggregate risk-weighted-asset overview and the related modelled-versus-standardised comparison disclosures. Preparers should therefore validate cross-template consistency before publication; as the connection is inferred from shared subject matter, confirm the specific template instructions and any explicit cross-references in the primary disclosure standard.

The leverage ratio exposure measure includes derivative exposures, and those exposures are measured using the counterparty credit risk methodology — SA-CCR for banks without internal model method approval — so the two provisions form a single measurement chain rather than parallel rules. A bank's IMM approval status therefore drives both its CCR capital calculation and the derivative component of its leverage ratio exposure measure. Confirm approval scope by transaction type before selecting the method, since an incorrect choice misstates both ratios simultaneously.

Internal audit and compliance are separate control functions under SAMA's governance expectations for banks, and the link signals that their mandates must be read together rather than in isolation. Typically internal audit provides independent assurance over the effectiveness of the compliance function, which constrains how a bank allocates responsibilities, reporting lines to the board or audit committee, and independence safeguards between the two functions. This relationship is inferred from the shared governance regime and the source excerpts are not available here, so verify the primary texts to confirm the precise assurance and reporting obligations before designing or defending a functional structure.

Treat these as parallel conduct/compliance expectations applied to two different licensed populations rather than one rule extending to the other: banks under the compliance-function principles, exchange centres under their own conduct principles. For a decision, apply the instrument that matches the entity's licence category, and use the sibling only as interpretive support; the link is inferred, so verify the primary texts before relying on read-across.

When assessing APR disclosure for a credit card product, read the consumer finance controls clarification together with the credit card rules: the clarification addresses withdrawal/termination rights, initial disclosure and APR calculation under the updated consumer finance controls, while the credit card rules impose the presentation requirement that APR and term cost be visually distinguished. The shared defined term (APR) and the common consumer-finance disclosure regime mean the calculation methodology and the display obligation are two halves of the same duty. Practically, an issuer must satisfy both the computation basis and the prominence requirement; the cross-reference is inferred, so confirm which version of the consumer finance controls is in force for the product in question.

Use these at different layers of the payments regime: the SIPS standards set systemic-risk, governance and operational-resilience expectations for designated payment systems, while the e-commerce technical support circular governs how supervised entities may deal with payment technical service providers. The connection is that outsourcing or dependency on such providers can feed operational risk into a systemically important system. For a decision, if an entity participates in or operates a designated system, apply the SIPS standards to the system itself and the technical-support requirements to the third-party relationship; the link is inferred, so verify designation and scope in the primary texts.

Read the SARIE operating-hours notice as an operational parameter sitting inside the broader SIPS framework: SARIE is the domestic settlement infrastructure to which systemic-payment-system standards on availability, settlement finality and business continuity apply, and the Ramadan/Eid schedule fixes the settlement window for that period. Seasonal hour changes therefore have compliance consequences for cut-off management and intraday liquidity expectations rather than being purely administrative. Participants should align internal settlement and contingency arrangements with the amended hours; the reference is inferred, so confirm the current-year notice and its stated effective dates.

These two instruments are best treated as separate compliance obligations that happen to share only the general branch-operations and conduct supervision context: one restricts offering products under a brand identity other than the licensee's, the other sets physical security surveillance requirements. Assess each independently against its own scope, and verify the primary texts before assuming any interaction, as the relationship here is ambiguous.

For an operational readiness decision covering Ramadan/Hajj, both circulars should be read together because they address the same seasonal period from different angles: one sets service-continuity and readiness expectations for currency exchange centers, the other fixes working hours for the season. The link is inferred from shared timing and SAMA's supervisory authority over supervised entities' service availability rather than an express cross-reference. Practically, a currency exchange center planning staffing and branch opening should satisfy both the readiness expectations and the applicable hours, and should verify the primary texts to confirm which entity types each instrument actually covers.

The relevance here is to onboarding and suitability decisions: income verification due diligence goes to the reliability of customer financial information, while the EMI fund-distribution circular concerns permissible activity and customer-facing conduct when investment products are offered through electronic money institution channels. The connection is inferred and not clearly a cross-reference, so it is best treated as a thematic overlap in customer due diligence and product-distribution controls rather than an obligation chain. A reader should verify scope in the primary texts, since the income-verification circular's addressees may not be identical to the entities permitted to distribute funds via EMI channels.

These are near-identical statements of the same OTC derivatives regime, so the decision point is version control: identify which instrument is the operative, current version before relying on reporting fields or risk-mitigation duties. The similarity reflects successive or parallel publications of the same trade repository reporting and risk-mitigation requirements rather than two independent obligations. Compliance should cite the current version and check for amended reporting tables or effective dates, verifying against the primary text.

For governance sign-off, these two topics cannot be approved in isolation: both sit within the same set of risk-mitigation techniques whose governing policies and procedures require board (or delegated authority) approval and periodic independent review. Portfolio reconciliation is also the practical trigger that surfaces the discrepancies dispute resolution must handle, so the obligations chain together within one instrument. A single approved policy framework covering documentation, confirmation, valuation, reconciliation, compression and disputes is therefore the compliant approach, with evidence of periodic review retained.

When completing a trade repository submission, the collateral fields and the common data fields form one report rather than separate filings, so field-level consistency across the tables determines whether the report is accepted as complete and accurate. The link is inferred from the shared reporting appendix structure, where common data identifies the report and its action type (including corrections to previously submitted erroneous fields) and collateral data populates valuation and margin attributes. Practically, an error in either table engages the correction mechanism, so remediation should be scoped across both rather than to the table where the error was first noticed; confirm field definitions in the primary appendix.

Treat list management as the upstream input control for screening: a screening decision is only as defensible as the currency, completeness and source authority of the designation lists it runs against. Both sit within the same TFS/sanctions instrument, so the obligation chain runs from maintaining and updating the applicable lists (UN and domestic designations) to applying them across customers, counterparties and transactions. Practically, if list update timeliness or scope is deficient, any 'no match' screening outcome is unreliable and the institution remains exposed on the underlying freezing duty. This linkage is inferred from structure rather than an express cross-reference, so verify the primary text before relying on it.

Read alert handling as the trigger stage of the freezing obligation, not a separate discretionary workflow: escalation timeframes must be short enough to allow freezing without delay once a true match is confirmed. Both provisions sit in the same sanctions/TFS instrument and form a single obligation chain from detection through escalation to asset freezing and reporting to SAMA and the competent authority. The decision consequence is that internal review or investigation steps cannot be used to defer the freeze, and unfreezing follows only the prescribed route. As this is an inferred structural link, confirm the exact timing and reporting wording in the source.

Before citing either document, establish which is the operative version: the two appear to be duplicate or near-identical publications of the same tariff guide for financial institution services. Where SAMA republishes the same instrument under separate references, the later or expressly current version governs and the other should be treated as superseded or a mirror. For a compliance decision on permitted fees or charges, cite the version confirmed as in force and check for any amendment or effective-date differences between the two, as this equivalence is inferred rather than stated.

Minimum paid-up capital should be assessed as a licensing condition, not merely a prudential metric: an applicant cannot be licensed for a given finance activity without meeting the capital floor set for that activity, and the requirement continues to bind after licensing. Both provisions sit within the same finance companies instrument, so the capital threshold operates as a gating condition within the licensing obligation chain administered by SAMA. Consequently, any change in activity scope, or a fall below the applicable floor, is a licensing issue requiring SAMA engagement rather than an internal capital-planning matter.

Do not read these as alternative statements of the same rule; identify which sits higher in the hierarchy before relying on either. The implementing regulation gives effect to the Finance Companies Control Law and elaborates its requirements, so where the two instruments address the same subject the implementing regulation supplies the operative detail while the parent law fixes scope and authority. For a decision, cite the specific provision in the instrument that is currently in force for the activity in question and check for supersession or amendment, since the overlap here is inferred from subject matter rather than an express cross-reference.

Treat these as one licensing regime read in sequence rather than two independent rulebooks: when advising on eligibility, capital, or application requirements for finance support activities, the amending instrument governs to the extent it revises the base Licensing Rules. Because both sit under the same finance-companies licensing hierarchy and address the same defined activity, the later text displaces or supplements the earlier on overlapping points while unamended provisions remain live. Use this pairing when deciding who inside the institution owns and signs off the enterprise-wide ML/TF/PF risk assessment: the AML guidance sets the substantive assessment obligation, while governance principles determine board and senior-management accountability, three-lines-of-defence allocation and the independence of the compliance/MLRO function. The connection is thematic rather than a direct cross-reference — governance is the delivery mechanism for the AML/CTF regime's requirement that risk assessment be documented, approved and kept current. Practically, a technically sound business risk assessment that lacks evidenced board approval and oversight is still a governance and AML deficiency; verify the specific approval and reporting wording in each instrument.

Before citing either item, resolve which is the authoritative version, since these appear to be the same ML/TF/PF business risk assessment guidance held twice in the knowledge base (for example an Arabic/English pair or a re-publication). Nothing in the substantive AML/CTF obligation changes as a result of the duplication — there is one obligation to conduct and document an enterprise-wide risk assessment, not two. Because this is inferred, check version numbers, issue dates and language of the primary documents so that policy references and regulatory correspondence point to a single controlling text.

Read these together when deciding how beneficial ownership is to be identified and verified for different customer categories: one addresses linkage to the Wathiq verification service for commercial-register entities, the other extends beneficial owner inquiry to the non-profit sector. Both operationalise the same CDD obligation to identify and take reasonable measures to verify beneficial owners, so the choice of source depends on the customer type rather than on a different legal standard. The consequence is that non-profit and association customers cannot be treated as out of scope for BO verification; confirm in the primary circulars the exact entity coverage and any mandatory-use language before setting onboarding policy.

These bear on the same question — how risk and recourse sit between an originating real estate finance company and a refinancing company when mortgage portfolios are transferred. The Rules for Regulating Real Estate Refinancing Companies provide the licensing and prudential framework for the refinancer, while the recourse-reduction instruction alters the originator's residual exposure on portfolios sold to SRC, which affects provisioning, capital treatment and contractual assignment terms. Since the link is inferred, verify in the primary texts the precise scope of the recourse reduction (which portfolios, which counterparty, from what date) before treating an exposure as derecognised or de-risked.

When a real estate refinancing company delegates any function to a third party, treat the outsourcing rules as the operative control layer rather than assuming the refinancing rules are self-contained. Both instruments sit under SAMA's finance company licensing and supervisory regime, so a refinancing company that meets the definition of a finance company inherits the outsourcing conditions (material activity classification, SAMA notification/no-objection, retained accountability, and audit access). This link is inferred, so confirm in the primary text that the refinancing rules do not carve out or modify the outsourcing conditions for the specific activity in question before relying on it.

If a financier is deciding how to secure and collect instalments, these two instruments should be read together as complementary limits on enforcement and collection mechanics rather than in isolation. Both address how a financier may take and use debt-collection instruments against a borrower — promissory notes as a security/enforcement instrument, and standing payment orders as an automated debit mechanism — and both operate within SAMA's finance and consumer-protection expectations about consent, disclosure and proportionate recovery. The practical consequence is that a control gap or borrower-consent defect under one mechanism is unlikely to be cured by reliance on the other; the reader should verify each instrument's own conditions in the primary text, as this relationship is inferred rather than expressly cross-referenced.

For a decision on protecting premises, systems and recorded footage, treat physical security specifications and the Cyber Security Framework as overlapping rather than alternative regimes. CCTV specifications govern the physical safety and security layer for supervised financial institutions, while the CSF's definition of cybersecurity extends protective obligations to the member organisation's information assets — which includes the digital recording, storage, retention and access-control aspects of a surveillance estate. Practically, a CCTV deployment that satisfies technical specifications may still fall short of CSF expectations for the data it generates; the reader should confirm the CSF's scope of applicability to their entity type in the primary text, as this link is inferred.

When self-assessing or reporting to SAMA, expect the same assessment logic to apply across cyber security and IT governance, so a single maturity methodology and evidence approach can serve both. Both frameworks use a predefined maturity model with graded levels as the supervisory measurement device, which means SAMA is evaluating capability depth against defined levels rather than binary compliance in either domain. The consequence is that a maturity rating asserted in one domain will be read against comparable expectations in the other; because the parallel is inferred, verify the specific level definitions and target maturity in each primary text, as they need not be identical.

A finance company designing its liquidity governance should read the liquidity risk management rules together with the liquidity requirements chapter, because one sets the governance and process expectations (including an ALCO with senior management, risk, treasury and financial control representation) while the other frames the liquidity risk management plan and associated requirements. They address the same prudential objective under SAMA's finance company regime, so governance arrangements and the liquidity plan are expected to be mutually consistent rather than developed separately. Note the differing normative force — recommendatory language on an ALCO does not lower any mandatory requirement in the liquidity requirements chapter; as this link is inferred, confirm which elements are binding in the primary text.

When judging whether a finance company's liquidity framework is adequate, stress testing and the contingency funding plan should be assessed as one chain rather than two separate deliverables: the scenarios and sensitivity analyses generate the shortfall estimates that the CFP's triggers, funding sources and escalation steps are supposed to answer. The link appears to rest on the same liquidity risk governance regime, under which the board approves the liquidity risk strategy, policies, CFP and stress testing framework together on at least an annual basis. Practically, a CFP that is not calibrated to the entity's own stress results (or stress work that never feeds the CFP) is a governance gap even if each document exists; as this connection is inferred, verify the specific liquidity rules text before relying on it in a finding.

Any decision about how an exposure is staged or classified cannot be taken independently of the default definition, because the definition is the trigger that drives movement into the impaired/defaulted classification and the associated provisioning treatment. Both sit within the same credit risk framework for finance companies, whose governance provisions require the board to approve credit risk policies covering identification, internal rating, collective assessment, measurement and reporting as a single set. For the reader, this means an inconsistent or narrowly drafted default definition will propagate into misclassification and understated provisions; the relationship is inferred from the shared instrument, so confirm the classification and default provisions in the primary text.

Where a finance company buys an individual consumer debt from another finance company, the transaction cannot be closed on the buyout instructions alone: the operational steps of settling the original exposure, releasing the consumer and moving the account or debt are governed by the separate timeframes rules for clearance letters and debt/account transfers. The buyout instructions are drafted against the earlier bank-to-bank consumer financing buyout framework and rely on those transfer and clearance mechanics rather than restating them. Consequently, compliance with agreed processing deadlines and the consumer's right to timely clearance is a condition of a lawful buyout; treat this as an inferred cross-reference and verify the operative articles of both circulars.

When pricing or documenting the purchase of an individual consumer finance debt, the new terms offered to the consumer must still be expressed using the standardized APR methodology, so a buyout decision is simultaneously an APR disclosure decision. Both instruments operate on the same consumer finance perimeter, and the APR rules exist to make retail finance offers transparent and comparable across providers, which is precisely the comparison a consumer makes when a debt is refinanced or transferred. The consequence is that a buyout offer with a non-conforming or non-comparable rate disclosure is a consumer protection breach independent of the buyout mechanics; the linkage is inferred, so check the scope and calculation provisions of the APR rules against the product concerned.

Registration of a finance lease contract in the register is the gateway condition for enforcement: only a contract that is registered can support a request for an executive bond extract under the dedicated rules, which is what allows the lessor to pursue enforcement without a fresh substantive proceeding. The rules on requesting and issuing such extracts are built on the register as the authoritative record of the contract and its parties. For the reader, a failure or delay in registering the lease undermines the later enforcement route regardless of the contract's validity between the parties; as the link is inferred, confirm the registration prerequisites and issuance conditions in the primary rules.

When scoping an AML/CTF programme, treat these two implementing regulations as a single combined compliance perimeter rather than alternatives: the AML Implementing Regulation elaborates the AML Law's defined terms and customer due diligence obligations, while the CTF Implementing Regulation elaborates the terrorism-financing law, including which financial activities and transactions fall within its scope. Because Saudi supervisory practice applies AML and CTF controls jointly to the same regulated entities, a customer, transaction or reporting trigger may be captured by one instrument even where the other is silent. The practical consequence is that a gap analysis or policy must be mapped against both texts, and any scope exclusion claimed under one should be checked against the definitions and covered-activity lists of the other. This link is inferred from subject-matter alignment; verify the specific defining articles in each primary text before relying on it.

For a remittance centre deciding whether its onboarding and monitoring controls are adequate, these two provisions of the same rulebook operate as one obligation chain and cannot be satisfied separately. The KYC principle sets the objective — establishing the true identity of the customer and understanding the expected business and transaction profile — while the CDD measures set the operative duties, including verifying that documents, data and information remain relevant and up to date, with intensified attention to high-risk customers and application to existing customers and beneficial owners. The consequence is that identity capture at onboarding alone will not discharge the obligation: ongoing review and refresh of records is a distinct, enforceable requirement, and deficiencies in either provision are likely to be cited together in supervisory findings.

When determining licensing scope and permitted activities under the payments regime, these two service definitions sit side by side in the same instrument and must be assessed independently for each business line. Account information service and payment initiation service are separately defined regulated activities within the open banking / PSP framework, so authorisation, consent, and conduct obligations attach to each on its own terms, and a firm performing both requires coverage for both. The consequence for the reader is that a permission or exemption established for one service cannot be read across to the other; confirm the precise definitions and any associated conditions in the primary text before scoping an application or a compliance assessment.

For a finance company drafting or reviewing customer documentation, these instruments should be read together as parts of the same finance-contract framework: the SAMA standard consumer finance contract governs the mandated form and content of the agreement with the consumer, while the finance lease executive bond circular addresses the enforcement instrument attaching to lease financing. Both derive from the finance companies regime and its consumer-protection obligations, so contract terms and the enforceability mechanism must be internally consistent. The practical consequence is that deviations from the standard contract may undermine reliance on the executive bond, and any lease documentation package should be checked against both. The connection is inferred from subject-matter proximity; verify the operative provisions in each primary text.

When a bank decides how to treat a customer account with no recent activity, these provisions of the same rules operate as a single sequenced framework rather than distinct regimes. The inoperative-account provisions set the defined stages and time thresholds — active, dormant, then unclaimed after the stated period from the last recorded debit transaction or documented contact — and the freezing provisions determine the restrictions and handling that follow once a stage is reached. The consequence is that any freeze or restriction must be justified by reference to the correct stage and its trigger date, and reclassification of an account changes the permitted actions; misclassifying the stage exposes the bank to both consumer-protection and operational findings.

When assessing whether a consumer credit decision meets responsible lending expectations, the Deductible Ratio cannot be treated as a stand-alone affordability test. The defined term itself points to the quantitative principles chapter for its calculation, and those quantitative limits sit alongside the qualitative principles (assessment of the consumer's circumstances, disclosure and suitability) as two halves of one obligation set under the same Responsible Lending Principles instrument. Practically, a file that satisfies the ratio ceiling can still fail the qualitative duties, so both must be evidenced. The linkage here is inferred from the shared instrument and defined term, so confirm the chapter allocation in the primary text.

If you are mapping outsourcing controls across a group containing both a bank and a finance company, treat these as parallel but separate regimes rather than one rule. The finance company rules sit under the Finance Companies Control Law and its Implementing Regulations, while the bank rules operate under the banking supervisory framework, yet both impose board-approved outsourcing policies, materiality assessment and record retention. The consequence is that a single group outsourcing policy may be workable in substance but each licensed entity must still demonstrate compliance against its own instrument, including any entity-specific notification or approval thresholds. As this is an inferred similarity, verify the specific articles applicable to each licence type.

For a decision on whether an instrument can be posted or recognised as collateral, note that these two provisions serve different prudential purposes and should not be conflated. The covered bond definition addresses asset quality and the ring-fenced cover pool for capital/liquidity treatment, whereas the margin eligibility rules govern what may be exchanged as initial or variation margin for non-centrally cleared derivatives and impose re-hypothecation restrictions. The practical effect is that covered bond status supports quality-based recognition but does not by itself resolve margin eligibility or reuse limits, which must be tested under the margin framework. The link is inferred conceptual overlap only; check both primary texts before relying on it.

When classifying covered bonds within the liquidity buffer, the definitional instrument and the LCR asset-tiering rules must be read together. The Level 2A criteria expressly admit qualifying covered bonds meeting a minimum rating, and whether a bond "qualifies" turns on the covered bond definition, including the statutory supervision and cover-pool requirements. The consequence is that a bond marketed as covered does not automatically attract Level 2A treatment unless it satisfies both the definitional and the rating/haircut and cap conditions. Confirm the qualifying criteria and haircuts in the primary liquidity text.

An applicant preparing a debt-based crowdfunding licence file should treat the guidelines as procedural guidance sitting beneath, not in place of, the substantive rules. The guidelines expressly rest on the Finance Companies Control Law and the debt-based crowdfunding rules, which supply the defined terms (including what constitutes a crowdfunding platform and company) and the ongoing conduct and prudential obligations. In practice, meeting the application checklist does not discharge the substantive requirements, and any conflict is resolved in favour of the rules and the parent law.

When deciding whether an account must be frozen because identification documents have lapsed, the bank is relying on the same customer identity data it is required to hold in the unified electronic registration system for bank accounts. Both provisions sit within the same account rules: the freezing rule presupposes that ID validity and expiry status are captured and maintained in the electronic record built on the prescribed classification. Practically, defects or gaps in the electronic record translate directly into failures to freeze on time, so the two should be assessed as one control chain rather than separate duties. This linkage is inferred from the shared instrument rather than an explicit cross-reference, so verify the primary text before relying on it.

Before allowing staff to apply the operating rules in Chapter IV — including any documented exception such as operating on a passport pending an Iqama — the bank must confirm those staff have completed the required KYC, AML/CFT and professional conduct training. The training principle is framed as a precondition for customer-facing and account-operating roles, so it conditions how Chapter IV is executed rather than sitting beside it. The consequence is that an exception to the operational rules does not relax the underlying KYC/AML expectations; it only shifts the documentary sequence. The reference is inferred from the structure of the rules, so confirm against the primary text.

Treat agent vetting and customer due diligence as two parallel obligation streams: completing due diligence on an agent does not discharge CDD on the underlying customer, and vice versa. Both draw on the same due-diligence methodology — identification, initial checks and ongoing periodic review — which is why the requirements read alike, but they attach to different counterparties and different risk exposures. The decision consequence is that a firm's onboarding file must evidence each separately where an agent is interposed. Note the two excerpts overlap, so the boundary between the provisions is ambiguous; verify the article text before treating one as satisfying the other.

If a real estate finance entity is considering an equity stake in the Saudi Real Estate Refinance Company, the decision is governed by the same provision that frames the company's secondary-market role: prior SAMA approval, acquisition at fair market value, and an aggregate shareholding ceiling of 30 percent of total shares. The shareholding permission exists to support secondary-market development in real estate finance, so the ownership limit is a structural safeguard rather than a routine investment rule. Practically, an entity cannot treat the stake as an ordinary investment decision — approval and the aggregate cap must be tested first. The conceptual link is inferred; confirm the applicable limits in the primary text.

When applying obligations expressed by reference to the Saudi Real Estate Refinance Company, check whether the operative defined term is the named entity or the generic licensed category. The other instrument defines a Real Estate Refinance Company as any joint stock company licensed to engage in real estate refinance activities, which is potentially broader than the single named company referred to in the shareholding provision. The consequence is a scoping decision: a rule drafted around the defined term may capture additional licensees, while the shareholding cap appears entity-specific. This alignment is inferred from wording similarity, so verify each instrument's own definitions section before extending scope.

Read these together when deciding how a specific funding source feeds into a bank's liquidity ratios: the first instrument sets out the LCR concept and methodology, while the second directs that funds raised through profit-sharing investment accounts be captured appropriately in both LCR and NSFR alongside the capital/risk-weighting treatment. The link is an obligation chain rather than a cross-reference — the PSIA guidance presupposes and applies SAMA's general prudential liquidity framework. Practically, a bank cannot treat PSIA balances under a bespoke liquidity approach; it must map them into the standard LCR/NSFR definitions. As this connection is inferred, confirm the exact PSIA treatment in the primary liquidity rules before finalising a classification.

If you are staffing or assessing a complaint handling unit, check whether the professional certification requirements bite on the individuals performing that function. The complaint-handling instrument defines the unit and its consumer-protection duties, while the certification instrument sets competency conditions for defined roles in supervised entities; the overlap is at the level of who may occupy the role. The consequence is that meeting the structural requirement for a complaints unit may not be sufficient if the certification regime separately covers those post-holders. This link is inferred, so verify in the primary texts whether complaint-handling staff fall within the scope of the certification requirements before relying on it.

Both instruments govern how an entity establishes confidence in a person's identity when the relationship is created without physical presence, so they should be applied cumulatively when designing a remote onboarding decision. The biometric verification instrument addresses identity assurance at the point of establishing the relationship; the minimum verification controls add sector-specific conditions for lending applications on top of the baseline controls. The practical effect is that a lender relying on biometric checks alone may still fall short of the additional lending-application controls, and both sit against the underlying CDD duty to verify identity. Because the connection is inferred rather than an express cross-reference, confirm the scope wording of each before treating one as satisfying the other.
